0.title: The Son of God on the Move: The Gospel According to Mark
0.overview:
Mark's gospel is the sound of boots on cobblestones. No genealogy, no annunciation, no infancy narrative — the very first sentence plants a flag and the rest of the book is a march: 'The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.' Everything else is commentary on that title. Before a parable is told or a sermon delivered, demons have been cast out, fevers have broken, a leper has been made clean, and four fishermen have walked away from their nets to follow a man they have known for minutes. Mark writes at full sprint.

The tradition connecting this gospel to the apostle Peter is ancient and remarkably consistent. Papias, writing around 125 AD, records that Mark was Peter's 'interpreter' and wrote down accurately — though not in strict chronological order — what Peter preached about the Lord's words and deeds. Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and Eusebius all confirm the connection. The internal evidence supports it: the gospel is saturated with the vivid, concrete, eyewitness detail of a man who was there — the green grass at the feeding (6:39), the look of anger on Jesus's face (3:5), the specific towns and houses and times of day. Peter's voice is everywhere. Mark's pen is the instrument by which that voice was preserved. The gospel was almost certainly written for a Roman audience — Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4), translates Aramaic phrases (3:17; 5:41; 7:34; 14:36; 15:22, 34), and sprinkles in Latin loanwords that would feel natural to Roman ears (centurion, legion, denarius, praetorium). Scholars place the composition in the late 50s to mid-60s AD, either during Peter's lifetime or in the immediate aftermath of his death.

Which Mark? The Gospel itself names no author, but the early church agreed that it was John Mark, whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the first believers (Acts 12:12). He set out with Paul and Barnabas and turned back (Acts 13:13), was the cause of their parting (Acts 15:37–39), was later restored to Paul’s confidence, he is very useful to me for ministry (2 Tim 4:11), and was with Peter in Rome, who calls him Mark, my son (1 Pet 5:13). That is the man the tradition makes Peter’s interpreter.

Why is it so much shorter than Matthew and Luke, with no birth story? Mark gives mostly what Jesus did, and gives a large share of the book to his last week, rather than long blocks of teaching. He begins where the apostles’ preaching began, with John the Baptist and the public ministry (cf. Acts 10:37–38), and leaves the birth to Matthew and Luke. Shorter is not lesser; what Mark gives is the most vivid of the four.

The word that unlocks Mark is euthys — immediately, at once, straightway. It appears some forty-one times. This is not careless repetition; it is a theological statement about the nature of the kingdom. When the King arrives, things happen. The blind see, the lame walk, the demons flee — and they do not do so on a leisurely timetable. The gospel's organizing question is not 'Who teaches about God?' but 'Who has authority over everything?' — over disease, over death, over the demonic, over the sea, over sin, over the law, over the grave. The answer Mark gives is Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God. The theological heart of the entire book is found in 10:45: 'The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.' Everything before that verse is the demonstration of who he is; everything after it is the unfolding of what that service costs. Mark is a passion narrative with a long introduction — and the introduction is glorious.

1.title: The Kingdom Breaks In
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. <sup>2</sup>As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, “Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, <sup>3</sup>the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight”— <sup>4</sup>John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>5</sup>And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>6</sup>Now John was clothed with camel’s hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. <sup>7</sup>And he preached, saying, “After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. <sup>8</sup>I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>9</sup>In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. <sup>10</sup>And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. <sup>11</sup>And a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” <sup>12</sup>The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. <sup>13</sup>And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him. <sup>14</sup>Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, <sup>15</sup>and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.” <sup>16</sup>Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>17</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>19</sup>And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. <sup>22</sup>And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. <sup>23</sup>And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, <sup>24</sup>“What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>25</sup>But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” <sup>26</sup>And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. <sup>27</sup>And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.” <sup>28</sup>And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee. <sup>29</sup>And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. <sup>30</sup>Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. <sup>31</sup>And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them. <sup>32</sup>That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. <sup>33</sup>And the whole city was gathered together at the door. <sup>34</sup>And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. <sup>35</sup>And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. <sup>36</sup>And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, <sup>37</sup>and they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out.” <sup>39</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons. <sup>40</sup>And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>41</sup>Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, “I will; be clean.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean. <sup>43</sup>And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, <sup>44</sup>and said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>45</sup>But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
1.overview:
No other chapter in the New Testament moves at the pace of Mark 1. Forty-five verses carry us from the wilderness prophet to a leper made clean — and along the way we see a baptism attended by the Holy Spirit and the Father's voice, a forty-day confrontation with Satan, four fishermen leaving their boats in a single morning, a man delivered from an unclean spirit in a synagogue, a fever cured with a touch, an entire town gathered at a doorstep after dark, and a solitary prayer in the pre-dawn dark before another preaching circuit begins. The word 'immediately' appears nine times. Mark is not interested in biographical completeness; he is interested in demonstrating authority — who this man is and what he does when he arrives.

The chapter divides into four movements: the prologue (vv. 1–13) establishes the cosmic identity of Jesus before his public ministry begins; the kingdom announcement (vv. 14–20) gives the content of his message and shows what responding to it looks like; the day in Capernaum (vv. 21–34) demonstrates his authority over the demonic and the physical in the most public possible setting; and the morning prayer followed by the preaching circuit (vv. 35–45) reveals the inner life that powers the outward mission, and ends with a healing that Mark's Jewish readers would have found staggering. The King has come. Everything is about to change.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Prologue: The Son Announced, Baptized, and Tested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mark's opening thirteen verses constitute a compressed prologue that accomplishes everything a careful reader needs before the public ministry begins. Three things are established: who Jesus is, what voices announce him, and that he has already engaged and survived the primary enemy. The Son of God is identified before a single synagogue hears him speak. This matters enormously for how we read everything that follows — every healing, every confrontation, every silencing of a demon is performed by the one the Father called 'my beloved Son' at the Jordan.

The temptation account in Mark (vv. 12–13) is the most compressed of the Synoptic versions — no dialogue, no three-part structure, only the bare essentials: the Spirit drives Jesus out, Satan is present, wild animals are there, angels minister. Mark gives us not the content of the temptation but its texture: isolation, exposure, the presence of the adversary, the sustaining of heaven. The brevity is itself eloquent. Mark's Jesus does not need to explain his victory over Satan. The reader will see the evidence throughout the gospel as demons flee before him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The baptism of Jesus (vv. 9–11) is one of the most theologically dense moments in Scripture. The Trinity appears in undisguised form: the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father speaks. The Father's words — 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased' — are a composite of Psalm 2:7 (the coronation Psalm of the Davidic king) and Isaiah 42:1 (the Servant of the Lord on whom God's Spirit rests). In a single sentence, Jesus is identified as both the Messianic King and the Suffering Servant. The two identities that the Old Testament held in tension are here placed on one person. The reader who knows their Hebrew Bible should feel the ground move.

Why was Jesus baptized with a baptism of repentance when he had no sin to repent of? The New Testament answer: he who knew no sin was being made sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21). His identification with sinful humanity at the Jordan is the beginning of the identification that will be completed on the cross. He goes into the water as the representative of those he came to save. He comes out of it as the Spirit-anointed King, confirmed by his Father, commissioned for the mission.
verseByVerse.examples: John in the wilderness wore camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey — the clothing and diet of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8). The garment was a prophetic uniform, a visible claim. He stood in the desert rather than Jerusalem for the same reason the word of God in every revival comes from the margins rather than the religious centre: the establishment had calcified, and God's next move was being prepared outside it. Then: the religious capital full of priests and scribes who had been waiting for centuries and missed the moment. Now: the same danger faces any church or tradition that mistakes institutional health for spiritual vitality. The voice of preparation rarely comes from where we expect it.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark’s first sentence is a title for the whole book: this is the beginning of the good news about Jesus, who is the Messiah and the Son of God.

The setting. Mark is probably the earliest Gospel, written in the AD 50s or 60s. Early church writers (Papias, about AD 120) say that John Mark wrote down the preaching of the apostle Peter, in Rome, for Christians who were mostly Gentiles and facing persecution under Nero. Mark was the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10), whose mother’s house in Jerusalem was a meeting place of the church (Acts 12:12), and who travelled with Paul and later with Peter (1 Peter 5:13). His Gospel is short, fast-moving and vivid. He uses the word “immediately” over forty times. Half the book is about the last week of Jesus’ life: Mark has been called a passion story with a long introduction.

The beginning. Like Genesis 1:1, “In the beginning”. Something new is starting. It may also mean that the whole story of Jesus’ life is only the beginning of the gospel, which continues to spread through the church.

Of the gospel. “Gospel” (euangelion) means good news. In the Roman world, the word was used for announcements of great public events, such as the birth or victory of an emperor. An inscription from 9 BC calls the birthday of Caesar Augustus “the beginning of the good news for the world”. Mark says the real good news is not about Caesar but about Jesus. In Isaiah, the good news is that God reigns and comes to save his people (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7).

Of Jesus Christ. “Jesus” means “the LORD saves”. “Christ” is the Greek for “Messiah”, the Anointed One, the King God promised to send. Not a surname but a title.

The Son of God. The title that frames Mark’s Gospel. Here at the start; at the baptism, the Father calls him his beloved Son (1:11); at the transfiguration again (9:7); and at the cross, a Roman centurion says, Truly this man was the Son of God (15:39). Demons know it too (3:11; 5:7). The question of the Gospel is who Jesus is, and Mark tells the reader the answer in the first verse.

Textual note. A few early manuscripts omit “the Son of God”. Most, including very early and diverse ones, include it. Verdict: probably original; it fits the shape of the whole Gospel.

In a sentence. Mark announces that his book is the good news of Jesus, the Messiah and the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. The news people need most is not the latest headline but the good news about Jesus. Who could you share it with this week?
verseByVerse.note: “Gospel” means good news. “Christ” is the Greek form of the Hebrew “Messiah” — the anointed one, the promised king. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: John’s opening: the Word who was God

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet, "Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way, the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark begins with Scripture. God had promised to send a messenger ahead of the Lord, a voice in the wilderness calling people to prepare the way. John the Baptist is that messenger.

As it is written in Isaiah the prophet. Mark combines three Old Testament texts: Exodus 23:20 (I send an angel before you), Malachi 3:1 (behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me), and Isaiah 40:3 (a voice cries: in the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD). He names Isaiah, the most prominent prophet and the source of the main theme, as Jewish writers sometimes did when combining texts.

Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way. In Malachi, God says the messenger will prepare the way before me. Here it is “your” way: the way of Jesus. The one whose way is prepared is the Lord God himself, come in Jesus.

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. In Isaiah 40, this voice announces comfort to God’s people in exile: their warfare is ended, their sin is pardoned, and God himself is coming to lead them home through the desert, in a new exodus.

Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Before a king visited, roads were repaired and straightened. John prepares hearts by calling them to repent. And the “Lord” whose way he prepares is, in Isaiah, the LORD, Yahweh. Mark applies it to Jesus. From its first lines, Mark’s Gospel identifies Jesus with the God of Israel.

What it does not mean. Not that Mark made a mistake in naming only Isaiah. Combining texts under the name of the leading prophet was an accepted practice. Later scribes, puzzled, changed it to “the prophets” in some manuscripts; the original reads Isaiah.

In a sentence. As the prophets promised, God sent a messenger to prepare the way for the Lord himself, who has come in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. What in your heart needs straightening out to make way for Christ? Repentance is how we prepare the way.
verseByVerse.note: Mark names Isaiah, the better-known prophet, though the first line comes from Malachi.

verseByVerse.quote: John appeared, baptizing in the wilderness and proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him and were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John appeared in the wilderness, baptising and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. People from all Judea and Jerusalem went out to him, confessing their sins, and were baptised in the river Jordan.

John appeared. Suddenly, after about four hundred years with no prophet in Israel. Mark tells us nothing of his birth (see Luke 1). God was speaking again.

Baptizing in the wilderness. The barren region near the Jordan, north of the Dead Sea. The wilderness was where Israel had been formed after the exodus, and where the prophets said God would begin again (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14).

And proclaiming a baptism of repentance. “Baptism” means washing, immersion. Jews washed for ritual purity, and Gentile converts to Judaism were washed. John called Jews to be baptised, as if they too needed to start again. “Repentance” (metanoia) means a change of mind and heart, turning from sin to God (see Matthew 3:2). The baptism expressed the repentance.

For the forgiveness of sins. Repentance leads to forgiveness. John’s baptism pointed to the forgiveness God would give through the one coming after him (v. 8; Acts 19:4).

And all the country of Judea and all Jerusalem were going out to him. “All” is a natural exaggeration for very many. The movement was huge.

And were being baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. The Jordan, where Israel had crossed into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). Confessing means openly admitting, naming one’s sins before God.

What it does not mean. Not that water baptism itself forgives sins. Forgiveness comes from God to those who repent and believe; baptism is the outward sign. Nor is John’s baptism the same as Christian baptism into the name of the Father, Son and Spirit (Matthew 28:19; Acts 19:1–5).

In a sentence. John called Israel to be baptised as a sign of turning back to God, and great crowds came, confessing their sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you need to name before God today? Confession is the doorway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).
verseByVerse.note: The Jordan runs south from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea. John’s baptism was a public washing that marked a turning from sin; confession came with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now John was clothed with camel's hair and wore a leather belt around his waist and ate locusts and wild honey. And he preached, saying, "After me comes he who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John dressed in camel’s hair with a leather belt, like the prophet Elijah, and lived on locusts and wild honey. He preached: one mightier than I is coming after me. I am not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. I have baptised you with water, but he will baptise you with the Holy Spirit.

Now John was clothed with camel’s hair and wore a leather belt around his waist. Almost exactly how Elijah is described (2 Kings 1:8). Malachi promised that Elijah would come before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). John is that Elijah (9:11–13).

And ate locusts and wild honey. The food of the desert, permitted by the law (Leviticus 11:22). John lived simply, apart from the comforts and compromises of the city.

After me comes he who is mightier than I. John points away from himself. His whole ministry is to point to Jesus.

The strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s task, so lowly that some rabbis said a disciple should never do it for his teacher. John says he is not worthy even of that. The greatest of the prophets (Matthew 11:11) sees himself as less than a slave before Jesus.

I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. John’s baptism was outward, with water. Jesus would do what only God can: pour out the Holy Spirit, as the prophets promised for the last days (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:26–27). This happened at Pentecost (Acts 1:5; 2:33). To be baptised with the Spirit is to be brought into new life by the Spirit, cleansed and indwelt. Every believer receives this (1 Corinthians 12:13).

What it does not mean. Not that Spirit baptism is a second experience after conversion for some believers only, as some Pentecostal traditions teach. Paul says all believers were baptised in one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Verdict: Spirit baptism happens at conversion; believers are then filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18).

In a sentence. John, dressed like Elijah, pointed away from himself to the mightier one coming, who would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point people away from yourself to Jesus. He is the one they need.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

parallels.desc: Elijah’s dress: hair and a leather belt

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptised by John in the Jordan.

In those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee. Mark introduces Jesus without a birth story or genealogy. He simply arrives, an adult of about thirty (Luke 3:23), from an obscure village. Nazareth is never mentioned in the Old Testament and was looked down on (John 1:46). The Lord whose way was prepared comes from nowhere important.

And was baptized by John in the Jordan. A surprise. John’s baptism was for repentance and confession of sins. Jesus had no sin to confess (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15). Why was he baptised? Matthew records his answer: to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:15). He identified himself with sinners, standing in the water with them, as he would later take their place on the cross (10:45). He obeyed every command of God on our behalf. And his baptism marked the start of his public ministry, when he was anointed with the Spirit for his work.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus needed forgiveness. He came to the water as the sinless one standing with sinners, not as a sinner himself.

In a sentence. Jesus came from obscure Nazareth and was baptised by John, standing with sinners though he had no sin.

On a Tuesday. Jesus stood with sinners in the water, so that sinners could stand with him before God. He is not ashamed to stand with you.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was a small village in the hill country of Galilee, never mentioned in the Old Testament.

parallels.desc: “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came up out of the water, immediately he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus came up out of the water, he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit coming down on him like a dove. A voice came from heaven: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

And when he came up out of the water, immediately. Mark’s favourite word, “immediately” (euthys), here for the first time. It gives his Gospel urgency.

He saw the heavens being torn open. “Torn open” (schizomenous) is a strong, violent word. Matthew and Luke say the heavens were opened; Mark says they were torn. Isaiah prayed: oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Now God has done it. Mark uses the same word only once more: when the temple curtain is torn in two at Jesus’ death (15:38). At the start and end of his ministry, the barrier between God and people is torn open.

And the Spirit descending on him like a dove. The Spirit anoints Jesus for his work as Messiah (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), signalling a new creation, or the dove of peace after the flood (Genesis 8:8–12).

And a voice came from heaven, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” The Father speaks directly to Jesus. The words combine Psalm 2:7 (you are my Son, spoken to the Messiah-King), Genesis 22:2 (your son, your only son, whom you love, spoken of Isaac, who was to be sacrificed), and Isaiah 42:1 (my chosen, in whom my soul delights, spoken of the suffering Servant). Jesus is the royal Son, the beloved Son who will be offered, and the Servant who will suffer. Before he has done anything in public, the Father delights in him.

The Trinity. The Father speaks, the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends: the three persons of the one God, revealed together.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism, as the early heresy called adoptionism taught. Mark’s first verse already calls him the Son of God. The baptism reveals and anoints who he already is.

In a sentence. As Jesus came out of the water, heaven was torn open, the Spirit descended on him, and the Father declared him his beloved Son.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, the Father’s delight in his Son covers you too (Ephesians 1:6). Rest in that today.

For worship. Worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.note: “Torn open” (schizō) is the word Mark uses again when the temple curtain is torn at Jesus’ death (15:38).

verseByVerse.quote: The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. And he was in the wilderness forty days, being tempted by Satan. And he was with the wild animals, and the angels were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately the Spirit drove Jesus out into the wilderness. He was there forty days, tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and the angels served him.

The Spirit immediately drove him out into the wilderness. “Drove out” (ekballei) is a strong word, the one Mark uses for casting out demons. The Spirit thrust him into the desert. The test was not an accident but God’s purpose. Matthew and Luke describe three temptations; Mark gives only the bare facts.

And he was in the wilderness forty days. Recalling Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where they were tested and failed (Deuteronomy 8:2), and Moses’ and Elijah’s forty days (Exodus 34:28; 1 Kings 19:8). Jesus relives Israel’s story and succeeds where Israel failed.

Being tempted by Satan. “Satan” means “adversary”. He is a real, personal enemy who tempted the first Adam and succeeded (Genesis 3). Now he tempts the last Adam. Temptation is not sin; Jesus was tempted and remained without sin (Hebrews 4:15).

And he was with the wild animals. Only Mark mentions this. The Judean desert had jackals, hyenas, leopards and snakes. Two meanings may be intended. The danger and loneliness of the place. And a picture of the new creation: Adam lived at peace with the animals before the fall, and Isaiah promised a day when the wolf would dwell with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6–9). In Jesus, the peace of Eden is returning. Mark’s first readers in Rome, who were being thrown to wild beasts in the arena under Nero, would take comfort that Jesus too had been among wild animals and was kept safe.

And the angels were ministering to him. Serving him, perhaps with food, as an angel fed Elijah in the desert (1 Kings 19:5–8). God cared for his Son.

In a sentence. The Spirit drove Jesus into the desert for forty days of testing by Satan, among wild animals, where angels served him.

On a Tuesday. Being tested is not a sign that God has abandoned you. Jesus was led into it by the Spirit. And God sent help.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Luke record the three temptations; Mark gives only the fact.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — The Kingdom Announced and the First Disciples Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transition from John to Jesus is marked by John's arrest. Mark notes it without elaboration — the forerunner's work is done, and the one he announced steps forward. The kingdom announcement of vv. 14–15 is the gospel compressed into four phrases: the time is fulfilled, the kingdom is at hand, repent, believe. This is not an offer to consider; it is the announcement of a reality that demands a response.

The calling of the first four disciples (vv. 16–20) is astonishing when read at face value. Jesus walks past a lake, says a sentence, and two sets of brothers leave their work, their equipment, their livelihoods, and their families to follow him. No extended conversation, no theological discussion, no discernment process. They came, he called, they went. Mark does not explain this — he presents it as the natural result of encountering a person with absolute authority.
verseByVerse.theology: 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel' (v. 15) — this four-part announcement is the theological thesis of the entire gospel. 'The time is fulfilled': the appointed moment in God's redemptive calendar has arrived. History has been building to this. 'The kingdom of God is at hand': the sovereign rule of God is not merely near as a future hope — it is present in the person of the King. 'Repent': turn, change direction, reorient the whole self. 'Believe the gospel': stake everything on the good news that the King has come. The kingdom is not a programme or an idea; it is a Person, and you are either with him or not.
verseByVerse.examples: Simon, Andrew, James, and John left their nets and their father without, as far as Mark tells us, a moment's hesitation. Zebedee is left in the boat with the hired servants — not abandoned cruelly, but left because the new claim on his sons was greater than the old. The call of Jesus has always done this: it places a weight on the scales that makes everything else feel lighter by comparison. Then: fishermen who knew the lake and the nets and the dawn routines. Now: every person who has heard the call and left something — a career, a worldview, a former self — to follow the one who calls. The response always precedes the understanding.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee, proclaiming the gospel of God, and saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
After John was arrested, Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God.

Now after John was arrested. Literally “handed over”. Herod Antipas imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to his brother’s wife (6:17–18). The same word is later used of Jesus being handed over to death (9:31; 10:33; 15:1). The forerunner’s fate foreshadows the Messiah’s.

Jesus came into Galilee. The northern region around the Sea of Galilee, with a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles, looked down on by people in Judea. Jesus began there, not in Jerusalem.

Proclaiming the gospel of God. “Proclaiming” means announcing as a herald. “The gospel of God”: the good news that comes from God and is about what God is doing.

In a sentence. When John was arrested, Jesus began announcing God’s good news in Galilee.

On a Tuesday. The silencing of one messenger did not stop God’s word. Opposition never stops the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Galilee was the northern region of the land, around the lake. John was imprisoned by its ruler, Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ message: the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.

The time is fulfilled. “Time” (kairos) means the appointed time, the decisive moment. The long wait of the Old Testament is over. Everything God promised is now coming true (Galatians 4:4).

And the kingdom of God is at hand. “The kingdom of God” is God’s reign: God acting as King to save his people and judge evil, as the prophets promised (Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14). It is not a place, nor merely a future heaven. “At hand” means it has come near; it is arriving in Jesus himself. His healings and exorcisms show it (3:23–27).

Repent. Turn around: a change of mind, heart and direction, away from sin and self-rule toward God (see v. 4).

And believe in the gospel. Trust the good news: rely on it, stake your life on it. Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning. You turn from sin and turn to God; you stop trusting yourself and start trusting Christ. Mark alone records “believe in the gospel”: the response to the kingdom is not first to do better, but to trust the good news.

What it does not mean. Not that repentance and faith earn the kingdom. They receive it. Nor that the kingdom is only spiritual and future, or only political and present. It is God’s saving reign, already begun in Jesus and to be completed at his return.

In a sentence. Jesus announced that the appointed time had come and God’s reign was arriving, and called everyone to turn to God and trust the good news.

On a Tuesday. Repent and believe is not only the first step of the Christian life, but every step. What do you need to turn from and trust God with today?
verseByVerse.note: “The kingdom of God” means God’s reign, his rule as King. “At hand” means it has come near.

verseByVerse.quote: Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men." And immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon and his brother Andrew casting a net, for they were fishermen. He said: follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men. Immediately they left their nets and followed him.

Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee. A freshwater lake about thirteen miles long and eight wide, full of fish, with fishing towns around its shore.

He saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea. A circular casting net, thrown by hand from the shore or shallow water. Simon, later called Peter, would become the leader of the apostles; Mark’s Gospel probably comes from his preaching. John’s Gospel tells us they had met Jesus before (John 1:35–42).

Follow me. Literally “come behind me”. Students usually chose their rabbi; Jesus chooses his disciples. He calls them not to a set of teachings but to himself.

And I will make you become fishers of men. “Men” means people. They would gather people into God’s kingdom as they had gathered fish. “I will make you become”: discipleship is a process; Jesus takes responsibility for forming them.

And immediately they left their nets and followed him. Their livelihood, left at once. Following Jesus costs something from the start.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must leave their job. These men were called to be apostles. But every disciple must put Jesus before everything, and every disciple is called to bring others to him.

In a sentence. Jesus called Simon and Andrew to follow him and become fishers of people, and they left their nets at once.

On a Tuesday. What “nets” would be hardest for you to leave if Jesus asked? Hold them loosely.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake about 13 miles long. A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. And immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little farther on, Jesus saw James and John, the sons of Zebedee, in their boat mending the nets. Immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him.

He saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in their boat mending the nets. Repairing nets after a night’s fishing. James and John, with Peter, became Jesus’ inner circle (5:37; 9:2; 14:33). Jesus nicknamed them “Sons of Thunder” (3:17).

And immediately he called them.

And they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him. Only Mark mentions the hired servants. Zebedee ran a business with employees; the family was reasonably well off. The brothers left a prosperous family firm, and their father. They did not leave him helpless; he had workers. But they put Jesus’ call above family and business.

In a sentence. Jesus called James and John, and they left their father and the family fishing business to follow him.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus may mean disappointing family expectations. Honour your family, but follow him first.
verseByVerse.note: James and John left “hired servants” with their father, so Zebedee ran a working fishing business.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–45 — Authority in Capernaum and Beyond
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What follows from verse 21 through verse 45 is a compressed day that functions as a demonstration of Jesus's authority across every domain. In the synagogue: authority over teaching and over the demonic. In the house: authority over disease. At the door after dark: authority over sickness and possession in numbers. Before dawn: the inner life of prayer that sustains the outer life of power. On the road: authority to cleanse the untouchable.

The crowd's reaction names exactly what Mark wants his readers to see: 'A new teaching — with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.' The scribes taught by citing precedent. Jesus taught declaratively — from his own authority, as one who does not need to appeal to a tradition because he is the source of the tradition.
verseByVerse.theology: The exorcism in the synagogue (vv. 21–28) raises the question of the Messianic Secret — one of Mark's dominant themes. The unclean spirit identifies Jesus accurately: 'the Holy One of God.' Jesus silences him and casts him out. Why the silence? Several things converge: the testimony of a demon is unreliable as a vehicle of revelation even when technically accurate; Jesus's identity must be understood through the cross, not merely through power encounters; and a premature popular messianism would derail the mission. Throughout Mark, Jesus consistently refuses to let the wrong voices tell the right story.
verseByVerse.examples: The leper of vv. 40–45 approaches Jesus with the most honest prayer in the chapter: 'If you will, you can make me clean.' Not 'if you are able' — he has already seen enough to know the ability is there. The question is the willingness. Jesus's response answers the question permanently: 'I will; be clean.' The will of God toward the broken and the defiled is never in doubt when he reaches out and touches the untouchable. Then: a man excluded from community, from worship, from human touch — brought back by a hand that chose to land on his skin. Now: the same question echoes in every person who approaches God uncertain whether he actually wants them. He does. He reaches. He wills it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went into Capernaum, and immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went into Capernaum, and on the Sabbath Jesus went into the synagogue and taught. The people were astonished at his teaching, because he taught them as one who had authority, not as the scribes.

And they went into Capernaum. A fishing town on the northwest shore of the lake, on a main trade route, which became Jesus’ base (2:1). Archaeologists have found remains of its synagogue and of a house venerated from early times as Peter’s.

And immediately on the Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. The synagogue was the local meeting place for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak (Luke 4:16; Acts 13:15).

And they were astonished at his teaching. “Astonished” means struck, overwhelmed.

For he taught them as one who had authority, and not as the scribes. The scribes were experts in the law who taught by quoting earlier teachers: “Rabbi so-and-so said”. Their authority was borrowed. Jesus spoke with his own authority, as the one whose word is final. Mark does not record what he taught here; the focus is on who he is.

In a sentence. In the Capernaum synagogue, Jesus amazed the people by teaching with his own authority, unlike the scribes.

On a Tuesday. When you read Jesus’ words, are you reading opinions to consider, or the words of the one with all authority?
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee. Scribes were the trained teachers of the law of Moses.

parallels.desc: the same astonishment after the Sermon on the Mount

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. And he cried out, "What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately a man in the synagogue with an unclean spirit cried out: what have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.

And immediately there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit. An “unclean spirit” is a demon: a fallen angel, morally impure, which defiles and torments the person it controls. In the place of worship, the presence of evil is exposed by the presence of Jesus.

What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? A Hebrew idiom: what is there between us? Leave us alone. “Us”: the demon speaks for the whole kingdom of evil spirits.

Have you come to destroy us? The demons know that Jesus has come to defeat them (1 John 3:8).

I know who you are, the Holy One of God. The demon recognises what the people do not: Jesus is the Holy One, set apart by God, God’s own. Demons in Mark repeatedly recognise Jesus’ identity (1:34; 3:11; 5:7). Knowing who Jesus is does not make them his followers; they believe and shudder (James 2:19). Some suggest that naming him was an attempt to gain power over him, as ancient magic believed that knowing a name gave control.

In a sentence. In the synagogue, a demon cried out that it knew Jesus to be the Holy One of God, come to destroy the powers of evil.

On a Tuesday. Knowing facts about Jesus is not enough; even demons know them. Do you trust and love him?
verseByVerse.note: An “unclean spirit” is a demon. “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, "Be silent, and come out of him!" And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus rebuked it: be silent, and come out of him! The unclean spirit threw the man into convulsions, cried out with a loud voice and came out of him.

But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent.” Literally “be muzzled”. Jesus silences the demon. Why, when it was telling the truth? Because Jesus would not accept testimony from demons, and because he did not want his identity proclaimed before people understood that the Messiah must suffer (1:34; 3:12). This is part of what is called the “messianic secret” in Mark.

And come out of him! A command. No ritual, no incantation, no appeal to a higher power, unlike the exorcists of the time, who used formulas and names. Jesus’ own word is enough.

And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. A final violent display, but it had to obey. Luke adds that it did not harm him (Luke 4:35).

What it does not mean. Not that every illness or mental disorder is demonic. The Gospels distinguish demon-possession from disease (1:34). Nor should Christians try to cast out demons by formulas. Jesus’ authority is his own.

In a sentence. Jesus silenced the demon and commanded it out, and it left the man with a final convulsion.

On a Tuesday. No power of evil can resist Jesus’ word. Whatever has a grip on you, it must obey him.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus uses no ritual, no formula and no appeal to another power — a command alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying, "What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him." And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the surrounding region of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were all amazed and asked each other: what is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him. And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout the region of Galilee.

And they were all amazed. Amazed at his teaching (v. 22), and now at his power.

What is this? A new teaching with authority! “New” (kainē) means new in kind, fresh. His teaching and his power go together: the word that teaches is the word that commands demons.

He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him. The evidence that the kingdom of God has arrived: Satan’s power is being broken (3:27).

And at once his fame spread everywhere. News travelled fast in the towns of Galilee.

In a sentence. The people were amazed at Jesus’ authoritative teaching and his command over demons, and his fame spread throughout Galilee.

On a Tuesday. Amazement is a beginning, not an end. Let wonder at Jesus become trust in him.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Now Simon's mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and the fever left her, and she began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leaving the synagogue, they went straight to the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John. Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever, and they told Jesus about her at once. He came, took her by the hand and lifted her up; the fever left her, and she began to serve them.

And immediately he left the synagogue and entered the house of Simon and Andrew. From public ministry to a private home. Jesus’ power is for ordinary households, not only for public spectacles.

Now Simon’s mother-in-law lay ill with a fever. Peter was married (1 Corinthians 9:5). A fever in the ancient world could be dangerous.

And immediately they told him about her. They brought her need to Jesus. That is the beginning of every answer to prayer.

And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up. A personal touch. “Lifted her up” is the word used for resurrection (16:6): a small picture of what Jesus came to do.

And the fever left her. Instantly and completely.

And she began to serve them. No time of recovery needed. Her response to healing was service, the mark of every disciple (10:45).

In a sentence. In Simon’s house, Jesus took his feverish mother-in-law by the hand and raised her up healed, and she served them.

On a Tuesday. Tell Jesus about the people you love who are suffering. And when he helps you, serve him.

parallels.desc: Peter was married, and his wife travelled with him

verseByVerse.quote: That evening at sundown they brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. And the whole city was gathered together at the door. And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening at sundown, people brought to Jesus all who were sick or oppressed by demons, and the whole town gathered at the door. He healed many who were sick with various diseases and cast out many demons. And he would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew him.

That evening at sundown. The Sabbath ended at sunset. Only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules about carrying burdens.

They brought to him all who were sick or oppressed by demons. News of the synagogue exorcism had spread. Mark distinguishes sickness and demonic oppression.

And the whole city was gathered together at the door. Peter, telling the story to Mark, could remember the crowd at his own front door.

And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and cast out many demons. “Many”, not necessarily “all”: a Hebrew way of saying a great number.

And he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. Jesus silenced them (see v. 25). He would not have his identity announced by demons, nor have people think of him merely as a wonder-worker before they understood his cross.

In a sentence. When the Sabbath ended, the whole town brought its sick and possessed to Jesus, and he healed many and silenced the demons who knew him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus received everyone who came to his door. Bring your needs, and the needs of others, to him in prayer tonight.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown. Only then could people carry the sick through the town without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. And Simon and those who were with him searched for him, and they found him and said to him, "Everyone is looking for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place, and there he prayed. Simon and those with him searched for him, and when they found him they said: everyone is looking for you.

And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark. After a long, exhausting evening, Jesus got up before dawn.

He departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed. “Desolate place” (erēmon) is the word for wilderness. Jesus withdrew from the crowds to be alone with his Father. Mark shows Jesus praying at three key moments, each at night: here, after feeding the five thousand (6:46), and in Gethsemane (14:32–39). If the Son of God needed time alone with the Father, how much more do we.

And Simon and those who were with him searched for him. “Searched” (katediōxen) means hunted him down, pursued him. They were eager to bring him back to the excited crowds.

And they found him and said to him, “Everyone is looking for you.” The disciples saw a great opportunity: popularity, crowds, success. They wanted Jesus to go back.

In a sentence. Jesus rose before dawn to pray alone, and the disciples hunted him down to bring him back to the crowds.

On a Tuesday. When will you be alone with God today? Guard that time, even when everyone is looking for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out." And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: let us go on to the next towns, so that I may preach there also, for that is why I came out. And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.

Let us go on to the next towns, that I may preach there also. Jesus refuses to be held by popularity. Prayer had clarified his purpose. The crowds wanted miracles; Jesus’ priority was preaching. The towns of Galilee were many and close together.

For that is why I came out. Perhaps “came out from Capernaum”, or more deeply, came from the Father into the world (John 16:28). His mission was to proclaim the kingdom.

And he went throughout all Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons. Word and power together.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus did not care about the sick in Capernaum. But the healings served the message, not the other way round. Good things can distract from the main thing.

In a sentence. Refusing to stay where he was popular, Jesus went on to preach throughout Galilee, because preaching was his purpose.

On a Tuesday. What has God called you to do first? Do not let good opportunities crowd out your main calling.

verseByVerse.quote: And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, "If you will, you can make me clean." Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, "I will; be clean." And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man with leprosy came to Jesus, knelt and begged him: if you are willing, you can make me clean. Moved with pity, Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him and said: I am willing; be clean. Immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean.

And a leper came to him. “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases (Leviticus 13–14). A leper was ritually unclean, had to live outside the town, wear torn clothes and call out “Unclean, unclean!” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Anyone who touched him became unclean. He was cut off from worship, family and all human touch. Curing leprosy was thought as hard as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7).

Imploring him, and kneeling said to him, “If you will, you can make me clean.” He had no doubt about Jesus’ power, only about his willingness. Would Jesus want to help someone like him?

Moved with pity. “Pity” (splanchnistheis) is deep, gut-level compassion. Some early manuscripts read “moved with anger” (orgistheis), perhaps anger at the disease and the misery it caused, or at the evil behind it. Verdict: the evidence is divided; “pity” is better supported, though “anger” may be the harder and therefore original reading. Either way, Jesus is moved deeply.

He stretched out his hand and touched him. Astonishing. Jesus touched the untouchable. Perhaps no one had touched this man for years. When Jesus touches a leper, the uncleanness does not pass to him; his cleanness passes to the leper.

And said to him, “I will; be clean.” The direct answer to the man’s question: I am willing.

And immediately the leprosy left him, and he was made clean. Not only healed, but clean: restored to God’s people and to worship.

What it does not mean. Not that we should pray “if you are willing” about forgiveness. God has promised to forgive all who come to him (1 John 1:9). We may pray “if you are willing” about healing or circumstances, which he has not promised.

In a sentence. A leper asked if Jesus was willing to cleanse him, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touched him and made him clean.

On a Tuesday. Is there something that makes you feel untouchable to God? Jesus is willing. Come to him.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he is willing to touch and cleanse the unclean.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart from others — so touching one was unheard of.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus sternly charged him and sent him away at once, and said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, for a proof to them." But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places, and people were coming to him from every quarter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sternly warned him and sent him away at once: see that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a proof to them. But the man went out and began to talk about it freely and spread the news, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but stayed out in desolate places, and people came to him from everywhere.

And Jesus sternly charged him. A strong word, expressing deep feeling.

See that you say nothing to anyone. Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a miracle-worker, or to stir up crowds with political hopes (see v. 34).

But go, show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded. The law required a priest to examine and declare a leper clean, with offerings of birds, lambs, flour and oil (Leviticus 14:1–32). Only then could he return to society and worship. Jesus respects the law and wants the man fully restored.

For a proof to them. A testimony to the priests that something extraordinary had happened.

But he went out and began to talk freely about it, and to spread the news. He disobeyed, out of joy. But disobedience, even happy disobedience, had consequences.

So that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places. The irony: the leper had lived outside the towns; now he could go in, and Jesus had to stay outside. Jesus took the leper’s place, a picture of what he would do at the cross (Hebrews 13:12).

And people were coming to him from every quarter.

In a sentence. Jesus told the cleansed leper to keep silent and go to the priest, but he spread the news, so that Jesus had to stay outside the towns.

On a Tuesday. Gratitude is good, but obedience is better. Ask how Jesus wants you to respond to what he has done for you.
verseByVerse.note: The cleansing involved the priest’s inspection, two birds, and offerings on the eighth day.

1.theology:
Chapter 1 establishes the theological framework for everything that follows. Jesus is identified from three directions before his ministry begins: by the Father ('my beloved Son'), by Scripture ('as it is written'), and by his own announcement ('the kingdom of God is at hand'). The reader is positioned to understand all subsequent events in light of these identifications. When the demons recognize him, when the crowds are astonished, when the disciples follow without explanation — the reader knows why.

The Messianic Secret — Jesus silencing the demons and commanding the healed not to speak — is not evasion but strategy. The kind of Messiah the popular imagination expected was a military deliverer. Jesus is doing something far more radical, and a premature popular messianism based on power-encounters would derail the mission before it reached its necessary destination. The secret must be kept until the cross redefines what messianic identity means. Fittingly, the climactic declaration will be made by a Roman soldier standing at the foot of the cross (15:39).
1.examples: The disciples in this chapter are responsive but unformed. They leave their nets, they follow, they find Jesus praying and report the crowds waiting — but they have no framework yet for what they are following. This is where discipleship always begins: responding to a presence before you have the categories to explain it. The categories will come, often painfully, over the three years ahead.

keyVerse.quote: The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.

2.title: Who Has Authority to Forgive?
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. <sup>2</sup>And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them. <sup>3</sup>And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. <sup>4</sup>And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. <sup>5</sup>And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” <sup>6</sup>Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, <sup>7</sup>“Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>8</sup>And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, “Why do you question these things in your hearts? <sup>9</sup>Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise, take up your bed and walk’? <sup>10</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the paralytic— <sup>11</sup>“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home.” <sup>12</sup>And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We never saw anything like this!” <sup>13</sup>He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. <sup>14</sup>And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>15</sup>And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. <sup>16</sup>And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>17</sup>And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>18</sup>Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?” <sup>19</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. <sup>20</sup>The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day. <sup>21</sup>No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. <sup>22</sup>And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins.” <sup>23</sup>One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. <sup>24</sup>And the Pharisees were saying to him, “Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?” <sup>25</sup>And he said to them, “Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>26</sup>how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?” <sup>27</sup>And he said to them, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. <sup>28</sup>So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the first gathering storm. Four episodes — the paralytic, the call of Levi and the dinner with sinners, the question about fasting, and the grain plucked on the Sabbath — form a sustained controversy sequence in which the question of Jesus's authority escalates from Who can forgive sins? to Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners? to Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? to Why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath? Each is a deeper probe of who this man thinks he is and by what right he does what he does. Read straight on into 3:6, where the Pharisees go out and take counsel how to destroy him, and you can watch a decision being reached. The shadow of the cross falls across this Gospel from chapter 2 onward.

The key that unlocks the chapter is the sentence Jesus speaks over the paralytic: Son, your sins are forgiven. The scribes immediately and correctly identify it as a claim to a divine prerogative — Who can forgive sins but God alone? Their premise is right; their conclusion about him is wrong. He is not blaspheming. The miracle that follows is the public receipt for the invisible claim, offered in terms Jesus himself set in advance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Paralytic and the Authority to Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The room (vv. 1–2). Jesus comes back to Capernaum and the town finds out within hours. The house fills, the doorway fills, the street outside the doorway fills — and Mark ends the sentence not with healing but with preaching. Whatever the crowd came for, what it got was the word.

The roof (vv. 3–4). Four men carry a fifth through the streets, find the door impassable, climb the outside stair, and dig through a mud-and-branch roof over the head of the preacher. Mark does not tell us their names, their theology, or whose ceiling it was.

The sentence nobody expected (vv. 5–7). Jesus looks at a paralysed man and speaks about his sins. The scribes say nothing aloud and think something precise: only God forgives sins, therefore this is blasphemy. Their premise is right out of Isaiah. Their conclusion about the man in front of them is the error the whole Gospel exists to correct.

The proof (vv. 8–12). Jesus answers the unspoken thought, stakes an invisible claim on a visible test, and the man walks home carrying the bed that carried him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the first place in Mark where Jesus does something that belongs to God alone, and it is worth being clear about why the scribes reacted as they did. A priest could pronounce a man clean; a prophet could announce that God had forgiven; a rabbi could teach the way of repentance. Nobody in Israel forgave sins in the first person. When God says I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isa. 43:25), the doubled pronoun is the whole point — pardon is his own act, not a delegated one.

So the scribes are not being obtuse. They have correctly identified that the man in the room has done something only the God of Israel does, and they draw the only conclusion their categories allow. Mark lets their logic stand unchallenged, because he intends the reader to run it to the end: if the premise is true and Jesus is not blaspheming, there is exactly one thing left that he can be.

Note also where the forgiveness happens. Not in the temple, ninety miles south, through a priest and a lamb. On earth (v. 10) — in a crowded fishing-village house, from the mouth of a carpenter, to a man who had not brought a sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: four men digging through someone else's roof because the door was blocked by people who had come to hear Jesus. The obstacle was not his enemies; it was the crowd around him.

Now: the friend or parent who keeps carrying a name to God when the person attached to it will not come — who has been carrying it for years, and has watched the door stay shut. Mark records that Jesus saw their faith, and did not ask the man on the mat for a statement first.

There is a warning folded into the same scene. The people blocking the door were not opponents. They were admirers who had got there early and would not move. It is possible to be so close to Jesus, and so pleased to be close, that you become the reason somebody else cannot reach him. The four went over the top of that crowd, and the crowd got a shower of dried mud for its trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus returned to Capernaum some days later, word spread that he was at home. So many people gathered that there was no room left, not even at the door, and he was preaching the word to them.

The connection. Mark 2:1–3:6 is a series of five conflict stories, in which Jesus is challenged by the religious leaders: over forgiving sins (2:1–12), eating with sinners (2:13–17), fasting (2:18–22), and the Sabbath (2:23–28; 3:1–6). Each reveals more of who Jesus is, and the opposition grows until the leaders plot to kill him (3:6).

And when he returned to Capernaum after some days. After his preaching tour of Galilee (1:39).

It was reported that he was at home. Probably Peter’s house (1:29).

And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. Houses in Capernaum were small, built of black basalt stone around a courtyard. The crowd filled the house and spilled into the street.

And he was preaching the word to them. “The word”: the message of the kingdom (1:15). Jesus’ priority was preaching, even when crowds came for healing (1:38).

In a sentence. Back in Capernaum, Jesus preached the word to a crowd so large that it filled the house and blocked the door.

On a Tuesday. People crowd to Jesus for many reasons. Make sure you come to him for his word.
verseByVerse.note: “At home” probably means Peter’s house in Capernaum (1:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four men came carrying a paralysed man on a mat. Unable to get near Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, dug through it, and let down the mat on which the paralysed man lay.

And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. Only Mark mentions that there were four, one at each corner of the mat. The man could not come on his own.

And when they could not get near him because of the crowd. The crowd was a barrier. They could have given up.

They removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay. Houses had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase. The roof was made of wooden beams covered with branches, reeds and packed mud or clay. The men climbed up, dug through the roof (literally “unroofed the roof”, then “dug it out”), and lowered the man down on ropes. Dust and clay would have fallen on the crowd. It was bold, inventive, costly and disruptive. Peter, whose house it probably was, would have remembered his roof being destroyed.

What their action shows. Faith that will not be stopped by obstacles. Love for a friend who could not help himself. Determination to get him to Jesus at any cost.

In a sentence. When four men could not get their paralysed friend through the crowd, they dug through the roof and lowered him to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Whom could you carry to Jesus: in prayer, by inviting them, by helping them past obstacles? Be one of the four.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. An opening could be dug through and repaired.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralysed man: son, your sins are forgiven.

And when Jesus saw their faith. Their faith was visible in their action. “Their”: the four friends, and probably the man himself.

He said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” Unexpected. Everyone expected him to say “Get up and walk”. Instead, Jesus addresses the man’s deepest need. “Son” (literally “child”) is tender. Paralysis would end at death; unforgiven sin would last for ever. The man’s greatest problem was not his legs but his guilt before God. “Are forgiven” is present tense: it is happening now, on Jesus’ word.

Sin and sickness. Was his paralysis caused by a particular sin? Not necessarily. Jesus denied that suffering is always caused by the sufferer’s own sin (John 9:1–3). But all sickness belongs to a world broken by sin. Jesus deals with the root first.

What it does not mean. Not that the friends’ faith saved the man apart from his own faith. But Jesus honoured the faith of those who brought him. Intercession matters.

In a sentence. Seeing their faith, Jesus first met the man’s deepest need, telling him his sins were forgiven.

On a Tuesday. Your deepest need is not your circumstances, but forgiveness. Have you received it from Jesus?

For worship. Thank Jesus that he speaks forgiveness to sinners, including you.
verseByVerse.note: “Son” is a warm address, like “my child.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the scribes sitting there questioned in their hearts: why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?

Now some of the scribes were sitting there. Experts in the law, perhaps sent to investigate this new teacher. They had seats, while others stood.

Questioning in their hearts. Silently.

Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Blasphemy means speaking against God or claiming for oneself what belongs to God alone. It was punishable by death (Leviticus 24:16).

Who can forgive sins but God alone? They were right. A person can forgive wrongs done to himself, but all sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4), and only God can forgive it (Isaiah 43:25). Either Jesus is blaspheming, or he is God. There is no third option. The scribes’ theology was correct; their conclusion about Jesus was wrong.

In a sentence. The scribes silently accused Jesus of blasphemy, rightly reasoning that only God can forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. The scribes saw the issue clearly: only God forgives. Who do you say Jesus is?
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: the same charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, "Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your bed and walk'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit what they were thinking, said to them: why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralysed man, your sins are forgiven, or to say, rise, take up your bed and walk?

And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves. Jesus knew their unspoken thoughts. Only God knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Answering the accusation that he claims God’s prerogative, he does something else only God can do.

Why do you question these things in your hearts?

Which is easier. A clever question. To say “Your sins are forgiven” is easier, because no one can see whether it is true. To say “Rise and walk” is harder, because everyone will see at once whether it works. But to actually do either requires the power of God.

In a sentence. Jesus read the scribes’ thoughts and asked which is easier to say: your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts. That is a warning against secret sin and a comfort in secret pain.

verseByVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic— "I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he said to the paralysed man: I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.

But that you may know. The visible healing will prove the invisible forgiveness.

That the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite name for himself, from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man receives authority, glory and an everlasting kingdom from God. “Authority” means the right and power to act. “On earth”: God’s heavenly authority to forgive is now exercised on earth, in person, by Jesus.

He said to the paralytic. Mark breaks the sentence to turn to the man.

I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home. Three commands, all impossible for a paralysed man. Carrying his own mat would show the healing was complete.

What it does not mean. Not that church leaders today have authority in themselves to forgive sins. They declare Christ’s forgiveness to those who repent and believe (John 20:23; 2 Corinthians 5:18–20), but the authority is his.

In a sentence. To prove he had authority on earth to forgive sins, Jesus commanded the paralysed man to get up, take his mat and go home.

On a Tuesday. Jesus has authority to forgive your sins. His word is as reliable as that man’s walking legs.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man receives everlasting dominion
