And immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. The shallow soil warmed quickly, so the seed sprouted fast. It looked promising.

And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. The roots could not reach water. The same sun that made it sprout killed it.

In a sentence. Seed on shallow, rocky soil sprouted quickly but withered in the heat for lack of roots.

On a Tuesday. Quick enthusiasm is not deep roots. How deep do yours go?
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it produced no grain.

Other seed fell among thorns. Ground where thorn roots remained, not yet visible.

And the thorns grew up and choked it. The thorns grew faster and took the light, water and nutrients.

And it yielded no grain. Only Mark adds this. The plant survived, but was fruitless.

In a sentence. Seed among thorns grew but was choked and produced nothing.

On a Tuesday. What thorns are growing beside God’s word in your life?

verseByVerse.quote: And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing, yielding thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold. And Jesus said: whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.

And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing. Deep, soft, clean soil. The seed grows steadily.

And yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold. A normal harvest was perhaps seven to tenfold. Thirty was excellent; a hundred was astonishing (Genesis 26:12). Despite all the losses, the harvest is abundant. God’s word will not fail.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Everyone has ears; not everyone listens. A call to hear with understanding and respond.

In a sentence. Seed in good soil produced an extraordinary harvest, and Jesus called everyone to listen carefully.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to make your heart good soil today.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus was alone, those around him with the Twelve asked him about the parables. He said: to you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.

And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. Disciples ask. Those who seek understanding come to Jesus.

To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God. “Secret” (mystērion) means a truth once hidden, now revealed by God. The secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, but in a hidden, unexpected way: like seed, not like a conquering army. “Has been given”: understanding is God’s gift (Matthew 16:17).

But for those outside everything is in parables. “Those outside” are those who have rejected Jesus (3:21–35, where his family stood “outside”).

So that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand. Isaiah 6:9–10. God sent Isaiah to preach to a people who would not listen, and his preaching would harden them. Jesus’ parables have the same effect on those who have already rejected him: the truth is there, but they do not grasp it. It is a judgment on hearts already closed.

Lest they should turn and be forgiven. “Turn” is repentance. The hardening confirms the choice they have made.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus wanted to prevent willing people from being saved. Those who wanted to understand came and asked, and he explained (v. 34). The hardening falls on those who refuse. And Jesus’ purpose in parables is also to reveal: a lamp is meant to be seen (v. 21). God is sovereign in revealing and hiding (Matthew 11:25–26), and people are responsible for refusing.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that the secret of the kingdom had been given to them, while for those outside, parables confirmed their refusal to understand.

On a Tuesday. When you do not understand Scripture, do what the disciples did: come to Jesus and ask.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The farmer sows the word. Those along the path are the ones in whom the word is sown, but when they hear, Satan comes immediately and takes away the word sown in them.

Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? This parable is the key to the rest. If you understand how the word is received, you can understand everything else.

The sower sows the word. The seed is the word: the message of the kingdom, God’s word. The sower is Jesus and all who preach his word after him.

And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. The first soil: hard hearts. The word lies on the surface and never sinks in. Satan, the birds, snatches it away: by distraction, mockery, doubt or simple forgetfulness. The god of this age blinds unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4).

In a sentence. The seed is God’s word, and in hard-hearted hearers Satan snatches it away at once.

On a Tuesday. After you hear God’s word, take time to reflect on it before the birds come.

parallels.desc: the god of this world has blinded the minds

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those sown on rocky ground are the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. But they have no root in themselves; they endure for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises because of the word, they immediately fall away.

Immediately receive it with joy. An enthusiastic, emotional response. It looks like conversion.

And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while. The response is shallow. It has not gone down into the heart and will.

Then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word. The scorching sun. Following Christ costs something. Mark’s first readers in Rome were facing exactly this.

Immediately they fall away. “Fall away” (skandalizontai) means stumble, be offended. As quickly as they came, they go.

What it does not mean. Not that joy is suspicious; good soil also receives the word with joy (1 Thessalonians 1:6). The problem is the lack of root. Nor do true believers finally fall away. Those who do show that their faith was never rooted (1 John 2:19).

In a sentence. Shallow hearers receive the word with quick joy, but without roots they fall away when trouble comes.

On a Tuesday. Pray for believers facing persecution, that their roots will hold.

verseByVerse.quote: And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Others are sown among thorns. They hear the word, but the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.

They are those who hear the word. They go further. The word takes root and grows.

But the cares of the world. Worries about life: money, health, family, work. Not open sin, but ordinary preoccupations that crowd God out.

And the deceitfulness of riches. Wealth deceives. It promises security and satisfaction and does not deliver. It makes people feel they do not need God (10:23–25; 1 Timothy 6:9–10).

And the desires for other things. Only Mark adds this: all the other wants that compete with God. Good things can become thorns when they take first place.

Enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. The plant survives, but bears nothing. A person may stay in church for years with no real fruit.

In a sentence. In preoccupied hearers, worry, wealth and other desires choke the word until it bears no fruit.

On a Tuesday. Name the thorns in your life: anxieties, money, other desires. Root one out this week.

verseByVerse.quote: But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But those sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold.

The ones who hear the word and accept it. “Accept” (paradechontai) means welcome, receive it fully. The good soil hears, welcomes the word into the heart, and holds it fast (Luke 8:15).

And bear fruit. The mark of good soil: a changed life, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23), good works, and others brought to Christ.

Thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold. Different amounts; every true believer bears some.

Where does good soil come from? Every heart is hard by nature. God makes the soil good: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), opens hearts (Acts 16:14) and gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Our part is to receive the word humbly (James 1:21).

The lessons. For hearers: what kind of soil are you? For witnesses and preachers: do not be discouraged when many do not respond. The sower sows widely, and the harvest will come. The problem is never the seed.

In a sentence. Good-soil hearers welcome the word and bear abundant fruit.

On a Tuesday. Keep sowing God’s word, whatever response you see. The harvest is God’s.

For worship. Thank God for making your heart receptive to his word.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest, nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.

Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick. The basket (modios) was a grain measure. No one lights a lamp to hide it.

For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest. The meaning in context: the kingdom is now hidden, spoken in parables, understood by few (vv. 10–12). But it is hidden in order to be revealed. The light will shine. One day everything will be made plain. Some see Jesus himself as the lamp: literally, “Does the lamp come?”

Nor is anything secret except to come to light. The secret of the kingdom will be proclaimed to all after the resurrection (9:9).

If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.

In a sentence. The kingdom is hidden now only so that it may be revealed, as a lamp is lit to be seen.

On a Tuesday. The light of Christ in you is not meant to be hidden. Let it be seen today.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

Pay attention to what you hear. Literally “see what you hear”. Listen carefully.

With the measure you use, it will be measured to you. A merchant’s picture. Here it applies to listening: the attention and response you give to God’s word determines how much understanding you receive.

And still more will be added to you. God is generous. Those who listen well receive more than they give.

For to the one who has, more will be given. Those who receive and respond to the truth receive more.

And from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Those who neglect the truth lose even what they had. Spiritual understanding not used is lost.

In a sentence. Listen carefully, because those who respond to God’s word receive more, and those who neglect it lose what they had.

On a Tuesday. How carefully do you listen to sermons and read your Bible? The measure you give is the measure you get.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seed that grows while you sleep (vv. 26–29). A parable found only in Mark, and it is the most relaxing thing in the chapter. A man scatters seed and then goes to bed, gets up, goes to bed, gets up — and the seed grows, and he knows not how. The growth is not his doing and never was.

The mustard seed (vv. 30–32). The proverbially smallest thing in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with branches enough for birds to nest in. Spoken to twelve unimpressive men whose movement looked like nothing at all.

As they were able to hear it (vv. 33–34). Mark tells us the teaching was calibrated: parables to the crowd, everything explained in private to the disciples. God gives truth at the rate a person can take it.

The storm (vv. 35–41). And then the chapter stops talking about the word and puts them in a boat. It was his idea to cross. The storm was not an interruption of obedience but the road it went down. He is asleep on a cushion; they are bailing; and the question they ask at the end — who then is this? — is the question the whole Gospel has been walking toward.
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is not a nature miracle among others; it is a disclosure of who is in the boat, and the disciples' own Scriptures gave them the answer to their question the moment they asked it.

In the Old Testament, mastery of the sea belongs to God and to nobody else. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29) — in a psalm about sailors at their wits' end who cried to the LORD in their trouble. It was God who shut in the sea with doors and said thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:8–11). To the ancient mind the sea was chaos itself, the one thing no king could command.

So who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? has exactly one possible answer, and it should have frightened them more than the weather did.

And hold the two halves of the scene together, because the chapter will not let you have one without the other. He was asleep because he was exhausted — a real man, worn out, on a boat cushion, so tired that a storm did not wake him. And he silenced the sea with a word. Fully man in his exhaustion, fully God in his voice, in the same four feet of a fishing boat.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: experienced fishermen, on their own lake, in their own boat, bailing with their hands and certain they were about to die — while the Lord of wind and wave slept four feet away.

Now: the same accusation, in the same words, from every believer in a storm — do you not care? And it is worth noticing that Mark preserved the accusation. The Gospel does not tidy up the prayer of frightened men into something more reverent. There is a place in Scripture for saying exactly that to God, and the Psalms are full of it: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Ps. 44:23).

Two things follow. First, he answered the panicked prayer before he corrected the panic — the storm was stilled, and then the question about faith was asked. He is not waiting for you to pray well before he acts. Second, their fear did not end when the danger did; Mark says they were filled with great fear after the calm. They were more frightened of the man in the boat than of the wind. That is not a failure. That is the beginning of knowing who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: the kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he does not know how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.

Only Mark records this parable.

The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. The farmer does his part: he sows.

He sleeps and rises night and day. He gets on with ordinary life. He cannot make the seed grow by worrying.

And the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. Growth is a mystery, beyond his control.

The earth produces by itself. “By itself” (automatē, from which “automatic”) means without visible cause. God makes it grow (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. Growth happens in stages, gradually, often unseen.

But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come. Joel 3:13: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. The harvest pictures the end of the age and the final judgment (Matthew 13:39). The kingdom grows quietly now, and will come to its harvest at the end.

The lesson. The kingdom grows by God’s power, not ours. We sow the word, and God gives the growth. This brings both relief and confidence: relief, because we do not have to make it grow; confidence, because God will bring it to harvest.

What it does not mean. Not that we should be passive. The farmer sows and reaps. But we cannot force growth: in our children, our friends, our church, or ourselves.

In a sentence. The kingdom grows by God’s hidden power, like seed growing while the farmer sleeps, until the harvest comes.

On a Tuesday. Have you been sowing the word in someone’s life without seeing results? Keep sowing, sleep well, and trust God with the growth.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this parable of the seed growing by itself.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe
the farmer waits for the precious fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: with what can we compare the kingdom of God? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which when sown is the smallest of all seeds on earth, yet when it grows it becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.

With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? Jesus invites his hearers to think with him.

It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth. The black mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the smallest seed farmers in Galilee commonly sowed. Jesus speaks as people spoke.

Yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches. The mustard plant could grow up to three metres high in one season.

So that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade. In the Old Testament, a great tree with birds in its branches pictures a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12). The kingdom of God, though tiny at first, will become great and shelter people from all nations.

The meaning. The kingdom began insignificantly: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary men, rejected by the leaders. It looked like nothing. Yet it would grow into a worldwide kingdom, as it has.

What it does not mean. Not that the world will become Christian before Christ returns, as postmillennialists teach. The parables of growth stand alongside the parables of mixed fields and continuing evil (Matthew 13:24–30). Verdict: amillennial: the kingdom grows powerfully through the whole gospel age, and comes to its fulness when Christ returns.

In a sentence. The kingdom starts as small as a mustard seed but grows into a great plant that shelters the nations.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise small beginnings: a small church, a single conversation, a little faith. God’s kingdom grows from mustard seeds.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.

With many such parables he spoke the word to them. Mark records only a few.

As they were able to hear it. Jesus adapted his teaching to his hearers’ capacity. Parables were both a mercy (making truth memorable and accessible) and a test (concealing it from the unwilling).

He did not speak to them without a parable. To the crowds.

But privately to his own disciples he explained everything. Those who came to him and asked received full understanding (v. 10). The difference between insiders and outsiders is not intelligence, but willingness to come to Jesus.

In a sentence. Jesus taught the crowds in parables as they could hear, and explained everything privately to his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Jesus explains his word to those who come close. Spend time with him in his word and prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, "Let us go across to the other side." And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That day, when evening had come, Jesus said: let us go across to the other side. Leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.

On that day, when evening had come. After a long day of teaching. Jesus was exhausted.

He said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” To the eastern shore, Gentile territory (5:1). Notice: Jesus said they would go to the other side. His word was a promise that they would arrive.

And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. “Just as he was”: he was already in the boat, from which he had been teaching (v. 1). A vivid detail, from an eyewitness like Peter.

And other boats were with him. Only Mark mentions this: another eyewitness detail.

In a sentence. At evening, Jesus told the disciples to cross the lake, and they set off with him in the boat.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus says “let us go to the other side”, he will get you there, whatever storms come.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that it was already filling. But Jesus was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke him and said: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?

And a great windstorm arose. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level, surrounded by hills. Cold air rushing down from the heights can create sudden violent storms. Experienced fishermen were terrified, so this was no ordinary storm.

And the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. The boat was sinking.

But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. Only Mark mentions the cushion, perhaps a sandbag used for ballast, or a leather pillow for the steersman. Jesus was truly human and truly exhausted. And his sleep showed complete trust in his Father (Psalm 4:8).

And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” Only Mark records this accusing question. The disciples thought he did not care. In storms, we often feel the same: God, do you not care? But he did care. He was with them in the boat.

In a sentence. A violent storm swamped the boat while Jesus slept, and the terrified disciples woke him, asking if he did not care that they were perishing.

On a Tuesday. If you feel that God does not care in your storm, tell him so honestly, as the disciples did. He is in the boat with you.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common. The cushion was probably the helmsman’s seat or a sandbag in the stern.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm
awake! why are you sleeping, O Lord?

verseByVerse.quote: And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus woke up, rebuked the wind and said to the sea: peace! Be still! And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

And he awoke and rebuked the wind. “Rebuked” is the word used for silencing demons (1:25). He addresses the wind as one rebukes a disobedient servant.

And said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” “Be still” (pephimōso) literally means “be muzzled”, the word used to the demon in 1:25. In the Old Testament, the sea often pictures chaos and evil, and only God can rule it (Psalm 65:7; 89:9; 107:23–30; Job 38:8–11).

And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. Normally the waves continue long after the wind stops. Here, instant calm. A great storm (v. 37), a great calm.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the wind and commanded the sea to be still, and there was instant and great calm.

For worship. Worship Jesus, whom the wind and the sea obey.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith? And they were filled with great fear and said to one another: who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith? “Still”: after all they had seen. Their fear showed they did not yet trust him. Faith here means trusting Jesus to keep his word (they would go to the other side, v. 35) and to care for them.

And they were filled with great fear. Literally “they feared a great fear”. Their fear of the storm became a greater fear: awe at Jesus himself. The storm had frightened them; the one who stopped it frightened them more. This is the fear of God (Jonah 1:16).

And said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” The question of the whole Gospel. Psalm 107:29 says of the LORD: he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. Jesus has done what only God does. The answer to their question is in Mark’s first verse: the Son of God.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus always removes the storms of life when we ask. Sometimes he calms the storm; sometimes he calms us in it. The story is first about who he is.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they still had no faith, and they were filled with awe, asking who he could be, that wind and sea obey him.

On a Tuesday. Let the question “Who is this?” grow your faith. The one in your boat commands the storm.

parallels.desc: who stills the roaring of the seas

4.theology:
Why parables? Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter and they should not be softened. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark says so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Three things resolve it. The words are a quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10, God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already shut its eyes for generations — settled judgement on hardened refusal, not fresh cruelty. The so that carries fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables meet a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist (cf. Rom. 1:24). And the door is never bolted — those around him with the twelve understood nothing either, and the one thing that separated them from the crowd walking home was that they stayed and asked.

Who is in the boat? In the Old Testament, command of the sea belongs to God alone: you rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9); he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29); thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11). So the disciples' closing question has exactly one possible answer. And Mark holds the two natures within four feet of each other: asleep from sheer exhaustion on the helmsman's cushion, and muzzling a hurricane with a word.
4.examples:
The four soils are not four historical types but four live possibilities in any congregation on any Sunday, and the third is the one that describes most Christians in a comfortable country.

The path was not made hard by a decision; it was made hard by traffic — the same feet over the same ground until nothing could get in. That is how hearts harden in real life: not by rejecting God but by hearing about him so often that the sound becomes familiar.

The rocky ground grows fastest, and grows fastest because the soil is shallow. The heat that kills it is the same sun that ripens the harvest in the next furrow. Roots are grown in private, in the boring stretches, and the test is simple: if the trial came this year, what exactly would you be drawing on?

The thorns are not sins. Jesus names them — cares, riches, and the desires for other things. Worry, money, and the ordinary wanting of ordinary stuff. This soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct, because there may be nothing in it to confess. It is diagnosed by what has quietly stopped: the praying, the reading, the conversation about Christ you have not had in a year — not refused, just crowded out.

And the good soil yields thirty, sixty, or a hundred — and all three are good soil. Jesus put thirty in the same category as a hundred. Some believers are given health and years and visible fruitfulness; some produce a marriage held together and a few names prayed for over decades in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in verse 20, and the barn does not sort them.

5.title: Legion, Daughter, and the Hand That Takes Hold
5.text: <sup>1</sup>They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. <sup>2</sup>And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. <sup>3</sup>He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, <sup>4</sup>for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. <sup>5</sup>Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones. <sup>6</sup>And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. <sup>7</sup>And crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” <sup>8</sup>For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” <sup>9</sup>And Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” <sup>10</sup>And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <sup>11</sup>Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, <sup>12</sup>and they begged him, saying, “Send us to the pigs; let us enter them.” <sup>13</sup>So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. <sup>14</sup>The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>16</sup>And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. <sup>17</sup>And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. <sup>18</sup>As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. <sup>19</sup>And he did not permit him but said to him, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” <sup>20</sup>And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled. <sup>21</sup>And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. <sup>22</sup>Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet <sup>23</sup>and implored him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” <sup>24</sup>And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. <sup>25</sup>And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, <sup>26</sup>and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse. <sup>27</sup>She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. <sup>28</sup>For she said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” <sup>29</sup>And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. <sup>30</sup>And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?” <sup>31</sup>And his disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” <sup>32</sup>And he looked around to see who had done it. <sup>33</sup>But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. <sup>34</sup>And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” <sup>35</sup>While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” <sup>36</sup>But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.” <sup>37</sup>And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. <sup>38</sup>They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. <sup>39</sup>And when he had entered, he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>40</sup>And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. <sup>41</sup>Taking her by the hand he said to her, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement. <sup>43</sup>And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is three impossible cases in a row, and the arrangement is deliberate. A man no one could restrain, a woman no one could cure, and a child who has already died — the whole range of human helplessness, met in one day and a boat ride.

It is also a chapter about uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of it without knowing that. Under the Law three things defiled by contact: a grave, a discharge of blood, and a pig. Mark has put all three in one chapter. Jesus lands in a graveyard among pigs to save a man who lives in the tombs; an untouchable woman takes hold of his clothes in a crowd; and he ends the day taking a corpse by the hand. Every one of those contacts should have made him unclean under the system he himself gave. Every one of them runs the other way instead.

The two halves are held together by twelve years — the length of the woman's suffering and the whole life of Jairus's daughter — and by one word. The father calls the girl his little daughter; Jesus calls the destitute, unclean woman in the street Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he addresses a woman that way. The chapter opens with a man nobody could chain and closes with a girl being handed something to eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The landing (vv. 1–5). The storm of chapter 4 was crossed to reach this beach, and the welcoming party is one man out of the tombs — chained, unchainable, screaming night and day, cutting himself with stones. Mark spends five verses establishing that this case is beyond every remedy human beings had.

The encounter (vv. 6–10). He runs and falls at Jesus's feet, and the voice that comes out of him tries to put Jesus under oath. Asked its name, it answers with the word for a Roman army: Legion.

The pigs (vv. 11–13). The demons beg to be sent into a herd, and are permitted — and the herd goes over the cliff. What they intended for the man is acted out on the hillside for everyone to see.

The town's verdict (vv. 14–17). The neighbours arrive, find the man dressed and talking sense, and are frightened. They do not ask Jesus to stay and do more. They ask him to leave, and he goes.

The commission (vv. 18–20). The one man who wants to come is told no — and given a district instead of a boat. He becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles, and his whole training was what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This chapter turns on ceremonial uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of its force without knowing that. Under the Law, three things made a person unclean by contact: a corpse or a grave (Num. 19:11–16), a discharge of blood (Lev. 15:25–27), and a pig (Lev. 11:7). Mark has put all three in one chapter, and the man in this scene is standing in all of them at once — living among tombs, on a hillside where pigs are grazing, in Gentile country.

The whole logic of the purity system ran one way: uncleanness is contagious and holiness is not. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse does not become clean. Which is why what happens next in this chapter is so startling. A woman whose bleeding has made her untouchable for twelve years puts her hand on Jesus, and she is healed rather than he defiled. He takes a dead girl by the hand, and she gets up. The current runs backwards.

That is not Jesus ignoring the Law. It is the Law's purpose arriving. The system taught Israel for centuries that sin and death spread and cleanness does not — so that when a man walked into Israel whose holiness was catching, they would know exactly what they were looking at. He is the one clean thing in the world that cannot be contaminated, and everything he touches is what changes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a Gentile town given a neighbour back — sane, dressed, sitting down — and a hillside of dead livestock, and it grieves the livestock and asks the Healer to go.

Now: the same trade is still on offer, and it is not usually made by wicked people. It is made by people who have counted the cost of Christ disrupting an arrangement that works — the business practice, the relationship, the private habit, the plans — and quietly concluded they would rather keep the pigs. Nobody in that town denied the miracle. They simply decided it was too expensive.

And note what he does when they ask. He does not argue, and he does not stay. He gets into the boat. That is one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospel: Jesus goes where he is asked to go, including away.

But he does not leave them without a witness. The man they had chained and could not hold is left behind in the district with nothing to offer but what had been done to him — and by chapter 7 the crowds on that side of the lake will come out to meet Jesus. One restored man, telling one town, and the ground was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to the other side of the lake, to the region of the Gerasenes. As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.

Meaning first. Mark 5 is a chapter of three rescues, each harder than the last. On the eastern shore Jesus meets a man possessed by a legion of demons, living among the tombs, beyond the reach of chains or neighbours, and with a word he sends the legion out and leaves the man sitting, clothed and in his right mind; the town, counting its drowned pigs, begs Jesus to leave, and the freed man is sent home to tell what the Lord has done. Back on the western shore a synagogue ruler, Jairus, begs Jesus to come to his dying daughter; on the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak and is healed, and Jesus stops to call her daughter. Then word comes that the girl has died, and Jesus goes in, takes her by the hand and tells her to get up. In every scene the same thing happens: what is unclean and dead does not defile him. His holiness and his life flow out to it.

The connection. Chapters 4:35–5:43 show Jesus’ authority over four enemies: the storm (nature), a legion of demons (the spiritual powers), chronic disease, and death itself. Each is a power no human can defeat. Mark sets them one after another so that by the end of the chapter there is nothing left in the list of what frightens human beings that has not been made to obey him.

They came to the other side of the sea. As Jesus had said they would (4:35), through the storm. And remember what it cost to get here. The last chapter ended with a hurricane at night and a boat filling with water, and this is the shore they were crossing to. Everything that happened on the lake happened on the way to this man. That is worth sitting with if you are inclined to think of the storm as an accident. Jesus said, let us go across to the other side, and the other side had one person on it who needed him. If the price of the crossing was a night that nearly killed twelve experienced sailors, he paid it, and he paid it for a man whose own town had given up on him.

To the country of the Gerasenes. Gentile territory on the eastern shore of the lake: the region of the Decapolis, ten Greek cities, pagan country with pig farms on the hillsides. It is the first time in this Gospel that Jesus sets foot outside Jewish land, and he goes there to fight.

Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? A reader with a map will notice a real puzzle, and it is better dealt with than hurried past. Manuscripts vary between Gerasenes, Gadarenes (Matthew 8:28) and Gergesenes. Gerasa was a large city about thirty miles southeast, far too far for a herd to run down a steep bank into the sea; Gadara was closer, about six miles off, but still not on the shore; Gergesa (perhaps modern Kursi) was on the shore itself, where steep slopes come down to the water. The likeliest answer is that the names refer to regions. Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that shore, and each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might say a village lies in greater London. The place was probably near Kursi, and the steep bank is still there. What looks like a contradiction is the ordinary looseness of naming a place by its nearest famous city, and the shoreline fits the story exactly.

One man or two? Matthew says there were two men (Matthew 8:28); Mark and Luke tell of one. That is no contradiction. Mark and Luke follow the one who spoke, begged to go with Jesus and was sent home to tell his story, and neither of them says there was only one. A reporter who tells you about the survivor who gave the interview has not denied that there was another.

And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. He has one foot on the beach. There is no interval, no walk into town, no settling in: the boat grounds and the man is coming down at them out of the rocks. And picture where he comes from. Tombs were caves cut in the hillside, and the limestone hills on that shore are full of them, some big enough to stand in. That is his address. A man is living in a graveyard, and the town knows it, and nobody has come to get him.

Unclean three times over. Note the word Mark uses for the spirit: unclean. Under the law a grave defiled anyone who went near it for seven days (Numbers 19:16). In this one scene the man is unclean three times over: demon-possessed, living among the dead, in a Gentile land near pigs. He is as far from God’s people as a person could be, outside the town, outside worship, outside every category human beings use to organise the living. And Jesus has crossed a storm to reach him.

Does demon possession happen today? The New Testament treats it as real, and nothing in it says the devil’s work ended with the apostles. Missionaries in places of open idolatry have often met things they could only describe this way. But Scripture also distinguishes the possessed from the sick (1:32–34), and most suffering of mind and body has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Two errors are to be avoided: seeing demons behind every illness, and denying that the devil works at all. And what drives out evil is not a technique, a ritual or a gifted specialist, but Christ himself, sought in prayer and trusted through his word (Ephesians 6:10–18; James 4:7).

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), sealed by him (Ephesians 1:13), and has been delivered from the domain of darkness and transferred to the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). A house cannot have two owners. Christians can be tempted, attacked and deceived, and they are told to resist the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9), but they are never told to fear being taken over by him. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). If you belong to Christ and are troubled, the answer is not to look for something living in you but to look to the one who lives in you.

So Mark has arranged the meeting with great care. On one side of the beach is a man out of the tombs, unclean, unreachable, the property of something that hates him. On the other is a man stepping out of a boat, wet through, who has just been asleep on a cushion in a hurricane. Nothing in the scene says which of them is stronger. The next twenty verses are about that.

In a sentence. As soon as Jesus landed in Gentile territory, a demon-possessed man came out of the tombs to meet him.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you know who is furthest from God: furthest by background, by behaviour, by the sheer improbability of him ever darkening a church door. Jesus crossed a storm to reach a man like that, and no one is beyond his reach or his concern. Pray for that person by name this week, and be ready to cross some small storm of your own (an awkward conversation, an inconvenient visit) on his account. And if you are the one who feels furthest away, notice who stepped out of the boat first.

For worship. The Son of God did not wait on the clean shore for the unclean to make their way to him. He set out across the dark water, slept through the storm, and stepped out onto a graveyard beach in pagan country because one ruined man was there. That is how he has always come: not to the healthy but to the sick, not to the places where he is welcome but to the places where he is needed. Before this man had asked for anything, the Lord of the sea had already crossed the sea for him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gergesenes, some Gadarenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lived among the tombs, and no one could bind him any more, not even with a chain. He had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he tore the chains apart and broke the shackles; no one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.

He lived among the tombs. Mark now slows right down. Three verses of pure description come before a word is spoken, and every clause does the same job: establishing that this man was past help. He did not hide among the tombs occasionally. He lived there. Driven out of society, he made a graveyard his home, and the dead were his company.

And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain. The word anymore tells the whole history. People had tried to control him with force, repeatedly. There had been a time when the town still attempted something, and it had stopped. Human strength cannot defeat demonic power.

He wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. Superhuman strength (compare Acts 19:16). Two different failures: iron chains torn apart, and the shackles, the metal cuffs on wrists and ankles, smashed. Mark, who has this from Peter, gives the detail like a man describing physical evidence he has seen.

No one had the strength to subdue him. There is the town’s final verdict, stated flatly. The word means to tame, the word you would use of an animal. They had reached the point of trying to tame a man, and failed at that too. Restraint had failed. Confinement had failed. There was no help available and nobody left who thought there might be. He was written off, and the writing off had been going on for years.

Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out. The screaming never stopped. Not a fit that came and went, but night and day, on the hillsides where the sound carried down to the town. The people of that district went to sleep hearing him.

And cutting himself with stones. Constant torment, self-harm, isolation, sleeplessness. Here Mark says the thing that will land hardest on a modern reader, and it should be handled gently, because a great many people know exactly what this verse is describing. Understand first what it tells us about the power in him. Everything the demons do to this man is aimed at his destruction. They have taken him out of his home, out of his town, out of human company, out of clothing, out of his own mind, and now they are using his own hands against his own body. That is the settled programme of the enemy wherever he is given room: not pleasure, not power, but ruin, and ruin worked where possible through the victim’s own hands. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy (John 10:10). The pigs in a few verses will act it out on a hillside for everyone to see.

What it does not mean. Not that people who harm themselves or suffer mental illness are possessed. The Gospels distinguish illness from possession (1:32–34), and pain, shame and illness are enough to explain most of what human beings do to themselves. Those who self-harm need compassion, safety and care, medical and spiritual. Going to a doctor is an ordinary mercy from God and not a failure of faith. But this man’s torment was demonic, and only Jesus could free him.

How can I tell whether a struggle is spiritual or medical? Usually you do not need to choose, because every human trouble is both: we are bodies and souls together, living in a fallen world with a real enemy. So do both things. See a doctor, and if a counsellor or medication is advised, accept it with thanks, as you would for a broken leg. And bring the whole thing to Christ in prayer, Scripture and the fellowship of his people, asking your pastor and elders to pray with you (James 5:14). Be wary of anyone who offers a quick spiritual diagnosis without knowing you well, and of anyone who tells you that faith means refusing treatment. The man in the tombs was beyond every remedy; most of us are not, and God normally heals through means.

The direction the story runs. If you are a person who hurts yourself, or you love one, take from this passage the direction the story runs. The man in the tombs, whom nobody could hold and nobody could help, is sitting quietly in a few verses, dressed, talking, in his right mind, with the marks of the stones still on his arms. And the one who put him back together did not flinch at meeting him at his worst, in a graveyard, screaming, bleeding and out of control. He came to that beach on purpose.

In a sentence. The man lived among the tombs, too strong to be chained, crying out and cutting himself day and night.

On a Tuesday. If you or someone you love is self-harming, please tell someone and seek help today: a doctor, a trusted friend, your pastor, or an emergency line if you are in danger. That is not weakness; it is taking hold of the help God has put within reach. And if you know someone the people around them have quietly given up on, refuse to join the town’s verdict. Write their name down, pray for them, and look for one ordinary kindness you can do them this week.

For worship. The enemy works by ruin, and he is very good at it: he isolates, strips, torments, and turns a man’s own hands against him. But he is not the strongest power on that hillside. Christ is the one who looks at what everybody else has chained and abandoned and walks towards it. He is not repelled by our worst, because he came to bear it. The marks of the stones did not keep that man from him, and the marks of the nails are the proof that nothing in us will keep us from him either.

parallels.desc: who sit in tombs, who eat pig’s flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. And crying out with a loud voice, he said, "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell down before him. Crying out with a loud voice, he said: what have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.

And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. The whole tragedy of the man is in that sentence, and you have to read it twice to feel it. He ran, across broken ground, from a distance, to get to Jesus, and then went down on his face in front of him. Who did the running? Mark does not tell us, and probably it cannot be separated. There is a man in there who has wanted help for years and has never once been able to get to it. And there is a power in there that has to come and bow before Jesus’ authority, because it cannot do anything else in the presence of the Son of God. Both are true, and they arrive at the same feet.

The posture of worship. It is not willing worship; it is the same involuntary prostration as on the beach in chapter 3 (3:11). But it is the rehearsal of a day when everything that has ever opposed him will do this: at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Philippians 2:10).

And crying out with a loud voice. The screaming that the district has heard for years is aimed now at one person.

What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? The question means, leave me alone; what is there between us (1:24)? And the theology is flawless. It is not the first time in Mark that the best confession in the district comes out of a demon (1:24; 3:11). “Most High God” was a title often used by or to Gentiles for the supreme God: it is Melchizedek’s name for him (Genesis 14:18–22), and Nebuchadnezzar’s (Daniel 3:26), and the slave girl’s spirit uses it in Philippi (Acts 16:17). On the pagan side of the lake even the demons use the local vocabulary, and they use it correctly. The demon knows exactly who Jesus is.

Right doctrine, no salvation. It still does them no good. That is the point Mark keeps making, and it will not go away: you can have the doctrine exactly right, use the right name, take the right posture, and be no nearer to being saved than you were before. The difference between this cry and a Christian’s is not accuracy. It is that this one means keep away from me.

I adjure you by God, do not torment me. Now look closely at what is happening, because it is remarkable and easily missed. To adjure someone is to put him under oath, and that was the standard technique of the professional exorcist in that world. You named a higher power and bound the spirit by it. The formula was the trade. So the demon is attempting an exorcism. It is trying to use the exorcist’s own tools on the exorcist, invoking God to bind the Son of God. The tormentor of the man begs not to be tormented. It is the last resort of something that has understood, in the first three seconds, that it is completely outmatched, and it does not work for even a moment.

Before the time. And there is the fear underneath. Matthew gives the sentence in full: Have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29). Demons know that judgment awaits them. They know there is a time. They know what is fixed for them, and they know who fixed it, and their only argument is about the schedule. The kingdom of darkness in this Gospel is not confidently opposing Christ. It is a defeated thing negotiating for a delay.

If demons believe the truth about Jesus, what makes my faith different? Saving faith is not only knowing who Jesus is; it is trusting him and coming to him to be saved. James says the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). They know he is the Son of God and they hate it; they want him to go away. A Christian knows the same truth and wants him to come nearer. So the test is not whether you can say the right words about Christ, but whether you rest on him, love him, and want to be with him. If you find in yourself even a weak longing for him, and grief that it is not stronger, that is not the faith of demons. It is the work of his Spirit.

In a sentence. The demon ran to Jesus, bowed, named him Son of the Most High God, and begged not to be tormented.

On a Tuesday. If the powers of evil frighten you, and there is no shame in that, notice who is on the ground and who is standing. The demons in Mark are never once calm in the presence of Jesus. They shout, they beg, they bargain, they go. He has not yet had to raise his voice. So when fear comes at night, or temptation presses, do not argue with it on its own terms. Go straight to Christ, speak his name in prayer, and stand on what he has already done.

For worship. There is no rival on the throne. The powers that hold men in chains cannot hold their ground before Jesus for a single moment; they fall on their faces, and they know his name better than his friends do. He is the Son of the Most High God, and every knee in heaven, on earth and under the earth is already bending in the direction of the day when it will bow. The darkness bargains for time, and he is the one who owns the time.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: For he was saying to him, "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" And Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Legion, for we are many." And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Jesus had been saying to him: come out of the man, you unclean spirit! And Jesus asked him: what is your name? He replied: my name is Legion, for we are many. And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.

For he was saying to him, Come out of the man, you unclean spirit. Mark drops the tense back a step to tell us what had already been happening: Jesus had already commanded it, and the whole exchange in verse 7 was the answer to that command. The screaming and the bargaining are what a thing does on its way out. And notice the command itself. No ritual, no formula, no invoking of a higher name, which is exactly what every exorcist in the ancient world needed, and precisely what the demon had just tried to use on him. Jesus does not appeal to an authority. He is one.

And Jesus asked him, What is your name? This is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus asks a demon its name, and it is worth asking why, because he plainly does not need the information. He is not gaining power over it by learning its name, as the magicians of the day believed. Two things are being done. The first is for the man. Everything that has happened to him has happened in the dark, unnamed and unexplained, for years. The thing that owned him is about to be forced to identify itself out loud, in front of witnesses, before it is thrown out. What has been destroying you is made to say what it is. The second is for the record. Mark wants his readers to grasp the extent of the possession, the scale of what they are watching, and only the enemy can supply that figure.

My name is Legion, for we are many. The word lands like a boot. A Roman legion had about six thousand soldiers: not a metaphor to anybody in that district but the thing that had marched up their road. A legion arrives, occupies and stays. It cannot be resisted, cannot be negotiated with, and does not leave. The name suggests a vast number of demons, organised like an army, and it describes exactly what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. It also tells you why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain a man. The man was a garrison.

Two occupations. The man was occupied by a hostile force, as the land was occupied by Roman legions; the tenth legion, stationed in the region, had a boar as its emblem, which gives the pigs in the next verses a sharp edge. So Mark quietly sets two occupations side by side. There is the one everybody in that country could see, with soldiers on the road and taxes to Caesar. And there is the one nobody could do anything about at all. Jesus walks up the beach and evicts the second with a sentence. He will deal with the first in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a cross outside Jerusalem and finds that it cannot hold him either.

And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. Begged. The strongest power in the district has been reduced to asking, and it will beg again in verse 12. Luke tells us what they were most afraid of: they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss (Luke 8:31), the place of their confinement. Weigh the whole encounter as the man on the ground would have heard it. He had been held by thousands, and he was worth a storm and a crossing to the one who came for him, and the thousands spent the entire conversation pleading.

Should Christians name demons, or bind spirits over places? No. This scene is not a method to copy. Jesus asked the name for the man’s sake and for ours, not because naming gives power; the demon’s own attempt to use a formula failed. Nowhere does the New Testament tell believers to interrogate spirits, map territorial demons, or command the devil by special words. The apostles, with their unique authority, cast out demons in Jesus’ name (Acts 16:18), but the instructions given to every Christian are plainer: be sober and watchful, resist the devil, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), take up the armour of God, which is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, the word of God and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18). Our weapon is not a technique but the Lord himself.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded the spirit to leave and asked its name, and it called itself Legion, for there were many demons.

On a Tuesday. However many forces seem to be against you, they are not too many for Jesus. Name what you are up against honestly before him in prayer: the habit, the fear, the accusation that keeps returning. Bringing it out of the dark and into his presence is half the battle. Then remind yourself whose word has the last say over it.

For worship. Six thousand were not too many for him. The garrison that no chain could hold heard one voice and began to plead. Jesus is not one authority among many, needing a stronger name to call upon; he is the Name. What the legions of hell and the legions of Rome could not stand against was not a better formula but the Son of God himself, who at the end let the second kind of legion crucify him in order to break the first kind for ever (Colossians 2:15).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him, saying, "Send us to the pigs; let us enter them." So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great herd of pigs was feeding on the hillside, and the demons begged him: send us to the pigs, let us enter them. So he gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside. Mark mentions them almost as scenery, and the detail confirms where we are. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and no Jewish district would have two thousand of them on a hillside. A herd that size shows this was Gentile country, and a valuable business: the pigs are somebody’s livelihood.

Send us to the pigs; let us enter them. The demons beg again. They have no power to resist Jesus; they can only plead. The Legion cannot go anywhere or do anything without permission, which tells you exactly how much of what happens in this world is unsupervised. Nothing.

So he gave them permission. Jesus permits it, for his purposes. Five words, and they raise every hard question in the chapter at once.

And the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. Two thousand animals over a cliff. A reader who cares about God’s justice, and about somebody’s ruined business, is entitled to ask what on earth this was for. Three things answer it, and none of them requires pretending the loss did not happen.

The demons did this. First, the demons drove the herd, not Jesus. He permitted their request, and in permitting it he let their intention show itself in the open. For five verses we have been told what they were doing to a man: the tombs, the chains, the screaming, the stones. Now the whole district gets to watch what that programme looks like when it runs unhindered: everything it enters goes straight over the edge and into the water. Demons destroy whatever they inhabit (John 10:10). The pigs are the man’s story acted out in a few seconds on a hillside. And it shows that the man was truly freed: everyone could see that the demons had gone.

The arithmetic of heaven. Second, one human being matters more to Jesus than two thousand pigs. One tormented man, restored to his mind, his clothes, his family and his town, and sent out as a herald of mercy, is worth more than any number of animals. Jesus had already said it in a synagogue argument: Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matthew 12:12). And a man than a pig. God’s care for animals is real: he feeds the ravens, he counts the sparrows, and Proverbs says the righteous man has regard for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10). But when the two are set against each other, there is no contest, and there never was.

The town’s reaction. Third, the reaction of the town settles the matter. Presented with a neighbour raised out of a living death and a hillside of dead livestock, they will grieve the livestock and ask the Healer to leave.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was careless with others’ property. He judged that a man’s freedom was worth more. And he is the Lord of all things: the cattle on a thousand hills are his (Psalm 50:10), and so were these pigs. The deeper question is the one the townspeople faced: what do you value more?

Why would Jesus grant a request from demons at all? Because their going into the pigs served his purposes, not theirs. It gave visible proof that the man was free, it exposed what the demons are, and it put the town’s heart to the test. Throughout Scripture God permits evil powers to act only within limits he sets, and he turns what they intend for harm into good (Job 1:12; 2:6; Genesis 50:20). The demons got what they asked for and lost everything: they wanted a home and ended in the sea. That is the pattern of every concession evil wins from God. It is never a defeat for him. It is always a rope by which it hangs itself.

In a sentence. Jesus let the demons enter a herd of two thousand pigs, which rushed down into the lake and drowned.

On a Tuesday. This scene puts an uncomfortable question to us, and it is not about pigs. There are still people who would rather keep their herd than lose their sins. The cost of Christ is always visible and always countable: the money, the relationship, the ambition, the private arrangement that works. What he gives is a man in his right mind, and that never appears in the accounts until later. Ask yourself where you have done the town’s sum this year, and come out against him, over something considerably less than two thousand pigs. And value people above possessions: the person who interrupts your plans is worth more than the plans.

For worship. Here is a Lord whose arithmetic is mercy. The market priced the herd and wrote off the man; Christ priced the man and let the herd go. Even the demons’ last request is in his hands, and their malice becomes the proof of his power. Nothing is unsupervised in his world. And the God who would trade two thousand pigs for one ruined Gentile would one day trade something infinitely greater, his own Son, for people like us.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a herd of two thousand shows this was Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country, and people came to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and saw the man who had been possessed by the legion sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. Of course they ran. They have two thousand animals at the bottom of a cliff and somebody is going to want an explanation. News spread quickly: town and countryside both. Within an hour the whole district knows.

And people came to see what it was that had happened. They come out in numbers, and Mark lets us watch them arrive at the scene.

And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion. Notice how they still describe him, even now. That is his name in this town: the demon-possessed man. It is what he has been called for years, and there is no other way anyone here knows how to refer to him. Then Mark gives three details, and they are three of the loveliest words in the Gospel.

Sitting there. Start with that, because it is the one people skip. This man has not sat down in years. He has been running the hills, tearing at chains, roaming the tombs night and day; whatever was in him never let him be still. And now, in the middle of the whole town, he is no longer running wild but at rest. Luke adds where: sitting at the feet of Jesus (Luke 8:35), which is the posture of a disciple at his teacher’s feet.

Clothed. He had been naked; Luke says so plainly (Luke 8:27). Somebody has given him a garment, and his dignity is restored along with his mind.

And in his right mind. The Greek is a single word meaning sound-minded, sane, self-possessed. He is no longer tormented. He can hold a conversation. He knows his own name, and he can hear his own thoughts for the first time in years.

A case everybody else had closed. Take the measure of what has just happened in the space of a few minutes. No process, no gradual rehabilitation, no years of careful work. He came down out of the rocks screaming and he is sitting on the ground with a borrowed coat on, listening. That is what Christ does with a case that everybody else has closed, and it is a picture of what he does for everyone he saves: peace, dignity and a renewed mind. And it is worth saying to anyone praying for a person who has been beyond reach for a long time, the addict, the one who is not in his right mind, the family member nobody knows how to help, that this town had reached the settled conclusion that nothing could be done. They were right about their own resources and wrong about the possibilities, and the difference arrived by boat.

And they were afraid. And there is the turn nobody expects. Not glad, not delighted for him, but afraid. The man they had feared and chained was now calm, and the power that did it frightened them more. It is the same fear that filled the boat after the storm (4:41): the fear of a power you cannot classify or control. In itself it is not a wicked reaction; awe in the presence of God is right. But what this town does with it in the next two verses is another matter entirely.

Is the change always this sudden? The freeing was instant, and so is the new birth: God gives a new heart, and a person passes from death to life (John 5:24; Ephesians 2:4–5). But what follows is usually slow. This man had to learn to live in a town, rebuild trust, and face people who remembered him; the sitting, the clothing and the right mind were the beginning of a life, not the end of it. So when you pray for someone, ask boldly for the decisive work only Christ can do, and then be patient with the long recovery afterwards, in them and in yourself. Christians are being transformed by the renewal of the mind (Romans 12:2), and that is a lifetime’s work.

In a sentence. The townspeople came and found the former demoniac sitting, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.

On a Tuesday. Think of a long-closed case on your prayer list, the person you stopped praying for because nothing ever changed. Open the file again today. And then look at your own life for the three marks of this man: is there rest at Jesus’ feet in it, or only running? Do you remember that you are clothed in a righteousness not your own? Are you letting his word renew your mind, or only the noise of the week?

For worship. Jesus is the one who sits the restless down, clothes the naked, and gives back the mind that was lost. He did it on that beach in a few minutes, and he does it for every sinner he saves: he brings us to rest at his feet, clothes us in his own righteousness (Isaiah 61:10), and makes us new. The man the town could only chain, Christ could only love, and his love was stronger than all their iron.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who had seen it described what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to leave their region.

And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. The eyewitnesses give their report, and Mark’s summary of it is quietly devastating: the man and the pigs. Both items, in one account, presented for the town’s consideration. Which mattered more to them? The town weighs them up.

And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. That is the third begging in this chapter, and it is the one that should stop us. A tragic reversal: the demons begged Jesus not to send them away; the townspeople beg Jesus to go away. Read it slowly, because it is one of the most sobering verses in the Gospel. Nobody in that district disputes what has happened. Nobody says it was a trick. They have the facts, they have the eyewitnesses, and they have their neighbour sitting in front of them in his right mind. And their considered, unanimous request is that the man who did it should get back in his boat.

Why did they want him gone? Mark does not explain, and he does not need to. They preferred their pigs and their comfort to the presence of the one who sets people free. His power threatened their way of life.
