They had just watched a hillside of assets go into the water, and they had understood something about Jesus that many people who admire him never grasp: he is not safe, and he does not stay within the budget. A man who can do that to a herd of pigs might do it to anything. Better to have the misery you have priced than the mercy you cannot. So they chose the graveyard they knew, and the terrible thing is that the choice is not exotic. It is the most ordinary transaction in the world.

And Jesus left. Jesus does not force himself on those who do not want him, and this is the most frightening thing here. Mark states it without comment in the next verse: as he was getting into the boat. No argument, no second attempt, no sermon on the shore about what they were throwing away. They asked him to leave and he left. Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone (Hosea 4:17) is a real sentence in the Bible, and it is the most terrifying kind of answered prayer there is.

Not the end of the account. Yet do not close the account there, because he does not. He is going, and he leaves the district the one thing it cannot chain, cut or drive away. He leaves a man with a story. And when Jesus returns to that side of the lake, the crowds come out to meet him (7:31–37; 8:1–10).

If I have pushed Jesus away before, has he left me for good? Not if you want him now. The danger in this passage is a settled preference for life without him, not a single moment of fear or refusal. The Gerasenes sent him away, and by chapter 7 that same region is bringing him their sick. Peter denied him three times and was restored on a beach (John 21:15–19). The very fact that you are troubled by having pushed him away is a sign that he has not left you to yourself. Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). So do not wait to feel worthy: ask him back today, and he will come.

In a sentence. Hearing about the man and the pigs, the townspeople begged Jesus to leave, and he went.

On a Tuesday. Ask it plainly of yourself, because this is what the passage is for. Is there any part of your life where you would rather Jesus stayed away, because his presence might cost you something? Not in theory, in fact. The relationship you know he would not sanction. The way you make your money. The evening habit. The plan for the next ten years you have never once put in his hands. Everybody has an answer, and the honest test is what you do when he walks up the beach and touches it. Name it to him today, and ask him to stay.

For worship. The Lord who could have compelled that town to receive him let them choose, and walked back to the boat. His patience is not weakness; it is the dignity of a King who will not be treated as a tool. And yet even as he left he did not abandon them: he planted a witness among them and came back. He is the God who is rejected and still sends messengers, who is shut out and still knocks (Revelation 3:20), and whose mercy outlasts the refusals of whole towns.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. And he did not permit him but said to him, "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you." And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed begged to go with him. But Jesus did not permit him. He said: go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you. He went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed.

As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. The fourth and last begging in this scene, and this one is a prayer any Christian would recognise. A true disciple’s request: the demons begged to enter the pigs, the townspeople begged Jesus to leave, and the freed man begs to stay with him. And look at the words Mark chooses: that he might be with him. That is not a wish for a boat ride. It is the exact phrase used of the appointing of the Twelve: so that they might be with him (3:14). The man is asking to be a disciple in the strictest sense. It is the best request in the whole chapter, made by the only person on that beach who has understood anything.

And he did not permit him. Stay with that, because it is one of the hardest sentences in Mark. He permitted the demons. He did not permit the man. It is the only time in Mark that Jesus refuses a request to follow him, and not because he did not want him, but because he had a different calling for him. The finest prayer offered on that shore, by the man with the most reason to offer it, asking for nothing but Jesus himself, and the answer is no.

When the best prayer is refused. If you have prayed the best prayer you know how to pray and been refused, you are in extremely good company, and this is the passage for you. Paul asked three times to have the thorn removed and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus himself asked in a garden that the cup might pass, and it did not (14:36). A no from Christ is not a sign that you asked badly or that he has stopped caring. Sometimes it is a redeployment.

Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you. Look what he is given instead: not a place in the boat but a district, not proximity but a commission. And notice where he is sent. Home: to his friends, to the town that chained him, to the neighbours who had heard him screaming on the hills for years, to the family that gave up. That is the hardest mission field on earth and it always has been. These are people who knew him before, who will remember what he was, and who cannot be impressed by a stranger’s testimony because they were there. Which is exactly why they are the ones who cannot argue with it.

Why is this man told to tell, when others are told to be silent? Elsewhere Jesus tells people to keep silent (1:44; 5:43). Here, in Gentile territory, where there was no crowd waiting for a Jewish Messiah to lead a revolt against Rome, and where Jesus would not be staying, he sends the man to tell. The danger that made silence wise in Galilee did not apply here. And the man is to tell what the Lord has done for him, not to proclaim a title. “The Lord” means God.

And how he has had mercy on you. His testimony was simple: what God had done, and God’s mercy. And note what the whole of his training consisted of. He had no theological education, no years with Jesus, no Scriptures at his fingertips. He had one thing: what happened to him. If you have ever thought you were not equipped to say anything about Christ to anybody, this man is the answer, and he had been out of his mind that morning.

And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan. Now catch what he has done with his instructions, because it is the most beautiful thing in the passage and almost everybody reads past it. Jesus told him to tell what “the Lord” had done; he told what “Jesus” had done. He made the substitution himself. Nobody taught him that. He had been a believer for about ten minutes, in a pagan district, with no Bible and no instruction, and he had already worked out that the man who had spoken to him on the beach and the Lord God of Israel were not two subjects. Mark’s point: what Jesus did, God did. His first sermon was better than the disciples’ theology, and they had been in the boat for months.

And everyone marveled. Ten cities, and one man with no qualifications telling the only story he had. When Jesus returned to this region later, crowds came to him (7:31–37; 8:1–10). The man became the first missionary to the Gentiles in this Gospel, and the town that begged Jesus to leave got him back, because the man they could not chain would not stop talking.

What if my story is not dramatic? Then tell it anyway, because the heart of this man’s message was not the drama but the mercy. Every Christian has the same two things to say: what the Lord has done for me, and how he has had mercy on me. Perhaps you grew up in a Christian home and cannot remember not believing; that is a story of mercy too, of God keeping you from what this man went through. Speak simply about what Christ means to you, what he has forgiven, how he has held you. Point to Jesus rather than to yourself, as this man did. You are not asked to impress anyone, only to be honest about the Lord.

In a sentence. The freed man begged to go with Jesus, but Jesus sent him home to tell what the Lord had done for him, and he proclaimed it throughout the Decapolis.

On a Tuesday. You do not need training to tell your friends what Jesus has done for you. Start with your own story, and start at home: with the family who knew you before, the colleague who saw the old you, the neighbour who has watched. Write down in three sentences what the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you, and pray for one opening this week to say them aloud.

For worship. This is the Lord who says no to our best prayers only because he has a better yes. He took a man out of the tombs in the morning and made him a herald to ten cities by the afternoon. And the man’s first sermon got the deepest thing right: Jesus is the Lord, and the mercy of God has a human face. Every Gentile believer since, every one of us on the far side of the lake, is the harvest of the God who sends his healed ones home to tell.
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

parallels.desc: Jesus later returns to the Decapolis

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–43 — Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The father (vv. 21–24). A synagogue ruler — a man of standing, from the very institution that has been building a case against Jesus — comes through the crowd and goes down on his face. His twelve-year-old is dying. Jesus goes with him, and there is not one word of negotiation.

The interruption (vv. 25–34). On the way, a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, ruined by doctors' fees, ceremonially untouchable, gets close enough to take hold of his clothes from behind. She is healed instantly — and then Jesus stops the entire procession to find her. Jairus stands and watches while his daughter dies.

The news (vv. 35–36). Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? — and Jesus overhears the sentence and speaks over the top of it: Do not fear, only believe.

The house (vv. 37–43). Professional mourners in full cry, and a man who says the child is sleeping, and a room that laughs at him. He puts them all out, takes a dead girl by the hand, and says two words in the language a mother would have used.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark has interleaved these two stories deliberately — his habitual sandwich — and the links are not decoration. Both turn on twelve years: the girl's whole life, and the length of the woman's suffering. The year that family received a daughter is the year this woman's life began to come apart. Both are called daughter — the one by her father, the other by Jesus. Both are healed by touch: she takes hold of his garment, he takes hold of her hand. And the same Greek verb, sōzō, runs through both — made well, and saved, are the same word.

Set side by side, they say one thing between them. The woman had exhausted every human resource over twelve years; the father had run out of time in an afternoon. Slow ruin and sudden catastrophe, and the same answer to both.

And the interruption is the point of the arrangement. From where Jairus is standing, the delay is fatal — Jesus stops to talk to a woman who is already healed, and while he talks, a child dies. But the delay is what Jairus is given to watch. He hears a desperate woman told your faith has made you well before he hears the words your daughter is dead. God's delays are not always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are the school in which faith is taught the thing it is about to need.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman who had tried everything else and everyone else, coming from behind, in a crowd, hoping to take what she needed without being seen.

Now: everybody who comes to Christ as a last resort, after the money, the specialists and the years have all run out — and finds that the last resort was the first and only real one all along. She had no right to be in that crowd and she knew it; her condition made her contagious under the Law, and every person she brushed against on the way through was defiled by her. She came anyway.

And notice that Jesus was not content to heal her anonymously. He stopped everything, in public, and drew her out — not to shame her, since she had done nothing wrong, but because he wanted more for her than a cure. She got a conversation, a word about her faith, a blessing of peace, and a name: Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he calls a woman that. She came for a healing and went away with a relationship. He always gives more than was asked, and it is never the part you were focused on.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet and implored him earnestly, saying, "My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live." And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus had crossed again by boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered around him beside the lake. Then one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, came, and seeing him, fell at his feet and begged him earnestly: my little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live. And Jesus went with him, and a great crowd followed him and pressed around him.

And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side. Back to the Jewish western shore, and the crowd is waiting on the beach. Then a man comes through it who should not be there.

Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name. Mark names him, which he rarely does, perhaps because Jairus was known in the church afterwards, a man people could go and ask. A ruler of the synagogue was not a preacher. He organised its services and cared for its building: the senior layman who appointed the readers, kept the building and held the respect of the town. He is the establishment. And the establishment, in this Gospel, has already held a meeting about how to destroy Jesus (3:6), and scribes have come from Jerusalem to declare him possessed (3:22). Every professional instinct and every social pressure in this man’s life points away from the beach he is walking down.

And seeing him, he fell at his feet. In front of everyone. A leading man humbles himself before Jesus, in front of the crowd: a dignitary on his face in the sand before an itinerant preacher his colleagues have written off. Desperation overcomes pride. That is what a dying child does to a man: it burns away everything he was worried about the week before. And there is a mercy hidden in it. The very grief that is destroying him has got him to the only place where help was.

My little daughter is at the point of death. The Greek is a diminutive: my little daughter, the word a father uses. A father’s anguish. She is twelve (v. 42), which Mark will tell us at the end almost as an afterthought: old enough in that world to be nearly a woman, and still his little girl.

Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live. He believes Jesus can heal her. “Made well” (sōthē) is literally saved. And notice the theology in a panicking man’s request. He has a method in mind: come, and lay hands on her. He assumes Jesus must be physically present and must touch her. He is about to discover that this is not remotely the limit of it, and that the delay he is about to endure is not the disaster it looks like.

Our way of asking. That is worth knowing about your own praying. Most of us come with the mechanism already specified: do it this way, by this date, through this means. God is not offended by that; he did not correct Jairus. He simply intends to answer more largely than the request was framed (Ephesians 3:20).

And he went with him. Jesus goes at once. Five words, and they are the gospel in miniature. No conditions. No questions about whether a synagogue ruler had been at the meeting in chapter 3. No lecture about coming sooner. No delay while the crowd is dismissed. Jesus goes where desperate faith brings him.

And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. And here Mark starts winding the tension. The crowd is not a backdrop; it is an obstacle. They are pressing in on all sides, and a man with a dying child at home is now moving at the pace of a mob through a village street. Every step is slower than it should be, and it is about to stop altogether.

The structure. Mark again sandwiches one story inside another: Jairus’s daughter (vv. 21–24, 35–43) frames the woman with bleeding (vv. 25–34). The two stories interpret each other: two daughters (v. 34), twelve years, uncleanness, faith, and the power of Jesus over disease and death. Mark wants you to read them together, so that the woman teaches Jairus what faith is, and the girl teaches the woman how far Jesus’ power reaches.

Does “saved” here mean healed or saved from sin? Both, in the way Mark tells it. The same Greek word covers rescue from illness, from danger, and from sin and judgment, and Mark uses it on purpose. Jairus means: heal her. But in this Gospel every healing is a sign of the larger salvation Jesus brings. The body made well points to the whole person made right with God, and one day to the body raised. So when we pray for healing we are asking for a small piece of what Christ will finally give in full. He may give it now; he will certainly give it at the resurrection (Romans 8:23).

In a sentence. Jairus, a synagogue ruler, fell at Jesus’ feet and begged him to come and heal his dying daughter, and Jesus went with him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your children to Jesus in prayer, as Jairus did, with humility and urgency. Name them one by one, whatever their age and whatever state they are in. And notice whether pride or reputation is keeping you from going to Christ, or from asking his people to pray with you, over something you cannot fix. Jairus lost his dignity on that beach and found the Lord of life.

For worship. The Lord of glory can be stopped in the street by a frightened father and turned towards a sickroom. He does not ask for credentials or remind anyone of old grievances; he simply goes. That is the heart of God made visible: he answers desperate faith not with a lecture but with his presence, and the one who walks beside Jairus through the crowd is the same who walks with every grieving parent who calls on his name.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years. She had suffered much under many doctors, and had spent everything she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.

And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years. Mark now does something novelists do: he stops the clock mid-journey and turns the camera on somebody else. A man with a dying daughter is left standing in the street while we are told about a woman in the crowd. Her condition was probably a chronic menstrual or uterine haemorrhage. And notice the twelve years, because Mark has built it in deliberately: Jairus’s daughter is twelve years old (v. 42). The year that family received a child is the year this woman’s life began to fall apart. One household had been counting birthdays while, somewhere in the same district, another woman had been counting the same years and losing everything.

Her situation. Under the law, a woman with a discharge of blood was ritually unclean for as long as it lasted, and anyone or anything she touched became unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). Anything she sat on was unclean; anyone who touched her bed or her chair was unclean until evening. For twelve years she had been excluded from the temple courts and from normal social contact, probably unable to marry or to stay married. She was physically weak, socially isolated and religiously excluded. No embrace, no hand on the shoulder, no worship, no place at anyone’s table. Whatever the bleeding was doing to her body, the loneliness had been doing something worse.

And who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had. Only Mark adds this frank detail, and his word is strong: she suffered under them. Ancient remedies for such conditions included unpleasant and useless treatments; the Talmud preserves a list of them, including carrying the ash of an ostrich egg in a linen rag. Twelve years of that, each new man with a new theory, each course of treatment a fresh humiliation. Luke, a doctor, softens it: no one could heal her (Luke 8:43). And she had spent everything. Whatever her family had, it is gone. She is not merely ill; she is destitute, and destitute in the specific way that leaves a person feeling foolish: she paid for all of it herself, one hopeful appointment at a time.

And was no better but rather grew worse. Hopeless. There is the sentence, and it is the one that will find some readers exactly where they live. Not merely that nothing worked, but that the whole twelve-year campaign of effort, money, hope and humiliation left her further down than she started. If you have a chronic illness, or a chronic anything, a marriage that every attempt has made colder, a child who has moved further away with each intervention, a besetting sin you have fought with every weapon you own and are visibly losing to, this verse is in your Bible on purpose. Mark takes two full verses to say that she had tried everything and was worse for it, and he does not soften it or hurry past it to the good part. And then, having established that there was no help anywhere, he tells you what she heard.

Was God saying her body was sinful? No. Ritual uncleanness in the law was not the same as sin. Childbirth, a skin disease, touching a dead relative while burying him: all made a person unclean, and none was wrong. The laws of cleanness were a living lesson for Israel that life and holiness belong together, and that death and everything that leaks life away are out of place in God’s presence. They pointed forward to the one who would make the unclean clean. Those ceremonial laws were fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind Christians (Hebrews 9:9–14; Westminster 19.3). No woman today is less welcome before God because of her body.

Is it wrong to keep seeking medical help? No. Mark is not mocking doctors, and Luke, who was one, tells the same story. Medicine is a good gift of God, and Paul himself travelled with the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14). The lesson is not that doctors are useless, but that they are limited, and that the last word on any case belongs to Christ, not to them. So keep the appointments, take the treatment, and bring the whole thing to him, the remedies that work and the ones that do not. Trust him above the means, and do not despise the means.

In a sentence. A woman had suffered bleeding for twelve years, spent all she had on doctors, and only grown worse.

On a Tuesday. Is there a long, hidden suffering you have tried everything to fix? Bring it to Jesus, not as a last resort after everything else, but by name and in detail. And look around your church for the person whose trouble has made them lonely: the chronically ill, the one who rarely comes because she is ashamed of something. A hand on the shoulder or a meal at your table may be the first in years.

For worship. Christ does not forget the people the world has stopped counting. The woman who had spent twelve years outside every circle of welcome was not outside his. He is the one in whom the long, dreary arithmetic of loss is finally cancelled: years spent, money gone, hope worn thin, and then the Lord of life passing down her street. He is the great Physician who charges nothing, and whose remedy has never once failed.
verseByVerse.note: A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch; twelve years meant twelve years of exclusion.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, "If I touch even his garments, I will be made well." And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She had heard the reports about Jesus, and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said: if I touch even his garments, I will be made well. And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.

She had heard the reports about Jesus. That is all she has. Not a meeting, not an introduction, not a promise made to her personally. She has heard what people are saying, and she acts on it. Faith, at its beginning, is very often no more than this: something you have heard about Christ, taken seriously enough to move on. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17).

And came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. Every word is loaded, and you have to know the law to feel it. She came from behind, secretly, because she was ashamed. She will not come at him face on; to approach openly would mean explaining, in front of a street full of people, what was wrong with her, and admitting that she had no business being in that crowd at all.

The risk she ran. Because that is the real risk, and it is not embarrassment. She knew that touching anyone would make them unclean. Every person she pushed past on her way through that press was defiled by her, under Leviticus 15, and none of them knew it. If she were recognised, this would not be a scene; it would be an uproar. She came anyway. Think what twelve years of being untouchable does to a person, and then think what it took to walk into a crowd.

The fringe of his cloak. Matthew and Luke say she touched the fringe, the tassel at the corner of the outer cloak that every Jewish man wore under the command of Numbers 15:38–39, to remind him of the commandments of the LORD. It was the furthest, lowest, most trailing edge of him. She is not reaching for his hand.

For she said, If I touch even his garments, I will be made well. Mark lets us hear her talking herself into it. “Made well” is again saved. Her faith was real, perhaps mixed with superstition, as though the power were in the cloth. But it was directed towards Jesus, and Jesus does not correct the theology. He never once, in this Gospel, refuses somebody for coming to him with a poor grasp of how it works. That is a considerable comfort. What saved this woman was not the accuracy of her understanding. It was that she put out her hand.

And immediately the flow of blood dried up. Instantly, after twelve years, stopped mid-street in the time it takes to touch a piece of cloth. No process, no convalescence, and, this is the point of the whole scene, the current ran the wrong way.

The contagion went backwards. Every law of uncleanness in Israel ran one direction: what is unclean contaminates what is clean, and never the reverse. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse is not raised (Haggai 2:11–13). That is how it had worked for fifteen centuries. This woman put her hand on a clean man and, by every rule she had been taught, she should have made him unclean. Instead she was made clean. That is not Jesus breaking the law. It is the law’s whole purpose arriving. Israel had been taught for centuries that sin and death spread and holiness does not, precisely so that when a man walked into their villages whose holiness was catching, they would know what they were looking at.

And she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. She knew it physically. Twelve years of it, and she felt it stop. “Disease” (mastix) means scourge, affliction: the word for a whip. She had been flogged by her own body for twelve years, and the whip was taken out of its hand.

Should Christians use prayer cloths, relics or holy objects? No. The power was not in the cloak, and Jesus says so in a moment: her faith, resting on him, made her well. God did once do unusual miracles through cloths taken from Paul (Acts 19:11–12), but those were signs confirming the apostles’ message in a unique moment, not a pattern for us. Scripture never tells us to seek healing through objects, and the medieval trade in relics shows where that road leads. We have something better than his cloak: direct access to Christ himself, at the Father’s right hand, through prayer in his name (Hebrews 4:16).

In a sentence. Believing that touching even his clothes would heal her, she touched Jesus’ garment from behind, and was instantly healed.

On a Tuesday. Even weak, mixed faith that reaches out to Jesus is met with his power. You do not have to have your theology tidy or your feelings settled before you pray. If all you have is what you have heard about him and a trembling hand, reach out with that today, over the thing you have been afraid to bring.

For worship. Here is holiness that is catching. In Christ the old direction of the world is reversed: the unclean touches the clean and is made clean, the dying touches the living and is made alive. That is the gospel in a village street. He took our defilement on himself at the cross so that his purity could flow to us, and the hem of his garment was only the beginning of what he would give.

parallels.desc: touching the fringe of his garment

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, "Who touched my garments?" And his disciples said to him, "You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, 'Who touched me?'" And he looked around to see who had done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned around in the crowd and said: who touched my garments? His disciples said: you see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, who touched me? And he looked around to see who had done it.

And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him. Healing came from Jesus’ own power, not from his clothes. He knew it had happened. This is a strange verse and it is worth being careful with, because it can be read as though healing were an electrical charge that leaked out of him without his knowledge. Two things rule that out. The first is that he asks the question at all: he stops, turns, and looks for the person. A power that simply drained away would not go looking for anybody. The second is what he says to her in a moment: your faith has made you well, not my cloak has. The healing was not mechanical, and it was not a transaction she managed to complete without him noticing. It was personal from both ends.

The cost of giving. What Mark is describing is the cost of it. Something went out of him. He is God in the flesh, and the giving is not free even to him, which is why, at the end of this Gospel, the giving will take everything he has.

Immediately turned about in the crowd and said, Who touched my garments? Jesus stopped, though a dying girl was waiting. He would not let the woman slip away unseen. And now the scene stops dead: a crowd in a village street, a man with a dying child beside him, and Jesus turning round to ask an apparently unanswerable question.

Did Jesus not know who had touched him? His question was not for his own information but to draw her out, as God asked Adam, Where are you? (Genesis 3:9). God knew where Adam was; he wanted Adam to come out. Even so, Mark does not hide that in his earthly life the Son accepted real human limits; Jesus says of himself that the day of his return is known only to the Father (13:32). He is fully God and truly man, and he wanted her face to face.

You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, Who touched me? You can hear the exasperation, and Mark has never minded making the Twelve look foolish. Peter thinks the question is absurd (Luke 8:45): everyone was touching him. It is a fair objection. But they have missed the distinction the whole Gospel turns on. The crowd was pressing against him; one woman took hold of him. Many touched him by accident; one touched him in faith. Jesus knows the difference. Contact is not faith. There were hundreds of hands on Jesus that afternoon and exactly one of them got anything.

In the crowd, but never touching him. That is worth putting to yourself in the plainest terms, because it is possible to spend a lifetime in the press. You can be in the crowd around Christ, in the building, in the congregation, in the family, brushing against him week after week, and never once have reached out for him on your own account. The people jostling him went home exactly as they came. The woman went home well.

And he looked around to see who had done it. Jesus wanted to meet her face to face. He is not going to let this be anonymous, and that is the surprising kindness of the passage, though it will not have felt like kindness to her. She had what she came for. The bleeding had stopped; she could have slipped out of that crowd and gone home cured, and nobody would ever have known. From her point of view, being found out was the worst thing that could happen. Jesus refuses to leave it there, and he is willing to hold up a dying child’s rescue in order to refuse it. He has something for this woman that she did not think to ask for, and it is worth the delay.

How do I reach out to him, rather than just being in the crowd? By coming to Christ yourself, personally, with your own need. Stop thinking of faith as something your family or church has and you share by being near it. Speak to him directly: tell him you are a sinner, that you have nothing to bring, that you trust him alone to forgive and make you clean, and ask him to receive you. Then keep reaching: in his word, read as his voice to you; in prayer, as to a person who is listening; at the Lord’s Table, receiving him by faith. The crowd brushes against Jesus. Faith takes hold of him and will not let go.

In a sentence. Jesus felt power go out from him and stopped to find who had touched him in faith.

On a Tuesday. In a crowd of people, Jesus knows the one who reaches out to him in faith. He knows you. Next Sunday, in the middle of the service, ask yourself whether you are pressing against him or taking hold of him. And this week, come to him once about something specific, not in a general way but as a person who needs him to act.

For worship. Christ is never lost in the crowd and never too busy for the one. Out of hundreds of hands he felt one hand of faith, and he stopped the whole procession to find its owner. That is how the Good Shepherd counts his flock: not as a mass but by name (John 10:3). And the power that went out from him that day was a foretaste of the day he would pour himself out entirely, so that all who reach for him might be made whole.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. And he said to her, "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling, fell down before him and told him the whole truth. He said to her: daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.

But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling. She could have stayed silent. The crowd was enormous, the question was unanswerable, the disciples had all but told him to drop it. She had only to stand still. She comes forward instead, and Mark tells us exactly what it cost: fear and trembling. She is physically shaking. She was afraid she would be rebuked for touching him in her uncleanness, exposed as the woman who had made half the street unclean, and condemned in front of everybody for taking what she had no right to take.

And fell down before him and told him the whole truth. Her whole story, publicly: twelve years of shame told in front of the crowd. Not a summary. The doctors, the money, the marriage if there was one, the reason she came from behind, what she had been hoping. The entire humiliating history, said out loud, in a public street, to a man she had just met. That is what confession is, and it is why we avoid it. Not the general admission that we are sinners, but the whole truth, in particular words, to the one person entitled to hear it. And nothing was owed. She was already healed. Jesus does not draw her out because the cure was incomplete or because he needed to check her credentials. He draws her out because he will not have a relationship with her that consists of her taking something from behind and running away.

And he said to her, Daughter. Stop there, because that one word is the reason he stopped the procession. It is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus calls a woman daughter. She has been nobody’s anything for twelve years: untouchable, unwelcome in worship, a name people lowered their voices about. And the first word out of his mouth gives her a place in a family. The woman no one wanted to touch is welcomed into God’s family. Remember what Mark is doing with this chapter. Jairus is standing a few feet away with his own daughter dying at home. Jairus has a daughter dying; Jesus has a daughter healed. And Jesus turns to a destitute, unclean woman nobody in that street would have looked at twice, and calls her the same thing.

Your faith has made you well. “Made you well” is saved you (sesōken): both healed and saved. He locates the power correctly, and it is worth noting for anyone with a superstitious streak: not her touch or his cloak, not the technique, not the crowd, not her boldness, but her faith in him. And her faith was small, frightened, theologically muddled, and reaching from behind. That is all it has ever taken. Faith saves not because it is impressive but because of who it takes hold of. The public declaration also restored her socially: everyone heard that she was healed and clean.

Go in peace. Shalom: wholeness, well-being, peace with God. It means far more than the absence of trouble; it is everything in its place, the whole person put right. She came for a body and is being sent away with a life.

And be healed of your disease. Permanently. The final clause is a word of permanence, and it settles her for ever. She had felt the bleeding stop and might well have spent the rest of her life waiting for it to start again, as anyone would after twelve years. He tells her, out loud, that it is over. And then, into the silence at the end of that sentence, the messengers arrive from Jairus’s house.

Does this mean that enough faith guarantees healing? No. Faith is the hand that reaches; Christ is the one who heals, and he heals as he wills. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be taken away and was told, My grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Timothy had frequent ailments and was told to take a little wine (1 Timothy 5:23), not to believe harder. A believer who is not healed has not necessarily failed to believe. Faith trusts Christ whether he heals now or raises us whole at the last.

Do I need to confess my sins publicly like this? Not usually. Confession is first to God, who already knows and wants to hear it from us (1 John 1:9). Confess to the person you have wronged, and seek their forgiveness (Matthew 5:23–24). James tells us to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another (James 5:16), which normally means a trusted brother or sister, a pastor or an elder, especially with a sin you cannot break alone. Public confession before the church is for public sins that have harmed the church. The point of this scene is not the size of the audience but the honesty: the whole truth told to Christ, who receives it with the word daughter.

In a sentence. The woman confessed everything in fear, and Jesus called her daughter, declared that her faith had saved her, and sent her away in peace.

On a Tuesday. Is there a whole truth you have never told him: not the general confession, but the particular thing in particular words? Tell it to him today, in fear and trembling if need be, and listen for the word he speaks to those who come. And if you have been carrying a secret alone for years, consider whether there is one wise believer you could tell, so that someone can pray with you.

For worship. The Son of God turned in a crowded street to give a stranger a family name. He is the one who takes the shamed and calls them sons and daughters, who receives the whole truth about us and does not flinch, who sends us away not merely cured but at peace with God. Behold what manner of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God (1 John 3:1), and it was spoken first, in this Gospel, to a woman nobody would touch.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler's house some who said, "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, "Do not fear, only believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, people came from the ruler’s house and said: your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue: do not fear, only believe.

While he was still speaking. Mark’s timing is exact and merciless. The word about the woman’s peace is barely out of his mouth when the men from the house arrive. The delay: while Jesus stopped for the woman, Jairus’s daughter died. Jairus, who has been standing through the whole interruption, hears what he has been dreading. He must have been in agony.

Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? Two sentences, and they are the world’s entire philosophy about death, delivered kindly by people who mean no harm. Death seemed final. Jesus could heal, but surely not raise the dead. Your daughter is dead: a fact. They are not wrong; she has died, and Mark will not let anyone soften this later. Why trouble the Teacher any further? There is the conclusion drawn from the fact, and it is the sentence to look at hard. Note what they call him: Teacher. That is their estimate of him and it is the reason for their advice. A teacher is a fine thing to bring to a sickbed and no use at all at a graveside. Their theology is not hostile; it is simply too small, and it produces the most reasonable pastoral advice in the world: stop praying about this one. It is finished. Do not bother him.

The kindly advice of unbelief. That advice still gets given, in exactly that tone, by people who are trying to be kind. The marriage is over; stop praying for it. He is seventy-eight and hardened; leave it. That door is closed. It is always said gently, and it is always based on a true fact and an inadequate estimate of Christ.

Matthew says the girl had already died. Matthew has Jairus say at the start that his daughter has just died (Matthew 9:18). Matthew tells the story briefly and gives its outcome from the beginning; Mark and Luke tell it in sequence, with the messengers arriving on the way. Both are true accounts of the same event, told at different lengths, as a man telling a story briefly might say his father died while the doctor was on the way, without walking through each telephone call.

The cost of the delay. Notice also what the delay has done. If Jesus had not stopped for the woman, he would have been at that house in time. From where Jairus is standing, the interruption killed his daughter: a stranger’s twelve-year complaint, which could have waited an hour, cost him everything. Hold that, because it is one of the hardest things about the way God works. His delays are real, they cost real people real things, and they are not accidents.

But overhearing what they said. Or ignoring what they said; the Greek can carry both: he heard it and refused to let it stand. He does not wait for the message to be relayed to Jairus, and he does not let it settle. He speaks over the top of it.

Do not fear, only believe. The heart of the story. Five words, and they are commands rather than comfort. He is not saying, do not worry, it will be fine. He is telling a man whose child has just died what to do with the next ten minutes. “Do not fear” and “only believe” are present tense: stop being afraid, keep on believing. Keep doing what you were doing when you came down that beach and fell in the sand. Nothing has changed about who I am. Jairus had believed Jesus could heal; now he must believe Jesus can raise the dead. And only is the tender word. He is not asking Jairus to feel confident, or to produce an emotion he does not have, or to understand why the woman came first. Just this one thing, and nothing else is required of you.

What the delay was for. And now see what the delay was actually for. The woman’s faith was an example for him. Jairus has just watched, at close range, a woman with a hopeless twelve-year case healed by touching a piece of cloth, and heard her called daughter, and heard her told to go in peace. He did not know it at the time, but he was being given the last lesson he would need, in the ten minutes before he needed it. God’s delays are not always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are the school.

What does only believe mean when Jesus did not raise the one I lost? It means trusting him with what he has not yet done. Jesus raised only a handful of people in his earthly ministry, and each of them died again. Those signs were not a promise that every Christian’s child will be restored this side of the grave, but a pledge of what he will do for all his people at the last day (John 11:25–26). If you have buried someone who trusted Christ, only believe means: he is not dead to Jesus, and Jesus will wake him. If you are unsure of the person’s faith, it means trusting the Judge of all the earth to do right (Genesis 18:25), and resting on his character. Fear says it is over. Faith says he has the last word.

In a sentence. News came that Jairus’s daughter had died, but Jesus told him, Do not fear, only believe.

On a Tuesday. When the worst news comes, hear Jesus’ words: do not fear, only believe. Think of the prayer you have quietly stopped praying because someone told you, kindly, that the case was closed. Take it up again. And when you are the one asked for advice about a hopeless situation, be careful not to say, do not trouble the Teacher. Say what Jesus said.

For worship. Christ is not merely the Teacher. When every human voice says it is too late, his voice speaks over the top of theirs. His delays are not neglect; they are the patience of one who never arrives too late, because death itself is not too late for him. The God who let Lazarus lie four days, and his own Son lie three, is the God whose timing is always perfect, and whose word to frightened people is still: only believe.

verseByVerse.quote: And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus allowed no one to follow him except Peter, James and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.

And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John. The crowd is dismissed. Whatever is about to happen in that house is not going to be a public demonstration, and the great press of people that has followed him from the shore is left in the street. This is the first time in Mark that these three are taken apart from the others, and it will not be the last. They are the inner circle, who would also see his glory at the transfiguration (9:2) and his agony in Gethsemane (14:33): witnesses of his deepest moments. So this is the beginning of an education, and notice the syllabus. The men who will be taken to watch him in glory, and taken to watch him in agony, are first taken to watch him in a dead child’s bedroom. And one of them tells the story to Mark years later, with the furniture still in it.

They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. The word is an uproar: that is what the house sounded like from the street. Understand what was going on inside, because it is not what a modern reader pictures. Mourning was loud, immediate and public. Even poor families hired flute players and at least one professional wailing woman; a man of Jairus’s standing would have had a houseful. Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23). They came fast, because burial was usually the same day in that climate, and their job was to make grief audible. The death had already been announced to the community.

Nobody sends for the mourners while there is a pulse. There is nothing false about the sorrow of the family, and nothing contemptible about the mourners either; this was simply how a village buried its children. But it does tell you one thing beyond dispute, and it settles a question that will come up in two verses. The professionals had already arrived. She was dead.

Jesus saw the commotion. Before he says anything, notice what Mark says he did first. He did not push through it or shout over it. He stood in the doorway of a house full of people making the loudest sound human beings make, and looked at it. He will stand at another graveside later and weep (John 11:35), knowing perfectly well that he is about to empty the tomb. The knowledge that he can undo it has never once made him indifferent to it. He is not embarrassed by grief and he does not hurry anyone through it, which is worth knowing if you are in a house like this one, or have been.

Is loud grief a lack of faith? No. Jesus wept, and so did Paul’s friends at Ephesus (Acts 20:37–38); devout men made great lamentation over Stephen (Acts 8:2). Paul tells believers not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), which is not a command to stop grieving but to grieve with hope. Tears at a graveside are not unbelief; they are love, and death is an enemy worth weeping over (1 Corinthians 15:26). What Jesus will rebuke in the next verse is not the tears but the certainty that death has the final word.

In a sentence. Taking only Peter, James and John, Jesus came to Jairus’s house, where the mourning had begun.

On a Tuesday. Jesus does not avoid places of grief. He walks right into them. So should his people. If someone you know is newly bereaved, do not wait until you know the right thing to say; go, sit, bring food, and let your presence say that they are not alone. And if you are the one grieving, do not hide your tears from him. He stands in the doorway and sees.

For worship. The Lord of life does not stand far off from death. He walks into the house where the wailing is loudest and looks at our grief with eyes that will soon weep at a tomb. He knows what he is about to do, and still he does not despise the sorrow. That is our High Priest, who sympathises with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15), and who entered the house of death itself so that he could open it from the inside.
verseByVerse.note: Peter, James and John were the inner three, with Jesus again at the transfiguration and in Gethsemane. Hired mourners were customary at a death.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered, he said to them, "Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child's father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he went in, he said to them: why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those with him, and went in where the child was.

Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping. This sentence has been seized on for two hundred years, and it deserves a straight answer, because a reader who has heard the objection needs to be able to put it down. The claim is that she was never really dead, a coma, a faint, a lucky misdiagnosis, so this is no resurrection at all. The reading collapses the moment you look at it. She was truly dead; the mourners knew it. Everyone present was certain: the messengers reported it as fact, and the house was already full of professional mourners in full cry. Those people made their living recognising death. They laughed at Jesus precisely because they knew a corpse when they saw one, and they had seen this one. Luke, who was a physician, states plainly what happened when Jesus spoke: her spirit returned (Luke 8:55).

So what does sleeping mean? It is not a second opinion on her pulse. It is his settled way of speaking about the death of people he intends to raise. For Jesus, death is like sleep, because he is about to wake her. Of Lazarus, four days in the tomb, he said, Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, and when the disciples took it literally he told them plainly, Lazarus has died (John 11:11–14). The New Testament uses sleep for the death of believers because they will be raised: those who have fallen asleep, and Christ the firstfruits of them (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:20). So the word is not a smaller claim than resurrection. It is a far larger one. To the mourners in that house, death was the end of the sentence. To the one standing in the doorway, it was as temporary as a night’s sleep, and waking this child would cost him no more effort than a parent leaning over a bed in the morning. He does not deny that she died. He announces that death, in his presence, has just become something you get up from.

Does sleep mean the dead are unconscious until the resurrection? No. The word describes how death looks from this side and how temporary it is, not what the soul experiences. It is the body that lies down and will be raised. Scripture is clear that believers who die go at once to be with Christ, conscious and blessed. Jesus told the dying thief, Today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The Westminster Confession puts it simply: the souls of the righteous, made perfect in holiness, are received at once into heaven (Westminster 32.1). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory. The Christian dead are awake in the presence of Christ, waiting for the morning of their bodies.

And they laughed at him. They ridiculed him. Their grief turned to mockery, and the swing is worth noticing: these people were wailing a moment ago and they are jeering now. Unbelief laughs at Jesus’ promises. It also tells you what the world does with the resurrection. It is not usually argued against. It is laughed at, and the laughter feels like sophistication (Acts 17:32). That room contained the only person present who knew what he was talking about, and he was the one being mocked.

But he put them all outside. Firmly: the mourners, the flute players, the neighbours, the crowd of opinion, all of them out of the door. “Put outside” (ekbalōn) is the word Mark uses for casting out demons. Jesus removes unbelief from the room.

And took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. Five people go in: Peter, James, John, and a father and a mother. Notice that the parents are not left in the corridor. Whatever is about to happen, they are going to see it, and they are going to be standing there when it happens. This is not a private miracle performed on their daughter and reported to them afterwards. He takes them in with him, into the room they had presumably been unable to leave. And the mother appears here for the first and only time in the story, unnamed, having been in that house all afternoon.

In a sentence. Jesus said the child was only sleeping, and when the mourners laughed, he put them out and went in with the parents and his three disciples.

On a Tuesday. For those in Christ, death is sleep, because he will wake them. Let that shape how you grieve (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and how you speak at a Christian funeral: honestly about the loss, confidently about the morning. And when your hope in the resurrection is laughed at, do not be embarrassed. You are standing where Jesus stood in that room.

For worship. To the Lord of life, the grave is a bed. What we call the end, he calls a night’s rest; what we mourn as final, he treats as something a child gets up from. He is the resurrection and the life, and those who believe in him, though they die, yet shall they live (John 11:25). The laughter of unbelief has been echoing for two thousand years, and it has never once kept him from walking into the room.

verseByVerse.quote: Taking her by the hand he said to her, "Talitha cumi," which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise." And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking her by the hand, Jesus said to her: talitha cumi, which means, little girl, I say to you, arise. Immediately the girl got up and began walking, for she was twelve years old, and they were overcome with amazement.

Taking her by the hand. Before a word is spoken, he takes hold of a dead child. Do not read past that. Under the law, touching a dead body made a person unclean for seven days and required a specific rite of purification (Numbers 19:11–13). Everyone in that room knew it. To take a dead girl’s hand was to walk out of that house defiled.

The third touch. It is the third time in this one chapter that Jesus has gone straight to the place where uncleanness lives. He landed in a graveyard and dealt with a man who lived among the tombs. He let an untouchable woman take hold of his clothes. And now he takes a corpse by the hand. Every one of those contacts should have run one way, and every one ran the other. Again, as with the woman, uncleanness does not pass to Jesus; his life passes to the dead. The tombs did not defile him; the man came out of them. The bleeding did not contaminate him; it dried up. And death does not get its seven days out of him. He takes hold of it, and it lets go. There is also, quite simply, the tenderness of it. He could have spoken from the doorway; he had stilled a hurricane from the stern of a boat. He goes and takes her hand, because that is what you do for a twelve-year-old, and because her mother and father are watching.

He said to her, Talitha cumi. Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke. Here Mark does something he does only a handful of times: he keeps the actual Aramaic. He is writing in Greek for readers in Rome and he stops to give them the sound of it, and then translates. He keeps his very words, perhaps because Peter never forgot them: a man remembering the exact syllables he heard in a small room thirty years earlier. It is not a magic formula, but the words a parent might use to wake a child in the morning. Talitha is an affectionate word for a little girl, perhaps from a word for a lamb: little lamb, get up.

Which means, Little girl, I say to you, arise. “I say to you”: by his own authority. No prayer, no invocation, no struggle. He does not ask the Father to raise her; he tells her to get up, and the authority in I say to you is the same authority that told a hurricane to be quiet. “Arise” (egeire) is the word used for resurrection (16:6), the word the angel will use of Jesus himself: he has risen.

And immediately the girl got up and began walking. Not weak and slowly recovering, but walking at once. She did not sit up weakly and need to be tended. She got up and started walking about the room, in front of her mother.

For she was twelve years old. Mark drops it in as a bracket, almost apologetically, to explain why a raised child could walk rather than needing to be carried. It is exactly the kind of detail nobody invents, and it quietly ties the two halves of the chapter together. The same number as the woman’s years of suffering: twelve years of a girl’s life, twelve years of a woman’s suffering, and both ended on the same afternoon by the same hands.

And they were immediately overcome with amazement. Literally, amazed with a great amazement. There is no adequate reaction to this and they did not manage one.

Was this the same as the resurrection Jesus will give us? Not quite. The girl was brought back to ordinary mortal life, and years later she died again. Jesus’ own resurrection was different: he was raised never to die again, in a body glorified and immortal (Romans 6:9), and he is the firstfruits of that harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). What happened in this room was a sign and a promise. The same voice, with the same authority, will one day speak to all who sleep in him, and they will rise not to die again but to live for ever, with bodies like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

The cost of the word. Two words in a child’s ear: that is what it cost him here. It will cost more than that at the end. When he stands outside another tomb and calls another name, it will be on his way to a grave of his own, and the hand that took this girl’s hand will be pierced by a nail, so that everyone who sleeps in him can be told, one morning, to get up.

In a sentence. Jesus took the dead girl’s hand, told her in Aramaic to get up, and she rose and walked.

On a Tuesday. Read 1 Corinthians 15 this week, slowly, as the long answer to this short scene. And if you are afraid of dying, or of the death of someone you love, picture this room: the hand that takes hold, the gentle word, the girl walking. That is what death is for those who belong to Christ. Tell a grieving friend about it, gently, when the time is right.

For worship. Praise to the Lord who speaks to the dead, and they rise. He takes hold of death with his bare hand and death lets go. He needs no formula and calls on no higher power; the Prince of life simply says, get up. One day he will say it over every grave where his people lie, and the whole sleeping church will rise to meet him (John 5:28–29). The hand that held a little girl’s hand was pierced for us, and it will never let go of the ones it has taken hold of.
verseByVerse.note: “Talitha cumi” is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke; Mark keeps his very words.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus strictly ordered them that no one should know about this, and told them to give her something to eat.

And he strictly charged them that no one should know this. Two instructions close the chapter, and they could hardly be less alike. The command is emphatic. And on the face of it, it is impossible. There is a street full of mourners outside who watched him go in, and a girl inside who is going to be seen in the village tomorrow. You cannot hide a resurrection for long.

Why the secret? The messianic secret again (1:44). Jesus did not want to be known chiefly as a wonder-worker, or to stir up political hopes, before his identity could be understood through the cross. In Galilee at that moment, a man who raises the dead becomes a national event within a week, and the word Messiah in that year meant a king who would drive out Rome. Jesus will not be crowned before he is crucified. He keeps the lid on as long as he can, because the truth about him has to be defined by a cross or it will be misunderstood entirely.

Not a performance. But there is something else in it here. He has just put the mourners out of the house and shut the door. He does not perform this. There is no crowd at the bedside, no audience, no demonstration. A father and a mother get their daughter back in a quiet room with four other people in it. He is not using this family. He is helping them.

And told them to give her something to eat. And there is the last sentence of the chapter, and it is one of the loveliest in the Gospel. A beautifully ordinary detail. It is proof that she was truly alive, not a ghost (compare Luke 24:41–43). And it is Jesus’ practical care: the girl needed food. The room is full of people beside themselves with amazement. A twelve-year-old is walking about who was dead five minutes ago. Her parents are past speech. And the Lord of life, having done the single most staggering thing anybody in that house will ever witness, says, in effect: she will be hungry. Nobody else in that room was capable of thinking about it. He was. The one who raises the dead also thinks about lunch.

The enormous and the domestic. Consider what that tells you about him. The same care that raises the dead notices that a child has not eaten. There is no gap in him between the enormous and the domestic. The God who spoke the sea into place is the one who thought about the girl’s meal, and it is the same tenderness in both directions. He did it again after his own resurrection: the risen Christ, having conquered death, lit a charcoal fire on a beach and cooked breakfast for seven tired fishermen (John 21:9).

Why was this kept quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because the time was different. Before the cross, the news of a wonder-worker would have been misunderstood as a political Messiah, and the crowds would have tried to make him king by force (John 6:15). After his death and resurrection, the full truth could be told: who he is and why he came. So the commission changes. Jesus himself sends his disciples to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). We are not under the secret; we are under the command to tell, and to tell it as Mark does, with the cross at the centre.

In a sentence. Jesus ordered silence and told them to give the girl something to eat.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares about practical needs, not only spectacular ones. So when you bring him something enormous, the diagnosis, the child, the grief that has flattened you, you are not distracting him from more important business. And when what you have is small and slightly embarrassing to mention, understand that he is the one who thought about the girl’s meal when nobody else did. Show care in ordinary ways today: the meal for the exhausted family, the lift, the practical thing nobody else has thought of.

For worship. The chapter began with a man nobody could chain and ends with a girl being handed a plate. Between them a legion was evicted, a woman was called daughter, and death was told to let go of a child, and the same hands did all of it. This is our Lord: mighty enough to command the abyss, humble enough to send for bread. There is nothing too great for his power and nothing too small for his love, and the one who conquered death for one little girl has conquered it for ever, for all who are his.

5.theology:
Legion, and two occupations. A legion was a Roman army unit of around six thousand men — the empire's instrument of occupation, the thing that arrives in your district and stays, that cannot be resisted and will not leave. That is the word the spirits choose for themselves, and it describes exactly what they had done to the man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. It also explains why nothing had worked. The town had been trying to chain a man; the man was a garrison. Mark sets two occupations side by side — the one everybody in that country could see, and the one nobody could touch — and Jesus evicts the second with a sentence, then deals with the first in his own way and at his own cost when Rome nails him up outside Jerusalem and finds it cannot hold him either.

Why the pigs? The demons drove the herd, not Jesus; he permitted their request, and in permitting it let their intention show itself in public. For five verses we have been told what they were doing to a man — the tombs, the chains, the stones. Now the district watches what that programme looks like unhindered: everything it enters goes over the edge. And the arithmetic of heaven is not the arithmetic of the market. Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (Matt. 12:12) — and a man than a pig.

Not dead but sleeping. This is not a claim that the girl had merely fainted. The professional mourners were already in the house, and they laughed because they knew a corpse when they saw one; Luke, a physician, records that her spirit returned (Luke 8:55). Sleeping is the Lord's settled way of speaking about the death of those he intends to raise — of Lazarus, four days in the tomb, he said the same and then said plainly Lazarus has died (John 11:11–14). It is not a smaller claim than resurrection but a far larger one: death, in his presence, has become something you get up from.
5.examples:
Then: a man begging to get into the boat, and told no.

It is the fourth begging in the chapter and the best request in it — that he might be with him, the very phrase used of the appointing of the Twelve (3:14). He is asking to be a disciple. Jesus permitted the demons and did not permit him.

Now: anyone who has prayed the best prayer they know how to pray and been refused. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9); Jesus asked in a garden that the cup pass, and it did not (14:36). A no from Christ is not evidence that you asked badly. Sometimes it is a redeployment — this man was given a district instead of a boat, and sent to the hardest mission field there is, which is home.

And notice his qualifications: none. No Scriptures, no training, no time with Jesus. One thing had happened to him, and that was the whole of his commission — tell them how much the Lord has done for you. Then watch what he did with it. Jesus said tell them what the Lord has done; he went out and proclaimed what Jesus had done. He made the substitution himself, ten minutes into the Christian life, in a pagan district with no Bible. His theology was ahead of the disciples' and they had been in the boat for months.

6.title: Refused at Home, Broken Bread, and a Prophet’s Head
6.text: <sup>1</sup>He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. <sup>2</sup>And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands? <sup>3</sup>Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household.” <sup>5</sup>And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. <sup>6</sup>And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching. <sup>7</sup>And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. <sup>8</sup>He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— <sup>9</sup>but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. <sup>10</sup>And he said to them, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. <sup>11</sup>And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>12</sup>So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. <sup>13</sup>And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. <sup>14</sup>King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>15</sup>But others said, “He is Elijah.” And others said, “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.” <sup>16</sup>But when Herod heard of it, he said, “John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.” <sup>17</sup>For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. <sup>18</sup>For John had been saying to Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.” <sup>19</sup>And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, <sup>20</sup>for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. <sup>21</sup>But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. <sup>22</sup>For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, “Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you.” <sup>23</sup>And he vowed to her, “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.” <sup>24</sup>And she went out and said to her mother, “For what should I ask?” And she said, “The head of John the Baptist.” <sup>25</sup>And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, “I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter.” <sup>26</sup>And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. <sup>27</sup>And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison <sup>28</sup>and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. <sup>29</sup>When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. <sup>30</sup>The apostles returned to Jesus and told him all that they had done and taught. <sup>31</sup>And he said to them, “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” For many were coming and going, and they had no leisure even to eat. <sup>32</sup>And they went away in the boat to a desolate place by themselves. <sup>33</sup>Now many saw them going and recognized them, and they ran there on foot from all the towns and got there ahead of them. <sup>34</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And he began to teach them many things. <sup>35</sup>And when it grew late, his disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the hour is now late. <sup>36</sup>Send them away to go into the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” <sup>37</sup>But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” And they said to him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give it to them to eat?” <sup>38</sup>And he said to them, “How many loaves do you have? Go and see.” And when they had found out, they said, “Five, and two fish.” <sup>39</sup>Then he commanded them all to sit down in groups on the green grass. <sup>40</sup>So they sat down in groups, by hundreds and by fifties. <sup>41</sup>And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the people. And he divided the two fish among them all. <sup>42</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. <sup>43</sup>And they took up twelve baskets full of broken pieces and of the fish. <sup>44</sup>And those who ate the loaves were five thousand men. <sup>45</sup>Immediately he made his disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, to Bethsaida, while he dismissed the crowd. <sup>46</sup>And after he had taken leave of them, he went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>47</sup>And when evening came, the boat was out on the sea, and he was alone on the land. <sup>48</sup>And he saw that they were making headway painfully, for the wind was against them. And about the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them, <sup>49</sup>but when they saw him walking on the sea they thought it was a ghost, and cried out, <sup>50</sup>for they all saw him and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>51</sup>And he got into the boat with them, and the wind ceased. And they were utterly astounded, <sup>52</sup>for they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. <sup>53</sup>When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret and moored to the shore. <sup>54</sup>And when they got out of the boat, the people immediately recognized him <sup>55</sup>and ran about the whole region and began to bring the sick people on their beds to wherever they heard he was. <sup>56</sup>And wherever he came, in villages, cities, or countryside, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and implored him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the widest swing in the Gospel: a village that will not have him, a mission that works, a prophet murdered at a birthday party, a hillside fed until it could eat no more, and a man walking on water in the last watch of the night.

It opens at Nazareth, where the questions asked about Jesus are exactly the right ones — where did this man get these things? what is the wisdom given to him? — and the conclusion drawn is the worst in the book. They knew his trade, his mother, his brothers by name, and the knowing is precisely what stopped them.

Then Mark does something structurally deliberate. He sends the Twelve out (vv. 7–13), interrupts them with thirteen verses on the death of John the Baptist — by far the longest passage in this Gospel about anyone other than Jesus — and only then lets them come back (v. 30). Anyone reading to find out what following costs has just been told, and told at length: the greatest man born of women dies alone in a cellar because a girl danced well and a weak king could not bear to look foolish in front of his officers.
