The second half answers the first. The crowd that ruins the disciples' day off is met with compassion rather than irritation, because he sees sheep without a shepherd; five loaves in his hands feed a district with twelve baskets over; and the men who could only do arithmetic are the ones who carry it out to the rows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Rejection, Mission, and the Death of John
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Home (vv. 1–6). He goes back to Nazareth and preaches in the synagogue he grew up in, and the village is offended. They know his trade, his mother, his brothers by name and his sisters by sight, and the knowledge is exactly what stops them. Mark records that he could do no mighty work there, and that he marvelled at their unbelief.

The sending (vv. 7–13). Twelve men are sent out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits and instructions to carry almost nothing. They preach repentance, cast out demons, and anoint the sick with oil — and they are sent before they understand very much at all.

The dungeon (vv. 14–29). Then Mark stops the mission dead and tells, at length and out of sequence, how John the Baptist died: a birthday party, a dance, a rash oath, a girl sent to ask her mother, and a head brought in on a serving dish. Herod is not a monster. He is a weak man who liked listening to a preacher and would not be changed by him.

Note where Mark has put that story. He interrupts the sending of the Twelve with a martyrdom, and only then lets them come back. Anyone reading this Gospel to find out what following costs has just been told.
verseByVerse.theology:
Could he not, or would he not? Verse 5 is one of the most startling sentences in Mark — he could do no mighty work there — and it should not be softened into he chose not to. Mark wrote what he wrote.

But read the exception clause, because it settles the meaning: except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power; he healed people in Nazareth that afternoon. The impossibility is moral, not mechanical. In a village that had decided in advance what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle — and Jesus does not do spectacle for people who have already ruled out the conclusion. He had refused exactly that to the Pharisees (8:11–12) and would refuse it to Herod himself (Luke 23:8–9).

Faith is not a mechanism that generates miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he deals with persons and not with material. Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it.

And he marvelled. There are only two things in the Gospels said to have astonished Jesus. He marvelled at the faith of a Roman officer who had no Bible and no upbringing in it (Luke 7:9), and he marvelled at the unbelief of the village that had raised him. The people with every advantage astonished him in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Herod, who feared John, knew he was a righteous man, protected him from a wife who wanted him dead, was greatly perplexed by his preaching — and heard him gladly. Gladly. He enjoyed it. He came back for more of it.

Now: the most searching portrait in the chapter, because Herod is not a scoffer and never was. He is the rocky ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace — the word received with real interest, real feeling, even real pleasure, and no root at all. Being moved by a sermon is not being changed by one, and the platter is the proof.

Everything was there in that man except the one thing that matters. He would not repent — and a man who will not repent will eventually have to silence the voice that keeps asking him to. It took a party, a dance and an audience to get it done, but it was decided long before the executioner was sent.

So the honest test is not whether you enjoy good preaching. Herod did. It is whether there is anything the preaching has actually cost you this year.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away from there and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished, saying, "Where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left there and went to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. On the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue, and many who heard him were astonished: where did this man get these things? What is this wisdom given to him? How are such mighty works done by his hands?

Meaning first. Mark 6 sets side by side two ways of meeting Jesus. It opens in his hometown, where the people who know him best are offended by him, and he can do few mighty works there. Then he sends out the Twelve with nothing but his authority, while Herod, haunted by guilt, remembers how he beheaded John the Baptist at a drunken banquet: the false shepherd-king who feeds the powerful and kills the prophet. Against that dark feast Jesus spreads a meal in the wilderness, where he has compassion on the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, teaches them, and feeds five thousand men with five loaves and two fish. That night he walks on the sea to his struggling disciples, passing by as God passes by and saying, Take heart; it is I. The chapter ends with whole districts bringing their sick to touch the fringe of his garment. The town that thought it knew him stayed as it was; those who knew they needed him were made well.

He went away from there and came to his hometown. Mark does not name it and does not need to: Nazareth, the small village in the Galilean hills where he grew up (1:9), a place of a few hundred people where he had lived for something like thirty years. Consider what going back meant. Everyone in that synagogue had known him since he was small. They had bought things from his workshop. Some of them had perhaps stood with him at his father’s funeral; Joseph has vanished from the record by now. He knew the seats they were sitting in.

And his disciples followed him. Mark mentions them because this is not a private visit. He has come home as a rabbi with a following, which is exactly the sort of thing a village finds hardest to swallow. And the disciples would see how his own town received him: a lesson before he sent them out (v. 7).

And on the Sabbath he began to teach in the synagogue. As a visiting teacher, invited to read and explain Scripture. Luke records a visit, probably an earlier one, when he read from Isaiah 61 and said, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (Luke 4:16–30). Mark gives only the reaction.

And many who heard him were astonished. Struck, overwhelmed. It is the same verb used of the crowd in Capernaum in chapter 1 (1:22), and there it opened towards faith. Here it goes the other way, and Mark lets you watch it turn. Astonishment is not faith.

Where did this man get these things? Listen to their questions, because every one of them is exactly right. This is a fair question, and the only fair question, with an answer they would not accept: from God. He has had no rabbinic training. Nobody in Nazareth taught him this.

What is the wisdom given to him? They can hear that it is wisdom. They are not pretending it was a poor sermon. And note the word given: they recognised that his wisdom came from somewhere beyond himself. They have half the answer in their own question and do not follow it.

How are such mighty works done by his hands? They had heard of his miracles, and they do not dispute them. News from Capernaum has reached them, and their objection is not that the reports are false.

Near is not the same as in. So here is a village asking precisely the right questions about Jesus of Nazareth (where does this come from, what is this wisdom, how are these things done) and arriving at the worst answer anyone in this Gospel arrives at. They are one honest step from the truth and they will not take it, because the step costs too much. That is not a first-century failure. It is entirely possible to acknowledge that the teaching of Jesus is extraordinary, that his influence is inexplicable, that something happened around him which ordinary categories do not cover, and to stop there, permanently, because the next sentence would rearrange your life. These people were not fools and they were not liars. They were near. And the whole tragedy of this passage is that near is not the same as in.

Is it enough to admire Jesus as a great teacher? No, and in the end it is not even possible. A man who claimed to forgive sins (2:5–10), to be Lord of the Sabbath (2:28), and to be the one whom the prophets foretold, was either telling the truth or was not good at all. Admiration that stops short of worship is not a compliment to him; it is a refusal to answer his question. The Nazareth question, where did he get these things, has only one honest answer: from the Father, because he is the Son. To admire him without bowing to him is to stand in the doorway of the synagogue and never go in.

In a sentence. In his hometown synagogue, Jesus’ teaching astonished the people, who wondered where he got such wisdom and power.

On a Tuesday. Astonishment at Jesus is not enough. The question where did this come from must lead to faith. If you have friends who speak warmly of Jesus but keep him at arm’s length, ask them gently what they make of his claims, not only of his teaching. And ask the same of yourself: which sentence of his are you admiring from a distance, when it is asking you to change?

For worship. The eternal Son of God went home and preached in the synagogue of his childhood, to neighbours who had watched him grow. He did not come with a new face or a borrowed name; he came as himself, and let them wonder. His wisdom is given from the Father, his mighty works are done by hands that once worked their timber, and both are offered to the very people most likely to despise them. That is the humility of our God: he comes near enough to be overlooked.
verseByVerse.note: His hometown is Nazareth.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us?" And they took offense at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us? And they took offence at him.

Is not this the carpenter? Here is where the astonishment curdles, and it turns on one word. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus himself is called a carpenter; Matthew’s version has the carpenter’s son (Matthew 13:55). The Greek tektōn means a builder or craftsman in hard materials: wood, and in that stony country very often stone as well. He made ploughs, yokes, doors, roof beams, furniture and houses. Jesus worked with his hands for years before his ministry.

They had his furniture. So for something like eighteen years the eternal Son of God did a trade in a village workshop, and the people in front of him had his work in their houses. There were roofs in Nazareth that afternoon that he had built. To the townspeople, this settled it: he was an ordinary tradesman, one of them. How could he be anything more? That is the offence, stated plainly. You cannot easily worship a man who fixed your door.

The son of Mary. A small phrase with a barb in it. Unusually, they identify him by his mother, not his father. Normally a man was called son of his father, even if the father was dead. To call a grown man his mother’s son in his own village was a slight, and the whisper behind it is not hard to hear: everyone knew Mary had been pregnant before her marriage, and the arithmetic had never quite worked (compare John 8:41). The town had its own explanation of his origins.

And brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not his sisters here with us? They name the brothers and gesture at the sisters, who are apparently sitting in the room. Jesus had four brothers and at least two sisters. James later led the church in Jerusalem and wrote the letter of James; Judas (Jude) wrote the letter of Jude. The most natural reading is that they were Mary and Joseph’s children born after Jesus. Matthew says Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son (Matthew 1:25), and Luke calls Jesus her firstborn (Luke 2:7), a word that quietly waits for others to follow.

Where Christians differ: Jesus’ brothers. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, and takes the brothers to be cousins (so Jerome). Orthodox tradition takes them to be Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. Verdict: the natural reading of the Gospels is that they were Mary’s younger children, Jesus’ half-brothers and half-sisters, born in the ordinary way. Nothing in Scripture requires otherwise. Mary’s honour is not a lifelong virginity. It is that she bore and raised the Son of God, believed God’s word (Luke 1:38, 45), and then mothered his brothers.

Does it matter whether Mary had other children? It matters a little, and in a particular direction. Nothing in the gospel hangs on it: Christ was born of a virgin, and that is the article of faith. But the idea of Mary’s perpetual virginity grew alongside the view that married love is somehow less holy, and that Mary should be honoured as more than a believing servant of God. Scripture gives her great honour as the mother of our Lord, and calls her blessed (Luke 1:48), but it never makes her an object of prayer or a mediator. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Reading the brothers plainly keeps Mary where she placed herself: among those who need a Saviour (Luke 1:47).

The brothers who came to believe. There is gospel gold in that little family list, so do not walk past it. During his ministry these brothers did not believe in him. John says it without softening: For not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Here in Nazareth they are among the offended, and three chapters back they came to take him home as a madman (3:21, 31). Then look where they are afterwards: in the upper room, praying with the believers after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). James becomes a pillar of the Jerusalem church, and writes the letter that opens, James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ. Judas, the Judas in this list, writes Jude. What turns a scornful younger brother into a man who signs himself the servant of his own sibling, and dies for it? Nobody is fooled by a brother. Something happened between Nazareth and Acts 1, and Paul names it in a single line: then he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7).

And they took offense at him. “Took offence” (eskandalizonto) is the root of our word scandal: they stumbled over him, and the thing they tripped over was that they knew him. Familiarity bred contempt. They knew his family, his trade and his ordinary life, and could not accept that God was at work in him. They had no category for the incarnation: God in an ordinary man. And there is the warning this verse leaves lying about for anyone raised in a Christian home or a long-attended church. Familiarity does not produce faith. It is quite capable of producing the opposite: a settled, comfortable, unastonished acquaintance with the most extraordinary Person who ever lived, filed under things you have always known.

Were those years in the workshop wasted? No. For most of his life on earth the Son of God did ordinary work for ordinary customers, and that was not a delay before his real work but part of his obedience. He was keeping the law perfectly in a carpenter’s shop, honouring his parents, giving fair measure, doing good work for people who would later despise him, and all of that is part of the righteousness credited to those who trust him. It also means your ordinary work matters to God. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23). A plumber, a nurse, a mother at home, a clerk at a desk, can serve Christ in the work itself, because Christ himself did.

In a sentence. His hometown could not accept that the carpenter they knew, with his ordinary family, could be more, and they stumbled over him.

On a Tuesday. Has familiarity with Jesus made you stop wondering at him? Ask God to make him fresh to you. Read one of the Gospels this week as if for the first time, and stop each time he does something no mere man could do. And as you go to your own work today, remember that the Lord of glory once stood at a workbench, and do your ordinary job for him.

For worship. The Word through whom all things were made took up a carpenter’s tools and made doors for Nazareth. The Son of the Most High was called the son of Mary with a sneer, and bore it. He grew up in a family that did not yet believe in him, and he loved them until the day he appeared to James. That is the depth of the incarnation: God among us, so ordinary to look at that his neighbours could not see him, so patient that his own brothers became his servants and his worshippers.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household." And he could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marveled because of their unbelief. And he went about among the villages teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: a prophet is not without honour except in his hometown, among his relatives and in his own household. He could do no mighty work there, except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. And he marvelled at their unbelief. And he went around the villages teaching.

A prophet is not without honor, except in his hometown and among his relatives and in his own household. He states it as a general rule, and it was probably a proverb already. But only Mark adds among his relatives and in his own household, and notice how the sentence narrows, step by step, getting more painful as it goes: the town, then the extended family, then the house he grew up in. The closer you get, the worse it gets. And he is speaking of himself. Even his family did not yet believe (3:21; John 7:5). His own brothers are in the room, and they are among the offended.

When your own family does not understand. If your family think your faith is a phase, an embarrassment or a mild derangement, if you dread the Christmas table because of the sighs, or have a mother who talks about it as though you had joined something, take this verse seriously and let it do its work. He was not spared this. He was refused in the village where he had been a good neighbour for thirty years, by relatives who could name every one of his brothers. And do not miss where his own brothers ended up. Nothing you can say to a family member will do what the risen Christ can do to them, and he had to rise from the dead to convince his.

And he could do no mighty work there. Now one of the most startling sentences in Mark, and it should not be smoothed away. Matthew says he did not do many mighty works there (Matthew 13:58). Mark says could not, and he wrote it deliberately. But read on, because the exception clause settles what it means.

Except that he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them. Whatever the limitation was, it was not a failure of power, as if he were helpless. He healed people in Nazareth that day. Sick men and women in that village got up well. Even in unbelief, a few came and were healed; his compassion was not withdrawn from those who sought him. The impossibility is moral, not mechanical. Miracles were signs meant to lead to faith; where people refused to believe, signs had no place. In a place that had already decided what he was, mighty works would have been mere spectacle, and Jesus does not perform. He refuses a sign to the Pharisees who demand one (8:11–12), and he will stand in silence in front of Herod Antipas, who wanted to see a miracle the way you would want to see a conjuror (Luke 23:8–9). And people did not bring their sick to someone they despised.

What it does not mean. Not that faith is a power that controls whether God can act. God is sovereign. Faith is not a mechanism that produces miracles, as though God were a machine and belief the coin you put in. It is the setting in which he ordinarily works, because he is dealing with persons and not with material. But faith receives what God gives, and unbelief closes the door. Unbelief does not disable God. It makes his help unwelcome, and he does not force it on a town that has made up its mind.

And he marveled because of their unbelief. Only twice in the Gospels are we told that Jesus marvelled, and it is worth putting the two together. He marvelled at a Roman officer, a Gentile soldier with no Bible, no upbringing in the covenant, no synagogue behind him, who said there was no need for him to come under the roof, only to say the word (Luke 7:9). And he marvelled here, at the village that had raised him, taught him the Scriptures, and heard him read them. Jesus was truly human and could be amazed. The people with none of the advantages astonished him in one direction. The people with all of them astonished him in the other.

And he went about among the villages teaching. Rejection did not stop him. No sulking, no long lament: he moved on to the next place and kept preaching. Rejection at home did not stop him for a single day.

Can my unbelief stop God from working in my life? Your unbelief cannot defeat God’s purposes, but it can keep you from receiving what he is offering. God is not limited by our weakness of faith; he heals the father who says, I believe; help my unbelief (9:24). What closes the door is not weak faith but settled refusal, the kind that has decided in advance what Jesus can and cannot be. So if your faith is small, bring it to him as it is, and ask him to increase it. If you notice that you have stopped expecting anything of him in some area of your life, confess that to him, and begin to pray about it again.

How do I love a family that rejects my faith? Patiently, warmly and without either preaching at every meal or hiding what you believe. Honour your parents (Ephesians 6:2), keep showing up, serve them in practical ways, and let your life speak before your words do (1 Peter 3:1–2). When they ask, answer gently and honestly. Do not take their scorn as a judgment on Christ or on you; he met it first. And pray for them by name, because their coming to faith will not depend on your arguments but on the risen Lord showing himself to them, as he did to James.

In a sentence. Rejected in his hometown, Jesus did few miracles there, marvelled at their unbelief, and moved on to teach in the villages.

On a Tuesday. If your own family or hometown does not honour your faith, Jesus understands. Keep going, as he did. And look for the opposite danger in yourself: are you so used to Christ that you have stopped expecting him to do anything? Pick one thing you have stopped praying for, and start again.

For worship. The Lord of all was refused in his own village, and did not withdraw his mercy; he laid his hands on the few who came and healed them. He marvelled at unbelief because he is truly man, and he went on to the next village because he is the faithful Saviour who does not sulk or retaliate. His own brothers mocked him and later worshipped him. There is no rejection so close to home that his patience cannot outlast it, and no family so hard that his resurrection cannot reach it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two, and gave them authority over the unclean spirits. He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts— but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called the Twelve and began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over the unclean spirits. He told them to take nothing for their journey except a staff: no bread, no bag, no money in their belts, but to wear sandals and not put on two tunics.

And he called the twelve and began to send them out two by two. The purpose for which he chose them (3:14). The word behind send out is apostellō, from which comes apostle, a sent one, and this is the moment the title starts to mean something. It is worth pausing on how little they knew. These men have not yet grasped who he is. Two chapters ago they were in a boat asking each other, who then is this? (4:41). They will fail to understand the loaves before this chapter is out. And he sends them anyway, with real authority, to preach. If you have been waiting to feel qualified before you say anything about Christ to anyone, notice that nobody in this group was.

Two by two. Never alone: for support, safety and credible witness. There is practical wisdom in it: a road at night, the danger of accusation, the sheer weight of doing it by yourself. There is also a legal reason: Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deuteronomy 19:15), and these men are bearing testimony. Jesus later sent out seventy-two in pairs (Luke 10:1), and the early church followed the pattern: Paul and Barnabas, Paul and Silas, Peter and John. It also means that every one of the Twelve went out with a colleague he had not chosen. Somebody was paired with Simon the Zealot and somebody was paired with Matthew the tax collector.

And gave them authority over the unclean spirits. His own authority, delegated. Note that it is given: not developed, not innate, not a technique they have learned by watching. Everything they are about to do runs on borrowed authority, which is exactly why it will fail in chapter 9 when they attempt it without dependence on God (9:28–29).

He charged them to take nothing for their journey except a staff. A walking stick for the road. Matthew and Luke say not even a staff (Matthew 10:10; Luke 9:3). It looks like a flat contradiction over the smallest of things, and a reader with Matthew open will spot it at once. It dissolves when the verbs are examined. Matthew’s word is acquire: do not procure, do not get hold of. Mark’s is take, in the sense of carry along. Perhaps Mark means take the staff you have, while Matthew means do not acquire another; or one Gospel speaks of a walking staff and the other of a club for defence. Either way, one plain instruction stands behind both: do not equip yourselves for this journey. Go exactly as you are, with the stick already in your hand and the sandals already on your feet. The point is the same: travel light.

No bread, no bag, no money in their belts. The list is deliberately stripped. No food. Coins were carried in folds of the belt. The bag was a traveller’s pack, or quite possibly a beggar’s bag for collecting gifts, which would have made them look like the wandering religious hucksters of the day. They must depend entirely on God’s provision through those who welcomed them.

But to wear sandals and not put on two tunics. No spare clothes. A second tunic was the ordinary traveller’s blanket, so they are being told to go without a change of clothes and without bedding. Simple, urgent, dependent. This is not asceticism for its own sake. It is engineered dependence. They will eat only if somebody feeds them, and sleep only if somebody takes them in, which means the mission cannot be conducted at arm’s length from the people it is for.

What it does not mean. Not a permanent rule for all missionaries. This was the instruction for one short mission in Galilee. Later Jesus reminded them of it, When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?, and then told them that things were now different: let the one who has a moneybag take it (Luke 22:35–36). The principles remain: urgency, simplicity, and dependence on God and on the hospitality of his people, not a ban on preparation.

Does this mean Christian workers should not be paid? No. The point of the instruction is that those who preach should live from those who receive the message, and that is exactly what Jesus says next: the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7). Paul argues the same: the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and elders who labour in preaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17–18). So it is right for churches to support their pastors and missionaries generously. And it is right for those workers to live simply, avoid the appearance of greed, and trust God rather than their reserves.

In a sentence. Jesus sent out the Twelve in pairs with authority over demons, telling them to travel light and depend on God.

On a Tuesday. What could you let go of to travel lighter in following Christ? A possession that owns you, a habit of keeping everything in reserve, the need to have every resource lined up before you obey? And consider who your partner is in serving Christ. If you have been trying to do it alone, ask a brother or sister to pray with you and go with you.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest sends out men who do not yet understand him, and gives them his own authority. He provides for them not from a treasury but through open doors and shared tables. That is how he has always fed his servants: daily bread, enough for the road. And the One who sent them empty-handed is the One who for our sake became poor, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
verseByVerse.note: Coins were carried in the belt; the “bag” was a traveller’s pack for supplies.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told them: wherever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place. And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you, when you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet as a testimony against them.

Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you depart from there. A small instruction with a surprising amount in it. Hospitality in that world was owed to travellers, and a visiting teacher with a following would attract offers. The temptation, once you were established in a village and word got round, was to move up: from the first house that took you in to a better one with a wealthier host and a more comfortable room. Do not move from house to house looking for better hospitality. Take the first door that opens and stay behind it.

What it protects. Two things are protected by that. The first is the poor family that risked something to receive them: they are not to be used as a stepping stone and then quietly left. The second is the message. A preacher who is visibly working his way towards the best address in town has already said something about himself that will drown out anything he says about Christ. And it is not an obsolete rule. There is a version of climbing available in every church and every ministry: the cultivation of the useful people, the warmth that increases with a person’s influence. The men who went out to those villages were told, before they preached a word, to stay in the house that had them.

And if any place will not receive you and they will not listen to you. Rejection was expected, as Jesus had just experienced in Nazareth. Jesus does not send these men out with the expectation of a clean sweep. He assumes refusal, names it, and gives them a way to leave that is neither bitter nor guilty.

When you leave, shake off the dust that is on your feet. Strict Jews returning from Gentile territory shook the dust off their feet, so as not to carry unclean soil into the holy land. It was a deliberate, visible gesture, and everyone knew what it meant: what belongs to you stays with you; we are not bringing it home. For the apostles to do this to a Jewish town was a startling sign. By rejecting God’s message, the town had made itself like pagan territory. Paul and Barnabas did it at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

As a testimony against them. A solemn warning, leaving them to God’s judgment, done in sorrow, not anger. It said, in a sign anyone could read: you have put yourselves outside. We came with what was ours to bring, and the responsibility now rests with you.

The mercy in the instruction. Here is the practical mercy in it, which is why it is in the Bible for people like us. They are told in advance what to do when it does not work. Jesus does not say, try harder, stay longer, keep pressing until they yield. He says, say your piece, and if they will not have it, go, and do not carry the town away with you in your shoes. That is worth taking to heart if you have talked to somebody about Christ for years and got nowhere, and have started to feel that his unbelief is a verdict on your competence. It may be, and it is worth examining. But this verse assumes the ordinary case is otherwise: the message was brought faithfully and was refused, and the refusal belonged to the hearer.

When should I stop talking to someone about Christ? Rarely, and never stop praying for him. The dust-shaking was a solemn act given to the apostles on a particular mission, marking towns that had heard and rejected the message; it is not a licence to write off a friend. But there is a lesson in it for us. When someone has clearly heard the gospel and has asked you to stop, respect that. Do not nag, argue at every meeting, or turn every conversation into a sermon. Keep the friendship, keep loving, answer if asked (1 Peter 3:15), and keep praying, because God can open a heart long after you have run out of words (Acts 16:14).

In a sentence. The apostles were to stay with those who welcomed them and solemnly shake off the dust of places that rejected them.

On a Tuesday. You are responsible for faithfully sharing the gospel, not for how people respond. Leave the results to God. You are responsible for the sowing; you never were responsible for the soil, and a man who cannot shake the dust off will eventually stop going anywhere at all. And look at how you treat the people who first welcomed you in your church or your work. Have you moved on to better company?

For worship. The Lord who sends his servants also carries the weight of the result. He does not make us answerable for hearts we cannot change; he alone opens and shuts (Revelation 3:7). And the God who warns towns of judgment by the dust on a preacher’s sandals is the same God who sent his messengers to them in the first place, because he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). Even his warnings are mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. They cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them.

So they went out and proclaimed that people should repent. The same message as John and Jesus (1:4, 15): turn back to God, for the kingdom has come near. Mark gives their message in a few words, and it is the same word Jesus opened with in chapter 1: repent and believe in the gospel. Repentance is not the same as being sorry. Remorse looks at yourself and feels bad; repentance turns round and goes the other way. The Greek word is about the mind being changed, and the Hebrew behind it is about a road being reversed. It is a direction, not a mood. And that is what twelve untrained men went from village to village saying. Not a technique for a better life, not a defence of Jesus’ credentials, but turn round.

And they cast out many demons. Sharing Jesus’ victory over Satan. The authority given in verse 7 turned out to be real in their hands, and when the seventy-two were sent out later they came back astonished at the same thing (Luke 10:17).

And anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them. Olive oil was used as medicine (Luke 10:34; Isaiah 1:6), and as a sign of God’s blessing and presence. This is the only place in the Gospels where anointing with oil accompanies healing, and it raises a fair practical question, because James tells the church to do the same thing: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord (James 5:14–15).

So what is the oil for? It is not medicine here; these healings are plainly not pharmacological. And it is not magic: nothing in the New Testament suggests the oil has power in it. It is a sign: something visible and physical, laid on the body of a sick person, saying that God is being asked to act here, on this man, now. Oil in the Old Testament marked out a person as set apart for God: kings, priests, the tabernacle furniture. To be anointed is to be designated as belonging to him and claimed for his purposes. And notice, before anyone builds too much on the oil, where James puts the power: And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. The Lord will. Not the oil, and not the elders.

What it does not mean. Not the sacrament of extreme unction or last rites, as the medieval church developed it, for preparing the dying for death. The anointing here was for healing. Reformed churches do not treat anointing as a sacrament, though some practise it in prayer for the sick, following James 5. Nor does it mean that every believer today has the apostles’ authority to heal at will. God still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills.

Should we expect healings like these today? These were signs given through the Twelve as they were sent out, part of the apostolic witness that confirmed their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). What continues is what James describes: the elders praying over the sick, with oil as a sign of setting them before the Lord. God hears such prayers and sometimes heals, often through ordinary means and sometimes beyond them. But no one is promised that every prayer for healing will be answered with recovery, and when healing does not come, the prayer has not failed. The final healing waits for the resurrection.

Should I ask my elders to pray over me when I am ill? Yes, if you are seriously ill. If you are seriously ill, the instruction in the New Testament is not to suffer privately and hope somebody remembers you in a service. It is to send for the elders of your church and ask them to come and pray over you. That is a specific, concrete thing you are entitled to ask for, and it is in your Bible. Many churches have quietly let it drop, which is a pity. James joins it to confession and forgiveness (James 5:15–16), so it is also a time to make sure all is well between you and the Lord, and then to rest in his will.

In a sentence. The Twelve preached repentance, cast out demons, and anointed and healed many sick people.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick in your church this week, by name, trusting God to answer as he knows best. If you are an elder, be ready to go when called. And if your own life needs not a mood but a turning, the message of the Twelve is for you: turn round, today.

For worship. Twelve men who could not yet answer the question who then is this went out and did all of this, on borrowed authority, because he sent them. Christ’s power does not depend on the brilliance of his servants. He is the one who drives out the darkness, heals the sick and calls sinners to turn, and he does it through weak hands so that the glory is plainly his. The Lord raises up the sick; the Lord forgives; and one day the Lord will raise up all his people whole.
verseByVerse.note: Olive oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing.

parallels.desc: anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord

verseByVerse.quote: King Herod heard of it, for Jesus' name had become known. Some said, "John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. That is why these miraculous powers are at work in him." But others said, "He is Elijah." And others said, "He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old." But when Herod heard of it, he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Herod heard of it, for Jesus’ name had become known. Some said: John the Baptist has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him. Others said: he is Elijah. Others said: he is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old. But when Herod heard of it, he said: John, whom I beheaded, has been raised.

King Herod heard of it. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. His official title was tetrarch, a minor ruler (Matthew 14:1), but people called him king, and Mark uses the title the locals used. He later asked Rome for the title of king, and was exiled instead.

For Jesus’ name had become known. The mission of the Twelve had spread his fame. Twelve men in six pairs have covered the district, and the noise has reached the palace. Then Mark gives us three popular verdicts on Jesus, and they are worth laying side by side.

Some said, John the Baptist has been raised from the dead. Others had the same idea as Herod.

Others said, He is Elijah. The prophet expected before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5).

And others said, He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old. All honourable opinions, all inadequate. The same list appears when Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is (8:28), and then turns and asks them. Note what the crowd is doing. It is reaching for the biggest category it already has. A prophet is the largest thing they can think of, so he must be one, or the greatest of them come back. It never occurs to anyone that a new category might be required. That instinct has not aged at all. Ask people today who Jesus was and you will be offered the same shape of answer at a lower altitude: a great teacher, a moral genius, a mystic, a revolutionary. All respectful, all far too small, and for the same reason: those categories cost nothing.

But when Herod heard of it, he said, John, whom I beheaded, has been raised. A guilty conscience, and one of the most chilling sentences in the Gospel, because of one word in it. Whom I beheaded. He could have said, John, who was beheaded. He could have blamed his wife, who wanted it; or the oath, which trapped him; or the guests, who were watching. Every one of those excuses was available and he had used them all at the time. Alone in his own head, months later, the sentence comes out in the first person, with the pronoun in it. Herod could not stop thinking about the man he had killed.

What guilt does. That is what a guilty conscience does: it keeps the accurate record. The moment Herod hears of miracles in Galilee his mind goes straight to the man he killed and produces a resurrection to explain it. He is not reasoning; he is haunted. He has become a man who cannot hear good news without hearing his own crime in it. Guilt does not fade because it is unaddressed. It goes underground and comes up sideways, in dreams, in irrational fears, in the inability to enjoy anything. A conscience that has not been dealt with does not stop working. It simply stops being useful and starts being a torment. And there is only one place in the world where it can be dealt with. Herod had a prophet in his cellar who would have told him where, the one who pointed to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and he preferred to keep listening rather than obey. Now he has a ghost. Mark now goes back to tell the story.

What do I do with a guilty conscience? Bring it to Christ, specifically and honestly, and do not try to manage it by yourself. Name the sin to God without excuses: not it happened, but I did it. Believe that the blood of Christ purifies the conscience from dead works (Hebrews 9:14), and that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9). Where you have wronged someone, put it right as far as you can. And if the guilt keeps returning after you have confessed and been forgiven, that is no longer conscience but accusation: answer it with the cross, where the debt was fully paid (Romans 8:1, 33–34).

In a sentence. People offered many explanations of Jesus, but Herod, haunted by guilt, thought he was John the Baptist raised from the dead.

On a Tuesday. A guilty conscience cannot be silenced by silencing the messenger. Bring your guilt to Christ. Is there something you have managed for years rather than confessed? Today is the day to bring it out. And when you hear people describe Jesus in the respectful, too-small categories of our day, ask them gently whether a great teacher would say the things he said.

For worship. The world has always tried to fit Jesus into its largest existing box, and he has never fitted. He is not one of the prophets come back; he is the one all the prophets were pointing to. And he is not a ghost to haunt the guilty, but the Saviour who came to set them free. The conscience that torments Herod can be quieted in one place only, at the cross of the Lamb whom John announced, and there it is quieted completely.
verseByVerse.note: “King” Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea; his official title was tetrarch.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her. For John had been saying to Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison, because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, whom he had married. For John had been saying to Herod: it is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.

For it was Herod who had sent and seized John and bound him in prison. Mark now backs up to explain, and the flashback is the longest passage in his Gospel about anyone other than Jesus. Everything in it is compressed elsewhere; here he slows down and gives you the whole squalid business. According to the historian Josephus, John was held at Machaerus, a grim hilltop fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea, miles from anywhere: the man who had baptised thousands in the open air of the Jordan valley, shut in a cell in a desert castle.

For the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, because he had married her. The family arrangement takes a moment to lay out and is worth the trouble, because the mess of it is the point. Herodias was the granddaughter of Herod the Great, and so the niece of both her husbands. She had been married to Antipas’ half-brother (called Philip in the Gospels). Antipas fell in love with her on a visit to Rome; both divorced their spouses and married each other. Antipas put away his first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, which would eventually cost him a war and an army. So a man leaves his wife for his brother’s wife, who is also his niece.

For John had been saying to Herod, It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife. “Had been saying”: repeatedly. This was not one outburst that Herod overheard. John said it, and said it again, and went on saying it, to the ruler’s face. The law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John confronted the ruler with God’s law, like Elijah before Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 21).

How John spoke. Look hard at what that sentence contains, because it is a model of something the church constantly gets wrong in one direction or the other. It is short: John does not deliver a treatise on marriage. It is specific: not a general denunciation of immorality in high places, which costs nothing and changes nobody, but this man and this marriage. It is addressed to the man himself: John says it to Herod, not about him in the safety of the Jordan valley to a crowd who already agreed. And it is about Herod’s sin, not Herod’s politics: John had no comment on the tetrarch’s taxes or his building projects. He confronted him on the thing he was answerable to God for.

The cost. It cost him his freedom and then his head. That is the price of speaking a name, and it always has been. It is perfectly safe to denounce sins in general, and sins that belong to people not present, and sins nobody in your circle is committing. The moment a name is attached, it becomes expensive, which is why the prophets are so few and the courtiers so many. A man who tells the king only what the king can bear is not a prophet. He is staff. Two things keep this from being a licence for the sharp tongue. John was not rude, and he was not indiscriminate: he had a word for the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers too (Luke 3:10–14), tailored to each. And he said it to the man’s face, repeatedly, in a way that risked everything he had, which is a very different thing from criticising the powerful at no cost, from a distance, to an audience that will applaud.

Was Herod’s marriage wrong only because of the law about a brother’s wife? No; it was wrong twice over. Each of them abandoned a living spouse without any ground God allows, and then they married within a forbidden degree of kinship. Scripture permits divorce only for adultery or for wilful desertion that cannot be remedied (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15; Westminster 24.5–6), and Jesus calls remarriage after any other divorce adultery (10:11–12). John’s sentence named the most public offence, but the whole arrangement was built on two broken covenants. The point is not that the powerful are worse sinners than others, but that their rank does not exempt them from God’s law about marriage.

Should Christians speak out against the sins of leaders today? Yes, with John’s wisdom. Pray for rulers first (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and honour them (1 Peter 2:17). When you speak, speak about what God’s word plainly says, not your political preferences dressed up as prophecy. Speak to the person where you can, not merely about him. Speak with grace, seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6), and be ready to pay for it. And remember that the first sins to deal with are your own: John’s courage before Herod grew out of a life that had already bowed to God.

In a sentence. Herod had imprisoned John because John kept telling him that his marriage to his brother’s wife broke God’s law.

On a Tuesday. God’s law applies to the powerful as much as anyone. Pray for courage to speak truth when love requires it. Is there a conversation you have been avoiding because the truth would cost you? Ask God for the courage to have it, kindly, directly and soon. And pray today for preachers and Christian leaders who are under pressure to say only what their hearers can bear.

For worship. God is no respecter of persons: his law reaches the palace as surely as the cottage, and he raises up prophets who will say so. The courage of John was not his own invention; it was the gift of the Spirit who filled him from the womb (Luke 1:15). And the Lord who sent John to Herod is the same Lord who sent his own Son to stand before Herod and Pilate in silence and then die for sinners of every rank. His truth is not cheap, and neither is his grace.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

verseByVerse.quote: And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herodias had a grudge against John and wanted to put him to death. But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man, and he kept him safe. When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly.

And Herodias had a grudge against him and wanted to put him to death. “Had a grudge” literally means held it in: a nursed, settled hatred. She would not let it go. This is not a flash of temper; it is a settled campaign, and she is waiting for her chance. Verse 21 will call it an opportunity, which means she had been looking for one. Bitterness kept and fed becomes murderous (Ephesians 4:31).

What the truth does to some people. Her reaction is worth noting for what it tells you about the effect of being told the truth. John’s sentence was aimed at Herod, but it was Herodias who could not live with it, because it named her position exactly: she was not his lawful wife. Every day that John stayed alive, that fact was alive in the kingdom. Some people, when a sin is named, repent. Some argue. And some set out to destroy the person who said it, because if the witness can be discredited or removed then perhaps the fact goes with him. It never does, but the attempt is one of the most reliable behaviours in human life, and it is why speaking plainly to power has always been dangerous.

But she could not, for Herod feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man. Only Mark tells us about Herod’s inner conflict, and it is the most searching thing in the chapter, because Herod is not a monster and everything in these two verses is to his credit, until it is not. He feared John: not in the sense of being frightened of a prisoner in his own dungeon, but with awe, the involuntary respect a slack man feels in the presence of a serious one. He knew John was right. Knowing that he was a righteous and holy man: Herod’s assessment is correct. He is not deceived about John’s character for a moment.

And he kept him safe. He protected John from Herodias, at least for a while. Against his own wife, who wanted him dead, the tetrarch used his authority to keep John alive.

Matthew says Herod wanted to kill John. Matthew says that Herod wanted to put him to death but feared the people (Matthew 14:5). Both are true. Herod’s feelings about John were divided, as Mark makes clear: he arrested him, feared him, protected him from Herodias and listened to him gladly. A man can want a voice silenced and still be drawn to it.

When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly. Herod listened to John often. John’s preaching disturbed him, unsettled his mind, left him at a loss. So the word was getting through: this is not a man who was bored. And yet he heard him gladly. He sent for him. He came back for more. Picture the scene, because it is extraordinary: the ruler of Galilee going down into his own prison to listen to the man he has chained there, being upset by what he hears, and returning to be upset again. He enjoyed hearing John, but would not obey him. He would not give up Herodias.

A divided heart. That is the most dangerous spiritual condition described anywhere in this Gospel, precisely because it looks so much like the real thing. Herod was disturbed, confused, drawn and resistant at the same time: attracted to the truth, unwilling to repent. Everything is present except one item. Interest, respect, emotion, protection of the preacher, genuine disturbance of conscience, and no repentance. The one thing John was actually asking for, week after week, was the one thing Herod would not do. Herodias stayed. He is the thorny ground of chapter 4 given a name and a palace (4:18–19): the word heard and choked by the desire for other things. And a man who will not repent must eventually silence the voice that keeps asking him to. Herod did not want John dead. He liked him. But the logic of an unrepented sin runs one way, and it took only a party, a dance and an audience to finish what had been decided long before.

Is it wrong to enjoy sermons? Not at all. Delight in God’s word is a mark of grace (Psalm 119:103), and it is right to be moved by faithful preaching. The danger is not enjoying it but stopping there. Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves (James 1:22). A simple test: after a sermon that moves you, ask what one thing it calls you to do, believe or stop, and tell someone. Enjoyment that leads to obedience is the Spirit at work. Enjoyment that replaces obedience is Herod in the dungeon, nodding.

In a sentence. Herodias hated John and wanted him dead, but Herod, knowing John was holy, protected him and listened to him gladly, though perplexed.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to enjoy sermons and admire preachers without ever repenting. Do you only listen, or do you obey? The question is not whether the sermon moved you. It is whether anything in your house is different because of it. Name one thing that has actually cost you something this year. And if a grudge is growing in you against someone who told you the truth, deal with it before it grows: forgive, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32).

For worship. God does not leave even a Herod without a witness. He placed a holy prophet in a tyrant’s cellar and let the tyrant hear him gladly, week after week. That is the patience of the Lord, who keeps speaking to divided hearts long after they deserve to be left alone. And he is the God who does what Herod would not: he gives what is dearest to him for the sake of what is right, and he gave his Son so that sinners who have resisted the truth might be made new.

verseByVerse.quote: But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. For when Herodias's daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. And the king said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you." And he vowed to her, "Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But an opportunity came when Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles, military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. When Herodias’ daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. The king said to the girl: ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you. And he vowed to her: whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom.

But an opportunity came. The opportunity Herodias had been waiting for. Mark’s word is literally a good day, a well-timed day. Herodias has been waiting for one, and the calendar hands it to her.

When Herod on his birthday gave a banquet for his nobles and military commanders and the leading men of Galilee. A lavish feast for the powerful, with plenty of wine. Note the guest list, because everything that follows turns on it. His nobles: the court. His military commanders: the army officers. The leading men of Galilee: the money and the influence of the province. This is every man in the region whose opinion Herod cares about, in one hall, on his birthday. It is the most public night of his year, and by the end of it a man will be dead.

For when Herodias’s daughter came in and danced, she pleased Herod and his guests. Josephus names her Salome. Mark does not, and calls her the girl in the verses that follow, a word for a young girl, not a woman; she was probably a teenager. Understand what has happened here, because the scene has been romanticised for centuries and the reality is squalid. For a princess to dance before drunken men at a banquet was shameful, and suggests a sensual performance, perhaps arranged by her mother. That is what hired entertainers were for, and their status was very low. Herodias sent her own daughter in to do the work of a dancing girl, in front of her stepfather and the entire military command of Galilee. She was willing to use her child that way to get what she wanted. That is the measure of the grudge.

Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you. A drunken, extravagant promise.

And he vowed to her, Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom. Now the oath, and there are three things wrong with it. It is theatre. Herod is performing for the room, buying a moment of admiration from his officers with a grand gesture, and the swearing is part of the show: he does not merely offer, he vows, and Mark says in verse 26 that it was oaths, plural. It is empty. Herod had no kingdom to give; he ruled at Rome’s pleasure, and he could not have given away a square mile of it without permission. The boast was hollow. And it is borrowed. Up to half of my kingdom echoes the Persian king’s words to Esther (Esther 5:3, 6; 7:2). Every Jew in that hall would have caught it, and the echo is unbearable, because in Esther that offer is used by a brave woman to save a nation from slaughter. Here the same words are used to fetch a prophet’s head on a plate.

A man who cannot say a small true sentence. The whole thing is a man who cannot say a small true sentence and cannot stop himself saying a large false one, and in a few minutes it will have him. Jesus warned against rash oaths (Matthew 5:33–37), and James repeats it: let your yes be yes and your no be no (James 5:12). The reason is exactly this scene. A man who inflates his words to impress a room will one day find himself standing behind a promise he never meant, in front of people he cannot bear to disappoint.

Should Christians take oaths at all? Yes, when it is solemn and lawful, but never casually. Jesus forbade the everyday swearing that props up our words because we are not otherwise trusted (Matthew 5:33–37). Yet God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God as his witness (2 Corinthians 1:23), and Reformed and Baptist confessions alike teach that a lawful oath in a court or on a solemn occasion is a proper act of worship (Westminster 22.1–3). What is forbidden is the rash oath, the oath to do evil, and the oath as performance. Let your ordinary word be so reliable that you rarely need more.

In a sentence. At Herod’s birthday banquet, his stepdaughter danced, and the drunken king swore to give her anything, up to half his kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Rash promises made in the moment can trap us. Be slow to promise, and never let a promise bind you to sin. Watch for the moments when you are performing for a room, at work, online, among friends, and notice how easily big words come. Practise the small, true sentence instead.

For worship. How different is the King we serve. Herod offered half a kingdom he did not own, as a drunken boast. Christ, who owns all things, gives his people the whole kingdom freely (Luke 12:32), and every promise he makes is yes and amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). Herod’s oath led to a prophet’s death; Christ’s oath, sworn by God himself, leads to life for all who flee to him for refuge (Hebrews 6:17–20). His word is never empty, and never theatre.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And she went out and said to her mother, "For what should I ask?" And she said, "The head of John the Baptist." And she came in immediately with haste to the king and asked, saying, "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter." And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She went out and asked her mother: what should I ask for? She said: the head of John the Baptist. She came in immediately with haste to the king and asked: I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter. The king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her.

And she went out and said to her mother, For what should I ask? She goes out, and that detail is worth having: the girl does not know what she wants. She has been given, in front of the whole court, an open cheque from a ruler, and she has to leave the room and go and ask her mother. Which tells you she was a child in every sense, and it tells you where the will in this story lives. The girl was the instrument of her mother’s hatred.

And she said, The head of John the Baptist. Herodias seized the moment. No hesitation, no pause to think of anything else. She has had the answer ready for months. And notice that she asks for nothing for herself and nothing for the girl: not land, not money, not jewels, not a position, and the offer was half a kingdom. There is nothing in the world Herodias wants as much as she wants that voice stopped. That is what a nursed grudge does to a person’s appetites. It eats everything else. Given one wish, unlimited, this woman spends it on a man in a cell who has done her no injury except to tell the truth about her.

And she came in immediately with haste to the king. Before Herod could sober up and change his mind. Mark piles up the words, immediately, with haste, and you can see a child hurrying to deliver a message, pleased to have an answer.

I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter. She has improved on it. Her mother said the head of John the Baptist. The girl adds two things: at once, and on a platter, a serving dish, as if it were another course at the feast. Grotesque. In a hall full of banqueting men, she asks for a man’s head to be carried in on the crockery. Mark does not comment. He does not need to. This is what happens to a child raised in that house.

And the king was exceedingly sorry. Herod regretted his oath. The word is strong, deeply grieved, and it is the word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:34). Herod’s distress is entirely real. He does not want this.

But because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her. And there it is: the whole reason a man is beheaded tonight. Because of his oaths: he had sworn, loudly, more than once. And his guests: there they sit, the nobles, the officers, the leading men of Galilee, every one of them looking at him and waiting. Fear of losing face before his powerful guests. He valued his reputation more than a righteous man’s life, and more than his own conscience. And here is the terrible piety of it. Herod keeps his word. He is scrupulous about an oath and murderous about a prophet, and he would have told you, quite sincerely, that a man must stand behind what he has sworn.

Was Herod bound to keep his oath? No. An oath to do evil binds no one; it should be repented of, not carried out (Westminster 22.4, 22.7). The law made provision for someone who had sworn rashly (Leviticus 5:4–6), and Jephthah’s vow stands in Scripture as a warning, not an example. Herod’s real bond was not to God but to the faces around his table. What he could not face was being the man who backed down in front of that room. Not conscience: he had already lost that argument, and he knew John was righteous and holy. Not law: no law said a prisoner should be executed to settle a dinner-party promise. He could not bear to look foolish in front of people whose opinion he had spent his life courting.

The fear of man. That is the most ordinary murder motive in the world, and the reason this passage is not really about ancient kings. Almost nobody does the worst thing he ever does because he wanted to. He does it because backing out in front of the people watching was unthinkable. The joke you laughed at. The thing you went along with because the room had already turned. The stand you did not take because of who would have seen you take it. Peter is eight chapters away from denying he ever knew Jesus, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, for exactly this reason. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25). Herod was a king with an army, and a girl and a room full of guests walked him into a murder he did not want to commit.

What if I have already made a promise I should not have? If keeping it would mean sinning, do not keep it; confess the rash promise to God and to the person, apologise, and bear the embarrassment. If it is merely costly or inconvenient, a godly person keeps his word even when it hurts (Psalm 15:4), unless the other person releases him. Either way, go humbly to the one you promised, explain honestly, and seek a way to make it right. The cross covers rash words too, and it is far better to look foolish before people than to do wrong before God.

In a sentence. Prompted by her mother, the girl asked for John’s head on a platter, and Herod, though sorry, would not break his word in front of his guests.

On a Tuesday. Fear of what others think leads people into terrible choices. Be willing to lose face rather than do wrong. Think of the room you are most afraid of disappointing: the boss, the friends, the family, the online crowd. Decide now, before the moment comes, what you will not do for their approval.

For worship. Herod feared his guests and killed a prophet. Christ feared his Father and gave his life. Before Pilate, Herod and the crowd he would not say the word that would have saved him, because he trusted the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He is the King who was never once trapped by the opinion of a room, and he frees his people from the snare of the fear of man by giving them a better fear, the fear of the Lord, which is the beginning of wisdom and the end of slavery to faces.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John's head. He went and beheaded him in the prison and brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately the king sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. He went and beheaded him in the prison, brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. When John’s disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb.

And immediately the king sent an executioner. Immediately: the whole thing takes as long as it takes a soldier to walk down to the cells and back. “Executioner” (spekoulatōr, from the Latin speculator) was a soldier of the guard who carried out executions. Mark uses the Latin word, perhaps because he was writing in Rome.

He went and beheaded him in the prison. A few words, and Mark will not embellish them. He does not describe the cell, or whether John was asleep, or whether anything was said. There is a door opening in the dark and a soldier with an order, and that is all we are told. Now stop and take in what has just happened, because it is one of the hardest things in the Gospel. This is the man Jesus called the greatest born of women (Matthew 11:11). The forerunner of the Messiah. The voice crying in the wilderness. The man who baptised the Son of God and saw the heavens torn open and the Spirit descend, and who said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29). The last and greatest of the prophets. And he died alone in a dungeon, killed at a drunken party to satisfy a vengeful woman and a weak man’s pride, with no last word recorded.

There is no rescue. That is the thing to sit with, and the Gospel does not soften it. Jesus was alive and a few days’ walk away, healing strangers, and John, who had been shut in that fortress long enough to send messengers asking, Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? (Matthew 11:3), was not delivered. The answer he got back was not, I am coming to get you. It was a message about the blind seeing and the poor having good news preached to them, and a beatitude: blessed is the one who is not offended by me (Matthew 11:6). So John died with the question answered and the door still locked.

Faithfulness is not a contract with providence. If you are serving God faithfully and your circumstances are getting worse rather than better, that is in your Bible on purpose, and it is not a sign that something has gone wrong. Hebrews knows this: some by faith stopped the mouths of lions and escaped the edge of the sword, and others, by exactly the same faith, were sawn in two and killed with the sword (Hebrews 11:33–37). The chapter puts them in the same list and calls it all faith.

And brought his head on a platter and gave it to the girl, and the girl gave it to her mother. Told plainly, without comment. The dish comes into the hall. It passes to a girl, and the girl carries it to her mother, and Mark stops the sentence there. Herodias has what she wanted. What she does with it, we are not told.

When his disciples heard of it, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. A last act of love, and the one clean act in the whole squalid story. John’s own disciples, men with no power and everything to lose, walking into a Herodian fortress to ask for a headless corpse, come and take the body and bury it properly. They could not save him. They could not avenge him. They could carry him, and they did.

Why Mark tells this story. It is the only story in Mark not directly about Jesus. Placed between the sending out of the Twelve (vv. 7–13) and their return (v. 30), it shows the cost of faithful ministry. The messenger is killed by a ruler who knows he is innocent, under pressure from others, and buried by his disciples. Every detail foreshadows Jesus’ own death: Pilate will know Jesus is innocent, yield to pressure, and Jesus will be laid in a tomb by friends who came and took the body (15:15, 45–46). The forerunner goes before him in death too. The difference is what happened next. Herod’s dungeon kept John. The tomb outside Jerusalem could not keep the one John had pointed to, and because it could not, the man in that cell is not finally a tragedy.

Why did God let John die like that? Scripture does not give us every reason, but it gives us enough to trust him. John’s work was complete: he had prepared the way and pointed to the Lamb, and he must decrease (John 3:30). His death became part of the testimony to Christ, showing what this world does with God’s messengers and what it would do with God’s Son. And death was not the end for him. To die in faith is to be with the Lord, and John now sees the face of the one whose sandals he was not worthy to untie. God does not promise his servants safety from suffering, but he promises that nothing, not even the sword, can separate them from his love (Romans 8:35–39).

In a sentence. John was beheaded in prison, his head was given to Herodias, and his disciples buried his body.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness to God may cost a great deal. Pray for those today who are imprisoned or killed for speaking God’s truth; find out the name of one persecuted church or believer and pray for them by name this week. And if your own faithfulness is costing you, at work, at home, in reputation, remember that you are in the line of John, and of the Lord he served.

For worship. The greatest born of women died in a cellar for the sake of the truth, and he died pointing to someone greater. The Lamb of God he announced would also be handed over by a ruler who knew he was innocent, and laid in a borrowed tomb by grieving friends. But the Lamb rose. Because he lives, John lives, and every martyr since lives with him, under the altar and before the throne (Revelation 6:9–11). The world has the last word only until the morning, and the morning belongs to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–56 — The Feeding, the Walking, and the Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rest that never happened (vv. 30–34). The apostles come back full of what they have done, and Jesus's first instruction is not a debrief but a retreat: come away and rest. They get into a boat — and the crowd works out where they are going, runs round the head of the lake on foot, and is waiting when they land. His response to a wrecked afternoon off is compassion, because they were like sheep without a shepherd.

The feeding (vv. 35–44). The disciples do the arithmetic and propose dispersal. Jesus hands the problem back: you give them something to eat. Then he seats a crowd of thousands in ranks on the spring grass, takes five loaves and two fish, and there is more left at the end than there was at the start.

The lake in the fourth watch of the night (vv. 45–52). He sends them off ahead and goes up the mountain alone to pray — and from up there, in the dark, he sees them straining at the oars. He comes to them on the water, and he means to pass by, in the language the Old Testament reserves for God showing himself.

Gennesaret (vv. 53–56). And then a summary paragraph of pure mercy: whole villages carrying the sick out into the marketplaces, and everyone who touched even the edge of his clothing made well.
verseByVerse.theology:
He meant to pass by them (v. 48) is the strangest clause in the chapter, and it is not what it sounds like. He is not trying to overtake them or slip past unnoticed. Passing by is the Old Testament's own vocabulary for God making himself visible.

When Moses asked to see the glory of God, the LORD put him in a cleft of the rock and said while my glory passes by I will cover you with my hand (Ex. 33:22). When Elijah stood at the mouth of the cave, the word was behold, the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:11). And Job, describing the God no man can lay hold of, says he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea — and then, three verses later, behold, he passes by me, and I see him not (Job 9:8, 11).

Walking on the sea and passing by, in the same sentence, out of the same book. Mark's readers who knew their Scriptures were not being told about a shortcut.

And then, when they scream, he speaks: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid. The middle phrase is egō eimi — literally I am, the words from the burning bush (Ex. 3:14). It is the ordinary way to say it's me, and in this setting, on that water, from that Person, it is very much more.

Which makes verse 52 the saddest verse in the chapter: they did not understand about the loaves, but their hearts were hardened. Mark uses of the Twelve the very word he used of the men in the synagogue who watched a withered hand restored and went out to plan a murder (3:5). Hardness is not a disease of unbelievers only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve exhausted men doing sums in front of a hungry crowd — two hundred denarii, most of a year's wages, and it still would not be enough — and hearing you give them something to eat.

Now: anyone facing a need that is plainly larger than their resources. The parent who has run out of wisdom. The pastor of a small church looking at a large town. The person asked to care for someone whose needs exceed anything they have.

Jesus is not asking them to solve it. He asks a different question, and it is the practical one: how many loaves do you have? Go and see. Not how many do you need — how many have you got. Go and count it.

Five loaves and two fish is an embarrassing answer to give in front of five thousand people, and it was the right answer, because the multiplication happens in his hands and not in theirs. Bring what you actually have, including how little it is. And notice who ended up carrying the twelve baskets of surplus: the men who had nothing to give, one basket each.
