And the Pharisees and the scribes asked him, "Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark pauses to explain. The Pharisees, and the Jews generally, do not eat without carefully washing their hands, holding to the tradition of the elders. Coming from the market, they do not eat without washing, and they keep many other traditions, such as washing cups, pots, copper vessels and dining couches. So the Pharisees and scribes asked Jesus why his disciples did not walk by the tradition of the elders but ate with defiled hands.

For the Pharisees and all the Jews. A generalisation: the Pharisees’ practice had spread widely and was respected by ordinary Jews, even if not all kept it strictly. And notice that Mark stops the narrative and explains the custom, in a bracket, for two whole verses. That tells you who this Gospel was written for. A Jewish reader would need none of this; it would be like explaining a kettle to an Englishman. Mark is writing for Gentiles, almost certainly for the church in Rome, and he keeps doing this: translating Aramaic phrases, converting money into Roman coinage, using Latin loan-words. The oldest Gospel we have was written for people outside the covenant, and that is quietly relevant to a chapter that ends with a Gentile woman and a Gentile deaf man.

Wash their hands properly. Literally, with a fist (pygmē). The exact meaning is uncertain. It may mean cupping one hand to pour water over the other, washing up to the wrist, or rubbing the fist in the palm. Whatever the gesture, it was a precise ritual.

Holding to the tradition of the elders. The key phrase, and everything in the passage turns on it. The tradition (paradosis, what is handed down) was the body of oral rules that the rabbis had built around the written law of Moses, to apply it to every situation and, as they said, to build a fence around the law so that no one would come near breaking it. It was later written down in the Mishnah (about AD 200), and it runs to a substantial book; there is a whole tractate on hand-washing, specifying the quantity of water, the position of the hands and the number of rinses. And the Pharisees believed, and this is the crucial point, that this oral tradition had been given to Moses on Sinai alongside the written law and was equally binding. Jesus will deny that flatly.

And when they come from the marketplace, they do not eat unless they wash. In the market you might brush against a Gentile, or a Jew who was unclean, or touch something unclean. So you washed, or even immersed yourself (the Greek is literally baptise themselves), before eating.

The washing of cups and pots and copper vessels and dining couches. Vessels could become unclean (Leviticus 11:32–35), and the tradition multiplied the rules. Mark’s list is faintly comic and probably meant to be: cups, pots, bronze vessels, the furniture you eat on. There were rules for all of it, and men had spent their lives mastering them. Some manuscripts lack and dining couches, which was probably added later; the meaning is unaffected.

Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? To walk is the Jewish way of speaking of how you live (the rabbis called their rules halakah, from the word for walking). The question is an accusation: your disciples are disobeying the recognised authorities, and you as their teacher are responsible. Now look hard at how they frame it, because the framing gives the whole game away. They do not ask why the disciples break the law of God. They ask why they do not walk according to the tradition of the elders. They know exactly which authority is being contravened, and they name it accurately, and they are perfectly confident that it settles the matter.

Where the authority has migrated. That is the position of a man who has stopped being able to feel the difference between what God said and what his tradition says God meant. He would tell you, sincerely, that he holds Scripture supreme. And when a real question arises, the answer he reaches for is the tradition, because that is where the practical authority has quietly migrated. It is worth asking, without cynicism, where the practical authority sits in your own convictions. When you are challenged about something you believe a Christian should or should not do, what do you reach for first: the text, or the settled instinct of the people you were formed by? The second is not always wrong. But a man who cannot tell which one he is using has already made the Pharisees’ mistake.

How do I tell a command of God from a human tradition? Ask three questions. Where does Scripture actually say this, read in context, not as a proof-text? Is it a command for all Christians, or wisdom for a particular situation? And would I think less of a faithful Christian who did it differently? Things like the length of a service, styles of dress, how often you have a quiet time, or which translation you read may be wise or unwise, but they are not commands. Keep your good habits gladly, but do not bind other people’s consciences with them. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2).

In a sentence. The tradition of the elders demanded ritual washings of hands and vessels, and the Pharisees challenged Jesus because his disciples ignored it.

On a Tuesday. Every church and family builds habits around obedience. Some are wise. But ask which of your rules come from God and which only from the way we do things. Write down two or three of your own unwritten rules for what a good Christian does, and check each against Scripture. Keep the wise ones; stop judging others by them.

For worship. The God who gave the law did not give it to be smothered. He spoke at Sinai with clarity and mercy, and the Son who stands before these scribes is the Word who spoke it. He has no need of a fence around his law, because he has come to fulfil it and write it on hearts. Blessed is the Lord whose commands are not burdensome (1 John 5:3), and whose yoke is easy (Matthew 11:30), unlike the heavy loads men tie on one another’s shoulders.
verseByVerse.note: Mark explains Jewish customs for readers who did not know them — likely Gentile Christians, perhaps in Rome. The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law.

parallels.desc: zealous for the traditions of my fathers

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written, 'This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.' You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered that Isaiah prophesied rightly about them, hypocrites that they were: this people honours God with their lips, but their heart is far from him; they worship him in vain, teaching human commandments as doctrine. They had left God’s commandment behind to hold on to human tradition.

Well did Isaiah prophesy of you. Jesus does not answer the question about hand-washing directly. He does not defend the disciples, explain the circumstances, or concede that the men might have washed. He goes to the root: the authority of their tradition, and the men making the complaint. And he opens with a quotation from the prophet they revered. Isaiah 29:13, written about Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, applied fully to these men. A prophecy can describe a recurring pattern that is fulfilled again and again, and supremely in the generation that met the Messiah.

You hypocrites. The only time Mark uses the word. A hypokritēs was an actor on a stage, someone wearing a mask, speaking lines. Their religion was performance: right on the outside, empty within. It does not necessarily mean conscious pretence, and it is important to see that, because otherwise the charge slides off us. Jesus is not merely saying they are lying. He is saying there is a gap between the performance and the person, and that the performance has taken over.

This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. The quotation was first spoken to a generation that was scrupulously religious, and that is what makes it lethal. Isaiah was not addressing idolaters who had abandoned the temple; he was addressing men who were keeping it all up. The heart, in the Bible, is the centre of the person: thought, will and love. Worship that is only on the lips is not worship. God looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). And the diagnosis is a measurement of distance. The lips are close. The heart is far. Both parts of that are true at once, and the first is what makes the second so hard to detect.

How would you know? That is the honest question, and it deserves a concrete answer rather than a shudder. Here is one test. What happens to your religion when nobody is watching? The lips are, by definition, the public part. Prayer that only happens in company, a Bible opened only where somebody might see, generosity that is known about: none of these is wrong, and all of them can be maintained by a heart that has quietly gone somewhere else. Subtract the audience and see what is left standing. Here is another. When did you last enjoy God? Not a service, or a sermon, or the company of Christians, but him. A heart that is far off can keep every observance and has usually stopped finding any pleasure in the Person the observances are about, and has stopped noticing that it stopped.

In vain do they worship me. “In vain” (matēn): pointlessly, emptily, to no effect. God does not accept it. This is worship that happens, offered to the right God, and achieves nothing. That should sober anyone who assumes that attendance is the same as acceptance.

Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. The second fault. Not only is their heart wrong; their authority is wrong. Not having human customs: every church on earth has those, and must. But teaching them as though they came from God. They put human rules on the same level as God’s word, and bind consciences where God has not bound them. Mark quotes Isaiah from the Greek translation (the Septuagint), which makes this point especially clearly.

You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men. The verdict. “Leave” (aphentes): abandon, let go. “Hold” (krateite): grip tightly. It is a picture of a man with both hands full who has to drop something to pick up something else. They had let go of God’s word with one hand while holding human tradition firmly with the other. Note the contrast: God’s commandment, men’s tradition. That is the distinction they had blurred. Nobody in that delegation thought of himself as abandoning the commandment of God. Every one of them would have said he was defending it. That is precisely why Jesus has to prove it, and in the next five verses he does, with a single devastating example.

Where Christians differ: Scripture and tradition. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Scripture and sacred tradition together form one deposit of revelation, both to be received with equal reverence, interpreted by the teaching office of the church. Protestants hold sola Scriptura: Scripture alone is the final authority, and every tradition, however old and useful, must be tested by it. Protestants value tradition (the creeds, the councils, the wisdom of the church) as a servant, not as a master. Verdict: this passage is one of the clearest grounds for the Reformation principle. Jesus judges a revered, ancient tradition, believed to come from Moses, by the written word of God, and condemns it where it contradicts that word.

But what about creeds and confessions, are they not tradition too? Yes, and good ones are a gift. The Apostles’ and Nicene Creeds, and confessions like the Westminster and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, are summaries of what the church has learned from Scripture. The difference is in their claim. They do not claim to be a second source of revelation; they claim to be faithful to the first, and they invite testing by it. The confessions themselves say that all synods and councils may err, and are to be used as a help in faith, not as its rule (Westminster 31.4). So read them, learn from them, and be humble before the wisdom of the saints, but let Scripture have the last word.

In a sentence. Jesus called the Pharisees hypocrites whose worship was empty, because they had abandoned God’s command and held fast to human tradition.

On a Tuesday. Before you sing on Sunday, ask whether your heart is near to God or only your lips. And measure every custom in your church by Scripture. Try the test this week: one act of devotion no one will ever see, a prayer in secret, a gift no one knows about (Matthew 6:6). Notice whether it feels like worship or like a loss.

For worship. God is not deceived by lips. He looks on the heart, and that is terrifying until we remember what he does with hearts. The same Lord who exposes the distance between our words and our love is the one who closes it. He gave his Son, whose lips and heart were never once apart, who honoured the Father perfectly in secret and in public, so that our hollow worship could be covered by his true worship. In Christ, the far-off heart is brought near (Ephesians 2:13).

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition! For Moses said, 'Honor your father and your mother'; and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went on, with biting irony: what a fine way they had of setting aside God’s commandment to establish their own tradition! For Moses said, Honour your father and mother, and whoever curses father or mother must be put to death.

You have a fine way of rejecting the commandment of God. “Fine” (kalōs, well, beautifully) is sarcastic: how skilfully you do it! It is one of the few places in the Gospels where you can hear Jesus being witheringly ironic, the tone of a man watching a skilled piece of work he despises. “Rejecting” (atheteite) means setting aside, declaring void. The word shows that their tradition did not simply add to the law; it cancelled it.

In order to establish your tradition. Some manuscripts read to keep your tradition. Either way, the tradition had become the goal, and God’s law the obstacle. And note the direction of the sentence. He is not saying they neglect the commandment while pursuing their tradition. He says they reject the commandment in order to establish the tradition. The setting aside is not a side effect. It is the mechanism. Now he proves it, and he chooses his ground with great care.

For Moses said. Note that Jesus treats Moses’ words as God’s commandment (v. 8) and God’s word (v. 13). What Moses wrote, God said.

Honor your father and your mother. He goes to the Ten Commandments: not to an obscure regulation but to the fifth word of the Decalogue, written by the finger of God, the first commandment with a promise (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16; Ephesians 6:2). Nobody in that delegation could plead ignorance or claim it was disputed. And he takes the commandment in its plain, practical sense, which is worth pausing on because we have sentimentalised it. It is not primarily about the manners of small children. In Jewish thought it included supporting your parents in old age, when they could no longer work. There were no pensions; children were their parents’ security. To honour your father meant to feed him when he could no longer work.

And, Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die. Exodus 21:17 (also Leviticus 20:9). “Reviles” means speaks evil of, curses, treats with contempt. The death penalty showed how seriously God took dishonouring parents. Jesus quotes the strongest form of the law to show what the Pharisees were evading. So he has now put down two immovable stones. God commanded the care of parents. God attached the severest possible sanction to its contempt. And in the next verse he will show the delegation a legal device, taught by their own school, that let a man walk away from both, and feel devout while doing it.

Obedience you can measure. One thing worth carrying. Jesus’ chosen example of what real obedience to God looks like is not a spiritual exercise. It is a middle-aged man paying his mother’s bills. When he wants a case that everybody can measure, he does not reach for prayer or fasting or the temple. He reaches for whether the old people in your family are being looked after, which is exactly where the New Testament keeps landing when it wants to test a religion. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27). If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8).

What if my parents were cruel, or are not Christians? You are still to honour them, but honour is not the same as obedience in everything, and it never means accepting abuse. Honour means treating them with respect as the parents God gave you, speaking of them without contempt, praying for them, and caring for their real needs when they are old, as far as you are able. It does not mean doing wrong at their request (Acts 5:29), keeping silent about abuse, or putting yourself or your children in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated, and if a parent has harmed you, wise distance and the help of your church and, where needed, the authorities are right. Even then, you can refuse bitterness and leave judgment to God, and still see that they do not go without food or care.

In a sentence. Jesus mocked the skill with which the Pharisees set aside God’s plain command to honour father and mother, a command God took with the utmost seriousness.

On a Tuesday. Honouring your parents includes caring for them when they are old. No religious duty excuses you from it (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). If your parents are living, ring or visit one of them this week, and ask honestly what they need. If they are gone, look around your church for an elderly person who has no children nearby.

For worship. The God who wrote the fifth commandment on stone kept it in flesh. His Son, hanging on the cross in agony, made sure his mother would be cared for (John 19:26–27). That is our Saviour: the eternal Son who became a son, honoured his earthly parents, and fulfilled every command we have broken. And the Father who commands us to honour our parents is the Father who never once fails his own children, and will not let the orphan or the widow go uncared for (Psalm 68:5).

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, 'If a man tells his father or his mother, "Whatever you would have gained from me is Corban"' (that is, given to God)— then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother, thus making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you say: if someone tells his father or mother that whatever support they would have had from him is Corban, that is, a gift dedicated to God, then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother. So you cancel God’s word by the tradition you hand down. And you do many things like this.

Corban. But you say: three words, and they carry the whole indictment. God said one thing; you say another. Jesus sets the two speakers side by side and lets the room hear it. Corban is a Hebrew word (qorban) meaning an offering, something brought near to God (Leviticus 2:1). Mark leaves it untranslated and then glosses it: given to God. A man could declare his property or money Corban, dedicated to the temple, set apart as though laid on the altar, no longer available for ordinary use. The vow did not always mean he handed it over at once; he might keep using it himself. But it could no longer be used for anyone else, including his parents.

Whatever you would have gained from me. The son speaks to his parents: the help you would have had from me is now dedicated. Perhaps in a quarrel, perhaps in anger, a son could take a vow that shut his parents out of his support. Watch how it was worked. A man has ageing parents. The fifth commandment obliges him to support them, and everyone knows it: the money he owes their care is a real, visible, calculable sum. He does not want to part with it, and he cannot simply refuse without disgrace. So he looks at his parents and says the word. Now his hands are tied by piety. The money is holy. He cannot spend it on his father, because it belongs to God, and a vow may not be broken.

Then you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother. This is the heart of the charge. Even if the son regretted the vow, the scribes held him to it, because a vow to God was sacred (Numbers 30:2). They used one law, about vows, to cancel another, about parents, and chose the interpretation that cancelled the greater command. The system had made repentance illegal. Later rabbis, to their credit, allowed such vows to be released in cases like this. And in practice the money very often never reached the temple at all. The vow made it unavailable to his parents; it did not necessarily make it unavailable to him. So an old man goes hungry, and his son is regarded as a devout person, and the machinery of religion has been used to produce exactly the outcome that God’s commandment existed to prevent.

Thus making void the word of God. “Making void” (akyrountes) is a legal word: annulling, cancelling the authority of a document, as you might annul a will. Human tradition had annulled God’s word.

By your tradition that you have handed down. Theirs, not God’s. They pass it on and it grows.

And many such things you do. Corban is one example, not the only one. Corban is not the disease. It is one symptom he happens to have picked up, because it was the clearest.

What it does not mean. Not that vows and giving to God do not matter. But no religious act can be a cover for neglecting the plain duties of love that God has commanded. God does not want gifts that are taken from the mouths of your parents.

Corban in modern clothes. Take the test this passage supplies, in its modern clothes, because the shape has survived perfectly and it is almost never consciously dishonest. It is the man so committed at church four nights a week that his mother has not had a visit since March. It is the money given to a fund while a brother in the same congregation cannot pay his heating bill. It is any arrangement in which something genuinely religious has been set in front of a plain duty God commanded, so that the duty can be quietly dropped without anybody feeling wicked. Ask it of yourself in one sentence: is anything I do for God currently costing somebody else something God told me to give them? That is Corban, whatever it is called, and there is no version of it that God accepts.

How do I balance caring for parents with my other duties? Scripture gives an order without making it a formula. Your first earthly duty is to your spouse and children (Genesis 2:24; 1 Timothy 5:8), and care for parents should not destroy a marriage. But within that, parents are not optional. Talk openly with your siblings about sharing the load, involve your parents in decisions where they are able, and use the help of others, including professional care, without guilt where it is needed. Ask your church for practical support; the early church cared for widows together (Acts 6:1–3). The aim is not that you do everything personally, but that your parents are honoured and not neglected.

In a sentence. By the Corban rule, the scribes let a man dedicate to God the support he owed his parents, and so they annulled God’s word by their tradition.

On a Tuesday. Watch for spiritual-sounding reasons to avoid costly love: I am too busy with church, that money is for the Lord. God is not honoured by neglect of the people he has given you. Look at your diary and your giving this week, and ask whether any of your religious commitments are crowding out a duty God has plainly given you.

For worship. Our God will not be bribed with gifts taken from the hungry. He sees through every holy-sounding word to the heart that is withholding love. And he does what the Corban son would not: he gave what was most precious to him not to shut others out but to bring them in. Christ did not shelter his riches behind a vow; he emptied himself and gave everything, so that we, who had no claim on him, might be provided for for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Property declared Corban — dedicated to God — could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the people to him again and said to them, "Hear me, all of you, and understand: There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him, but the things that come out of a person are what defile him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus called the crowd to him again and said: listen to me, all of you, and understand. Nothing outside a person that goes into him can defile him. What comes out of a person is what defiles him.

And he called the people to him again. Jesus turns from the experts to the crowd. He has been talking to a delegation of scholars from Jerusalem. Now he turns away from them, raises his voice, and calls the crowd over: the ordinary people who have been standing at the edge of the argument. This is not a private debate; it concerns everyone. He is about to say something the experts will not like, and he says it to everybody.

Hear me, all of you, and understand. A solemn call to attention, like he who has ears to hear (4:9). Both verbs are commands, and the second one is doing real work. He is not asking for attention; he is asking them to think. What follows is weighty, compressed and easy to misunderstand.

There is nothing outside a person that by going into him can defile him. A revolutionary statement. Read it as a Jew standing in that crowd would have heard it, because we are so far from the world it detonated in that we hardly feel the blast. The whole system of food laws (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14) and the Pharisees’ hand-washings rested on the idea that what you eat or touch can make you unclean before God. Pork, shellfish, rabbit, camel, birds of prey: unclean. Contact with a corpse, a leper, a discharge: unclean. It ran through every meal, every kitchen, every market transaction, every relationship with a Gentile neighbour. It was not a dietary preference; it was the boundary marker of the people of God, and men had died in the Maccabean persecution rather than eat pork. And Jesus says: not in the deepest sense. Uncleanness that separates you from God is not a matter of what goes into your stomach.

But the things that come out of a person are what defile him. Real defilement is moral, not ceremonial. It comes from within. Jesus does not explain the riddle yet; he calls it a parable (v. 17), and explains it to the disciples in private. That statement is either an outrage or it is the arrival of the thing the whole system was pointing to. There is no third option, which is presumably why he told them to understand.

The picture fulfilled. Here is what makes it the second. The food laws had always been a picture: a daily, physical, unavoidable lesson in the difference between clean and unclean, drummed into a nation three times a day for fifteen centuries so that they would know in their bones that holiness matters and that not everything is acceptable to God. A picture is not abolished when the thing it pictured arrives. It is fulfilled, and put away. What the picture was teaching all along is that there is such a thing as defilement, and he is about to tell them where it actually lives.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament food laws were wrong or foolish. God gave them, for a time, as a picture of holiness and to mark Israel off from the nations. Jesus reveals what they were pointing to, and that their time is ending.

Does this mean it does not matter what I take in, what I watch, read or drink? No. Jesus is speaking about the food laws, not about everything that enters through the eyes and ears. Sin comes from the heart, but what we feed the heart matters: Keep your heart with all vigilance (Proverbs 4:23). The lustful look is adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28), and Paul says, I will not be dominated by anything (1 Corinthians 6:12). Drunkenness is still sin (Ephesians 5:18). What Jesus denies is that any food can make you unclean before God, not that your choices about what you look at and consume are morally neutral.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 16: If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from 4:9 and 4:23, a sentence Jesus certainly said, which a scribe perhaps wrote in the margin and a later copyist took into the text. The ESV puts it in a footnote, which is why the verse numbers jump from 15 to 17. The verse numbers themselves are not ancient; they were added in the sixteenth century, long after the manuscripts. So when translators went back to the earliest copies and found the sentence absent, they could not renumber the entire New Testament; they left the number empty and put the words in a footnote.

Has something been taken out of my Bible? No. The reverse has happened: we have older and better copies than were available four hundred years ago, and where those copies show that a sentence crept in later, honest translators tell you in the margin instead of quietly leaving it in. Nothing Jesus taught is lost; the same words stand in 4:9 and 4:23. A faith that would not let you see its own manuscripts would have something to hide. This one prints the workings at the bottom of the page.

In a sentence. Jesus told the crowd that nothing entering a person from outside can defile him; what defiles is what comes out of him.

On a Tuesday. You cannot make yourself clean before God by what you avoid eating, touching or watching, important as those choices are. The problem is deeper: it is the heart. So when you guard your eyes and your habits this week, do it as care for a heart that belongs to Christ, not as a way of earning cleanness he has already given.

For worship. For fifteen centuries God taught his people the grammar of clean and unclean, line upon line, meal upon meal, and then the Teacher himself arrived to say what it all meant. He is the substance to which the shadows pointed. The Lord who gave the food laws had the authority to fulfil them, and he did it not by lowering the standard of holiness but by moving it to where it always belonged: the heart. And there, where no washing can reach, his blood can.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 16: “If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house and left the people, his disciples asked him about the parable. And he said to them, "Then are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, since it enters not his heart but his stomach, and is expelled?" (Thus he declared all foods clean.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had left the crowd and gone into the house, his disciples asked him about the parable. He said: are you also without understanding? Do you not see that whatever goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but his stomach, and passes out? (So he declared all foods clean.)

And when he had entered the house and left the people. The pattern of Mark 4: public teaching in riddles, private explanation to the disciples (4:10, 34). The men who get the explanation are the ones who stayed and asked.

His disciples asked him about the parable. Parable here means a riddle, a saying that needs unlocking. Matthew tells us Peter asked (Matthew 15:15). They call it a parable, which tells you they knew something large had been said and had no idea what.

Then are you also without understanding? “Also”: like the crowd, like the Pharisees. There is a weariness in it. He has been at this a while, and these are the men who have watched everything. It is a rebuke that runs through Mark’s middle section, as the disciples keep failing to understand (6:52; 8:17–21). But note that he answers. The rebuke and the explanation come in the same breath, as they did in chapter 4 (4:13). He does not withhold teaching from slow disciples; he sighs, and teaches them.

Since it enters not his heart but his stomach. The logic is simple, almost crude, and deliberately so. Food goes to the digestive system, not to the heart, the moral and spiritual centre. It cannot reach the place where a person is clean or unclean before God. Whatever route moral corruption takes into a man, it is not that one. He is drawing a distinction the whole system had blurred: between ceremonial uncleanness, which was about ritual standing, and moral defilement, which is about what a man actually is. The Pharisees had spent so long on the first that they had come to treat it as the second, and had ended up, as the last paragraph showed, ceremonially spotless and robbing their parents.

And is expelled. Literally, goes out into the latrine. Mark is frank: food passes through the body and out. It has no effect on your soul.

Thus he declared all foods clean. The key phrase, and one of the most consequential parentheses in the Bible. It is worth being clear about who is speaking. That is Mark’s comment, in brackets, drawing out the implication for his readers: an inspired comment on what the saying meant. Jesus’ words meant the end of the food laws. And Mark wrote, by every early account, with Peter’s preaching behind him.

Peter learned it slowly. Peter was in that house. He heard this explanation with his own ears, in a private room, from the Lord himself. And years later, on a rooftop in Joppa, God let down a sheet full of unclean animals and told him to kill and eat, and Peter said, By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean. He had to be told three times, What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:9–16). Then he went to a Gentile’s house, and was called before the Jerusalem church to explain himself, and years after that Paul had to rebuke him publicly at Antioch for pulling back from Gentile tables (Galatians 2:11–14). The church settled it at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), and Paul taught it plainly (Romans 14:14; Colossians 2:16–17; 1 Timothy 4:3–5). So the parenthesis in verse 19 is the note of a man who has finally understood something he was told to his face a long time before.

The comfort in a slow learner. Take the comfort in that, because you probably need it. It is entirely possible to be taught a truth clearly, by Christ himself, in Scripture, and to go on for years without it having landed, and then to have it land, at last, in a way that reorganises everything. That is not a sign that you were never taught. It is what learning actually looks like in creatures like us. Peter needed the sermon, a vision, a Gentile household, a church council and a public rebuke, and he got there. And note what this verse cost him: he is the one who tells us, through Mark, that he had been told all along.

Why the food laws ended. They had a purpose: to separate Israel from the nations and to teach that God is holy and his people must be distinct (Leviticus 20:24–26). In Christ, the wall between Jew and Gentile is broken down (Ephesians 2:14–15), and the gospel goes to all nations. Holiness is now marked not by diet but by a changed heart. The shadow gives way to the substance (Hebrews 9:10).

Textual note. In the Greek, declaring clean is a participle, and older translations (like the King James) attached it to the latrine: purging all meats. Most modern scholars, following the ancient interpreters Origen and Chrysostom, take it as Mark’s comment on Jesus’ words, as the ESV does.

So are Christians free to eat any food? Yes. The food laws of Moses no longer bind anyone in Christ: Peter was told, What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15), and Paul says that everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4). Love may still limit that freedom. A Christian should not insist on his rights in a way that wounds a weaker believer (Romans 14:13–21; 1 Corinthians 8:13), and those who keep kosher out of conscience or for the sake of witness to Jewish friends are free to do so. What no one may do is make food a condition of standing with God.

Then which Old Testament laws still apply? Reformed Christians have long distinguished three kinds of law in the Old Testament. The ceremonial laws (sacrifices, food laws, purity rites) were shadows of Christ and are fulfilled and set aside (Hebrews 10:1). The civil laws governed Israel as a nation and expired with that state, though their general justice still teaches us. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflects God’s own character and still binds everyone, not as a way to be saved but as the shape of a grateful life (Westminster 19.3–5). Not every verse fits neatly into one box, but the principle is sound: ask how a law points to Christ, and how Christ applies it to his people.

In a sentence. Jesus explained that food goes into the stomach, not the heart, and cannot defile anyone, and so he declared all foods clean.

On a Tuesday. You are free to eat with thanks (1 Timothy 4:4). But use that freedom with love towards those whose consciences are weaker (Romans 14:20–21). Thank God for your next meal as a gift from the Lord who made all foods clean. And if there is a truth from Scripture you have heard a hundred times and never let land, ask him to make it land this week, as he did for Peter.

For worship. With one sentence the Lord of the Sabbath became the Lord of the kitchen, and the wall that had divided Jew from Gentile at every meal began to come down. He has the authority to do it because he is the Lawgiver himself. And he is patient enough to teach the lesson again and again to a slow apostle, by a sermon, a vision and a rebuke, until it is learned. All foods are clean because he has made the eaters clean, and his table is open to the nations.
verseByVerse.note: The food laws of Leviticus 11 had marked Israel off from the nations; Mark draws out that Jesus set them aside.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "What comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said: what comes out of a person is what defiles him. For from within, out of the human heart, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride and foolishness. All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person.

For from within, out of the heart of man. Fix the location before the list, because the location is the doctrine. The source of sin is not outside us, in our environment, our food, our upbringing or the company we keep, though all these can tempt and shape us. The source is the heart, and the heart in the Bible is not the seat of the emotions only but the control room of the person: what you love, choose, decide and are. The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick (Jeremiah 17:9). This is the biblical doctrine of human sinfulness: we sin because we are sinners.

Evil thoughts. First, and rightly, because they are the root of the rest. “Thoughts” (dialogismoi) means reasonings, schemes, the plans of the mind. Every evil act begins as an evil thought.

The list. Twelve vices follow. The first six are in the plural in Greek, and describe acts. The last six are singular, and describe dispositions. It repays reading them one at a time rather than letting them blur. Sexual immorality (porneiai): any sexual activity outside marriage. Theft, murder, adultery: three of the Ten Commandments, named flatly. Coveting (pleonexiai): greed, the restless desire to have more, the tenth commandment and the engine under a great deal of the rest. Wickedness (ponēriai): malice, the active desire to harm. Deceit (dolos): cunning, trickery, the bait on a hook. Sensuality (aselgeia): unrestrained, shameless indulgence, flaunting appetite without caring who sees, the loss of the capacity to be embarrassed. Envy: literally an evil eye, the grudging look at another’s good. Slander (blasphēmia): abusive speech against God or people. Pride (hyperēphania): arrogance, showing yourself above others, used only here in the Gospels. Foolishness (aphrosynē): not lack of intelligence but moral folly, the senselessness of the person who lives as if there were no God (Psalm 14:1).

Notice the mixture. Murder sits in a list with envy; adultery next to pride; theft beside foolishness. We would have graded them. Jesus does not, because he is not ranking behaviours by their social damage. He is naming what comes out of one source.

All these evil things come from within, and they defile a person. Not hands, cups or food. These. The Pharisees were careful about washing hands and careless about the heart. Jesus reverses their priorities.

Follow your heart? Put that against the way our own culture talks, because the collision is total. The modern account of human trouble is almost entirely external. People go wrong because of what was done to them, because of what surrounds them, because of systems and pressures and pasts. Some of that is true, and Scripture never denies it; the Bible is fierce about oppression and tender about wounds. But the modern remedy follows from the modern diagnosis: change the environment, remove the influences, and what is underneath will come right. And the counsel that follows is the one you will hear anywhere: trust yourself, follow your heart. Jesus says the heart is where it comes from. That is either the most pessimistic sentence in the chapter or the most hopeful, depending entirely on what comes next, because a diagnosis is not a verdict, and this one is the reason the gospel exists.

The uncomfortable test. Look at the list and find the ones you would have quietly excluded from your own account of yourself. Most of us can manage the first few from a distance. Try coveting. Try envy: the small drop in your stomach when a colleague does well. Try slander, which does not require a lie, only a true thing said to lower someone. Try pride. If those are in you, and they are, then they did not come in from outside, and no adjustment of your circumstances will remove them, and no washing of hands will touch them.

What it does not mean. Not that outward actions do not matter, or that a person who sins in deed can excuse himself because his heart is good. The point is the reverse: the heart is not good, which is why the deeds are evil. And not that outside influences are harmless. But removing temptation will not make a sinful heart clean. Only God can do that, by giving a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26; Psalm 51:10).

The only remedy that reaches. So what is the remedy? Not a better system, and not a stricter one. God promised the only one that reaches this far, centuries before: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). That is what the man in front of them had come to do. He is not offering to clean the outside of the cup. He is offering to make the man new, and he will do it by being treated as defiled himself, made sin for us who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that what comes out of a human heart can finally be something other than this list.

If I am a Christian, why do I still find these things in my heart? Because the new heart God gives is real, but the old sin is not yet gone. At conversion God gives new life and new desires, and sin no longer reigns (Romans 6:14), but it still remains and fights (Galatians 5:17; Westminster 13.2). The difference is that a Christian now hates these things, confesses them, and fights them by the Spirit, and is slowly changed. Finding envy or pride in yourself is not proof that you were never born again; being untroubled by it would be more worrying. Bring each one to Christ as you notice it, and remember that his blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).

Does this mean what was done to me does not matter? No. Scripture takes seriously the harm others do, and God is the defender of the wronged (Psalm 10:14, 17–18). Abuse, neglect and trauma shape people deeply, and they need care, justice and time. But Jesus is clear that our own sins come from our own hearts, and that is actually good news: if my sin came only from outside, I would be helpless until my circumstances changed. Because it comes from my heart, Christ can deal with it directly, forgiving it and changing me, whatever my circumstances. You can be both a person who was wronged and a sinner who needs grace, and Christ is enough for both.

In a sentence. What defiles a person is the evil that comes out of the heart: thoughts, acts and attitudes that show the heart itself is corrupt.

On a Tuesday. When you sin today, do not blame circumstances or other people. Trace it to your heart, confess it, and ask God for the clean heart only he can create. Pray Psalm 51:10 each morning this week: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.

For worship. The Lord sees to the bottom of us. Nothing in the list surprises him, and none of it repels his grace. He knew what was in man (John 2:25), and he came anyway. He did not merely wash the outside; he took the defilement of our hearts on himself at the cross, and gives us a new heart in its place. The God who diagnoses so truly is the God who heals so completely, and every clean desire in a Christian’s heart is his own handiwork.

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — Two Healings Beyond Israel’s Borders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Tyre (vv. 24–30). Having just dismantled the boundary between clean and unclean, Jesus walks across it. He goes north into pagan Phoenicia, tries to stay hidden, and fails within hours — because a woman with a demonised daughter has heard he is there. What passes between them is the hardest exchange in the Gospel and one of the greatest lessons in prayer anywhere in Scripture.

The Decapolis (vv. 31–37). Then a long looping journey back down the eastern side of the lake — through Gentile country the whole way — and a man is brought to him who is deaf and can barely speak. Jesus takes him away from the crowd, uses touch instead of words because touch is the only language the man can receive, looks up, groans, and says one word.

The two halves belong together and the order is not accidental. The teaching cleared the ground: nothing outside a man defiles him. The healings show what that means in practice — a Phoenician mother and a Gentile deaf man, both of them outside every boundary Israel had, both of them served.

And the crowd's verdict at the end is bigger than they know: he has done all things well.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was Jesus being cruel to the Syrophoenician woman? It is the first question any honest reader asks, and it deserves a straight answer rather than an embarrassed one.

Three things take the sting out without softening the difficulty. The word first (v. 27) is the hinge: let the children be fed first. That is not a refusal; it is an order of service, and it implies a second course. Paul states the same order without apology — to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Rom. 1:16). The dogs are under the table (v. 28), and the picture is domestic: not the scavengers of the street but the household pets under the table while the family eats. They are inside the house. And the outcome is the loudest commentary of all — he grants what she asks, immediately, at a distance, and Matthew records him saying O woman, great is your faith! (Matt. 15:28).

He was not insulting her. He was handing her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find the door. She did, in one sentence, and it is the only exchange in the Gospels where someone answers Jesus back and he says they are right.

And the deaf man's healing is the new creation beginning. The crowd's he has done all things well echoes Genesis 1:31 — God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. And he even makes the deaf hear and the mute speak is Isaiah's sign of the age of the Messiah: then... the ears of the deaf unstopped... and the tongue of the mute sing for joy (Isa. 35:5–6). They meant only that this healer was impressive. They were quoting the first page of the Bible and the promise of the last days in the same breath.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who could not hear, brought by friends who could — because he could not hear the news, could not ask, and could not have explained what he needed.

Now: every person who is carried to Christ by somebody else. It is the four on the roof in chapter 2 all over again, and it is worth noticing how often in this Gospel the person healed did not get there under their own power.

And look at how he handles him. He takes him aside from the crowd privately. A deaf man in a jostling crowd is a man being stared at and unable to follow a word of it. Jesus removes him from the audience before he touches him — which is a rebuke to every way of helping people that requires the helped to be visible.

Then he uses touch, because touch is the only language the man has: fingers into the ears, saliva on the tongue, a look up to heaven to say where this is coming from. It is not a ritual; it is a conversation conducted in the only vocabulary available. He tells the man what is about to happen to him in signs he can read.

And he sighed. Standing in front of one ruined pair of ears, the Creator groans — as Paul says the whole creation is making, and we with it, waiting for redemption (Rom. 8:22–23). He is not indifferent to what has been done to his world. He feels it, in the body he took, over one man nobody has named.

verseByVerse.quote: And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. And he entered a house and did not want anyone to know, yet he could not be hidden. But immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him and came and fell down at his feet. Now the woman was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth. And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From there Jesus went to the region of Tyre and Sidon. He entered a house and wanted no one to know, but he could not be hidden. Immediately a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard of him, came, and fell at his feet. She was a Gentile, a Syrophoenician by birth, and she begged him to drive the demon out of her daughter.

The placing of the story. Mark puts this straight after Jesus declared all foods clean. The barrier of the food laws between Jew and Gentile has just been removed in principle, and now Jesus goes into Gentile territory and a Gentile woman receives his blessing. The teaching is followed by the picture. He has just said that nothing outside a man can defile him, and now he walks straight over the boundary he has dissolved.

And from there he arose and went away to the region of Tyre and Sidon. He leaves Israel. Tyre was a great Phoenician port about 40 miles (65 km) northwest of Capernaum, in modern Lebanon, with Sidon further north. It was Gentile, pagan, and historically an enemy of Israel: the country of Jezebel’s father (1 Kings 16:31), a city the prophets denounced (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28), a place a devout Jew would not go without a reason. Yet Jesus had said that if his mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented (Matthew 11:21), and people from there had already come to hear him (3:8).

And did not want anyone to know. He was seeking rest and privacy with his disciples, away from Herod’s territory and the crowds, and perhaps time to teach them. It is the rest that never happened in chapter 6, attempted again by leaving the country. He wants a house, a door, and nobody knowing where he is.

Yet he could not be hidden. His fame had gone before him. The words have a double bottom. On the surface, his reputation has crossed the border ahead of him, and even in Phoenicia people know. Underneath, it is simply not possible for this Person to be concealed. Whatever room he enters, he is what he is.

A woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit. “Little daughter” (thygatrion) is a tender word, the same as Jairus used (5:23). A mother’s desperate love drives her. She has a daughter at home with an unclean spirit, which means she has already tried everything Tyre had to offer.

And fell down at his feet. The posture of a suppliant, of worship. She asks as one who has no claim. Consider what she has already had to overcome to be lying on that floor. She is a woman, approaching a male Jewish teacher, uninvited, in a private house, on behalf of a child who is not present. Every social convention in the region is against it.

Now the woman was a Gentile. Literally a Greek: Greek-speaking, Greek in culture, and so a Gentile, not a Jew.

A Syrophoenician by birth. From Phoenicia, which was part of the Roman province of Syria (as distinct from the Libyan Phoenicians of North Africa, around Carthage). Matthew calls her a Canaanite (Matthew 15:22), reaching for the ancient word, the name of the peoples Israel was commanded to drive out of the land. Everything about her is outside: a woman, a Gentile, from a pagan city, with a demon-possessed child. Not Jewish by blood, by religion or by language, and descended from the nations under the ban. There is no category of outsider she does not occupy.

And she begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter. She kept on asking. Matthew records the disciples’ reaction, which is entirely in character: Send her away, for she is crying out after us (Matthew 15:23). And into that scene, a foreign woman on the floor of a borrowed house, asking repeatedly for a child she has left at home, comes the hardest sentence Jesus speaks to anyone in this Gospel.

Was Jesus sent only to Israel? In his earthly ministry, first to Israel. Matthew records Jesus saying, I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24). That was the shape of his ministry before the cross: Christ came first as a servant to the circumcised (Romans 15:8), and the nations would be reached after his death and resurrection (Matthew 28:19). But the promise to Abraham was always that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and the word first in verse 27 shows that the Gentiles were not excluded but were to come in their turn. This woman is an early firstfruit of that harvest, and so are we.

In a sentence. In Gentile Tyre, where Jesus sought privacy, a Syrophoenician mother fell at his feet and begged him to free her daughter from a demon.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far outside to come to Jesus. Bring him your children’s needs as this mother did, on your knees. And notice who in your town is as far outside as she was: by background, religion or reputation. Pray for them as people Jesus has already crossed borders to reach.

For worship. The Son of God could not be hidden, not in a house in Tyre, not in a tomb in Jerusalem. He walked into the land of Jezebel and let a Canaanite mother fall at his feet. That is how wide his mercy reaches: past every border that his own people drew, to the very nations they were once told to drive out. The God of Israel is the God of all the earth, and the outsider on the floor is nearer to his heart than the inspectors from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a Gentile port city on the coast north-west of Galilee. “Syrophoenician” means a Phoenician from the Roman province of Syria; Matthew calls her a Canaanite.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "Let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: let the children be fed first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.

A hard saying. This sounds harsh, and it is meant to be taken seriously, not explained away. It is the one saying of Jesus that makes readers wince, and a commentary that hurries past it is not worth reading. But it must be read carefully, so take it apart properly. Understand first the picture he has drawn: a family at a meal, bread on the table, children being fed, and dogs, which in this house are under the table rather than out in the yard.

Let the children be fed first. The children are Israel, God’s covenant people; it is God’s own word for the nation: Israel is my firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). The bread is the blessing of the Messiah’s ministry, and Mark’s readers have just watched five thousand people fed from five loaves. Jesus’ mission in his earthly life was first to Israel (Matthew 15:24; 10:5–6). This was God’s order of salvation: to the Jew first and also to the Greek (Romans 1:16). Note the word first, which only Mark records. A man who says first has a second course in mind. It implies that the Gentiles will be fed after. The door is not shut; there is an order. She is not being told there is no place for her; she is being told about the timing.

For it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs. Dogs was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles, as unclean as street dogs, and that has to be admitted rather than explained away. But Jesus uses a diminutive, kynaria, little dogs: house dogs, pets under the table, not the scavengers that ran in packs outside the town. The picture is of a household at a meal: you do not take food from the children’s plates and give it to the family pets. And that matters enormously, because it means the animal in his picture is inside the house. He has drawn a scene in which the outsider is already in the room.

Why speak like this? Several reasons come together. First, it states the truth of salvation history: Israel had a covenant priority that she did not. Second, it tests her faith, as God tested Abraham and Jacob, and draws it out into the open. Jesus already knew what he would do. He tests faith to bring it out, not to break it, as he did with Jairus, kept standing in the street while his daughter died. Third, the saying was a parable, an opening she could enter. His tone and look we cannot see; the house-dog word and the first were not a closed door. He has handed her a picture with a door in it, to see whether she would find the door. Everything she needs is in his own sentence. And watch what he actually does: he grants her request, immediately, at a distance, and Matthew records what he said about her: O woman, great is your faith! (Matthew 15:28). That is the loudest commentary available on the tone of verse 27, and it is not the commentary of a man who has just insulted somebody.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus despised Gentiles, or was racist, or that he learned from her to widen his mission, as some modern readers suggest. He had already healed Gentiles (5:1–20) and declared all foods clean (v. 19). He is in control of this conversation from beginning to end.

How it must have felt from the floor. And it is worth being honest about that. She did not have Matthew’s account or a commentary. She had a hard sentence and a sick child, and what she did with it in the next verse is the reason we still know who she was.

Does God still test us like this? Yes, though not usually with words spoken aloud. Sometimes our prayers meet silence, delay, or what looks like a refusal, and Scripture tells us that the testing of our faith produces steadfastness (James 1:2–4) and that faith, tested by fire, is more precious than gold (1 Peter 1:6–7). God does not test us to discover what is in us; he already knows. He tests us to bring it out, to strengthen it, and to show us his faithfulness. When God seems hard, do not conclude that he is against you. Look again at what he has said, as she did, and you will often find a door in it.

In a sentence. Jesus told the woman that Israel must be fed first, like children at a meal before the house dogs, testing her faith while leaving the door open.

On a Tuesday. When God seems to say no, or not yet, do not walk away. Keep coming. His delays often draw out faith. If a prayer of yours has met only silence, read again the promises of God that bear on it, and bring them back to him.

For worship. Even the Lord’s hardest word to her had a door in it. He spoke of the order of salvation, children first, and in the same breath placed the dogs under the table, inside the house. That is the way of our God: his severity is never without mercy, and his tests are always invitations. He held back the bread for a moment only so that she might discover how much was on the table, and he is the same Saviour who keeps nothing back from those who keep coming.
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table. “First” implies the Gentiles’ turn will come.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first and also to the Greek

verseByVerse.quote: But she answered him, "Yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answered: yes, Lord; yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.

Yes, Lord. She accepts what he has said. She does not argue that she deserves the bread, or protest the word dogs. She does not say the comparison is unfair, or that she has as much right as anybody, or that she is offended. She agrees with his description of her: yes, the children come first; yes, I am not one of them. That is not weakness. It is the opposite. She has stopped arguing about her standing, which is the argument she could never win, and she is about to argue about his generosity, which is an argument nobody has ever lost. “Lord” (kyrie) can mean simply sir, but here it carries more: she acknowledges his authority. She is the only person in Mark to call Jesus Lord.

Yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs. Brilliant faith. She takes his own picture and finds hope inside it. She picks up his own word, the household dog, the one inside, and stands on it. He put the animal under the table; she is simply pointing out where he put it. Yes, I am a dog, not a child. But dogs in a house are fed too: the crumbs that fall from the table belong to them. Nothing is taken from the children. The crumbs are not the loaf; feeding a dog under the table does not deprive a single child of a mouthful. I am not asking for the children’s bread, only a crumb. And a crumb of your power is enough to heal my daughter. She has understood, apparently by instinct, that there is always overflow where he is. Mark’s readers have just counted twelve baskets of it (6:43).

The only one who won an argument with Jesus. It is the only place in the four Gospels where somebody answers Jesus back in an argument and he tells them they are right. She has argued with Jesus from Jesus: not from her rights, her need, or her daughter’s suffering, though all three were real and she might have pleaded any of them, but from his own words and his own character.

Faith that wins. What makes her faith great (Matthew 15:28)? She is humble: she claims nothing. She is persistent: she does not give up at an apparent refusal. And she is confident: she believes there is so much grace in Jesus that even what falls from the table is enough. She takes the place of having no claim and appeals to his abundance. That is exactly what faith is.

The contrast. In this chapter, the religious experts heard Jesus’ word and resisted it, and even the disciples failed to understand (v. 18). This Gentile woman understood his parable at once and answered it with faith.

How to pray like her. That is the lesson in prayer, and it is worth having in plain terms because it is the difference between persevering faith and mere nagging. She came with a desperate need and met what looked like a closed door. She did not take offence and walk away. She also did not stand outside the door pleading louder in the hope of wearing him down. She listened to the very word that sounded like a refusal, took hold of it, and pressed further in. Her confidence did not rest on her own persistence; it rested on his goodness, which is why she could hold on through an apparent no. So if you are praying into silence, or into an answer that so far looks like no, learn her method rather than merely admiring her. Do not read the delay as the final verdict. Take God at his revealed character and his promises and press into them. Plead the crumbs. Plead his own word back to him: you said, you promised, you are the God who. That is not impertinence; it is the way every great prayer in Scripture is built, from Abraham at Sodom to Moses on the mountain (Genesis 18:22–33; Exodus 32:11–14).

Within his purpose, not against it. Hold it with the balance Scripture keeps everywhere. This is not a technique for bending God to your will. The Lord himself, praying in Gethsemane with perfect faith, added, Yet not what I will, but what you will (14:36), and the cup did not pass. Her persistence was answered because it was persistence within his purpose, not against it. So pray like her, refusing to let go, and trust like him, that the Father’s no, when it comes, is as wise and as loving as his yes.

Is it presumptuous to argue with God in prayer? Not when you argue from his own word and character, humbly, as she did. Scripture is full of such prayers: Abraham pleading for Sodom, Moses reminding God of his promises, the psalmists asking how long. God invites it: Put me in remembrance; let us argue together (Isaiah 43:26). What is presumptuous is demanding things God has not promised, or arguing from our own deserving. She said, Yes, Lord, first. Agree with God about yourself, then plead his mercy, and you are on the ground every saint has stood on.

In a sentence. Agreeing that she had no claim, the woman asked only for the crumbs that fall to the house dogs, trusting that a crumb of his grace was enough.

On a Tuesday. Take one request you have been bringing to God and rebuild it on her pattern. First, Yes, Lord: agree with what God says about you, that you have no claim. Then, yet: bring a specific promise or truth about his character and plead it. Write it down and pray it each day this week.

For worship. There is so much bread at Christ’s table that the crumbs are enough to cast out a demon. That is the abundance of our Lord, and this Gentile mother saw it before the apostles did. We come to God in exactly her posture: no merit, no claim, but complete confidence in the abundance of his mercy. Yes, Lord; yet. Blessed be the Saviour who is pleased when we argue from his goodness, and who never once has been out-asked by the faith he himself gives.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, "For this statement you may go your way; the demon has left your daughter." And she went home and found the child lying in bed and the demon gone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to her: because of this answer, go; the demon has left your daughter. She went home and found the child lying on the bed, and the demon gone.

For this statement you may go your way. Literally, because of this word. Her answer expressed faith, and Jesus honoured it. He names the thing that moved him, and it was her sentence, the one she made out of his own. Matthew records his words: O woman, great is your faith! Be it done for you as you desire (Matthew 15:28). And it is worth noting where the two great commendations of faith in the Gospels land: this woman, and a Roman centurion (Luke 7:9). Neither of them Jewish. Neither of them raised on the Scriptures. Both of them, in the Lord’s own judgment, ahead of anyone in Israel.

The demon has left your daughter. Past tense: it is already done. Healing at a distance. The girl was not present; Jesus did not go to her, touch her or speak to the demon. In this Gospel that is unusual: Mark’s exorcisms are close-range, physical, noisy. Here there is a sentence in one house and a quiet room in another. His word, spoken in one house, freed her in another. Only one other healing in the Gospels is like this: the centurion’s servant (Matthew 8:5–13), also for a Gentile, also commended for great faith. In both, the Gentile is blessed from a distance, perhaps a picture of how the nations would receive Christ’s blessing after his ascension, without seeing him.

Most of our praying is at a distance. That is worth having. The people we are most desperate about are usually not in the room: the child in another city, the friend in a hospital we cannot get to, the person who will not see us. Nothing in this account requires proximity. He said it where she was, and it was true where the child was.

And she went home. She believed his word without any sign, and went. These words are the last act of her faith and easy to miss. She has been given a sentence and nothing else: no sign, no accompanying miracle, no proof. She turns round and walks back, quite possibly a long way, on nothing but what he said. That is what faith always finally looks like: going home on the word.

And found the child lying in bed and the demon gone. “Lying” (beblēmenon, thrown down) may suggest she had been exhausted by the final convulsion, as with the boy in 9:26. Now she is at rest. The demon is gone, permanently. Mark’s detail is beautifully understated. A child who had been thrown about by an unclean spirit is lying down, quiet, resting. Her mother came in and found her at peace.

Does my faith help someone who does not believe? Yes, in this sense: God hears the prayers of his people for others, and acts in answer to them. This girl was freed because her mother believed and asked. Paul prayed for Israel’s salvation (Romans 10:1), and the church prayed for Peter in prison (Acts 12:5). But no one can believe on another’s behalf for salvation; each person must come to Christ himself (John 3:36). So pray for your unbelieving children and friends with confidence, because God is pleased to use prayer to open hearts. And leave the result with him, trusting that he is good and wise in what he does.

In a sentence. Because of her answer of faith, Jesus freed her daughter by a word from a distance, and she went home to find the child at peace.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s word reaches where you cannot. Pray for those far away, and trust him to act. Make a short list of the people you love who are out of your reach, by distance or by their own choice, and pray for each by name. Then go about your day on the strength of his word, as she went home.

For worship. And so a Phoenician woman, with no covenant, no Scriptures, no synagogue and no standing, got what she asked for from the God of Israel because she believed he was generous and would not stop saying so. The children were fed first. But the crumbs were enough to cast out a demon, and the second course, when it came, would be the nations of the earth sitting down at the table. Our Lord’s word runs faster than any messenger and further than any road, and wherever it goes, the darkness leaves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, in the region of the Decapolis. And they brought to him a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus left the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, into the region of the Decapolis. People brought to him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and begged him to lay his hand on him.

Then he returned from the region of Tyre and went through Sidon. A long detour, and the route has puzzled readers for centuries; it is worth tracing on a map. Tyre is on the coast. Sidon is about 25 miles (40 km) north of Tyre, the wrong direction entirely for the Sea of Galilee. Then he went southeast, around, to the Decapolis on the eastern side of the lake. A journey of perhaps 120 miles (200 km) on foot, possibly months on the road, and its one consistent feature is that almost every mile of it is Gentile ground. Jesus was spending time in Gentile territory, perhaps to be alone with his disciples, away from Herod and the crowds of Galilee. He has left Israel and is taking the long way round through the nations.

In the region of the Decapolis. The Ten Cities, a league of Greek cities, mainly east of the Jordan. This is where he met the man among the tombs, where the townspeople begged him to leave, and where he left one restored madman with a story and no training (5:1–20). The man went out and proclaimed in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marvelled. Now Jesus comes back, and instead of being asked to go, he is met by people bringing him their sick. Mark does not connect the dots for you. He does not need to. One man told one district what had happened to him, and when the Lord returned, the ground was ready. The witness had borne fruit.

A man who was deaf and had a speech impediment. The man does not come. He is brought. And think about why, because it is not incidental. He is deaf, which in that world meant he had never heard the reports about Jesus, could not have overheard the conversation about where he was, and could not have asked. Whatever he knew, somebody had to get across to him without words. “Speech impediment” (mogilalon) means speaking with difficulty, perhaps because he had become deaf and could not hear himself. The word appears only here in the New Testament and once in the Greek Old Testament, in Isaiah 35:6: then shall the tongue of the mute sing for joy. Mark has chosen a word that points to Isaiah’s prophecy of the coming of God to save. See verse 37.

And they begged him to lay his hand on him. Friends brought him, as so often (2:3). He could not hear of Jesus or ask for himself, so they ask on his behalf. It is the four on the roof again (2:3–5), and it is one of the most frequent patterns in this Gospel: a person who could not get to Jesus, and someone who would not let that be the end of it. So the whole way this man came to Christ was other people. They heard, they went, they made him understand, and they carried the request for him. If you are carrying somebody like that, praying for a person who cannot or will not pray, who does not understand enough to ask, who has no idea you have been at it for years, this is the man in the Bible for you. Nobody records the names of the people who brought him. They are simply they, and without them he would have lived and died deaf.

How do I bring someone to Jesus who cannot or will not come? Pray for him, first and persistently, because only God can open ears (Acts 16:14). Then do what these friends did: go where he is, find a way to communicate he can understand, and bring him into contact with Christ, through a kind word, a Gospel to read, an invitation to hear the word preached, or simply your own life of love. Do not wait for him to ask. Many people come to Christ because someone carried them: a praying mother, a patient friend, a church that welcomed them. Your name may never be recorded, but your carrying is seen.

In a sentence. After a long journey through Gentile lands, Jesus came to the Decapolis, where people brought him a deaf man who could hardly speak.

On a Tuesday. Some people cannot come to Jesus by themselves. Be one who brings them. Think of one person who is cut off from hearing the gospel, by disability, language, illness, age or hostility, and ask how you could help them hear it this month.

For worship. The Lord took the long way round through the nations, and the seed one healed man had scattered was already growing. He is the God whose word does not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11), who prepares the ground before he arrives, and who welcomes those carried to him as gladly as those who walk. No one is too cut off to be reached, because he comes to the places where the outsiders live.
verseByVerse.note: Going from Tyre through Sidon to the Decapolis is a long loop through Gentile territory.

parallels.desc: the healed man proclaims in the Decapolis

verseByVerse.quote: And taking him aside from the crowd privately, he put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. And looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, "Ephphatha," that is, "Be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking him aside, away from the crowd, Jesus put his fingers into his ears, spat and touched his tongue. Then, looking up to heaven, he sighed and said to him, Ephphatha, which means, Be opened.

And taking him aside from the crowd privately. Before anything else, notice this, because it is the mark of the man. There is a crowd; there always is. And Jesus takes hold of him and walks him out of it. A gentle consideration. Think what a jostling crowd is like for a man who cannot hear. He can see faces turned towards him, mouths moving, people pointing, the whole apparatus of being discussed, and he cannot follow one word of it. He is the object of attention and shut out of it at the same time. Jesus deals with him alone, face to face. It was also part of his wish not to become known as a wonder-worker (v. 36). That is a rebuke to every way of helping people that requires the helped to be visible: the testimony extracted, the need described in public, the person made into an occasion. He took him aside.

He put his fingers into his ears, and after spitting touched his tongue. This is one of the most elaborate things Jesus does in any healing in Mark, and modern readers find it odd. It is not odd once you ask the obvious question: how do you tell a deaf man what you are about to do? You cannot say it. So he says it in the only language available: sign language. Fingers into the ears: this is what I am dealing with. Saliva on the tongue: this too. Saliva was widely believed in the ancient world to have healing power, so the gesture would have read to that man as treatment being applied, but Jesus is not using medicine. He speaks to the man in the only language he could understand, and makes clear that the healing comes from him. It is a conversation, conducted entirely in signs, with a man who has perhaps never heard a sentence. He could have healed him from where he stood, as he had just healed a girl many miles away with a word. He goes to the trouble of being understood, by one man, in the man’s own language.

And looking up to heaven. Towards the Father, the source of power, in prayer (6:41; John 11:41). The man could see this too: help comes from God.

He sighed. A deep groan (estenaxen). Why would he sigh like that? He is not straining; the healing costs him no effort at all, and he will do it with one word. This is not exertion. It is grief at the ruin sin and suffering have brought on the world, and compassion for this man.
