They were exceedingly astonished and said to him: then who can be saved? Jesus looked at them and said: with man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.

Then who can be saved? The right conclusion. If even the rich, who seemed most blessed, cannot, then no one can. They had heard correctly.

Jesus looked at them. A deliberate, steady look, Mark’s third “look” in this passage (vv. 21, 23).

With man it is impossible. Yes, they had understood. Salvation is not difficult for human beings; it is impossible. No one, rich or poor, can save himself. Not by keeping commandments, giving money, or any effort. This is the heart of the gospel’s bad news: we are unable.

But not with God. For all things are possible with God. And this is the good news. What man cannot do, God does. An echo of the angel to Sarah: Is anything too hard for the Lord? (Genesis 18:14). Salvation is God’s work from beginning to end: he gives the new heart, he grants repentance and faith, he draws us (John 6:44; Ephesians 2:8–9). If God can save a rich man, and he can (Zacchaeus, Joseph of Arimathea), he can save anyone. The camel can go through the needle if God takes it through.

What it does not mean. Not that people have no responsibility to repent and believe. But even our repentance and faith are God’s gifts, the fruit of his grace, not our contribution to it.

In a sentence. Jesus told his astonished disciples that salvation is impossible for human beings but not for God, for whom all things are possible.

For worship. Pray for the hardest cases you know with confidence. Salvation is impossible with man, which is why it is always God’s work.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter began to say to him: see, we have left everything and followed you. Jesus said: truly, I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands for my sake and for the gospel who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

See, we have left everything and followed you. Peter contrasts the disciples with the rich man: we have done what he would not. It is true (1:18, 20). Matthew adds his question: What then will we have? (Matthew 19:27). There is a hint of self-congratulation.

There is no one who has left. Jesus does not rebuke Peter. He promises reward. Following him costs: home, family, property. In the early church, many converts were disowned by their families or lost their property (Hebrews 10:34).

For my sake and for the gospel. As in 8:35, only Mark adds “and for the gospel”. The cost is borne for Jesus and his message.

Who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time. Not only in heaven, now. How? In the family of God. The one who loses his earthly family gains brothers, sisters and mothers in the church (3:34–35), homes opened to him, and a share in all that belongs to the people of God (Acts 2:44–46). Notice that “fathers” is missing from the list of what is received: in God’s family, there is one Father (Matthew 23:9).

With persecutions. Only Mark adds this, and it is honest. The reward is not a comfortable life. Following Jesus brings persecution as well as family. Mark’s readers in Rome knew this well.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the rich man’s question (v. 17). What he would not give up everything for, they will receive.

But many who are first will be last, and the last first. A warning, perhaps to Peter. The rich and powerful, first in this world, may be last in the kingdom. The disciples, last in the world’s eyes, will be first. But also: those who think of themselves as first, because of their sacrifices, may find themselves last. Reward is grace, not wages earned (Matthew 20:1–16).

In a sentence. Jesus promised that everyone who leaves family and property for him and the gospel will receive a hundred times more now, in God’s family, with persecutions, and eternal life to come.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you family or property, look around at the church. These are your brothers, sisters and mothers. And if you have a home, open it to those who have lost theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Walking ahead (vv. 32–34). Mark gives us a picture worth stopping over: a road going up to Jerusalem, Jesus striding out in front, and behind him a group that is amazed and a crowd that is frightened. Then he tells them, for the third and most detailed time, exactly what is waiting — handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised.

The request (vv. 35–45). And immediately James and John ask for the two best seats. The other ten are furious, which is not righteous indignation but competition. So Jesus lays down the law of his kingdom — the great one is the servant, the first is the slave — and grounds it in himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Jericho (vv. 46–52). The last miracle before Jerusalem. A blind beggar shouts a messianic title that none of the disciples has yet used, is told to be quiet by the crowd, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road to the cross.

The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark 10:45 is the theological centre of this Gospel, and every word repays weighing.

A ransom — lytron — was the price paid to set a captive free: the sum laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block. Jesus says his own life is that price.

And a ransom is a substitute — one thing given instead of another. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, the many going free because the One is handed over.

Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many, and by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous (Isa. 53:11–12). That word many rings through the prophecy, and Jesus claims it as his own errand.

And to whom is the price paid? Not, as some early teachers imagined, to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim. The debt is owed to the justice of God — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself.

Here, then, is why he came. Not first to teach, or to heal, or even to model servanthood, though he did all three. To die in the room of sinners who could never buy themselves back. Nineteen verses earlier the disciples asked then who can be saved? and were told with man it is impossible, but not with God. This is how.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question — What do you want me to do for you? — asked twice in fifteen verses.

It is put to James and John in verse 36 and to a blind beggar in verse 51. Mark has done that deliberately, and the two answers are the whole chapter.

James and John ask for glory. They open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and then name the two best seats in the kingdom. They get a redirection and a warning.

Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight. He gets exactly what he asks for, immediately.

Now: the question is still being asked, and most of us answer it more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank-cheque prayer — do what I have decided — dressed up religiously. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And notice what makes Bartimaeus's answer better. It is not humility as a technique. He asked for the thing he actually needed, from someone he had correctly identified, having first asked for mercy rather than a favour. He had no credentials, no standing, and no way of repaying anybody — which is precisely the child of verse 15, arriving at the other end of the chapter with nothing in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. They were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Taking the Twelve aside again, he began to tell them what was going to happen to him.

And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem. The first time Mark names the destination. Jerusalem stands about 2,500 feet (750 m) up in the Judean hills, so one always went “up” to it, especially from the Jordan valley, which is below sea level. The road from Jericho climbs about 3,500 feet (1,000 m) in 15 miles (25 km).

And Jesus was walking ahead of them. A vivid picture, probably from Peter’s memory. Jesus leads, resolute, going to his death on purpose. Luke says: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). He is not dragged to the cross; he walks ahead to it. A shepherd goes before his sheep (John 10:4).

And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. Something in his manner awed them. Two groups may be meant: the Twelve, who were amazed, and the wider group of followers, who were afraid. They sensed that something terrible lay ahead.

And taking the twelve again. Aside, privately, as before.

He began to tell them what was to happen to him. He knows. Nothing will take him by surprise.

In a sentence. On the road up to Jerusalem, Jesus walked ahead of his awed and frightened followers and began to tell the Twelve what would happen to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walks ahead of you into every hard road. Follow him there.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes. They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles. They will mock him, spit on him, flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.

The third prediction. The fullest and most detailed of the three (8:31; 9:31). It reads almost like a summary of chapters 14–16, and Mark’s readers would recognise each step.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. “See” (idou): look, pay attention.

Delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes. Betrayed into the hands of the Jewish leaders (14:10, 43).

And they will condemn him to death. The Sanhedrin’s verdict (14:64).

And deliver him over to the Gentiles. New detail. The Jewish leaders did not have the right to carry out executions under Roman rule (John 18:31), and so they would hand him to Pilate (15:1). God’s Messiah would be rejected by both Jews and Gentiles; the whole world is guilty (Acts 4:27).

And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. Every one was fulfilled: mocking (14:65; 15:17–20, 29–32), spitting (14:65; 15:19), flogging (15:15), killing (15:24, 37). Isaiah had foretold it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). Roman flogging, with a whip of leather straps weighted with bone or metal, was so savage that men sometimes died under it.

And after three days he will rise. Again the promise. It is always there.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve in detail that in Jerusalem he would be betrayed, condemned, handed to the Gentiles, mocked, spat upon, flogged and killed, and would rise after three days.

For worship. He knew every detail of what he would suffer, and still walked ahead. That is the measure of his love.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to him and said: Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask. He said to them: what do you want me to do for you? They said: grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.

The contrast. Each time Jesus predicts his suffering, the disciples respond with something that shows they have not understood: Peter’s rebuke (8:32), the argument about greatness (9:34), and now this. Immediately after hearing that he will be spat on and killed, two of his closest friends ask for the best seats.

James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Two of the inner three, who had been with him on the mountain. Matthew says their mother asked on their behalf (Matthew 20:20). She was probably Salome, possibly the sister of Mary, which would make them Jesus’ cousins (compare 15:40 with Matthew 27:56 and John 19:25). Family closeness may have encouraged the request.

Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you. A blank cheque. They approach Jesus as one might approach a king, asking for a favour before stating it. Herod had made such a promise (6:22–23), with disastrous results.

What do you want me to do for you? Jesus will ask the very same question of blind Bartimaeus (v. 51). The two requests are a study in contrast: they ask for glory, he asks for sight.

Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory. To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour and power. They believe he is the Messiah, and that he will reign in glory. They have seen that glory on the mountain. But they want the glory without the cross, and they want it for themselves, above the others. Ironically, those who will be at his right and left when he is “enthroned” will be two criminals on crosses (15:27).

In a sentence. Straight after Jesus predicted his suffering, James and John asked him for the highest places of honour in his glory.

On a Tuesday. What are you asking Jesus for? Make sure your prayers are not a request for position but for his will.
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: you do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptised with the baptism with which I am baptised? They said: we are able. Jesus said: the cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptised you will be baptised; but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant; it is for those for whom it has been prepared.

You do not know what you are asking. They do not know what his glory involves, or the path to it.

The cup that I drink. Key image. In the Old Testament, the “cup” is often a picture of God’s judgement and wrath, which the wicked must drink (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15–28). Jesus will pray in Gethsemane: Remove this cup from me (14:36). The cup he drinks is the wrath of God against sin, which he takes in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty that sinners deserved.

Or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized. “Baptism” here means being overwhelmed, submerged, as by a flood of waters (Psalm 42:7; 69:1–2). Jesus speaks of his coming suffering and death as a baptism (Luke 12:50).

We are able. Brave and ignorant.

The cup that I drink you will drink. Jesus predicts that they will indeed suffer. James was the first of the apostles to be martyred, beheaded by Herod Agrippa about AD 44 (Acts 12:2). John suffered exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9) and, by tradition, lived to an old age. But their cup will not be the same as his. Only he drinks the cup of God’s wrath for sin. Theirs is the cup of suffering for his sake (Colossians 1:24 speaks of this in a different sense).

But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant. Not that Jesus lacks authority, but that he submits to the Father’s will (13:32). The places are assigned by the Father.

But it is for those for whom it has been prepared. Prepared by God, in his eternal purpose. The places of honour in the kingdom are not won by ambition or asking, but by God’s sovereign appointment. Matthew adds: by my Father (Matthew 20:23).

In a sentence. Jesus told James and John they did not understand that his glory comes through the cup of suffering and wrath; they would suffer too, but places of honour are the Father’s to give.

On a Tuesday. Following Christ will involve a cup of suffering. But he has drunk the cup of wrath, so you never will.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the ten heard this, they began to be indignant at James and John. Jesus called them to him and said: you know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.

They began to be indignant at James and John. Not because the request was wrong, but because the two had got in first. The ten had the same ambitions.

And Jesus called them to him. All twelve. This is for all of them.

Those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles. “Considered”, “seem to rule”: a hint of irony. Their power is not what it looks like; the real ruler is God.

Lord it over them … exercise authority over them. Both verbs have a prefix (kata-) that means power used downward, against people, to dominate. The world’s pattern of leadership is power over others for the leader’s benefit. Rome knew this well.

But it shall not be so among you. A flat contradiction. Not “it should not”, but “it is not”: this is not how my community works.

Whoever would be great among you must be your servant. “Servant” (diakonos): one who waits at table.

And whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. “Slave” (doulos) goes further still: one who belongs to another and has no rights. Two steps down: servant, slave. The way up is down. Greatness in the kingdom is measured by service.

What it does not mean. Not that there is no authority in the church. Elders are to lead and be obeyed (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12). But Christian authority is exercised as service, for the good of others, never for the leader’s benefit (1 Peter 5:1–3).

In a sentence. When the others resented James and John, Jesus taught that in his kingdom, unlike the world, greatness is shown by being a servant and the first must be the slave of all.

On a Tuesday. If you lead at work, home or church, ask: am I using my power for others or for myself?

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

The key verse of Mark. This one sentence sums up the whole purpose of Jesus’ coming. It explains the three passion predictions and everything that follows in chapters 11–16.

For even the Son of Man. The Son of Man of Daniel 7, to whom all nations will give service (Daniel 7:14). If anyone had the right to be served, it was he.

Came not to be served but to serve. “Came”: implying that he came from somewhere, from heaven, with a purpose. And the purpose reversed every expectation. The King came as a servant. He washed his disciples’ feet (John 13:1–17). He took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7).

And to give his life. The supreme service: his life itself. Not taken from him but given (John 10:18).

As a ransom. Key word. A “ransom” (lytron) was the price paid to free a slave, a prisoner of war, or someone condemned to death. In the Old Testament, the firstborn were redeemed with a payment (Numbers 3:46–48), and a man whose ox had killed someone could pay a ransom for his own life (Exodus 21:30). We are slaves of sin and under the sentence of death (Romans 6:23). Jesus pays the price of our freedom with his own life. The price is not paid to Satan, as some of the early fathers thought, but to the justice of God, whose law we have broken.

For many. “For” (anti) means “in place of”, “instead of”. This is substitution: he gives his life in place of theirs. The background is Isaiah 53, the suffering servant, who poured out his soul to death… yet he bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12; also 53:10–11). Jesus is that servant. His death is a substitutionary payment, bearing the penalty of sin in the place of sinners.

Who are the many? “Many” contrasts the one who dies with the great number of those for whom he dies. The phrase comes from Isaiah 53, where the servant bears the sin of many and makes many to be accounted righteous. Reformed theology reads this as definite: Christ gave his life as a ransom for his people, those the Father had given him (John 10:11, 15; 17:9), and his death actually secures their freedom. A ransom that is paid frees the captive. Other traditions read “many” as “all”, a universal offer. Verdict: the ransom is real and effective; it does not merely make freedom possible but actually purchases it for the many. This is definite atonement. And the gospel offer still goes freely to all, since no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).

In a sentence. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as the price that frees many, in their place.

For worship. You were bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20). Worship the servant King who gave his life as your ransom, and serve others as he served you.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Jericho. As he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! Many rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me!

The placing. The second healing of a blind man, matching the one at Bethsaida (8:22–26). Between them, Jesus has taught about the cross and his disciples have been blind to it. Now, at the end of the section, a blind man sees and follows Jesus on the way. He is a model disciple, set against James and John.

And they came to Jericho. About 15 miles (25 km) north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. The last stop before the climb to the city. Pilgrims for Passover passed through in crowds.

As he was leaving Jericho. Luke says as he drew near to Jericho (Luke 18:35). There were two Jerichos, the ancient ruined city and the new Herodian town a short distance away; Jesus may have been leaving one and approaching the other. Matthew mentions two blind men (Matthew 20:30); Mark names the one who was perhaps known to the early church.

Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus. The only person healed in Mark who is named. “Bar” is Aramaic for “son of”, so Mark translates. Naming him suggests he was known to Mark’s readers, a living witness in the church.

Jesus of Nazareth. The crowd’s name for him, a man from a small town.

Jesus, Son of David. Bartimaeus’ name for him, and a far greater one. “Son of David” is a messianic title: the promised king from David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1). This is the first time in Mark anyone uses it. The blind man sees what the crowd does not. The Messiah was expected to give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1). And Jesus does not silence him: the hour for the secret is ending. He is about to enter Jerusalem as the Son of David (11:10).

Have mercy on me! The cry of one with no claim, only need. The prayer of the tax collector (Luke 18:13). The church has prayed it for centuries (Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy).

And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. Like the disciples with the children (v. 13). A beggar was a nuisance.

But he cried out all the more. Persistent, unembarrassed, desperate faith. He knows this is his one chance; Jesus is passing by and will not come this way again.

In a sentence. As Jesus left Jericho, blind Bartimaeus cried out to him as the Son of David for mercy, and would not be silenced.

For worship. Pray the beggar’s prayer: Son of David, have mercy on me. And don’t let anyone shame you out of crying to Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped and said: call him. They called the blind man, saying to him: take heart; get up; he is calling you. Throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.

And Jesus stopped. On his way to the cross, with the weight of the world on him, Jesus stops for one blind beggar.

Call him. He does not go to Bartimaeus. He calls him to come, and Bartimaeus must respond. And he involves the crowd: those who had rebuked him are now told to call him.

Take heart. Get up; he is calling you. Three short commands, and the crowd changes its tune. These could be the words of every evangelist: take heart, get up, Jesus is calling you.

And throwing off his cloak. A beggar’s cloak was spread on the ground to collect coins, and was his covering at night (Exodus 22:26–27). It was all he had. He throws it aside. The rich man would not leave his possessions (v. 22); the beggar leaves his only one, without being asked.

He sprang up and came to Jesus. Eager, joyful, at once. A blind man, guided by the voice.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped and called Bartimaeus, who threw off his cloak, sprang up and came to him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is calling you. What cloak do you need to throw aside to come to him?
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: what do you want me to do for you? The blind man said: Rabbi, let me recover my sight. Jesus said: go your way; your faith has made you well. Immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.

What do you want me to do for you? The same question as to James and John (v. 36). They asked for glory; he asks for mercy and sight. It is obvious what a blind man wants, but Jesus asks him to say it: to express his need and his faith.

Rabbi. Literally Rabbouni, “my master”, a more personal and reverent form, used elsewhere only by Mary Magdalene at the empty tomb (John 20:16).

Let me recover my sight. “Recover” suggests he once could see.

Go your way; your faith has made you well. “Made you well” (sesōken) is literally “has saved you”, the same word as for the woman with the bleeding (5:34). Physical healing and spiritual salvation are both in it. His faith was the empty hand that received what Jesus gave; the power was Jesus’.

And immediately he recovered his sight. No touch, no saliva, no second stage. Just the word.

And followed him on the way. The last words of the section, and the most important. Jesus told him to go his way; his way was Jesus’ way. “On the way”: the road to Jerusalem and the cross (v. 32). He is the picture of the true disciple, which the Twelve should be: his eyes opened, he follows Jesus to the cross. This is what Mark wants for his readers.

In a sentence. Asked what he wanted, Bartimaeus asked for his sight, received it at once through faith, and followed Jesus on the way to Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Has Jesus opened your eyes? Then follow him on the way, wherever it leads.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. Not a contradiction but a difference of purpose: Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt; Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others. Mark's silence is not denial but a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in.

"Why do you call me good?" is not a denial that Jesus is good or that he is God, and he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Good Teacher was easy flattery; Jesus stops him and asks whether he knows what he is saying. Either the word should not have been used — or it is right, and the man must reckon with who is standing in front of him. A door held open, not a door shut.

And v. 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom (lytron) is the price paid to buy a captive out of bondage. The word rendered for is anti — in the place of, one thing given instead of another — so he does not merely die for our benefit but in our stead. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12), that word many tolling through the prophecy and claimed here by Jesus as his own errand. And the price is not paid to the devil, as some early teachers imagined — he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27) and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, and God in the person of his Son pays it himself.
10.examples:
Then: the same question asked twice, fifteen verses apart. What do you want me to do for you? — to James and John (v. 36), and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

The brothers open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and name the two best seats in the kingdom. Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight.

Now: most of us pray more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank cheque dressed up religiously — a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgement. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And note what actually makes Bartimaeus's answer better. Not humility as a technique. He had correctly identified who was passing — Son of David, a messianic title not one of the disciples had yet used out loud — and he asked for mercy, which is what you ask for when you have no claim of any kind and the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking.

And then there is the cloak (v. 50). A beggar's outer cloak was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch coins, his bed at night, his shelter, and the one possession the Law protected (Ex. 22:26–27). It was everything he owned. He flung it aside, blind, with no idea where it landed, because it might slow him down by four seconds.

Set that against the man at the start of the chapter, asked to give up his possessions and going away sorrowful because he had a great many. One had much and would not let go of any of it; one had a single thing and did not think about it twice. Mark put them at opposite ends of the same chapter on purpose.

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>16</sup>And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. <sup>17</sup>And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>18</sup>And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. <sup>19</sup>And when evening came they went out of the city. <sup>20</sup>As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. <sup>21</sup>And Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. <sup>23</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. <sup>24</sup>Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. <sup>25</sup>And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.” <sup>27</sup>And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, <sup>28</sup>and they said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>30</sup>Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” <sup>31</sup>And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>32</sup>But shall we say, ‘From man’?”—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. <sup>33</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
11.overview:
After ten chapters of hushing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to the throne — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said the king would come. The crowd throws down cloaks as they did for Jehu, spreads leafy branches cut from the fields, and shouts the Passover psalm at him: Hosanna — save now. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do, and by Friday the road is empty.

Then he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves, because it is late.

What he does the next morning is therefore not a loss of temper. He had seen all of it the night before, slept on it, and walked two miles back. And Mark wraps the temple inside a fig tree to tell you what it means: a tree in full leaf and no fruit, cursed on the way in; the tables overturned; and on the third morning the tree dead to its roots. Israel's worship that week was magnificent from a distance. He came near, and found leaves.

Out of the dead tree comes the great teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness. And the chapter ends with the Sanhedrin asking the right question — by what authority? — and being handed one question in return that would have led them home, and spending it instead on a calculation about the crowd.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Entry, the Fig Tree, and the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The entry (vv. 1–11). After nine chapters of silencing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to be king — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said. The crowd sings the Passover psalm at him. Then he walks into the temple, looks around at everything, and goes out to Bethany because it is late.

The tree (vv. 12–14). The next morning, hungry, he goes to a fig tree in full leaf and finds nothing on it — and Mark adds the detail that makes the whole thing intelligible: it was not the season for figs. He curses it, and the disciples hear him.

The temple (vv. 15–19). And then he does to the temple what he has just done to the tree. Tables over, seats over, the traffic stopped — and two verses of Scripture that between them tell the leadership exactly what their house has become.

The lesson (vv. 20–26). Next morning the tree is dead to the roots, and out of that comes the great passage on faith, prayer and forgiveness.

Mark has wrapped the temple inside the fig tree deliberately. The tree is the temple: leaves and no fruit, an advertisement with nothing behind it, and it is finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree for having no figs out of season? The objection is old and it deserves a proper answer, and the answer turns on the leaves.

A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after. In early spring the branches put out small green knobs — the paggim — which are edible, and a hungry traveller ate them. The leaves follow. So a tree standing in full leaf is making a claim: there is fruit here.

The main harvest was months away, which is exactly why Mark tells us it was not the season for figs. He is not embarrassed by the detail; he supplies it, so that no reader can mistake this for agricultural pique. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own appearance, and it had none.

And then look where Mark has put it. He splits the story in two and wedges the temple between the halves — curse (vv. 12–14), temple (vv. 15–19), withered (vv. 20–21). It is his habitual sandwich, and it is never accidental. The tree interprets the temple.

Israel's worship at that moment was in full leaf: the courts crowded, the sacrifices running, the festival packed, the money changing hands. From a distance it looked like the healthiest religion in the world. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), found nothing, and the next morning both the tree and the temple were under sentence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a den of robbers — the phrase everybody quotes and almost nobody reads properly.

A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they divide the takings and feel perfectly safe. That is the charge, and Jeremiah, whom Jesus is quoting, spells it out: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' (Jer. 7:9–11).

Now: the accusation is not primarily about commerce in church buildings. It is about using religion as a safe house — going out into the week, doing what you do, and coming back on Sunday to feel delivered.

That is a test anyone can run. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about the way you conduct your business, or less? If a man can hold a grudge for eleven years, cut corners at work, be cold at home — and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without changing any of it, then he has not been worshipping. He has been using the den.

And note where the tables were standing. The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew was permitted to pray — which is why Mark alone keeps Isaiah's full phrase, for all the nations. The arrangement that made the insiders comfortable had physically evicted the outsiders, and nobody had noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples. He told them: go into the village ahead of you, and as soon as you enter it you will find a colt tied up that no one has ever sat on. Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks why you are doing this, say: the Lord needs it and will send it back here at once.

Setting. The last week of Jesus’ life begins. Mark devotes six of his sixteen chapters (11–16) to this one week, which shows where the weight of the gospel lies: in the death and resurrection of Jesus. The week is Passover, when Jerusalem’s population swelled with pilgrims, perhaps several times over.

Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives. Two villages on the eastern slopes of the Mount of Olives, the ridge just east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron valley. Bethany, about two miles (3 km) from the city, was the home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus, where Jesus stayed during this week (v. 11). The Mount of Olives was associated with the coming of the Lord: on that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4).

You will find a colt tied. A young donkey (Matthew 21:2 mentions its mother as well). Jesus knew it would be there: either by divine foreknowledge, or by a prior arrangement with the owner. Either way, he is in control. Every step of this week is deliberate.

On which no one has ever sat. An animal used for a sacred purpose had to be one that had never been put to ordinary work (Numbers 19:2; Deuteronomy 21:3; 1 Samuel 6:7). This colt is set apart for the King.

The Lord has need of it. “The Lord” (ho kyrios) could mean simply “its master” (Jesus as the one with the right to it), but Mark’s readers would hear the fuller meaning. The Lord of all creation borrows a donkey.

And will send it back here immediately. A promise to return it. The King borrows; he does not seize, as kings did (1 Samuel 8:16–17).

In a sentence. Approaching Jerusalem for the last week of his life, Jesus deliberately sent two disciples to bring an unridden colt for him to ride.

On a Tuesday. “The Lord has need of it.” What do you have that he might want to borrow for his purposes? Hold it ready.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

parallels.desc: a heifer on which a yoke has never come

verseByVerse.quote: And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went and found a colt tied at a door, outside in the street, and they untied it. Some of the people standing there said: what are you doing, untying the colt? They told them what Jesus had said, and the people let them go.

And found a colt tied at a door outside in the street. Precise details, as if from an eyewitness: the door, the street, the bystanders. Everything happened exactly as Jesus said.

What are you doing, untying the colt? A natural question: two strangers taking someone’s donkey.

And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. The word of Jesus was enough. Perhaps the owners knew him, or had been asked in advance. Either way, Mark shows the disciples obeying, and Jesus’ word coming true in every detail. If his word about a donkey can be trusted, so can his word about his death and resurrection (10:33–34).

In a sentence. The disciples found the colt exactly as Jesus had said, and when questioned, repeated his words and were allowed to take it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word comes true in small things and great. Obey it in the small ones, and trust it for the great.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. Many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches they had cut from the fields.

And he sat on it. A deliberate act of prophetic symbolism. Jesus had walked everywhere. Now, for the last two miles, he rides. The prophet Zechariah had foretold: Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion! … Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). Mark does not quote it (Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 do), but the action speaks for itself. Jesus is publicly claiming to be the King. The time for secrecy is over.

A donkey, not a horse. Kings went to war on horses. A donkey was the mount of peace. Solomon rode David’s mule to his coronation (1 Kings 1:33–40). Zechariah goes on: he shall speak peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). Jesus comes as a king, but a humble king of peace, not a warrior to overthrow Rome.

And many spread their cloaks on the road. A gesture of homage to a king. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the people spread their garments under him (2 Kings 9:13).

And others spread leafy branches. John specifies palm branches (John 12:13), which gives us “Palm Sunday”. Palm branches had been waved when Simon Maccabeus liberated Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 13:51), and they were symbols of Jewish nationalism. Branches were also used at the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:40). Mark’s word means leafy branches, perhaps straw from the fields.

In a sentence. Jesus rode the colt toward Jerusalem, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of the humble king, and the crowds honoured him with cloaks and branches.

For worship. Lay down your cloak before the King: give him the honour and the things that are yours.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!

Hosanna! Key word. A Hebrew expression (hôšî‘â nā’) meaning “save, we pray” or “save now”, from Psalm 118:25. Over time it had become a shout of praise and acclamation, like “hurrah” or “God save the king”. Both meanings fit: the crowd praises Jesus, and unknowingly prays for exactly what he has come to do.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Psalm 118:26. Psalm 118 was one of the Hallel psalms (113–118) sung at Passover, and pilgrims would sing it as they approached Jerusalem. It was a greeting for pilgrims arriving at the temple. But “he who comes” had also become a title for the Messiah (Matthew 11:3). The crowd sings it to Jesus. And the same psalm speaks of the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22), which Jesus will quote against the leaders (12:10).

Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Only Mark records this line. It makes the political hope explicit: they expect Jesus to restore David’s kingdom, perhaps by overthrowing Rome. The kingdom is indeed coming, but not as they imagine. Within days, the crowd will be shouting for his crucifixion (15:13–14).

Hosanna in the highest! “In the highest” means in the highest heavens: let the angels and God himself join the praise, or, save us, O God who is in the highest.

What it does not mean. Not that the crowd understood Jesus. They acclaimed him as a political Messiah. But their words were truer than they knew. He is the Son of David, and he has come to save.

In a sentence. The crowds hailed Jesus with the pilgrim psalm, crying “Hosanna” and blessing the coming kingdom of David, not knowing how truly they spoke.

For worship. Christians still sing these words at the Lord’s Supper and in worship. When you say “Hosanna”, mean both: praise him, and ask him to save.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. When he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the Twelve.

And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. Not the palace, not the Roman fortress. The Messiah goes straight to the house of God. Malachi had promised: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple … But who can endure the day of his coming? (Malachi 3:1–2).

The temple. Herod’s temple, under construction for more than forty years (John 2:20), was one of the wonders of the ancient world: white marble and gold, on an enormous platform covering about 35 acres (14 hectares). The Greek word here (hieron) means the whole temple complex, with its courts, not just the sanctuary building.

And when he had looked around at everything. An inspection. Only Mark records it. Jesus looks at everything, as a master inspects his house, or as God looks for fruit from his vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7). Tomorrow he will act on what he saw.

As it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. He stayed in Bethany each night of this week (v. 19; 14:3), perhaps with Lazarus and his sisters, and on the last night on the Mount of Olives (Luke 21:37). Jerusalem was overcrowded at Passover, and also dangerous for him.

What it does not mean. Not an anticlimax. Mark tells this deliberately: the King has come, looked, and will judge. The quiet inspection prepares for the cursing of the fig tree and the cleansing of the temple.

In a sentence. Jesus entered Jerusalem and went to the temple, where he looked around at everything, before returning to Bethany for the night.

On a Tuesday. The Lord looks at everything in his house: in his church, and in your life. What does he see?
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, as they came from Bethany, he was hungry. Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it: may no one ever eat fruit from you again. And his disciples heard it.

The structure. Mark sandwiches the cleansing of the temple between two halves of the fig tree story (vv. 12–14, 20–21), as he often does (3:20–35; 5:21–43; 6:7–30). Each story interprets the other. The fig tree is the temple: full of leaves (religious activity), with no fruit (true worship and righteousness). And the withered tree shows what will happen to the temple: it will be destroyed (13:2).

He was hungry. Truly human.

A fig tree in leaf. Fig trees in Palestine produced leaves in March or April, and with them, or even before, small early knobs (paggim) that were edible, though not very tasty, and that local people ate. The main crop came in June and later. A tree in full leaf ought to have had these early fruits. If it had leaves but no early fruit, it would not bear at all that year. Its leaves were a false advertisement.

For it was not the season for figs. Mark’s note explains why there were no ripe figs: it was Passover, early spring. But this makes the point sharper, not weaker. The tree’s leaves claimed fruit it did not have. The cursing is not a fit of temper at an innocent tree. It is an acted parable, like the prophets’ symbolic actions (Jeremiah 13:1–11; 19:1–13).

The fig tree in the prophets. The fig tree was a recognised picture of Israel. When I would gather them, declares the Lord, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered (Jeremiah 8:13). Hosea and Micah use the same image (Hosea 9:10, 16; Micah 7:1). God came looking for fruit in his people and found none.

May no one ever eat fruit from you again. The only miracle of judgement in the Gospels. A sentence pronounced on fruitless religion.

And his disciples heard it. Mark notes this for the sequel (v. 21).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was unreasonable or petulant. And not that God has rejected the Jewish people for ever (Romans 11:1–2, 25–29). The judgement fell on the temple and the leadership that rejected their Messiah, and the temple was destroyed in AD 70.

In a sentence. Finding a fig tree full of leaves but with no fruit, Jesus cursed it, an acted parable of God’s judgement on the fruitless temple.

On a Tuesday. Leaves without fruit: religious activity without faith, love and obedience. God is looking for fruit (John 15:8; Galatians 5:22–23).
verseByVerse.note: Leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came to Jerusalem. He entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple. He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons, and he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.

What was happening in the temple. All the trading took place in the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, the only part of the temple where non-Jews could come to pray. Beyond it, warning notices threatened death to any Gentile who went further. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice that were certified unblemished, and it was easier to buy them on the spot than to bring them from far away. They also needed to pay the annual temple tax in a particular coinage, the Tyrian shekel, because Roman coins bore the emperor’s image. So the money-changers exchanged currency, at a profit. This trade was controlled by the high priestly family, and was a source of their great wealth.

And began to drive out those who sold and those who bought. A dramatic, physical act. He did not just preach against it. He emptied the market.

He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. Pigeons (doves) were the sacrifice the poor could afford (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8), as Jesus’ own parents had offered (Luke 2:24). Profiting from the poor in the house of God was especially offensive.

And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. Only Mark records this. The temple courts were used as a short cut between the city and the Mount of Olives. Jesus stopped the traffic. The house of God was not a thoroughfare.

Cleansing or judgement? Both. It was a cleansing: the temple was being restored, for a moment, to its purpose. But it was also an acted prophecy of judgement, like the fig tree. Jesus was not reforming the temple, but announcing its end. He himself would be the new temple (John 2:19–21; 14:58), the place where God meets his people.

One cleansing or two? John records a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22). Some think there was only one, placed differently for theological reasons. But there is no difficulty in Jesus doing it twice, at the beginning and end of his ministry, and the details differ.

In a sentence. Jesus drove out the traders and money-changers from the Court of the Gentiles, overturned their tables, and stopped the temple from being used as a short cut.

On a Tuesday. What commercial or worldly business has crept into the place where you meet with God? Let him overturn the tables.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers." And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was teaching them and saying: is it not written, My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations? But you have made it a den of robbers. The chief priests and the scribes heard it and were looking for a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.

Is it not written. Jesus explains his actions from Scripture. He combines two prophets.

My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations. Isaiah 56:7. Isaiah foresaw a day when foreigners and eunuchs, excluded people, would be welcomed to worship in God’s house. Only Mark includes “for all the nations”, which matters, because the market was in the one court where the nations could pray. The Gentiles had been squeezed out by commerce. And “my house”: Jesus speaks of the temple as his Father’s, and his own.

But you have made it a den of robbers. Jeremiah 7:11, from Jeremiah’s great sermon at the gate of the temple, before its first destruction by Babylon in 586 BC. The people thought the temple would protect them whatever they did. Jeremiah warned that God would destroy it, as he had destroyed Shiloh (Jeremiah 7:12–14). A “den” is where robbers hide after their crimes, a safe place. The leaders were not just cheating in the temple; they were using the temple as a refuge from the consequences of their sins. The quotation carries the threat with it: as before, the temple will be destroyed.

And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him. The first time the chief priests appear as Jesus’ enemies in Mark. Until now the opposition was mainly from Pharisees and scribes. Now the temple authorities, whose income and authority he had challenged, join in. The plot to kill him begins in earnest (14:1).

For they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. They could not arrest him openly, because the crowds were with him.

And when evening came they went out of the city. Back to Bethany.

In a sentence. Quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah, Jesus accused the leaders of turning God’s house of prayer for all nations into a robbers’ hideout, and they began plotting to kill him.

For worship. The church is God’s house of prayer for all nations. Is your church a place where outsiders can come and pray, or have other things crowded them out?
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark keeps “for all the nations” from Isaiah’s words.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples

verseByVerse.quote: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered." And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. Peter remembered and said to him: Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered. Jesus answered them: have faith in God.

They saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. Not a gradual decline. Completely dead, from the roots up, within a day. Complete judgement (Hosea 9:16: their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit; Job 18:16).

And Peter remembered. Mark’s source, very likely.

Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered. Astonishment.

And Jesus answered them, Have faith in God. A surprising response. Jesus does not explain the fig tree. He turns to faith. Why? Because the temple, the centre of Israel’s worship, is under judgement. Where will God’s people now meet with him? Not in a building, but through faith in God, and prayer. The temple was meant to be a house of prayer (v. 17); with the temple gone, the disciples will pray directly to God, in faith. And the disciples will need great faith in the days ahead.

In a sentence. The next morning, Peter pointed out that the cursed fig tree had withered to its roots, and Jesus told them: have faith in God.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not faith in faith, or in a building, or in your own prayers. Have faith in God.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, whoever says to this mountain, be taken up and thrown into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.

Whoever says to this mountain. “This mountain”: they were on the Mount of Olives, or within sight of the temple mount, Mount Zion. Moving a mountain was a proverbial expression for doing something impossible (1 Corinthians 13:2; rabbis who were great scholars were called “uprooters of mountains”). But “this mountain” may also be pointed. The temple mount, the great obstacle of unbelief and opposition, can be removed by God in answer to prayer. Zechariah prophesied that the Mount of Olives would be split in the day of the Lord (Zechariah 14:4), and that before Zerubbabel a great mountain would become a plain (Zechariah 4:7).

Be taken up and thrown into the sea. From the Mount of Olives, on a clear day, you can see the Dead Sea.

And does not doubt in his heart. “Doubt” (diakrithē) means to be divided, to waver between two opinions (James 1:6–8).

But believes that what he says will come to pass. Faith that rests entirely on God.

Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. “Have received” (elabete) is a past tense: believe it as already given. Faith counts God’s answer as certain before it is seen (Hebrews 11:1).

What it does not mean. Not a blank cheque for anything we want, or a technique for making God do our will by believing hard enough. Prayer in faith is prayer according to God’s will (1 John 5:14–15), in Jesus’ name (John 14:13–14), from a heart that seeks his kingdom (Matthew 6:10, 33). Jesus himself prayed in faith that the cup might pass, and submitted: not what I will, but what you will (14:36). The promise is about the power of God, not the power of positive thinking.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that prayer in undivided faith in God can remove mountains, and that whatever is asked in such faith, believing it already given, will be received.

For worship. What mountain stands in your way: a sin, a person who resists the gospel, a situation? Pray to God about it with faith that he is able.

parallels.desc: faith like a grain of mustard seed
ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father in heaven may also forgive you your trespasses.

And whenever you stand praying. Jews commonly prayed standing (1 Samuel 1:26; Luke 18:11, 13), with hands lifted.

Forgive, if you have anything against anyone. Faith is the first condition of answered prayer (v. 24); forgiveness is the second. Unforgiveness blocks prayer. You cannot come to God holding a grudge. “Anything against anyone”: no exceptions.

So that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses. The only time Mark has “your Father in heaven”, so common in Matthew, and close to the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12, 14–15). “Trespasses” (paraptōmata): false steps, stumbling off the path.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn God’s forgiveness by forgiving others. God forgives because of Christ, freely. But a person who has truly received God’s forgiveness will forgive others (Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:32), and a person who refuses to forgive shows that he has not understood or received it. Refusing to forgive is incompatible with asking to be forgiven. Nor does forgiveness mean pretending that wrong was not wrong, or always restoring trust at once. It means letting go of the debt and the desire for revenge, and leaving judgement to God (Romans 12:19).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 26: But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts, and was probably added from Matthew 6:15. The ESV puts it in a footnote.

In a sentence. When you pray, forgive anyone you hold anything against, so that your Father may forgive you.

For worship. Before you pray today, ask: is there anyone I have not forgiven? Let it go before God, then pray.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The challenge. They come back into the city and the full weight of the establishment is waiting: chief priests, scribes and elders — the three constituencies of the Sanhedrin, which is to say the supreme court of Judaism has sent a delegation to meet him in the temple courts.

Their question is the right one and the only one: by what authority are you doing these things? A man has stopped the temple trade, halted the traffic across the courts, and is now teaching daily on the premises. Somebody has to ask who authorised it.

The counter-question. Jesus offers to answer if they will answer one of his: was John's baptism from heaven or from man?

It is not evasion, and it is not a debating trick. John's commission was the same kind as his own — direct from God, without institutional sanction — so anyone who can assess the one can assess the other.

The calculation. And Mark lets us listen in while they work out what to say, which is the most damning thing in the chapter: they weigh both answers by what each will cost them, and the question of what is actually true never comes up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does Jesus refuse to answer? It looks at first like a rabbinic sparring move, and it is much more than that.

He is not withholding truth from honest enquiry — he has never once done that in this Gospel. He explained the parables privately to anyone who stayed and asked (4:10, 34); he answered a scribe who asked about the greatest commandment and told him he was not far from the kingdom (12:34); he answered the rich man who ran and knelt (10:17-22).

What he refuses is to give an answer to men who have already demonstrated they will not deal honestly with an answer. They have John's case in front of them — a prophet the entire nation recognised — and they cannot bring themselves to say publicly what they think about him, because both possible verdicts are expensive.

And that is a settled principle, not a mood: do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs (Matt. 7:6). He will stand silent in front of Herod, who wanted a miracle for entertainment (Luke 23:9), and largely silent before Pilate.

So the withdrawal of light is itself a judgement — and a merciful one, because more truth given to a man determined to reject it only deepens the guilt of the rejecting.

And note what their answer costs them. We do not know is a lie, spoken publicly by the highest religious authority in Israel, about the most famous prophet of their own generation. To protect their position they declared themselves incompetent — and having done so, they had no ground left from which to judge anybody's authority, including his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If we say, "From heaven," he will say, "Why then did you not believe him?" But shall we say, "From man"? — and they were afraid of the people.

Read the deliberation again and notice what is missing from it. Two options are weighed. Each is assessed for consequences. And at no point does anybody in that huddle ask: which of these is true?

That question is simply absent. These are the most religiously educated men in the nation, standing in the temple, discussing a prophet's commission — and truth is not one of the factors.

Now: the mechanism is not first-century and it is not confined to unbelievers. It is the standing temptation of any institution, church or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it.

It is the doctrine quietly not preached because of who would leave. The sin not named because of who is in the family. The question about your own life you have never taken to God because you already know roughly what the answer costs.

And it ends the way it ended here: not in a lie you tell somebody else, but in we do not know — a shrug that feels like humility and is in fact a decision. They walked away with their positions intact and no answer at all, and it is the last conversation they have with him before they arrest him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came again to Jerusalem. As he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes and the elders came to him and said: by what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?

And as he was walking in the temple. In the colonnades around the courts, where teachers gathered with their students (John 10:23). Jesus walks in the temple as though he owns it, which, in a sense, he does.

The chief priests and the scribes and the elders. The three groups that made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council of seventy-one members, presided over by the high priest. The same three groups Jesus had named in his first prediction of his death (8:31). This is an official delegation.

By what authority are you doing these things? “These things”: above all the clearing of the temple, but also the triumphal entry, the teaching, everything. The temple was under the authority of the high priest; who gave this Galilean the right to interfere? It is a legitimate question for the guardians of the temple. But it is also a trap. If Jesus claimed his authority came from God directly, they could charge him with blasphemy. If he claimed human authority, they could dismiss him; he had no rabbinic ordination and no official position.

Or who gave you this authority to do them? The real answer, which they will not hear, is the Father (1:11; 9:7).

In a sentence. An official delegation of the Sanhedrin demanded to know by what authority Jesus had acted in the temple, and who had given it to him.

On a Tuesday. The question of Jesus’ authority is the question for every person: does he have the right to command your life?
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.

I will ask you one question. Answering a question with a question was a recognised rabbinic method of debate. It is not an evasion. The answer to his question is the answer to theirs.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? “The baptism of John” stands for his whole ministry: his preaching of repentance and his baptism. “From heaven” is a reverent Jewish way of saying “from God”, avoiding the divine name. Did John’s ministry come from God, or was it a merely human movement?

Why this question? Because John had pointed to Jesus. He had announced the coming of one mightier than himself (1:7), and at Jesus’ baptism by John, the Spirit descended and the Father spoke (1:10–11). If John was from God, then his testimony about Jesus was true, and Jesus’ authority came from God. The two are bound together. To accept John is to accept Jesus.

Answer me. Only Mark records the repeated demand. Jesus is in charge; he is now examining them.

In a sentence. Jesus replied by asking whether John’s baptism came from God or from men, since the answer to that settled the source of his own authority.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the question we ask God is already answered by what he has shown us. Have you responded to what you already know?
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But shall we say, 'From man'?"—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And Jesus said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They discussed it with one another: if we say, from heaven, he will say, why then did you not believe him? But shall we say, from man? They were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus: we do not know. And Jesus said to them: neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

And they discussed it with one another. Notice what they do not ask: is it true? They ask only: what are the consequences of each answer for us? They are not seeking truth but calculating.

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him? They had not believed John. Luke records that the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not being baptised by him (Luke 7:30).

But shall we say, From man? The sentence breaks off. Mark finishes it for them.

They were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. John had been executed by Herod, and was revered by the people as a martyr prophet. To deny him publicly in the temple, during Passover, could provoke a riot. Luke adds that they feared being stoned (Luke 20:6).
