So they answered Jesus, We do not know. A confession of failure. The religious authorities, whose job was to judge true and false prophets (Deuteronomy 18:20–22), declared themselves unable to judge the greatest prophet of their generation. They disqualified themselves from judging Jesus.

Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. Not a refusal to tell the truth, but a refusal to give it to those who would not receive it (Matthew 7:6). They had already decided. And yet, in the parable that follows, he does tell them, in a form they cannot miss (12:1–12): he is the beloved Son.

In a sentence. Afraid of either answer, the leaders said they did not know whether John was from God, so Jesus refused to tell them the source of his authority.

On a Tuesday. “We do not know” is sometimes not honesty but evasion. Don’t let fear of the consequences keep you from saying what you know is true about Jesus.

11.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree out of season? The answer turns on the leaves. A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after — in spring the branches put out small edible knobs, the paggim, and a hungry traveller ate them. So a tree in full leaf is making a claim. Mark's clause it was not the season for figs is not an embarrassment but the key: he supplies it so no reader mistakes this for pique over a missed breakfast. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement, and it had none.

And the placement is the interpretation. Mark splits the story and wedges the temple into the gap — curse, temple, withered — his habitual sandwich, never accidental. The fig tree was Israel's own image for itself (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13), and the sentence pronounced here is carried out on the building in 13:2.

A den of robbers (Jer. 7:11) is the most misquoted phrase in the chapter. A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens; it is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe. Jeremiah spells it out at the temple gate: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' The charge is not commerce in church. It is using religion as a safe house.

And v. 17 keeps a clause the other Gospels drop. Matthew and Luke both quote Isaiah 56:7 and stop before the final phrase; Mark keeps for all the nations — the Gospel written for Gentiles preserving the clause about Gentiles. Isaiah 56 is God's promise about the foreigner and the eunuch, the two categories explicitly excluded under the old arrangements; and the trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew could stand. The arrangement had physically evicted the very people the verse was about.
11.examples:
Then: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours — a promise that has been made to carry a weight it was never meant to bear.

What it does say: pray with enormous boldness, ask for what is far beyond your resources, expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption. We are in danger of praying for nothing much in case nothing happens, and the whole point of the mountain is that it is too big.

What it does not say: that sufficient certainty compels God. That reading makes prayer a technique and God a force, and it is refuted most decisively by the man saying it — within days, in a garden a few hundred yards away, he asks his Father to remove the cup and adds yet not what I will, but what you will (14:36), and the cup does not pass. If unqualified confidence always secured the request, that prayer is unintelligible. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9); John, who heard this saying, wrote in the qualifier himself — if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 Jn. 5:14).

Now: to the reader who asked and did not receive — your faith was very likely not the problem, and blaming it only adds a second grief to the first. Believe boldly, ask for great things, and trust him enough to want his will more than your own, knowing that his no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you hoped for.

And note what he says next (v. 25), with no pause: whenever you stand praying, forgive. Having promised that a believing man can move a mountain, he immediately names the thing that blocks the pipe. There is a name — you thought of it while reading this — and the instruction is not to feel differently, but to put it down, deliberately, now, and again whenever it comes back.

12.title: The Beloved Son and the Widow’s Two Coins
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And he began to speak to them in parables. “A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. <sup>2</sup>When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. <sup>5</sup>And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. <sup>6</sup>He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>7</sup>But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ <sup>8</sup>And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. <sup>9</sup>What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. <sup>10</sup>Have you not read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; <sup>11</sup>this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” <sup>12</sup>And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away. <sup>13</sup>And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. <sup>14</sup>And they came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?” <sup>15</sup>But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, “Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.” <sup>16</sup>And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” <sup>17</sup>Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. <sup>18</sup>And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, <sup>19</sup>“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>20</sup>There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. <sup>21</sup>And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. <sup>22</sup>And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. <sup>23</sup>In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>24</sup>Jesus said to them, “Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? <sup>25</sup>For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>26</sup>And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? <sup>27</sup>He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.” <sup>28</sup>And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup>And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ <sup>31</sup>The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” <sup>32</sup>And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. <sup>33</sup>And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” <sup>34</sup>And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. <sup>35</sup>And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? <sup>36</sup>David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ <sup>37</sup>David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” And the great throng heard him gladly. <sup>38</sup>And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces <sup>39</sup>and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>40</sup>who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.” <sup>41</sup>And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. <sup>42</sup>And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. <sup>43</sup>And he called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. <sup>44</sup>For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”
12.overview:
This is the last day Jesus ever taught in the temple, and it is one long interrogation. Three delegations come at him in turn, each with a question designed to finish him, and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything at all.

He opens by answering the challenge they refused to answer, with a story. A vineyard is planted at great expense, leased out, and the owner sends for his share — and the tenants beat one servant, humiliate another, kill a third, and go on doing it. Then, having nobody else, the owner sends a beloved son, which in this Gospel is a phrase that has twice come out of heaven. They recognise him, kill him, and throw him out of the vineyard. Mark says the leaders understood the parable perfectly — and went away to arrange the arrest.

Then the traps: a coin with Caesar's face on it, and a riddle about a woman with seven husbands. He answers the first in sixteen words that have shaped Christian political thought ever since, and the second from a single present-tense verb in the burning bush.

Then one honest scribe asks a real question and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And the chapter ends with Jesus sitting down opposite the treasury, watching people give, and calling his disciples over to look at a widow putting in two of the smallest coins in the empire — everything she had to live on, three days before he did the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — The Tenants, Caesar’s Coin, and the Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable (vv. 1–12). They asked by what authority he acts, and refused to answer his question. So he tells them a story about a vineyard, and it is the least veiled parable he ever told: an owner, a run of beaten and murdered servants, and finally a beloved son. They understood it perfectly — Mark says so — and went away to arrange the arrest.

The coin (vv. 13–17). Pharisees and Herodians together again, opening with flattery and closing a trap with two jaws: endorse the tax and lose the crowd, oppose it and be reported for sedition. He asks for a coin, asks whose face is on it, and gives an answer nobody has improved on.

The riddle (vv. 18–27). Then the Sadducees, with a seven-husbands puzzle designed to make resurrection look absurd — and he answers them from the one part of the Bible they accepted, out of a single present-tense verb.

Three challenges from three different quarters, all in one day, all of them designed to end him — and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything else.
verseByVerse.theology:
Render to Caesar (v. 17) cuts in two directions at once, and both must be held.

On one side, a real obligation. Jesus does not say the tax is illegitimate or that a man of God may treat the government as an enemy to be defied. The coin is Caesar's; give it to him. Paul draws the same line plainly: the governing authority is God's servant for the ordering of society, so pay your taxes, keep the law, honour the office (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy, and a faith that despises all earthly authority has not understood this verse.

On the other side, the obligation is bounded. Caesar may claim the coin; he may not claim the soul. The image on the denarius marks what is his; the image of God stamped on the man marks what is God's — and what is God's, Caesar must never be given.

So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. The moment the state demands what belongs to God alone — worship, or the violation of God's clear command — the Christian renders to God and not to Caesar. We must obey God rather than men, the apostles answered the very Sanhedrin that plotted this trap (Acts 5:29). It is the fault line the martyrs died on: they would pay any tax Rome levied and pray for its emperor, but they would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that title was God's.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the Sadducees, and the ground Jesus chooses to fight them on.

They were the aristocratic priestly party who ran the temple — wealthy, powerful, politically pragmatic — and they held that only the five books of Moses carried full authority. They also say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8).

Which is why Jesus does not answer from the obvious places. He could have quoted Daniel — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Dan. 12:2) — or Isaiah 26:19, and they would simply have waved those books away. Instead he beats them on their own chosen ground, reaching into the Torah, into the burning bush that every priest knew by heart, and finding the resurrection in a present-tense claim: I am the God of Abraham. Not was. Abraham has been dead four hundred years and God speaks of him in the present tense.

Now: he does not merely win the argument. He wins it inside the fence they built themselves, proving that the hope they denied was lying all along in the only Scriptures they would accept.

And note the diagnosis he gives first: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those are the two ways to go wrong, and they are still the two. Some err because they do not know the text; some because they know the text and have quietly decided what God is not able to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to speak to them in parables. "A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus began to speak to them in parables. A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a pit for the winepress and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to collect from them his share of the fruit of the vineyard.

Setting. The same scene as 11:27–33: in the temple, to the chief priests, scribes and elders, who had just asked by what authority he acted. Jesus refused to answer directly. Now he answers in a parable, and they understand it perfectly (v. 12).

A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower. Every listener would recognise Isaiah’s song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), which uses almost the same words. There, the vineyard is Israel, the owner is God, and he looked for good grapes and found only wild ones: he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed (Isaiah 5:7). The fence kept out animals; the winepress was a pit cut in rock where grapes were trodden; the tower was for a watchman, and for storage. The owner did everything to make it fruitful.

And leased it to tenants. This is the change from Isaiah. In Isaiah, the vineyard is at fault. Here, the tenants are: the leaders to whom God had entrusted his people. Absentee landlords leasing to tenant farmers were common in Galilee, and so was resentment of them. The tenants would pay rent with a share of the harvest.

And went into another country. God had entrusted Israel to its leaders and given them time.

When the season came, he sent a servant. A new vine takes about four years to produce a crop (Leviticus 19:23–25). Then the owner sent for his share. The servants are the prophets, often called God’s servants (Jeremiah 7:25; Amos 3:7).

In a sentence. In a parable drawing on Isaiah’s vineyard, Jesus told of an owner who prepared a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and sent a servant for his share of the fruit.

On a Tuesday. God has given you everything you need to bear fruit for him. What fruit is he looking for in your life this season?
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They took the servant, beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again the owner sent another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. He sent another, and they killed him. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.

The history of Israel’s prophets. The parable summarises centuries. God sent prophet after prophet to call his people to repentance and fruitfulness, and they were rejected, persecuted and killed (2 Chronicles 24:19–22; 36:15–16; Nehemiah 9:26; Jeremiah 26:20–23; Matthew 23:29–37; Acts 7:52; Hebrews 11:36–38). Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned; Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court; tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two.

And sent him away empty-handed. The fruit was withheld. God received nothing from them.

They struck him on the head. Literally “beheaded” or “wounded in the head”. Some think Mark’s readers would hear an echo of John the Baptist (6:27), the latest of the servants.

And so with many others. The owner’s patience is extraordinary, beyond anything a real landlord would show. That is the point: God’s patience with his rebellious people was astonishing (2 Peter 3:9).

In a sentence. The tenants beat, insulted and killed servant after servant, as Israel’s leaders had rejected God’s prophets through the centuries.

On a Tuesday. How have you treated God’s messengers when they called you to repent? Thank God for his patience, and don’t presume on it.

parallels.desc: they mocked the messengers of God

verseByVerse.quote: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying: they will respect my son. But those tenants said to one another: this is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. And they took him, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.

He had still one other, a beloved son. Key words. “Beloved son” is exactly what the Father called Jesus at the baptism (1:11) and the transfiguration (9:7). Here Jesus answers the leaders’ question about his authority (11:28): he is not one more servant, one more prophet. He is the Son. The owner’s last and greatest messenger. And “beloved” may again mean “only”, as with Isaac (Genesis 22:2).

Finally he sent him to them. “Finally” (eschaton): last of all. There is no one after the Son. God’s final word (Hebrews 1:1–2).

They will respect my son. The patience of the owner goes beyond reason. The Father’s love for his rebellious people led him to send his Son.

This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours. Under the law of the day, land without an heir might pass to those who had occupied and worked it. The tenants recognise exactly who he is and kill him for that reason. This exposes the leaders: their rejection of Jesus is not ignorance but rebellion. They want the vineyard, God’s people, for themselves, without God. And “Come, let us kill him” is what Joseph’s brothers said about the favoured son (Genesis 37:20).

And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. The final insult: leaving the body unburied. Jesus is predicting his own death, and his enemies’ part in it, to their faces. Matthew and Luke say they threw him out and then killed him (Matthew 21:39; Luke 20:15), which matches Jesus’ crucifixion outside the city wall (Hebrews 13:12).

In a sentence. Last of all, the owner sent his beloved son, and the tenants, recognising him as the heir, killed him to seize the vineyard for themselves.

For worship. God sent his only, beloved Son to rebels like us. He knew what we would do, and sent him anyway. This is love (1 John 4:9–10).
verseByVerse.note: “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration.

verseByVerse.quote: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?

What will the owner of the vineyard do? Matthew records that the listeners themselves answered (Matthew 21:41), and so condemned themselves, as David did when Nathan told him the parable of the lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

He will come and destroy the tenants. Judgement on the leaders who rejected the Son. Fulfilled in AD 70, when Rome destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and the priestly aristocracy and the Sanhedrin came to an end.

And give the vineyard to others. To whom? To new tenants: the apostles and the leaders of the church, Jewish and Gentile, who would care for God’s people under Christ (Matthew 21:43: a people producing its fruits). Notice: the vineyard is not destroyed. God’s people continue; the wicked tenants are replaced.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Psalm 118:22–23, from the same psalm the crowds had sung at his entry (11:9). Jesus changes the picture from a vineyard to a building, perhaps because of a play on words in Hebrew between “son” (ben) and “stone” (eben). The builders are the leaders. They examined the stone and threw it away as useless. But God made it the cornerstone (or capstone), the most important stone in the building, which holds the walls together. The rejected Son will be vindicated by God, in the resurrection. The apostles preached exactly this (Acts 4:10–11; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Ephesians 2:20).

This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. The rejection and the vindication are both God’s work. Human evil and divine purpose meet at the cross (Acts 2:23). The result is wonderful.

In a sentence. The owner will destroy the wicked tenants and give the vineyard to others, and the rejected stone will become the cornerstone by God’s marvellous doing.

For worship. The one rejected by the world is the cornerstone of God’s new temple, the church. Build your life on him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were looking for a way to arrest him, but they feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.

For they perceived that he had told the parable against them. They understood perfectly. Unlike the parables of chapter 4, which outsiders did not understand (4:11–12), this one was plain. They knew they were the tenants and he was claiming to be the Son.

And they were seeking to arrest him. And so they began to do exactly what the parable said they would do. Rather than repent, they plot to kill the Son.

But feared the people. Again (11:18, 32). The crowd protected him for now. They will need to take him secretly, at night, through a traitor (14:1–2, 10–11).

In a sentence. Understanding that the parable was aimed at them, the leaders wanted to arrest Jesus at once but held back for fear of the crowd.

On a Tuesday. To recognise yourself in God’s word is not enough. It must lead to repentance, not resentment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his words. They came and said: Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. You are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not? But knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them: why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.

A series of tests. Mark now records three questions put to Jesus by different groups (vv. 13–34), and then one he puts to them (vv. 35–37). Each is meant to trap him. Each fails. This is the Messiah being examined in the temple, like a Passover lamb examined for blemishes before being sacrificed. He is found without fault.

Some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians. An unlikely alliance, as in Galilee (3:6). The Herodians supported Herod’s family, and therefore the Roman rule that kept them in power. The Pharisees resented Roman rule as an insult to God’s people. They are united only by their hatred of Jesus.

To trap him in his talk. “Trap” (agreusōsin) is a hunting word, used of catching wild animals.

Teacher, we know that you are true. Flattery, to set him up. But every word was true. He was true, impartial, and taught the way of God. They said it without believing it.

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? The tax was a poll tax, a head tax paid by every adult directly to the Roman treasury. It had been imposed when Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, and provoked a revolt led by Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37), who taught that paying it was treason to God, the only king. It was a symbol of subjection. The trap: if Jesus said yes, he would lose the crowd, who hated the tax and hoped he would liberate them. If he said no, the Herodians could report him to the Romans as a rebel. Either answer would destroy him.

But, knowing their hypocrisy. He saw through the flattery to the trap.

Bring me a denarius and let me look at it. A silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer, and the coin in which the tax was paid. Jesus apparently did not carry one. They did, even in the temple.

In a sentence. Pharisees and Herodians flattered Jesus and then tried to trap him with the question of paying the Roman tax, and he asked them for a coin.

On a Tuesday. Flattery is a trap. Be wary of praise that comes with a question attached.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought one. He said to them: whose likeness and inscription is this? They said: Caesar’s. Jesus said to them: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. And they marvelled at him.

Whose likeness and inscription is this? The denarius of Tiberius, emperor at the time, bore his portrait and an inscription: “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus”. On the other side: “high priest”. To devout Jews it was doubly offensive: a graven image (Exodus 20:4), and a claim to divinity.

Caesar’s. They answer, and by producing the coin, have already shown that they use Caesar’s money and benefit from Caesar’s rule.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. “Render” (apodote) means give back, pay what is owed. Not “give” as a gift, but repay a debt. The coin bears Caesar’s image; it is his; give it back. Those who use the roads, coinage and order that Rome provides owe taxes. Paul and Peter teach the same (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). The state has a legitimate, God-given authority in its own sphere.

And to God the things that are God’s. The deeper point. What bears God’s image? Human beings (Genesis 1:26–27). The coin belongs to Caesar because it bears his image; you belong to God because you bear his. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, all of you. And Caesar’s claims are limited by God’s. Caesar’s inscription claimed divinity; Jesus denies it. Caesar is owed taxes, not worship. When Caesar demands what belongs to God, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

And they marveled at him. The trap had failed. He had neither endorsed Roman rule unconditionally nor called for revolt. He had put both in their place.

Where Christians differ: church and state. Christians have understood this saying in many ways: as dividing life into two separate spheres (secular and sacred); as subordinating the church to the state; or as subordinating the state to the church. Verdict: Jesus does not make Caesar and God equal partners. Everything belongs to God, including Caesar (Romans 13:1). The state has real but limited authority under God, and Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes and honouring rulers. But their final loyalty is to God, and they may not give the state what belongs to God alone.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that what bears Caesar’s image should be given back to Caesar, and what bears God’s image, ourselves, to God.

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes honestly. And remember whose image you bear: give yourself wholly to God.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and asked him: Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no child, the man must marry the widow and raise up children for his brother. There were seven brothers. The first married, and died leaving no children. The second married her, and died leaving no children, and the third likewise. None of the seven left children. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.

And Sadducees came to him. The only time they appear in Mark. The Sadducees were the aristocratic, priestly party, including the high priestly families who controlled the temple. They were wealthy and politically conservative, cooperating with Rome. In theology they accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative, and rejected the oral tradition of the Pharisees.

Who say that there is no resurrection. Mark explains for his readers. The Sadducees also denied angels and spirits (Acts 23:8), and life after death. They argued that the resurrection was not taught in the books of Moses.

Moses wrote for us. They appeal to Deuteronomy 25:5–10, the law of levirate marriage (from Latin levir, brother-in-law). If a man died without children, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son would carry on the dead man’s name and inheritance, so that his name may not be blotted out of Israel. (The book of Ruth involves a version of this.)

There were seven brothers. A ridiculous story, probably a standard argument the Sadducees used to mock the Pharisees’ belief in the resurrection. They meant to show that the resurrection leads to absurdities. If Moses commanded levirate marriage, and the resurrection would make it absurd, then Moses could not have believed in the resurrection.

In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? The trap is meant to make Jesus look foolish, on the assumption that life after the resurrection is just like life now.

In a sentence. The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, tried to make it look absurd with the story of a woman who married seven brothers in turn.

On a Tuesday. Mocking questions about the faith are nothing new. Don’t be thrown by them; Jesus has answers.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: is this not why you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.

Is this not the reason you are wrong. “Wrong” (planasthe) means to wander, to go astray, to be deceived. The Sadducees, the educated elite, the guardians of the temple, are lost.

Because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Two causes of error, still the two causes of most theological error. They do not know the Scriptures: they do not see what they actually teach (v. 26). And they do not know the power of God: they cannot imagine that God can raise the dead and make a new kind of life, different from this one. They have shrunk God to the size of their own imagination.

For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage. Resurrection life is not simply this life continued. Marriage belongs to this age. Its purposes, companionship, the bringing of children into the world, and the picture of Christ and the church, will be fulfilled. In the new creation there will be no death, so no need for children to continue the family line, and no levirate marriage. The whole basis of their story falls apart.

But are like angels in heaven. Not that we become angels, or lose our bodies or our identities. But like angels, we will not die (Luke 20:36), and will not marry. And the Sadducees did not believe in angels either; Jesus corrects them on that too.

What it does not mean. Not that married love is lost, or that spouses will not know each other in heaven. Every relationship will be taken up into something greater: perfect love for God and for one another, in the marriage of Christ and his bride, the church (Revelation 19:7–9), to which every earthly marriage points.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Sadducees they were wrong because they knew neither the Scriptures nor God’s power: in the resurrection there is no marriage, for the risen are like the angels.

On a Tuesday. When you are puzzled by a question about heaven, remember the two keys: what Scripture says, and how great God’s power is.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.

Have you not read in the book of Moses. Jesus answers from the books the Sadducees accepted.

In the passage about the bush. This is how passages of Scripture were located before chapter and verse numbers were added (in the 13th and 16th centuries). The burning bush is Exodus 3, where God appeared to Moses.

I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Exodus 3:6. God said this to Moses centuries after the three patriarchs had died. Note the tense: “I am”, not “I was”.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. Jesus’ argument. God describes himself in terms of a covenant relationship with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. A covenant relationship with God cannot be broken by death. If God is still their God, they must still exist, alive to him (Luke 20:38: for all live to him). And if God is their God, he will keep his promises to them, which concerned not only their souls but their bodies, the land, an inheritance. The living God will not leave his friends in the grave. Their continuing life with God leads to the resurrection of their bodies.

A deep argument. Jesus grounds the resurrection not in a single proof text but in the character of God and his covenant faithfulness. The God who binds himself to his people by covenant is the God who will raise them (Hebrews 11:16).

You are quite wrong. Only Mark records this final sentence. “Greatly mistaken.”

In a sentence. Jesus showed from the burning bush that God is still the God of the long-dead patriarchs, and so they live to him and will be raised, for he is the God of the living.

For worship. If God is your God, death cannot end your relationship with him. Worship the God of the living.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The one honest question (vv. 28–34). After a day of traps, a scribe asks something he actually wants to know — which commandment is the most important. He gets the Shema and Leviticus 19, agrees warmly, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And after that, nobody dares ask anything at all.

The question he asks them (vv. 35–37). So Jesus asks one instead, and it is the deepest thing he says in public. If the Christ is David's son, why does David call him Lord?

The warning (vv. 38–40). Then a warning about the men in the long robes who love the greetings and the best seats, say long prayers for show, and devour widows' houses.

The widow (vv. 41–44). And he goes and sits down opposite the treasury and watches people give — and the last thing he does in this temple before he leaves it forever is point out a woman putting in two of the smallest coins in circulation.

Mark has put her immediately after devour widows' houses, and that is not an accident.
verseByVerse.theology:
Psalm 110 and the deepest disclosure in the Gospel. Jesus takes the most quoted psalm in the New Testament and asks a question nobody could answer.

Everyone agreed the Christ would be David's son — the promise ran through the whole Old Testament (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Isa. 11:1). And in Psalm 110, David writes: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand. The first LORD is God; the second is somebody David calls my Lord.

In that culture the point is unanswerable. Honour ran upward from son to father, never downward. A man does not call his own descendant his lord.

So: how can the Christ be David's son and David's Lord at once? Mark records no answer, and the crowd hears him gladly, and nobody says a word.

The answer is that both are true, and it takes the whole New Testament to say it. Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity.

And notice which verse of the psalm he quotes: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. He asks this in the temple, on the Tuesday, surrounded by the men who will have him killed on the Friday. They are the enemies in the sentence, and he quotes it to their faces.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God.

The scribe has answered magnificently. He has the doctrine of God right, the summary of the law right, and the priorities right — he even says out loud, as a temple professional, that love of God and neighbour outweighs the whole sacrificial system, which is a remarkable thing for such a man to concede.

And Jesus does not say you are in. He says not far.

Now: that is the most uncomfortable commendation in the Gospel, because not far is still outside, and it is the address of a great many people who have been in church all their lives.

The gap between near and in is not a gap in knowledge. This man's theology was better than the Twelve's. The gap is a Person. He was standing three feet away, and the question was never whether the scribe could give the right answer about the law but whether he would follow the man who was about to keep it for him.

So it is worth asking plainly: could you give the right answers, and never have come? Right doctrine is the beginning and it is not the destination. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it — and Mark never tells us whether this man did.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the scribes came up and heard them disputing. Seeing that Jesus answered them well, he asked him: which commandment is the most important of all? Jesus answered: the most important is, Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength. The second is this: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these.

And one of the scribes came up. A different kind of questioner. He is impressed, not hostile. Matthew suggests it was still a test (Matthew 22:35), but Mark shows his sincerity (v. 34).

Which commandment is the most important of all? The rabbis counted 613 commandments in the law: 248 positive and 365 negative. They debated which were “heavy” and which “light”, and whether one could summarise the whole. Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, had said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. That is the whole law; the rest is commentary.

Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. Deuteronomy 6:4, the Shema (Hebrew for “hear”), recited twice daily by devout Jews, the great confession of Israel’s faith. There is one God, and only one. He is not one of many gods to be divided among; he alone is God, and so he alone is to be loved with everything. Only Mark includes the Shema itself before the commandment. The command to love flows from who God is. And Christians confess the same one God, as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 8:6).

And you shall love the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 6:5. Love here (agapēseis) is not mainly a feeling but a commitment of the whole person, shown in loyalty and obedience (John 14:15).

With all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength. Deuteronomy has heart, soul and might; Jesus adds “mind”. The four are not separate parts but the whole person, from every angle: your will and affections, your life, your thinking, your energy. Nothing held back.

The second is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:18. Jesus was asked for one commandment and gave two. The second flows from the first and is inseparable from it (1 John 4:20–21). “As yourself”: with the same care and attention you naturally give to your own needs. Not a command to love yourself first, but an assumption that you already do.

There is no other commandment greater than these. All the others hang on them (Matthew 22:40). Love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10).

What it does not mean. Not that we can be saved by loving God and neighbour. No one has ever kept these two commandments fully, except Jesus. They expose our need (Romans 3:20). But in Christ, forgiven, we begin to keep them by the Spirit (Romans 8:4).

In a sentence. Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus gave the Shema’s command to love the one God with your whole being, and joined to it the command to love your neighbour as yourself.

For worship. Pray through the four: Lord, I love you with my heart, my soul, my mind, my strength. Where is my love for you incomplete?
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribe said to him: you are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him; and to love him with all the heart, with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbour as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. When Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him: you are not far from the kingdom of God. And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.

You are right, Teacher. Only Mark records the scribe’s response. A rare moment: a scribe agrees with Jesus.

And there is no other besides him. Deuteronomy 4:35; Isaiah 45:21.

Is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. A remarkable thing to say in the temple courts, where sacrifices were being offered all around them. He echoes the prophets: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6–8). He has understood what the chief priests had not. The temple’s sacrifices, without love, were empty, like the leaves of the fig tree (11:13).

When Jesus saw that he answered wisely. “Wisely” (nounechōs): thoughtfully, with understanding.

You are not far from the kingdom of God. Words of encouragement, and of challenge. Not far, but not yet in. What did he lack? To see that he could not keep these commandments, and to recognise and follow the one who was speaking to him, the King. Understanding the law is not the same as entering the kingdom. A person can be very close and still outside.

And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. Jesus has answered every challenge. His opponents are silenced.

In a sentence. The scribe agreed that love for God and neighbour is greater than all sacrifices, and Jesus told him he was not far from the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Being close is not enough. If you understand the gospel but have not come to Christ, don’t stay “not far”. Come in.

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus taught in the temple, he said: how can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son? And the great crowd heard him gladly.

Now Jesus asks the question. After being tested by everyone, Jesus asks the decisive question, about who the Messiah is.

How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? They were right to say it (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5). Bartimaeus had called Jesus Son of David (10:47), and the crowds had hailed the kingdom of David (11:10). But is that all the Messiah is: a human descendant of David, a new king like David?

David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared. Jesus affirms that David wrote Psalm 110, and that he wrote it inspired by the Spirit. Scripture is God’s word through human authors (2 Peter 1:21).

The Lord said to my Lord. Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse most often quoted or alluded to in the New. In Hebrew: “Yahweh said to my Adonai”. God (the LORD) speaks to David’s Lord, someone David calls his master.

Sit at my right hand. The place of supreme honour and authority, sharing God’s throne.

Until I put your enemies under your feet. Victory over every enemy. Conquered kings had the victor’s foot placed on their necks (Joshua 10:24).

David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son? The puzzle. In the ancient world, a father did not call his son “lord”; the son honoured the father. If David calls the Messiah “my Lord”, the Messiah must be greater than David. How can he be both David’s descendant and David’s Lord? The answer, which Jesus leaves them to find: he is the Son of David by human birth, and the Son of God, David’s Lord, by nature (Romans 1:3–4). Both human and divine. Jesus is claiming that the Messiah is more than a human king, and pointing to himself. At his trial, he will apply Psalm 110 to himself directly (14:62).

And the great throng heard him gladly. The ordinary people enjoyed seeing the experts outmatched.

In a sentence. Quoting Psalm 110, Jesus showed that the Messiah is more than David’s son, since David calls him Lord, pointing to his own divine identity.

For worship. Jesus is David’s son and David’s Lord, fully man and fully God, now seated at God’s right hand until every enemy is under his feet. Worship him as both.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: And in his teaching he said, "Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his teaching he said: beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honour at feasts, who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.

Beware of the scribes. Not every scribe; one had just been commended (v. 34). But the pattern was common enough to be a danger.

Who like to walk around in long robes. Long, white, linen robes, sometimes reaching to the ground, marked out men of learning and rank. They “like” them: the problem is the love of display.

And like greetings in the marketplaces. Respectful public greetings, with titles: Rabbi, master. People stood when a scribe passed.

And have the best seats in the synagogues. The bench at the front, facing the congregation, where everyone could see them.

And the places of honor at feasts. Seats nearest the host. Their religion is a means to status and honour.

Who devour widows’ houses. Widows were the most vulnerable people in Israel, without a husband’s protection; God commanded special care for them (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17). Scribes were not supposed to be paid for teaching, and relied on gifts. Some apparently exploited widows’ generosity, or charged them for legal advice, or managed their estates and took advantage, eating up their property.

And for a pretense make long prayers. Long, public prayers that make them look holy, while they cheat the vulnerable. The hypocrisy of Isaiah 29:13 again (7:6).

They will receive the greater condemnation. Greater because they knew the law better than anyone (James 3:1; Luke 12:47–48), and because they used religion to cover their sins. There are degrees of punishment in hell, according to knowledge and privilege.

In a sentence. Jesus warned against scribes who love religious status, exploit widows and pray long prayers for show, for they will receive greater judgement.

On a Tuesday. Watch your own heart for the love of being seen and honoured, especially if you lead in church. God judges teachers more strictly.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.

The contrast. Straight after the scribes who devour widows’ houses comes a widow, perhaps one of their victims. And this is Jesus’ last scene in the temple, his last public teaching in Mark.

And he sat down opposite the treasury. The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, so called because women could go that far and no further. There were thirteen trumpet-shaped collection chests there, each marked for a different purpose.

And watched. Jesus watches how people give. He still does.

Many rich people put in large sums. Perhaps noisily: coins thrown into the trumpet-shaped chests would rattle. Jesus does not condemn them.

A poor widow. “Poor” (ptōchē): destitute, a beggar’s poverty.

Two small copper coins, which make a penny. The lepton (plural lepta) was the smallest coin in circulation, a tiny copper coin worth about 1/128 of a denarius, a day’s wage. Mark translates it into Roman currency for his readers: two lepta made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin. She could have kept one; she gave both.

In a sentence. Sitting opposite the temple treasury, Jesus watched the rich put in large sums and a poor widow put in two tiny coins.

On a Tuesday. Jesus sees what you give, and how. Give as one who knows he is watching.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, with collection chests for offerings. Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called his disciples to him and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called his disciples and said to them: truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

And he called his disciples to him. This is a lesson for them, and for every disciple.

This poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing. More than everyone, more than all the rich together. How? God measures gifts not by the amount but by the cost, and by the heart.

For they all contributed out of their abundance. From their surplus. It did not affect their lives. They would not miss it.

But she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on. Literally “her whole life” (holon ton bion autēs). She gave everything and kept nothing, trusting God to provide her next meal. This is the giving of total trust.

The wider meaning. She stands in contrast to the rich man who would not give up his possessions (10:22), and to the scribes who devour widows’ houses (v. 40). She has done, in a small way, what the first commandment requires: loved God with all her strength, with all she had (v. 30). And she is a picture of what Jesus is about to do: give everything, his whole life, for others. The next time Mark mentions an offering of everything, it is the cross.

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? Some argue that Jesus is not praising her but lamenting a temple system that took the last coins of the poor, continuing his condemnation of the scribes. Verdict: there is truth in that context, as the scribes who devour widows’ houses stand just before her, and Jesus will predict the temple’s destruction next (13:2). But his words are clearly commendation: she “put in more than all”. He honours her faith and devotion, whatever the corruption of those who received it.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must give away everything they have, or that the amount of giving does not matter. But it shows that God values sacrificial, trusting giving, and that no gift is too small if it is given wholeheartedly.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that the widow had given more than all the rich, because they gave from their surplus, and she gave everything she had to live on.

For worship. Does your giving cost you anything? Give as an act of worship and trust, not leftovers.

12.theology:
Render to Caesar cuts in two directions and both must be held. It establishes a real obligation — the coin bears his image, so give it to him, and Paul says the same (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy. And it bounds that obligation absolutely: Caesar may claim the coin, but what bears God's image belongs to God, and man bears it (Gen. 1:27). So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) was said to this same council. The martyrs paid every tax Rome levied and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord.

The Sadducees and the ground he chose. They were the priestly aristocracy who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied resurrection, angels and spirits alike (Acts 23:8). So Jesus does not quote Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19; they would have waved those away. He goes into the Torah, into the burning bush every priest knew by heart, and finds the resurrection in two words: I am the God of Abraham — spoken centuries after Abraham died. A covenant of that kind cannot be ended by the death of one party without God's own word failing. He wins the argument inside the fence they built themselves.

David's son and David's Lord. In Psalm 110:1 the first LORD is the divine name and the second is my lord, a title of superior rank. In that culture honour ran upward only; no man called his own descendant his master. So how is the Christ both? Mark records no answer, and the whole New Testament is the answer: descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity. And note the line he quotes — until I put your enemies under your feet — spoken in the temple to the men who would kill him on Friday.
12.examples:
Then: two lepta, the thinnest coins in circulation, dropped into a bronze trumpet-mouthed chest that made almost no sound.

And the detail that undoes you is that there were two. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known and nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Now: the measure is not the amount but what is left afterwards. The rich gave real gifts, honestly, and nothing in their lives changed on the way home. She gave and had nothing — all she had to live on.

That cuts both ways. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And the gift you are embarrassed by — the small amount from a pension, an hour from someone who has almost no hours — is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

Is he commending her or lamenting her? Both, and the passage is stronger for holding them together. He has just denounced the men who devour widows' houses, two verses earlier, and the building her money maintains has forty years left. He does not commend the machinery for taking it. And he commends her without a single qualification — she gave to God in the only way available to her, and because he said so out loud, a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth.

And note where he was sitting. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and he spent one of his last hours in that temple watching a woman put in everything she had to live on. She is the only other person in the story who does what he is about to do on Friday.

13.title: Stay Awake
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” <sup>2</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <sup>4</sup>“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus began to say to them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>7</sup>And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>8</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. <sup>10</sup>And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. <sup>11</sup>And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. <sup>12</sup>And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. <sup>13</sup>And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>15</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, <sup>16</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>17</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>18</sup>Pray that it may not happen in winter. <sup>19</sup>For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. <sup>20</sup>And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. <sup>21</sup>And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>22</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. <sup>23</sup>But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. <sup>24</sup>But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, <sup>25</sup>and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. <sup>26</sup>And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. <sup>27</sup>And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. <sup>28</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>29</sup>So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>30</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>31</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>32</sup>“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. <sup>33</sup>Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. <sup>34</sup>It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. <sup>35</sup>Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— <sup>36</sup>lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. <sup>37</sup>And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.”
13.overview:
They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the stonework — and he was right to. Herod's platform covers thirty-five acres; the largest block still visible weighs several hundred tons; Josephus says the gold front was too bright to look at in the morning sun. Building had been going on for some forty-six years when Jesus first spoke of it (John 2:20), and it was not finished until AD 63.

Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and seven years after the last workman went home it was gone.

Four disciples take him aside on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when and how they will know. What follows is the longest teaching in Mark before the passion, and its most striking feature is what it refuses to give. He describes signs and then says they do not mean what people will say they mean — the end is not yet. He describes the fall of Jerusalem in detail, and the flight, and the unequalled distress, and sets it inside a generation. And then, at v. 32, the discourse turns a corner: of his own coming there is no sign, no timetable, and no one knows the day — not the angels, not even the Son.

What is left, four times over, is a command. Stay awake — which the parable at the end defines not as scanning the horizon but as being found at your post, doing the work you were left. And in the next two chapters Mark walks his reader through all four watches of the night, and the disciples fail at every one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Signs, Perseverance, and the Abomination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stones (vv. 1–4). They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the masonry, and Jesus says that not one of those stones will be left standing on another. Four of them come to him privately on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when.

The age (vv. 5–13). His answer begins by taking away the thing they wanted. Deceivers will come; wars will come; earthquakes and famines will come — and none of it means what people will say it means. The end is not yet. The church will be beaten in synagogues and hauled before governors, betrayed by brothers and fathers and children, hated by everyone. And in the middle of the list, one line that is not a disaster at all: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

The crisis (vv. 14–23). Then something specific: an abomination standing where it ought not to be, and instructions so urgent that a man on his roof is not to go downstairs for his belongings. Forty years later, Roman legions came up the valley.

Notice what the discourse never gives them: a date. It gives signs that will be misread, warnings that will be needed, and one command repeated four times — stay awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and Jesus answers about the temple and about his own coming, and the seam between them is visible if you look for it.

Everything down to v. 30 is hedged with signs and set inside a timeframe: false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, unequalled distress — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of those things did happen, in the horror of AD 70, some forty years on. That is why the fig tree can say the season is near, at the very gates.

Then look at the hinge in v. 32: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. The but turns a corner. From here Jesus says the opposite of everything before — no sign, no timetable, nobody knows, it arrives like a householder in the night.

So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgement on Jerusalem, marked with signs and dated inside a generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date. Read this way — and it is the reading the seams of the text ask for — Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He said the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He said his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 10) — one bright, forward-driving line dropped into the middle of a catalogue of disasters.

It is the only item in the list that is not something to be endured but something to be done, and the little word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people.

Now: that turns the whole grim catalogue inside out. The wars and betrayals and floggings are not the church waiting helplessly for the end. They are the conditions under which the gospel travels — and often it travels furthest precisely by way of those dragged before governors and kings (v. 9). Paul reached Caesar's household because he was arrested. The persecution is not an interruption of the mission; it is one of its engines.

So the age between the resurrection and the coming has a task, and not merely a fear. Every tribe that hears is the clock of the world moving one turn closer to the dawn — which is why a Christian reading the news is not simply watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him: look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings! Jesus said to him: do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.

Setting. Chapter 13 is the longest single speech of Jesus in Mark, often called the Olivet Discourse because it was given on the Mount of Olives (v. 3). It answers two questions: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will happen at the end? It stands between Jesus’ last day of public teaching in the temple and the account of his death. Jesus leaves the temple for the last time. He will not return.

And as he came out of the temple. A solemn departure. In Ezekiel’s vision, the glory of God left the temple and went to the mountain east of the city before the temple was destroyed by Babylon (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23). Now Jesus leaves the temple and goes to the Mount of Olives (v. 3).

Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings! The disciples were Galileans, from the country, and Herod’s temple was overwhelming. Herod the Great began rebuilding it in 20/19 BC, and the work went on until AD 63, only seven years before it was destroyed. It was built of white stone, much of it covered with gold, so that from a distance, said the historian Josephus, it looked like a mountain covered with snow. Some of the stones were enormous: Josephus speaks of stones 25 cubits long (about 37 feet, 11 m). Stones of about that size can still be seen in the Western Wall. The rabbis said: whoever has not seen Herod’s temple has never seen a beautiful building.

There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down. An astonishing prediction. The emphatic double negative in Greek (ou mē) means it will surely happen. Fulfilled in AD 70, when the Roman general Titus captured Jerusalem after a terrible siege. The temple was burned and then demolished. Josephus describes it: the city was so completely levelled that visitors could hardly believe it had ever been inhabited. The great retaining walls of the platform survived, but the temple buildings themselves were thrown down. The fig tree had withered (11:20).

In a sentence. As his disciples admired the magnificent temple, Jesus predicted its complete destruction, fulfilled when Rome levelled it in AD 70.

On a Tuesday. The most impressive human achievements, even religious ones, will not last. Build your life on what cannot be thrown down (Hebrews 12:27–28).
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with some stones many yards long. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately: tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?

And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple. The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley, and from it the whole temple mount can be seen spread out below. Jesus sits, the posture of a teacher, and of a judge, facing the temple he has just condemned. Zechariah prophesied that the Lord would stand on this mountain on the day of the Lord (Zechariah 14:4).

Peter and James and John and Andrew. The first four disciples called (1:16–20). This is private teaching for those who will lead the church.

When will these things be? The destruction of the temple. When?

And what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished? “All these things”, “accomplished” (synteleisthai, brought to completion). The disciples probably assumed that the destruction of the temple would be part of the end of the world. Matthew makes this explicit: what will be the sign of your coming and of the close of the age? (Matthew 24:3). Jesus’ answer will separate the two: the destruction of the temple will come within their generation (v. 30), but the end of the age at a time no one knows (v. 32).

Where Christians differ: how to read this chapter. Some (preterists) take the whole discourse as fulfilled in AD 70. Some (futurists, especially dispensationalists) take most of it as describing a future tribulation before a millennium. Others see it as speaking of both, with the near event foreshadowing the far. Verdict: the best reading, held widely in Reformed and amillennial interpretation, is that verses 5–23 speak mainly of the period leading to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which also serves as a pattern of the troubles of the whole church age; verses 24–27 speak of the second coming of Christ at the end of the age; verses 28–31 return to the destruction of the temple within that generation; and verses 32–37 speak of the unknown day of the end. There is no secret rapture here; the gathering of the elect is at Christ’s visible return (v. 27).

In a sentence. Sitting opposite the temple on the Mount of Olives, Jesus was asked privately by four disciples when it would be destroyed and what sign would precede it.

On a Tuesday. It is right to ask Jesus about the future. Listen to his answer, which is mainly about how to live until he comes.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.
