parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus began to say to them, "See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am he!' and they will lead many astray. And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus began to say to them: see that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, I am he! and they will lead many astray. When you hear of wars and rumours of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.

See that no one leads you astray. Jesus’ first concern is not information but protection. He does not give a timetable; he gives warnings. The word “see” or “watch” (blepete) runs through the chapter (vv. 5, 9, 23, 33).

Many will come in my name, saying, I am he! Not claiming to be Jesus himself, but claiming the role he holds: I am the Messiah (Matthew 24:5), or even using the divine name, “I am” (egō eimi, see 6:50). In the years before AD 70, many such figures arose: Theudas, who promised to part the Jordan (Acts 5:36); “the Egyptian”, who led thousands into the desert (Acts 21:38); and others whom Josephus describes, promising signs of deliverance. Every age since has had its false messiahs and false prophets.

And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. “Be alarmed” (throeisthe): be frightened, shaken. Wars are not signs that the end is about to come.

This must take place. “Must” (dei): God’s plan, as with the cross (8:31). Nothing is out of his control.

But the end is not yet. Key phrase. These events are not the end; do not mistake them for it.

Nation will rise against nation … earthquakes … famines. These describe the whole period between Christ’s first and second coming. In the decades before AD 70 there were wars on the Roman frontiers, a severe famine in the 40s (Acts 11:28), and major earthquakes, including one that destroyed Laodicea in AD 60 and one at Pompeii in 62. But such things have marked every generation.

These are but the beginning of the birth pains. Key image. The prophets used labour pains as a picture of the sufferings that precede God’s new age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9; Micah 4:9–10). Jewish writers spoke of “the birth pangs of the Messiah”. The pains are real and terrible, but they are not meaningless. They lead to birth. Creation is groaning in labour for the new world (Romans 8:22).

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples not to be deceived by false messiahs or alarmed by wars, earthquakes and famines, which are the beginning of the birth pains, not the end.

On a Tuesday. When the news is full of wars and disasters, don’t panic, and don’t follow those who claim to know the date of the end. God is in control, and this is labour, not death.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

verseByVerse.quote: But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be on your guard. For they will hand you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. When they bring you to trial and hand you over, do not be anxious beforehand about what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.

But be on your guard. Literally “see to yourselves”. From world events to the disciples’ own experience.

For they will deliver you over to councils. “Deliver over” (paradōsousin): the same word used of Jesus being handed over (9:31; 10:33). The disciples will follow their master’s path. “Councils” (synedria) were local Jewish courts, as well as the Sanhedrin in Jerusalem.

And you will be beaten in synagogues. Synagogues had authority to discipline Jews by flogging: forty lashes less one (2 Corinthians 11:24, where Paul says he received this five times).

And you will stand before governors and kings for my sake. Fulfilled in Acts: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5); Paul before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 24–26), and finally before Caesar.

To bear witness before them. Persecution becomes an opportunity for the gospel. The courtroom becomes a pulpit.

And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. Key verse. “Must” again (dei): God’s purpose. Before the end comes, the gospel must go to all the nations. This is the real “sign” of the age between the comings: not wars, but mission. By AD 70, the gospel had reached across the Roman world (Romans 1:8; Colossians 1:6, 23). But the mission continues until the end (Matthew 24:14; 28:19–20).

Do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say. A promise for times of persecution, not an excuse for not preparing sermons. When believers stand trial for Christ, they need not rehearse their defence in fear.

For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. The Spirit will give them the words, as he did for Peter (Acts 4:8) and Stephen (Acts 6:10).

In a sentence. Jesus warned that his disciples would be persecuted and tried before Jewish and Gentile authorities, giving them opportunity to witness, while the gospel goes to all nations, and the Spirit gives them words.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for Christians on trial for their faith around the world. And when you are asked about your faith, trust the Spirit to help you speak.
verseByVerse.note: The councils were local Jewish courts; synagogues had the authority to flog.

parallels.desc: Peter and John before the council

verseByVerse.quote: And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brother will hand brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

And brother will deliver brother over to death. Persecution at its most painful: betrayal by your own family. The prophet Micah described a time when a man’s enemies are the men of his own house (Micah 7:6). Jesus had said he came not to bring peace but a sword, dividing families (Matthew 10:34–36). In the persecution under Nero, the Roman historian Tacitus records that Christians were informed on by others, and many were convicted. It still happens today in many countries, especially to converts from other religions.

And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. “All”: by all kinds of people, Jews and Gentiles. Tacitus describes Christians as hated for their “abominations” and as haters of the human race. The reason: “my name”. They are hated because they belong to Jesus.

But the one who endures to the end will be saved. “Endures” (hypomeinas): remains under the weight, perseveres, does not give up. “To the end”: to the end of his life, or to the end of the age. “Will be saved”: not saved from death, but saved eternally.

Where Christians differ: endurance and perseverance. Some take this to mean that a true believer can lose salvation if he does not endure. Verdict: endurance is required, and it is real; those who fall away permanently show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). But God himself keeps his elect so that they will endure (v. 20; John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The perseverance of the saints means that the saints do persevere, because God preserves them. The warning is one of the means God uses to keep them.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that even family members would betray believers to death, and they would be hated for his name, but those who endure to the end will be saved.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you family relationships, you are not alone, and he knows. Keep enduring, and trust him to keep you.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down or enter his house to take anything out, and let the one in the field not turn back to take his cloak.

Now a specific sign. In answer to the disciples’ question (v. 4), Jesus gives the sign that the destruction of the temple is about to happen.

The abomination of desolation. Key phrase, from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11). An “abomination” is something detestable to God, especially an idol. “Of desolation” means that causes desolation, making the temple empty and abandoned, because God’s people can no longer worship there. Daniel’s prophecy was first fulfilled in 167 BC, when the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes set up an altar to Zeus on the altar of burnt offering in the temple and sacrificed pigs there. The book of 1 Maccabees calls it a desolating sacrilege (1 Maccabees 1:54). Jesus says it will happen again.

Standing where he ought not to be. Notice “he”: Mark uses a masculine participle with a neuter noun. The abomination is a person, or represented by one. Luke explains it plainly for Gentile readers: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). It refers to the Roman armies, with their idolatrous standards, coming to desecrate and destroy the temple. In AD 70, after the temple was captured, Roman soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and offered sacrifices to them, according to Josephus. Earlier, in AD 67–68, Jewish rebel factions (the Zealots) had occupied the temple, committed murders in it, and installed a false high priest, which some see as part of the fulfilment.

Let the reader understand. An aside, to the reader of Mark’s Gospel, or of Daniel. Think about this; you need to understand it.

Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Flee; do not try to defend the city or the temple. The early church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophecy, fled before the siege to Pella, in the hills beyond the Jordan, and were spared.

Let the one who is on the housetop not go down. Houses had flat roofs, used for rest and work, with stairs on the outside. Leave at once, by the outside stairs; don’t go inside even to collect belongings.

And let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. A man working in the field would leave his outer cloak at the edge of the field or at home. Don’t go back for it. The danger is that sudden.

In a sentence. When they saw Daniel’s abomination of desolation, the desecration of the temple by Rome, the disciples were to flee from Judea at once, without stopping for anything.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ warnings are given so that his people can obey them in time. Take his word seriously when it tells you to flee from danger (1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:14).
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple; it was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.

And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Jesus’ compassion. Flight would be hardest for them.

Pray that it may not happen in winter. Winter rains made the roads muddy and the river crossings, especially the Jordan, impassable. Prayer can affect the circumstances of what God has decreed.

For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been. The language echoes Daniel 12:1: there shall be a time of trouble, such as never has been since there was a nation till that time. The siege of Jerusalem was horrifying. Josephus, who was there, reports famine so severe that a mother ate her own child, the crucifixion of up to five hundred captives a day around the walls, and over a million deaths (probably an exaggeration, but conveying the scale). For the Jewish people, it was a catastrophe unlike any before it.

And never will be. This shows Jesus is speaking of a historical event within history, not the very end; there will be time after it.

And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. “Saved” here means survived physically. The siege of Jerusalem lasted about five months. If it had gone on longer, no one would have survived.

But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. “The elect” (eklektous): God’s chosen people, those he chose for salvation. The double expression, “the elect, whom he chose”, is emphatic. God’s sovereign choice of his people governs even the length of a war. He limits suffering for their sake. History is controlled by God for the good of his elect (Romans 8:28).

In a sentence. The siege of Jerusalem would bring unparalleled suffering, but God shortened those days for the sake of the people he had chosen.

On a Tuesday. God sets limits on the suffering of his people. He will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13).
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: And then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'Look, there he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then if anyone says to you, look, here is the Christ! or, look, there he is! do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.

Look, here is the Christ! or Look, there he is! During times of crisis, people look for a deliverer, and will follow anyone who claims to be one. During the siege of Jerusalem, Josephus records, false prophets told the people to wait for signs of deliverance in the temple, until it burned with them inside.

Do not believe it. Christ’s return will not be a local event that needs to be announced by someone (v. 26; Matthew 24:26–27). It will be seen by all, like lightning across the sky.

For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders. Miracles are not proof of truth. Satan can perform counterfeit signs (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13–14). Deuteronomy 13:1–3 warned that a prophet who performs a sign but leads you after other gods is false. The test is not power but truth.

To lead astray, if possible, the elect. “If possible” implies it is not possible. God’s elect may be shaken, but they will not finally be deceived, because God keeps them (John 10:27–29). But the warning is real. God keeps his elect partly through such warnings.

But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. Forewarned is forearmed. Jesus has given his people everything they need to recognise deception.

In a sentence. Jesus warned against false messiahs and prophets whose signs could deceive even the elect, if that were possible, and said he had told them everything beforehand.

On a Tuesday. Test every teacher by Scripture, not by impressive signs or the size of the crowd. You have been told beforehand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The coming (vv. 24–27). Sun darkened, moon gone out, stars falling, the powers shaken — and then the Son of Man, coming in clouds with great power and glory, sending out angels to gather his people from the four winds. It is Daniel 7 arriving, spoken by a man three days from a public execution.

The fig tree (vv. 28–31). A lesson in reading signs, and the most argued-over verse in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. And then a claim no creature could make — heaven and earth will go, and his words will not.

The hinge (v. 32). But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows — not the angels, not the Son. Everything before this verse had signs. Nothing after it does.

The command (vv. 33–37). A householder goes away, leaves each servant a job, tells the doorkeeper to stay awake — and might come back at any of the four watches of the night. Stay awake, four times over, and the last words are addressed past the four men on the hillside to everybody.

And Mark's reader is about to walk through all four watches in the next two chapters, with the disciples failing at every one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against the deity of Christ. Arius built on it in the fourth century; it is still reached for today. If Jesus did not know the day, the argument runs, he cannot be God.

The answer the church has always given is not a dodge but the heart of who Christ is: the one person, the eternal Son, took to himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God, so that from the incarnation there are two natures in the one Lord. According to his divine nature he is omniscient, upholding the universe; according to his human nature he learned to speak, grew tired, and — as Luke says plainly — increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. So the single person can truly say I do not know as a man, while as God he knows the hour perfectly.

It is no more a contradiction than that the same Jesus could sleep in the stern of a boat and then stand up and silence the storm with a word (4:38–39). The one he did as a weary man; the other as the Lord of creation.

And Mark has set the proof of it one verse earlier, for anyone with eyes. In v. 31 this same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own words above the entire created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day.

The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. That is not a prophet who overreached in v. 31, nor a mere man who was honest in v. 32. It is God become man — and this verse, far from disproving his deity, is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a householder goes away and leaves his servants each with his work, and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake.

Notice how the parable defines watchfulness, because it is not what the word suggests. The servants are not told to sit at the window scanning the road. They are given jobs. Watching, in this parable, is doing what you were left to do — and the doorkeeper's post is itself a task.

Now: which corrects both of the standard mistakes about the Lord's return.

One is the anxious calculation that treats every crisis as a countdown and produces confident predictions and quiet retractions. The other is the practical forgetting that lives as though he is not coming at all.

Jesus rules out both with one image. The man who is ready is not the man who worked out the date; it is the man found at his post, doing his work, whenever the door opens. Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes (Matt. 24:46).

So the honest question is not when? — he has refused that four times. It is: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it? If he came back this evening, would he find you at the post or asleep in it? That is a question about this week's ordinary duties, and it is the only question this chapter finally asks.

verseByVerse.quote: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

But in those days, after that tribulation. “But”: a contrast with what came before. “After that tribulation”: after the distress of the siege (v. 19), and the whole period of the church age that it represents. Jesus does not say how long after.

The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light. Isaiah 13:10, about the fall of Babylon; also Joel 2:10, 31; 3:15. The prophets used cosmic images like these to describe great acts of God’s judgement in history: the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13), of Edom (Isaiah 34:4), of Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7–8). It was their way of saying: the world is turned upside down, the powers are falling; God is acting.

And the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. Isaiah 34:4. The “powers” (dynameis) may be the heavenly bodies, or the spiritual powers that people worshipped through them (Ephesians 6:12). Either way, the whole created order is shaken by the coming of its maker (Haggai 2:6; Hebrews 12:26–27).

Where Christians differ: AD 70 or the end? Some (preterists, and some others such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright) take verses 24–27 as prophetic imagery for the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s vindication in AD 70, since the prophets used such language for historical judgements. Others take it as the end of the world and the second coming. Verdict: “after that tribulation” marks a new stage, and the gathering of the elect from the whole earth (v. 27) and the coming of the Son of Man in glory (8:38; 14:62) describe the visible return of Christ at the end of the age, as the New Testament elsewhere teaches (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). The cosmic imagery may be partly symbolic, but it points to a real event that ends history.

In a sentence. After the tribulation, the heavens themselves will be shaken, the prophets’ picture of God coming in judgement, here pointing to the end of the age.

On a Tuesday. Everything you can see will one day be shaken. Fix your hope on the kingdom that cannot be shaken.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.

And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds. Daniel 7:13–14 again: one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven, to whom is given everlasting dominion. In Daniel, he comes to the Ancient of Days, to receive the kingdom. Here, he comes to earth in glory. “They will see”: all people. His return will be visible and public, not secret (Revelation 1:7).

With great power and glory. The contrast with his first coming: then in weakness, now in power. The one about to be crucified will return as Lord of all.

And then he will send out the angels. His angels, his servants (8:38).

And gather his elect from the four winds. “His elect”: Christ’s chosen people. The angels gather them from everywhere, the four points of the compass. This is the great ingathering of all God’s people at the end, foretold by the prophets as the regathering of scattered Israel (Deuteronomy 30:4; Isaiah 43:5–6; Zechariah 2:6). Now it includes believers from every nation, since the gospel will have been preached to all nations (v. 10).

From the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. From one horizon to the other: nowhere is too far.

No secret rapture. Some (dispensationalists) teach that believers will be secretly taken from the earth before a seven-year tribulation, and that this passage describes a later stage. Verdict: the gathering of the elect happens at Christ’s visible coming in glory, after the tribulation (v. 24), just as Paul describes the gathering of believers to meet the Lord at his public return with a shout and a trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 2:1). There is one return of Christ, public and glorious, at which his people are gathered to him.

In a sentence. All will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory, and he will send his angels to gather his chosen people from every corner of the earth.

For worship. Every believer, wherever they are, whenever they died, will be gathered to Christ at his coming. Live in that hope, and pray: Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.

From the fig tree learn its lesson. “Lesson” is literally “parable”. A different use of the fig tree from 11:13, though they are on the same mountain.

As soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves. Unlike most trees in Israel, which are evergreen, the fig loses its leaves in winter. When the sap rises and new leaves appear, in late spring, summer is near. You can read the signs.

So also, when you see these things taking place. “These things”: the events Jesus has described, leading up to the destruction of the temple (vv. 5–23), especially the abomination of desolation (v. 14). The disciples had asked for a sign (v. 4); this is it.

You know that he is near, at the very gates. “He” or “it”: the Greek can mean either. “It” would be the destruction of the temple, the event they asked about. Most translations take it as “he”, the Son of Man. Either way, the point is that when the signs appear, the event is close, as near as someone standing at the city gate.

In a sentence. As fig leaves signal that summer is near, so the events Jesus described would show that the end of the temple was at the gates.

On a Tuesday. Learn to read the times in the light of Scripture, not to calculate dates but to stay alert and faithful.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

This generation will not pass away until all these things take place. “This generation” (hē genea hautē) everywhere else in Mark means the people living at the time (8:12, 38; 9:19). “All these things”: the events of verses 5–23, leading to the destruction of the temple, the event the disciples asked about (v. 4: when will these things be?). And so it happened: the temple was destroyed in AD 70, about forty years later, within the lifetime of many who heard him.

Where Christians differ: this generation. Some take “this generation” to mean the Jewish race, or the human race, or the generation alive at the end, which sees the signs. Some critics conclude that Jesus expected the end of the world within a generation and was mistaken. Verdict: the plain meaning is Jesus’ contemporaries. “All these things” refers to the events leading to the destruction of the temple, which did take place within that generation. Jesus then carefully distinguishes “that day” (v. 32), the day of his coming, whose timing no one knows. He was not mistaken.

Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. An astonishing claim. In the Old Testament, it is God’s word that stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8; Psalm 119:89). Jesus claims the same for his own words. They are more permanent than the universe. This is an implicit claim to be God. And it guarantees everything he has just said: the temple will fall, he will return, the elect will be gathered. You can stake your life on his words.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly promised that the events leading to the temple’s destruction would happen within that generation, and declared his words more lasting than heaven and earth.

On a Tuesday. Everything else in your life will pass away. Jesus’ words will not. Build on them.

parallels.desc: the word of our God will stand forever

verseByVerse.quote: "But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.

But concerning that day or that hour. “But”: a contrast. Jesus turns from “these things” (v. 30), which would happen within a generation, to “that day”. In the Old Testament, “that day” is the day of the Lord, the day of final judgement and salvation (Amos 8:9; Zechariah 14:4–9). Here, the day of the Son of Man’s coming (v. 26).

No one knows. No human being can know when Christ will return. Every attempt to set a date has been, and will be, wrong. The very fact of claiming to know is a mark of a false teacher.

Not even the angels in heaven. Who stand in God’s presence.

Nor the Son. A remarkable statement, and one the church would never have invented. How can the Son of God not know? The classic answer, from the early church fathers and the Reformers: Jesus speaks according to his human nature. As a true man, with a true human mind, he grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), and did not know everything. In his divine nature, he is omniscient. In becoming man, the Son voluntarily accepted the limits of a human mind, and did not use his divine knowledge in his human consciousness except as the Father willed. This is part of his humbling (Philippians 2:6–8). And it shows his perfect obedience: he does not seek to know what the Father has not revealed.

But only the Father. The Father has fixed the time by his own authority (Acts 1:7).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus is less than fully God, as Arians argued from this verse. Notice the order: men, angels, the Son, the Father. Jesus places himself above the angels, alongside the Father, as “the Son”, a unique title. It is a claim to deity even in the moment of confessing his human limitation.

In a sentence. No one knows the day or hour of Christ’s return, not the angels, not the Son in his human nature, but only the Father.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus did not know the day, ignore anyone who claims to. Your task is not to calculate but to be ready.

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.

Be on guard, keep awake. The practical point of the whole discourse. Because you do not know when, be ready always. “Keep awake” (agrypneite): stay sleepless, alert, watchful.

For you do not know when the time will come. “Time” (kairos): the appointed moment.

It is like a man going on a journey. The man is Jesus, who is about to leave (by his death, resurrection and ascension), and will return.

And puts his servants in charge, each with his work. While he is away, every servant has a task. Waiting for Christ is not passive. Every believer has work to do (Ephesians 2:10; 1 Corinthians 15:58).

And commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. The doorkeeper had to be ready to open the door the moment the master knocked, at any hour. Perhaps a picture of church leaders, who must keep watch over the household (Hebrews 13:17), or of every believer.

In a sentence. Because no one knows the time, Jesus’ followers must stay alert, like servants each doing their work and a doorkeeper keeping watch while their master is away.

On a Tuesday. What work has the master given you to do while he is away? Be doing it when he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore stay awake, for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning, lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: stay awake.

In the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning. The four Roman watches of the night, roughly 6–9 p.m., 9–12, 12–3 a.m., and 3–6 a.m. The master might come at any of them. And Mark’s readers would notice that these four times are the times of the passion night that follows: the Last Supper in the evening (14:17), Gethsemane and the arrest at night (14:32–50), Peter’s denial at cockcrow (14:72), and the handing over to Pilate in the morning (15:1). At each of these times, the disciples failed to watch.

Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. In Gethsemane, Jesus will come three times and find them sleeping (14:37, 40, 41). Sleep is a picture of spiritual unreadiness: complacency, carelessness, being absorbed in this world (Romans 13:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 5:4–8).

And what I say to you I say to all. Not only to the four disciples, but to all believers in every age, including Mark’s readers and us.

Stay awake. The last word of Jesus’ teaching before the passion. The final command: watch.

In a sentence. Since the master may come at any hour, Jesus commanded all his followers to stay awake, so that he will not come suddenly and find them asleep.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus came today, would he find you awake: living for him, doing his work, ready to meet him? Live this day as if it might be the day.
verseByVerse.note: These are the four Roman watches of the night, roughly from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.

13.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and the seam between the two answers is visible if you look for it. Everything down to v. 30 carries signs and a timeframe — false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of them did happen, in AD 70. Then v. 32 turns the corner: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. From there, the opposite of everything before — no sign, no date, nobody knows. Read this way, Jesus was not mistaken by a day: the temple fell in their lifetime as he said, and his own coming remains unmarked as he said.

Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against Christ's deity, from Arius onwards. The answer is not a dodge but the heart of the incarnation: the one person, the eternal Son, took a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God. As God he knows the hour; as man he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. It is the same structure as sleeping in a boat from exhaustion and then silencing the storm with a word (4:38–39) — the one as a weary man, the other as Lord of creation.

And Mark set the proof one verse earlier. In v. 31 the same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own sentences above the created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day. The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. This verse is not a problem for his deity; it is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.

And the signs will work (v. 22). Jesus does not say the wonders will be faked. Pharaoh's magicians duplicated the plagues (Ex. 7:22); Deuteronomy legislates for a prophet whose sign comes to pass and who then leads you to other gods (Deut. 13:1–3). The supernatural is not self-authenticating. It works is never by itself a reason to follow anybody; the test is always the doctrine underneath (1 Jn. 4:2–3).
13.examples:
Then: in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning — the four watches of the Roman night, listed as the hours at which the master might come home.

And Mark writes all four into the next two chapters, in order. When it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17). At midnight, Gethsemane — where he asks them to watch, comes back and finds them sleeping, three times, and says could you not watch one hour? (14:37). At cockcrow, the courtyard, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72). And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests delivered him to Pilate (15:1).

The parable's own words are the passion narrative's words. Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep — and he came to them in the garden at his hour of greatest need and found them asleep.

Now: do not read that as an indictment only. The men who failed it in the garden are the men he died for, restored on a beach, and sent to the ends of the earth. But do not imagine you would have stayed awake either. They loved him, they meant it, they were exhausted — and they could not manage an hour.

And note how the closing parable defines watchfulness: the servants are given jobs, each with his work. Not scanning the road; working. The man who is ready is not the one who calculated the date but the one found at his post when the door opens. So the question this chapter finally asks is answerable this week: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it?

14.title: The Cup, the Kiss, and the Fire
14.text: <sup>1</sup>It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, <sup>2</sup>for they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people.” <sup>3</sup>And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. <sup>4</sup>There were some who said to themselves indignantly, “Why was the ointment wasted like that? <sup>5</sup>For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they scolded her. <sup>6</sup>But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>7</sup>For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. <sup>8</sup>She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. <sup>9</sup>And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.” <sup>10</sup>Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. <sup>11</sup>And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>12</sup>And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, “Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>13</sup>And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him, <sup>14</sup>and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>15</sup>And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us.” <sup>16</sup>And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>17</sup>And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. <sup>18</sup>And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.” <sup>19</sup>They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Is it I?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. <sup>21</sup>For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>22</sup>And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” <sup>23</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. <sup>25</sup>Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>27</sup>And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ <sup>28</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>29</sup>Peter said to him, “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” <sup>30</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” <sup>31</sup>But he said emphatically, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And they all said the same. <sup>32</sup>And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” <sup>33</sup>And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. <sup>34</sup>And he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.” <sup>35</sup>And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. <sup>36</sup>And he said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” <sup>37</sup>And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? <sup>38</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>39</sup>And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. <sup>40</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him. <sup>41</sup>And he came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>42</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>43</sup>And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. <sup>44</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.” <sup>45</sup>And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>46</sup>And they laid hands on him and seized him. <sup>47</sup>But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>48</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? <sup>49</sup>Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.” <sup>50</sup>And they all left him and fled. <sup>51</sup>And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, <sup>52</sup>but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. <sup>53</sup>And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. <sup>54</sup>And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. <sup>55</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. <sup>56</sup>For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree. <sup>57</sup>And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, <sup>58</sup>“We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’” <sup>59</sup>Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. <sup>60</sup>And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>61</sup>But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” <sup>62</sup>And Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” <sup>63</sup>And the high priest tore his garments and said, “What further witnesses do we need? <sup>64</sup>You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?” And they all condemned him as deserving death. <sup>65</sup>And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, “Prophesy!” And the guards received him with blows. <sup>66</sup>And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, <sup>67</sup>and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.” <sup>68</sup>But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you mean.” And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed. <sup>69</sup>And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, “This man is one of them.” <sup>70</sup>But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, “Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.” <sup>71</sup>But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak.” <sup>72</sup>And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.
14.overview:
The longest chapter in Mark, and the clock runs in hours. Two days before Passover the chief priests decide to take him quietly — not during the feast — and are overruled by their own accomplice, so that the Lamb dies at Passover after all.

Mark wraps that plot around a woman in Bethany who breaks a flask of nard worth a year's wages over his head. The room calls it waste; he calls it beautiful, and says she has anointed him for burial. Then Judas goes out and sells him for less than the perfume cost.

In a borrowed upper room he takes the Passover bread — the meal that had looked backwards to Egypt for fourteen centuries — and turns it round: this is my body, and this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. Then they sing the Hallel and walk out into the dark.

What follows is the most exposed scene in the Gospels. In an olive grove, appalled and shaking, he asks his Father to take away the cup — the Old Testament's cup of wrath — and adds the words that hold the world together: yet not what I will, but what you will. Three times he comes back to friends who cannot stay awake for an hour.

Then a kiss, an armed crowd, and every one of them running. Upstairs in the high priest's house he answers the direct question at last — I am — and is condemned for it. Downstairs, at a charcoal fire, Peter says, in effect, "I am not", three times, and a bird calls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Anointing, Betrayal, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The plot and the perfume (vv. 1–11). Two days before Passover the chief priests are looking for a way to take him quietly. Mark then interrupts them with a woman in a house in Bethany breaking a flask of nard over his head — and closes the sandwich with Judas going to the priests for money. The plot frames the anointing, and the anointing interprets the plot: while men calculate the price of his death, a woman prepares his body for burial.

The upper room (vv. 12–21). Two disciples are sent into the city with a sign — a man carrying a water jar — and find everything as he said. And at the table, with the twelve reclining round him, he says that one of them will hand him over, and none of them looks at Judas.

The Supper (vv. 22–26). He takes the bread of the Passover, the meal that had commemorated the exodus for fourteen centuries, and says this is my body. He takes the cup and says this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

Then they sing, and go out into the night.
verseByVerse.theology:
He is not attending the Passover. He is the Passover.

For fourteen hundred years Israel had killed a lamb, put its blood where the destroyer would see it, and eaten a meal standing up, ready to leave — and told their children that this was the night God brought them out. Every element of that meal pointed backwards.

Jesus takes it and turns it round. The bread is his body. The cup is my blood of the covenant — which is Moses's phrase at Sinai, where he threw blood over the people and said behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Ex. 24:8), and it is Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on hearts, with sins remembered no more (Jer. 31:31–34).

So there is a new exodus, and he is the lamb of it, and the blood goes not on a doorframe but into a cup that is handed round a table and drunk.

And poured out for many is Isaiah 53 — the Servant who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12) — and it is his own word from 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many. Not a tragedy that overtook him. A ransom, deliberately paid, for a definite number of people whom he knew by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman breaks a flask worth a year's wages over his head, and the room objects that it could have been sold for the poor.

The objection is not stupid. Three hundred denarii would have fed a great many families, and the New Testament is fierce about the poor. But Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 15:11 at them — you always have the poor with you — and it is worth knowing that the verse he is quoting goes on: therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land. He is not excusing anyone from generosity. He is saying that this particular week will not come again.

Now: and then the sentence for everyone who has ever felt they had nothing worth giving: she has done what she could.

Not what she should have. Not what somebody more capable would have. What she could — which was one thing, and she did it, and he called it beautiful and said it would be told wherever the gospel went. It has been, for two thousand years, and Mark does not even record her name.

That is the measure. Not the scale of the service but whether it was the whole of what you had.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, for they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him, for they said: not during the feast, or there may be an uproar from the people.

Setting. The passion narrative proper begins. Chapters 14–15 cover about thirty-six hours, told in great detail. The early church told this story more than any other, and Mark’s account was probably shaped by years of preaching it.

Two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Passover (Hebrew Pesach) recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt, when the angel of death passed over the houses marked with a lamb’s blood (Exodus 12). The lamb was sacrificed on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, and eaten that evening, which by Jewish reckoning was the start of 15 Nisan. The Feast of Unleavened Bread was the week that followed (Exodus 12:15–20), and the two were spoken of together. Jesus will die as the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him. The plot that began in Galilee (3:6) and grew in Jerusalem (11:18; 12:12) now becomes a settled plan. They had already decided to kill him; the only question was how.

Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people. Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims, many from Galilee who supported Jesus. Passover, the feast of liberation, was a time of high nationalist feeling, and the Roman governor brought extra troops to the city. A public arrest could start a riot. So they planned to wait until after the feast. But God’s timing overruled theirs. Judas’s offer (v. 10) made a quiet arrest possible, and Jesus died at the feast, as the Passover lamb, exactly when God had planned.

In a sentence. Two days before Passover, the leaders plotted to arrest and kill Jesus quietly, intending to wait until after the feast for fear of the crowds.

On a Tuesday. Human plans are made, but God’s purpose stands (Proverbs 19:21). Even the plots of his enemies serve his timing.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt; Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that followed it. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims.

parallels.desc: the council resolves to kill him

verseByVerse.quote: And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly, "Why was the ointment wasted like that?
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly. She broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly: why was the ointment wasted like that?

The structure. Another of Mark’s sandwiches. The plot of the leaders (vv. 1–2) and the betrayal by Judas (vv. 10–11) are the bread; the woman’s devotion is the filling. Hatred and treachery on either side, and in the middle, extravagant love.

In the house of Simon the leper. Presumably a man Jesus had healed, since a leper could not host a dinner. Otherwise unknown. John places this dinner six days before Passover, and Mark may have placed it here for its meaning rather than its date (John 12:1–8).

As he was reclining at table. At a formal dinner, guests lay on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, with their feet away from the table.

A woman came. Mark does not name her. John tells us she was Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus (John 12:3). Luke records a different anointing earlier, by a sinful woman in Galilee (Luke 7:36–50).

With an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly. Alabaster was a soft, translucent stone, used for perfume jars, often with a long, sealed neck. Nard (spikenard) was a fragrant oil from a plant that grew in the Himalayas, imported at great expense from India. “Pure” (pistikēs) may mean genuine, unadulterated. It may have been a family treasure, or her dowry, or her savings.

And she broke the flask and poured it over his head. She broke the neck to pour it all out: nothing held back, and the jar could not be used again. Anointing the head was how kings were made (1 Samuel 10:1; 2 Kings 9:6). “Messiah” means anointed one. Without knowing it, perhaps, she anointed the King. John says she also anointed his feet (John 12:3).

Why was the ointment wasted like that? Matthew says the disciples said this (Matthew 26:8); John, that Judas did (John 12:4–5). To them, it was waste. Love always looks like waste to those who calculate.

In a sentence. At a dinner in Bethany, a woman broke an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume and poured it all on Jesus’ head, and some were indignant at the waste.

For worship. Is there anything you are holding back from Christ because it seems too precious to “waste” on him? Nothing given to him is wasted.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor." And they scolded her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor. And they scolded her.

More than three hundred denarii. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer, so three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages, with no work on Sabbaths and feast days. An enormous sum to pour out in a moment.

And given to the poor. It was customary to give gifts to the poor on the evening of Passover. And it sounds very spiritual. But John tells us that Judas said this not because he cared about the poor but because he was a thief and took from the money bag (John 12:6).

And they scolded her. “Scolded” (enebrimōnto) is a strong word: snorted at her, rebuked her harshly. She had done something beautiful, and was attacked for it.

In a sentence. They complained that the perfume, worth a year’s wages, should have been sold and given to the poor, and they harshly rebuked her.

On a Tuesday. Be slow to criticise others’ devotion to Christ. Pious-sounding objections can hide a cold heart.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages. John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus said, "Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus said: leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I tell you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.

Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? Jesus defends her.

She has done a beautiful thing to me. “Beautiful” (kalon): good, fine, lovely. Not only right, but beautiful. Love for Jesus that does not count the cost is beautiful to him.

For you always have the poor with you. An echo of Deuteronomy 15:11: For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor. Jesus does not dismiss the poor. Quoting this verse reminds them of the command to give.

And whenever you want, you can do good for them. Only Mark has this. The opportunity to help the poor is always there. Use it.

But you will not always have me. This moment is unique. Jesus is about to die. The opportunity to honour him in person will soon be gone.

She has done what she could. Only Mark has this. She could not stop his death, but she did what was in her power.

She has anointed my body beforehand for burial. Bodies were anointed with spices and perfumes for burial. Jesus would die as a criminal, and there would be no time to anoint his body properly; the women who came to do it on Sunday morning would find the tomb empty (16:1). So this was his only anointing. Did she understand? Perhaps more than the disciples. Either way, Jesus gives her act a meaning: it was for his burial.

Wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world. A remarkable prediction, two days before his death: the gospel will be preached throughout the world (13:10). And it has been, along with her story.

What she has done will be told in memory of her. And it is, as you read this. The disciples criticised her; Jesus made her famous.

In a sentence. Jesus defended the woman, calling her act beautiful, an anointing of his body for burial, and promised it would be told wherever the gospel is preached.

On a Tuesday. Do what you can for Christ. It may not seem much, but he calls it beautiful.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray him to them. When they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he looked for an opportunity to betray him.

Then Judas Iscariot. “Iscariot” may mean “man of Kerioth”, a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the Twelve who was not a Galilean. Or it may come from sicarius, “dagger-man”, a revolutionary.

Who was one of the twelve. Mark stresses this (vv. 10, 20, 43). The betrayer was one of the inner circle, chosen by Jesus, who had shared his life for three years.

Went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. He went to them; they did not come to him. Why did he do it? The Gospels give several reasons. Greed: he was a thief (John 12:6) and asked what they would give him (Matthew 26:15). Satan: Satan entered into him (Luke 22:3; John 13:2, 27). Perhaps also disillusionment: Jesus was not the political Messiah he expected, and was talking about dying. The story in Mark suggests a link with the anointing: the “waste” of a year’s wages may have been the last straw.

And when they heard it, they were glad. This solved their problem (vv. 1–2). An insider could tell them where to find Jesus at night, away from the crowds.

And promised to give him money. Matthew says thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), the price of a slave (Exodus 21:32), and fulfilling Zechariah 11:12–13.

And he sought an opportunity to betray him. A deliberate, continuing search.

What it does not mean. Not that Judas was a helpless puppet, forced by God or Satan. He chose freely and was fully responsible (v. 21). Yet his evil act was within God’s plan, foretold in Scripture (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18; Acts 1:16). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both fully true (Acts 2:23).

In a sentence. Judas, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests offering to betray Jesus, and they gladly promised him money.

On a Tuesday. Being close to Jesus outwardly is no guarantee of a true heart. Examine yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), and guard against the love of money (1 Timothy 6:10).
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, "Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?" And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him: where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover? He sent two of his disciples and said to them: go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him.

On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb. Thursday, 14 Nisan. Strictly, the feast of Unleavened Bread began on 15 Nisan, but in popular usage the day the lambs were sacrificed was included. On the afternoon of the 14th, the lambs were slaughtered at the temple by the thousands. Each household, or group of at least ten, brought a lamb; the priests caught the blood in bowls and poured it at the altar. The lamb was then roasted whole and eaten that night, within the walls of Jerusalem.

The date of the Last Supper. Mark, Matthew and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal. John seems to place Jesus’ death on the afternoon when the Passover lambs were being slaughtered (John 18:28; 19:14), which would make the supper a day earlier. Many explanations have been offered: that different groups used different calendars, or that John’s phrases refer to the whole week of the feast. However it is resolved, both accounts present Jesus’ death as the fulfilment of Passover.

Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover? Preparation involved buying and sacrificing the lamb, and preparing the unleavened bread, wine, bitter herbs and sauce.

A man carrying a jar of water. Carrying water was normally women’s work; men carried wineskins. A man with a water jar would stand out. Either Jesus foreknew it, as with the colt (11:2), or he had arranged it secretly, to keep the location from Judas until the last moment. Either way, Jesus is in command.

In a sentence. On the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, Jesus sent two disciples into the city to follow a man carrying a water jar to the place where they would eat the Passover.

On a Tuesday. Jesus prepares the way for what he asks you to do. Follow his instructions one step at a time.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us." And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house: the Teacher says, where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? He will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready; prepare for us there. The disciples set out, went to the city, found it just as he had told them, and prepared the Passover.

The Teacher says. The owner apparently knew Jesus, and would recognise the phrase. Perhaps he was a disciple.

Where is my guest room. “Guest room” (katalyma) is the same word used for the inn in Bethlehem where there was no room (Luke 2:7). At his birth, there was no room. At his last meal, a room is ready.

A large upper room furnished and ready. Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair. “Furnished”: with couches and cushions for reclining. Many think this was the house of Mark’s mother, Mary, where the church later met in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12), and perhaps the upper room of Acts 1:13 where the disciples gathered after the ascension. This cannot be proved, but it would explain some of Mark’s detailed knowledge.

And found it just as he had told them. Again, as with the colt (11:6): Jesus’ word comes true exactly.

In a sentence. The disciples found the large upper room exactly as Jesus had said, and prepared the Passover there.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus’ word is reliable in such small details, it can be trusted in everything.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?" He said to them, "It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was evening, he came with the Twelve. As they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said: truly, I tell you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another: is it I? He said: it is one of the Twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.

And when it was evening. The Passover was eaten at night, after sunset (Exodus 12:8).

One of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. An echo of Psalm 41:9: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me. To betray someone you had eaten with was a particularly shocking betrayal in that culture, because sharing a meal created a bond of loyalty.

They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, Is it I? In Greek, the question expects the answer no: “Surely not I?” They were shocked, but each knew he was capable of it. None suspected Judas.

One who is dipping bread into the dish with me. At the Passover, they dipped unleavened bread and bitter herbs into a common bowl of sauce (charoseth, made of fruit and nuts). Several might share one bowl. Jesus does not name Judas publicly here, but identifies the betrayer as one of those closest.

For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him. “Goes”: to his death. As it is written means in Scripture, in passages such as Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 and Psalm 41. Jesus’ death is not an accident or a defeat. It is God’s plan.

But woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! Yet God’s plan does not excuse Judas. “Woe” is a cry of lament and of judgement together. Divine sovereignty and human responsibility stand side by side.

It would have been better for that man if he had not been born. A terrible sentence. Judas’s end was worse than non-existence. This implies conscious, everlasting loss, not annihilation, and shows that Judas was not saved in the end (John 17:12).

In a sentence. At the Passover meal, Jesus revealed that one of the Twelve who shared his dish would betray him, as Scripture foretold, yet woe to that man.

On a Tuesday. “Is it I?” is a good question to ask yourself. Never assume you are beyond the capacity for betrayal.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said: take; this is my body. And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. He said to them: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

The Passover meal. The meal followed a set order. The head of the household explained the meaning of each element, retelling the story of the exodus: the lamb (God passed over our houses), the unleavened bread (we left Egypt in haste), the bitter herbs (the bitterness of slavery). Four cups of wine were drunk at fixed points. Jesus now gives the bread and the cup a new meaning, about himself. The old Passover gives way to the new.

He took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them. The same four actions as at the feedings (6:41; 8:6). “Blessing” means thanking God over it, in the traditional Jewish blessing: Blessed are you, Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth.

Take; this is my body. Jesus gives the bread a new meaning: it represents his body, about to be broken in death for them. Not the bread of affliction from Egypt, but his own body. “Take”: they must receive it. Salvation must be personally received.

And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks. “Given thanks” (eucharistēsas), from which we get “Eucharist”. Probably the third cup of the Passover meal, called the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the meal (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25).

And they all drank of it. All, including Judas, it seems (Luke 22:21).

This is my blood of the covenant. Key words. An echo of Exodus 24:8, when Moses sealed the covenant at Sinai: Behold the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you. A covenant was ratified by sacrifice and blood. Jesus’ death is the sacrifice that seals a new covenant between God and his people, the new covenant promised by Jeremiah, in which God writes his law on hearts and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8–9).

Which is poured out for many. “Poured out”: the blood of sacrifice poured out at the altar (Leviticus 4:7). “For many”: Isaiah 53:12 again, as in 10:45. His blood is shed in the place of many, for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28). This is the heart of the gospel: the substitutionary, atoning death of Christ.

Where Christians differ: the Lord’s Supper. Four main views. Roman Catholic teaching holds transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine becomes the body and blood of Christ, while their appearance remains; the Mass is a sacrifice. Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with and under” the bread and wine. Zwingli taught that the Supper is chiefly a memorial, “is” meaning “represents”. Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that Christ is truly and spiritually present, and that believers, by faith and through the Holy Spirit, truly feed on Christ, though his body is in heaven. Verdict: Calvin’s view is the best reading. When Jesus said “this is my body”, his body was sitting at the table, and the disciples would not have thought they were eating his flesh; he speaks as he did in “I am the door”. But the Supper is more than a reminder. It is a real communion with Christ by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 10:16), in which believers are nourished by him. And it is not a repeated sacrifice; Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14).

In a sentence. At the Passover, Jesus gave the bread as his body and the cup as his blood of the covenant, poured out for many, establishing the new covenant through his death.

For worship. Every time you take the Lord’s Supper, you proclaim his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). Come to the table by faith, and feed on Christ.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I tell you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God. And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine. “The fruit of the vine” is the phrase used in the Jewish blessing over wine. This is Jesus’ last meal before his death. Some think he did not drink the fourth Passover cup, the cup of completion, and that he would finish it only in the kingdom.

Until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God. A promise of the messianic banquet, the great feast at the end of the age (Isaiah 25:6–9; Matthew 8:11; Revelation 19:9). Even on the night of his betrayal, Jesus looks beyond the cross to the kingdom. He will die, but he will rise and reign, and he will eat and drink with his people again. The Lord’s Supper looks back to the cross and forward to that feast.
