And when they had sung a hymn. The Passover meal ended with the second part of the Hallel psalms (Psalms 115–118 or 114–118). Jesus sang, among other words: The cords of death encompassed me (Psalm 116:3), I shall not die, but I shall live (Psalm 118:17), and The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). He sang those words on his way to Gethsemane.

They went out to the Mount of Olives. Across the Kidron Valley, east of the city, to Gethsemane. Luke says this was his custom (Luke 22:39), so Judas knew where to find him.

In a sentence. Jesus vowed not to drink wine again until he drank it new in the kingdom of God, and after singing the Passover psalms, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

For worship. Jesus sang on the way to the cross. Sing in your hard times too, especially the psalms; they are the songs he sang.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The warning (vv. 27–31). On the walk out he tells them they will all fall away — and in the same breath tells them where to meet him afterwards. Peter says he will not, and says it twice, and the rest say the same.

The garden (vv. 32–42). Then the most exposed scene in the Gospels. He takes three men further in, tells them his soul is sorrowful to the point of death, falls on the ground and asks his Father to take the cup away — and adds the words that hold the world together. Three times he comes back and finds them asleep.

The arrest (vv. 43–52). Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and identifies him with a kiss. A sword is drawn, an ear comes off, and Jesus asks whether they think he is a robber. Then everybody runs — including a young man who gets away leaving his only garment in a soldier's hand.

And in three of the four watches of the parable he preached two nights ago (13:35), the disciples are asleep or running, and he is awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane depends on it, and the answer is not the general dread of dying.

Men far less brave than Jesus have gone to horrible deaths singing — including thousands of his own martyrs, many of them under torture, some of them within living memory of this night. If the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have the awkward position of a Lord less composed at the prospect than his servants.

The cup is an Old Testament image, and it is fixed. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8). Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17). Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it (Jer. 25:15).

The cup is the wrath of God against sin. That is what is set in front of him in that garden, and it is why a man who had faced hurricanes and legions without a flicker is on the ground shaking.

And he drank it. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21). Which means there is nothing left in that cup for anyone who is in him — the reason a Christian can face death more calmly than Christ did in the garden is precisely that Christ was not calm in the garden.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has said a word, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those two verses in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure has happened. Not after they repent. Not on condition of anything. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards.

And the word he uses is a shepherd's word — I will go before you, the way a shepherd walks ahead of the flock. He has just quoted Zechariah about the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zech. 13:7); now he says he will gather them again himself.

Now: and the angel at the empty tomb repeats it, with one addition that has comforted more failing Christians than almost any other line in Scripture: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7).

The one who was named in the failure is named in the restoration. If you have failed him badly and are wondering whether there is a road back, notice that the road was mapped and announced before you ever took the wrong turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: you will all fall away, for it is written, I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.

You will all fall away. “Fall away” (skandalisthēsesthe): stumble, be tripped up. Not just Judas: all of them. They will desert him.

I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Zechariah 13:7. In Zechariah, God himself strikes the shepherd: Awake, O sword, against my shepherd… Strike the shepherd. “I will strike”: the death of Jesus is God’s act, as well as the act of wicked men. The Father strikes the Son, in judgement for the sins of his people (Isaiah 53:10: it was the will of the Lord to crush him). This is penal substitution in the words of the prophet.

But after I am raised up. Again, he promises resurrection, alongside the prediction of their failure.

I will go before you to Galilee. Like a shepherd going ahead of his flock (10:32; John 10:4). The scattered sheep will be gathered again. The angel at the tomb will repeat the promise (16:7). Their failure will not be the end. He will restore them.

In a sentence. Jesus predicted that all his disciples would desert him, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy of the struck shepherd, but promised to go ahead of them to Galilee after he was raised.

On a Tuesday. Christ knows your failures before you commit them, and he has already planned your restoration.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Even though they all fall away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he said emphatically, "If I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him: even though they all fall away, I will not. Jesus said to him: truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. But he said emphatically: if I must die with you, I will not deny you. And they all said the same.

Even though they all fall away, I will not. Peter’s sincere love, and his pride. He thinks he is stronger than the others. He contradicts Jesus, and Scripture.

This very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. Very precise. “Today, this night”: before the day is out (Jewish days began at sunset). Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice, a detail perhaps from Peter himself. A cockcrow around 3 a.m. gave its name to the third watch of the night (13:35).

But he said emphatically. “Emphatically” (ekperissōs): vehemently, over and over.

If I must die with you, I will not deny you. He meant it. Peter was not a coward. In a few hours he will draw a sword against an armed crowd (v. 47; John 18:10). But courage in a fight is different from courage alone in a courtyard.

And they all said the same. All of them; and all of them fled (v. 50).

In a sentence. Peter insisted he would never desert Jesus, but Jesus predicted that he would deny him three times that very night, and still Peter and the others protested their loyalty.

On a Tuesday. Self-confidence is not faithfulness. Don’t trust your own strength; depend on Christ’s (1 Corinthians 10:12).
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went to a place called Gethsemane. He said to his disciples: sit here while I pray. He took with him Peter, James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. He said to them: my soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.

Gethsemane. The name means “oil press”. An olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, where olives were crushed for their oil. John calls it a garden (John 18:1). Olive trees still grow there, some very old. Here, Jesus will be pressed.

Sit here while I pray. As at the beginning of his ministry (1:35) and at key moments (6:46), Jesus prays.

And he took with him Peter and James and John. The three who saw his glory on the mountain (9:2) now see his agony. James and John had said they could drink his cup (10:39); Peter had said he would die with him (v. 31). Now they will see what that cup is.

And began to be greatly distressed and troubled. Two very strong words. “Greatly distressed” (ekthambeisthai): overwhelmed with horror, shocked. “Troubled” (adēmonein): in anguish, deeply disturbed. Mark does not soften the picture. Jesus, who calmly faced storms, demons and enemies, is now overwhelmed.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. An echo of Psalms 42–43: Why are you cast down, O my soul? His sorrow is so great it almost kills him. Luke tells us his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44).

Why such anguish? Many martyrs have faced death calmly, even joyfully. Was Jesus less brave than them? No. Jesus faced something no martyr has faced: the cup of God’s wrath against sin (v. 36), separation from the Father (15:34), being made sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). It was not death itself but what death meant for him: bearing the judgement of God in the place of sinners. The holy Son, who had known only the Father’s love, was about to bear his wrath. This is the measure of what our sin deserved, and of his love.

Remain here and watch. “Watch” (grēgoreite): keep awake. The same word as in 13:35–37. He wants their company, and their prayer.

In a sentence. In Gethsemane, Jesus took the three closest disciples with him, and was overwhelmed with horror and sorrow so deep it almost killed him.

For worship. Jesus was truly human, and felt horror and grief. He knows the darkness you feel, and he faced a darkness far deeper, for you.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. He said: Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.

And going a little farther, he fell on the ground. Luke says about a stone’s throw (Luke 22:41). Jews normally prayed standing (11:25). He fell to the ground, prostrate, in anguish and submission.

That, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. “The hour”: the appointed time of his suffering and death (v. 41; John 12:27).

Abba, Father. “Abba” is Aramaic for “father”, the word a child used at home, warm and intimate, though it was also used by adult children. Jews did not normally address God as “Abba” in prayer. Jesus did, because he was the Son. Mark preserves the Aramaic word, and Paul tells us that by the Spirit, believers too can now cry “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). We pray as sons and daughters because of the Son.

All things are possible for you. Jesus believes what he taught (10:27).

Remove this cup from me. The cup of God’s wrath (10:38; Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). A true request, from a true human will, shrinking from the horror of what lay ahead. If there were any other way to save sinners, let it be found.

Yet not what I will, but what you will. The key words. Jesus submits his human will to the Father’s. There was no other way, and he accepted it. This is the obedience that undid Adam’s disobedience (Romans 5:19). Adam in a garden said “my will”; Christ in a garden said “your will”. And this is the model for all Christian prayer: honest about our desires, and submitted to God’s will (Matthew 6:10).

What it does not mean. Not that there was conflict or sin in Jesus, or that his will was against the Father’s. His human will naturally shrank from suffering, as it should; to desire suffering for its own sake would be unhealthy. But he willingly submitted it. The early church taught, from this passage, that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in perfect harmony (the Third Council of Constantinople, 681).

In a sentence. Prostrate on the ground, Jesus asked his Father, if possible, to remove the cup of suffering, yet submitted wholly to the Father’s will.

For worship. When you pray, tell God honestly what you want, and then pray as Jesus did: not what I will, but what you will.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came and found them sleeping, and said to Peter: Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

And he came and found them sleeping. Exhausted, late at night, after a large meal and wine, and grief (Luke 22:45). But Jesus had told them to watch, and at the moment of his greatest need, they slept. The warning of 13:36 comes true: lest he come suddenly and find you asleep.

Simon, are you asleep? Not “Peter”, the rock, but his old name, Simon. The man who promised to die for him could not stay awake for him.

Could you not watch one hour? A gentle reproach, more sad than angry.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. “Temptation” (peirasmon): a test, a trial, the testing that could make them fall. It is coming within the hour. Their only defence is watchful prayer. This is the Lord’s Prayer in action: lead us not into temptation (Matthew 6:13).

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. “Spirit” here means the human spirit, the inner person with its good intentions; “flesh” means human nature in its weakness. Peter’s spirit was willing; he really did want to stand by Jesus. But his willingness was not enough. Good intentions without prayer fail. This is the experience of every believer (Romans 7:18–25; Galatians 5:17).

In a sentence. Finding them asleep, Jesus asked Peter why he could not watch one hour, and urged them to watch and pray, since the spirit is willing but the flesh weak.

On a Tuesday. Good intentions are not enough. Before temptation comes, pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.

And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. Repetition is not vain repetition when it is the cry of the heart (compare Matthew 6:7). Matthew records the second prayer: My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done (Matthew 26:42). The submission deepens.

For their eyes were very heavy. Literally “weighed down”. Mark is honest: they couldn’t help it, physically. But that is the point: the flesh is weak.

And they did not know what to answer him. The same words used of Peter on the mount of transfiguration (9:6). On the mountain of glory and in the garden of agony, the three failed in the same way. They had no excuse.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed the same prayer again, and returned to find them asleep again, ashamed and without an answer.

On a Tuesday. It is all right to pray the same prayer more than once. Keep praying until your will is shaped to God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came the third time and said to them: are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.

And he came the third time. Three times he prayed, three times they slept. Three times Peter will deny him.

Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? Or, with irony: “Sleep on now, and take your rest.” It is too late now.

It is enough. An obscure word (apechei), which may mean “it is settled”, “enough of this”, or even “the money has been paid” (it was used for receipts). Whatever the exact meaning: the time for prayer is over, and the time of action has come.

The hour has come. The hour he prayed might pass (v. 35). It has not passed; it has come. And Jesus rises to meet it.

The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. The prediction (9:31; 10:33) is fulfilled. “Sinners”: the Jewish leaders, who considered themselves righteous and Gentiles sinners, are themselves the sinners into whose hands he is given.

Rise, let us be going. Not to run away, but to go out to meet the betrayer. Jesus is not caught; he goes forward. The anguish is over. Having prayed, he has peace and resolve.

See, my betrayer is at hand. He sees the torches coming.

In a sentence. Finding them asleep a third time, Jesus announced that the hour of his betrayal had come and rose to go and meet the betrayer.

On a Tuesday. Prayer turns anguish into resolve. Pray until you can rise and face what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the Twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests, the scribes and the elders. The betrayer had given them a sign: the one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard. When he came, he went up to him at once and said: Rabbi! And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.

Judas came, one of the twelve. Mark repeats it again. The horror is that it was one of his own.

And with him a crowd with swords and clubs. Probably the temple police, under the authority of the chief priests, with servants, and perhaps some Roman soldiers (John 18:3, 12 mentions a cohort and its commander). A large force for one unarmed teacher and eleven tired men.

The one I will kiss is the man. It was dark, and they might not recognise him among the disciples. A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher, a sign of respect and affection. Judas turned it into a signal of betrayal. Joab had kissed Amasa as he killed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10). Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Proverbs 27:6).

Lead him away under guard. “Under guard” (asphalōs): securely. Judas perhaps feared that Jesus would escape, as he had before (Luke 4:30).

Rabbi! And he kissed him. The verb is intensive (katephilēsen): he kissed him fervently, warmly, perhaps repeatedly. The most chilling detail in the passion narrative. Matthew records Jesus’ reply: Friend, do what you came to do (Matthew 26:50).

And they laid hands on him and seized him. The Son of Man is in the hands of men.

In a sentence. Judas arrived with an armed crowd from the leaders and identified Jesus by greeting him warmly as Rabbi and kissing him, and they seized him.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to show outward affection for Jesus while betraying him. Let your love for him be real.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled." And they all left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Jesus said to them: have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled. And they all left him and fled.

But one of those who stood by drew his sword. Mark does not name him. John tells us it was Peter, and that the servant was named Malchus (John 18:10). Perhaps Mark, writing while Peter was alive or recently martyred, protected him. Luke tells us Jesus healed the ear (Luke 22:51), his last miracle of healing before the cross, done for an enemy. Matthew records Jesus’ rebuke: all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52).

And cut off his ear. Probably aiming at his head. Peter was keeping his promise to fight (v. 31), but it was the wrong kind of loyalty. Jesus’ kingdom does not advance by the sword (John 18:36).

Have you come out as against a robber. “Robber” (lēstēn) can mean a bandit, or an armed revolutionary, like Barabbas (15:7). They treat him as a dangerous rebel. He will be crucified between two such men (15:27).

Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. He had been in public all week. Their night-time arrest exposed their cowardice and their fear of the people.

But let the Scriptures be fulfilled. All of this is foretold. Perhaps Isaiah 53:12 (numbered with the transgressors), and Zechariah 13:7 (the struck shepherd, v. 27). Jesus is not a victim of circumstance. He submits to the Scriptures, which are his Father’s will.

And they all left him and fled. All of them, as he said (v. 27). The ones who had said they would die with him (v. 31). The Shepherd is struck, and the sheep are scattered. Jesus now faces his trial and death alone.

In a sentence. When one disciple struck the high priest’s servant with a sword, Jesus rebuked the crowd for arresting him like a bandit, submitted to the Scriptures, and all the disciples deserted him.

On a Tuesday. Don’t defend Christ with the world’s weapons: violence, anger, manipulation. And when you have deserted him, remember he went on alone for you, and came back for you.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. They seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.

Only Mark records this. A strange, brief episode. Who was he, and why is it here?

A young man. Many have suggested he was Mark himself, which would explain why the story is included at all: a small signature, like an artist painting himself into the corner of a picture. If the Last Supper was in his mother’s house (v. 15), he may have followed from there, hastily dressed. It cannot be proved, but it is an old and attractive suggestion.

With nothing but a linen cloth about his body. Linen was expensive, suggesting a family of some wealth. He had perhaps been asleep and thrown on a sheet.

And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. The ultimate picture of desertion. Even the one who tried to follow fled, leaving everything behind, in shame. Amos 2:16 speaks of the day of judgement: he who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day. Everyone deserted Jesus. Not one was left with him.

The contrast. The disciples had left everything to follow Jesus (10:28). Now this young man leaves everything to escape him. And there is another linen cloth in Mark: the one Joseph will wrap Jesus’ body in (15:46). And another young man: the one in white at the empty tomb (16:5).

In a sentence. A young man who tried to follow Jesus was seized, but slipped out of his linen cloth and fled naked, a picture of the total desertion of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. If you have ever fled from Jesus in shame, you are in good company, possibly that of the Gospel’s own author. He restores those who run away.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the young man. Many have guessed he was Mark himself, but the text does not say.

parallels.desc: he who is stout of heart shall flee away naked in that day

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 53–72 — The Trial and the Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The council (vv. 53–65). He is taken to the high priest's house and the whole Sanhedrin assembles in the middle of the night. They look for evidence to justify a verdict they have already reached, and cannot find any that holds — the witnesses contradict each other, even about the temple saying. He says nothing at all. Then the high priest puts the direct question, under oath, and he answers it in full for the first time in this Gospel: I am — and adds Daniel 7 and Psalm 110 to it. The robes are torn, the sentence is passed, and men begin to spit at him.

The courtyard (vv. 66–72). And Mark cuts, in the same building, to the one disciple who followed. A servant girl looks at Peter across a fire; a second challenge comes; then the bystanders place his accent. Three times, escalating — a denial, a denial, and finally oaths and a curse.

Then a bird calls, and he remembers, and the strongest of the twelve goes to pieces.

Mark has interleaved the two scenes deliberately: upstairs, Christ confesses and is condemned for it; downstairs, Peter denies and is safe.
verseByVerse.theology:
The trial was illegal, and the record shows it. By the standards later codified in the Mishnah, capital cases were to be tried in daytime, in the temple's own hall, never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival, and a conviction could not be handed down on the same day as the trial — an acquittal could, but a death sentence required a night to pass first. This proceeding breaks all of it. It is held at night, in the high priest's residence, at Passover, with sentence passed at once.

How much of that code was in force in AD 30 is genuinely debated. But Mark's own account convicts them without any of it, in one sentence: the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death (v. 55). That is not a court. A court seeks the truth and then decides the penalty; this one had the penalty and went looking for grounds.

And I am is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of demons silenced and healed men hushed, and now, under oath, with nothing left to protect, he answers plainly. Egō eimi — the words of the burning bush (Ex. 3:14) — and then two texts fused: seated at the right hand of Power (Ps. 110:1), which he had put to them as a riddle two days earlier (12:36), and coming with the clouds of heaven (Dan. 7:13).

He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the high priest tears his garments (v. 63) — the formal gesture required of a judge on hearing blasphemy.

And it is worth knowing what the Law said about that particular man's clothes. The high priest was under a standing prohibition: he shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Lev. 21:10). The office was not permitted the ordinary signs of mourning.

So on the night the Sanhedrin condemned Jesus for blasphemy, the high priest of Israel broke the Law of Moses to do it. Every man in that room was more concerned with the letter of the law than anybody alive, and the one they killed for breaking it was the only one in the building keeping it.

Now: and then they spat at him and covered his face and hit him and said Prophesy! — a game, apparently, of making the blindfolded man name who struck him.

They did not know that he had prophesied, that afternoon and the night before, with total accuracy: that one of the twelve would betray him, that all of them would run, and that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed twice.

While they were demanding a prophecy, the last of those predictions was coming true below them, in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl.

verseByVerse.quote: And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They led Jesus to the high priest, and all the chief priests, the elders and the scribes came together. Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest, and he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.

And they led Jesus to the high priest. Caiaphas, high priest from AD 18 to 36 (Matthew 26:57; John 18:13–14). John records a first hearing before Annas, his father-in-law, a former high priest who still held great power (John 18:13–24).

And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. The Sanhedrin, the council of seventy-one, or at least a quorum of it. A night-time meeting was irregular. By later Jewish law (the Mishnah), capital trials could not be held at night or on the eve of a feast, and a death sentence could not be passed on the same day as the trial. If those rules applied then, this trial broke them. They were in a hurry, determined to finish before the feast and before the crowds could react.

The structure. Another Mark sandwich. Peter in the courtyard (v. 54), Jesus before the council (vv. 55–65), Peter in the courtyard (vv. 66–72). Inside, Jesus confesses who he is, and is condemned. Outside, Peter denies who he is, and saves himself. Mark invites us to compare.

And Peter had followed him at a distance. Brave enough to follow, when the others had fled. But “at a distance”.

Right into the courtyard of the high priest. Wealthy houses were built around an open courtyard. John tells us that another disciple, known to the high priest, got Peter in (John 18:15–16).

And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. Spring nights in Jerusalem, at 2,500 feet, can be cold. Peter sits with the very men who arrested Jesus. The fire’s light will reveal his face (v. 67).

In a sentence. Jesus was taken to the high priest before the gathered council, while Peter followed at a distance into the courtyard and warmed himself among the guards.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus “at a distance” is dangerous. Notice where you are warming yourself, and with whom.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.

Were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death. The verdict was decided before the trial began. They were not looking for truth, but for evidence to justify a decision already made.

But they found none. A remarkable admission. In three years of public ministry, no genuine evidence could be found against him. He was innocent, the spotless lamb (1 Peter 1:19).

For many bore false witness against him. They broke the ninth commandment to convict the Son of God: You shall not bear false witness (Exodus 20:16). The psalmist had foretold it: false witnesses have risen against me (Psalm 27:12; 35:11).

But their testimony did not agree. The law required at least two witnesses whose testimony agreed for a conviction, especially in a capital case (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15). Under the law, a false witness was to receive the punishment he intended for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:18–19).

In a sentence. The council searched for evidence to justify killing Jesus, but even the false witnesses contradicted each other.

On a Tuesday. If you are falsely accused, remember that Jesus was. Commit your cause to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, "We heard him say, 'I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.'" Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying: we heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands. Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.

We heard him say, I will destroy this temple. A distortion of something Jesus actually said. John records that early in his ministry, Jesus said: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21). He had not said he would destroy it; he had said, if you destroy it. And he had predicted the temple’s destruction (13:2), but not that he would do it.

That is made with hands … not made with hands. “Made with hands” was a phrase used of idols (Acts 7:48; 17:24). The witnesses may have been twisting Jesus’ teaching that a new temple was coming, not a building but a people, built around himself (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Peter 2:5).

The irony. The false testimony was, in a deeper sense, true. By putting Jesus to death, they would destroy the temple of his body; in three days he would rise; and his resurrection would bring into being the true temple, not made with hands, the church. And the temple made with hands would be destroyed forty years later. This charge will be thrown at him again on the cross (15:29).

Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. The charge failed on a technicality.

In a sentence. Witnesses twisted Jesus’ words about the temple into a threat to destroy it, but even they could not agree.

For worship. You are part of the temple not made with hands, built on the risen Christ. Live as the place where God dwells.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest stood up in the middle and asked Jesus: have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you? But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And Jesus said: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.

Have you no answer to make? Frustrated, with the case collapsing, Caiaphas tries to make Jesus incriminate himself.

But he remained silent and made no answer. Isaiah 53:7: like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth. He would not defend himself against lies.

Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? The direct question. “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God”, avoiding the divine name. “The Christ, the Son of the Blessed”: the Messiah, the Son of God. Matthew says Caiaphas put Jesus under oath (Matthew 26:63). The question echoes Mark’s first line (1:1).

I am. Key words. Jesus’ plainest claim in Mark. The messianic secret is over. Now, when it will cost him his life, he says openly who he is. “I am” (egō eimi) may also echo the divine name (Exodus 3:14; Mark 6:50).

And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power. Psalm 110:1, combined with Daniel 7:13. “Power” is another reverent way of saying “God”. Jesus claims to be the one who sits at God’s right hand, sharing his throne (12:36).

And coming with the clouds of heaven. Daniel 7:13. The Son of Man who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. Jesus is saying: you are judging me now, but I will judge you. “You will see”: they would see his vindication, in his resurrection and ascension, in the fall of the temple, and finally at his return. The prisoner is the judge.

In a sentence. Silent before false charges, Jesus answered the high priest’s question openly: he is the Messiah, the Son of God, who will sit at God’s right hand and come with the clouds of heaven.

For worship. He confessed the truth at the cost of his life. He is who he said: the Christ, the Son of God, seated at God’s right hand. Bow before him.
verseByVerse.note: “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God.” Jesus’ “I am” is his plainest claim in Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest tore his garments and said, "What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?" And they all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high priest tore his garments and said: what further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision? And they all condemned him as deserving death. Some began to spit on him, to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him: prophesy! And the guards received him with blows.

And the high priest tore his garments. Tearing one’s clothes was a sign of grief or horror, and the required response of a judge on hearing blasphemy. Ironically, the high priest was forbidden by the law to tear his garments (Leviticus 21:10), though this probably referred to his official robes. Caiaphas was playing his part.

What further witnesses do we need? Relief: the problem of the witnesses is solved.

You have heard his blasphemy. Blasphemy, under the law, was punishable by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). Strictly, it meant using the divine name irreverently. Claiming to be the Messiah was not in itself blasphemy; others had done it. But claiming to sit at God’s right hand and come on the clouds, sharing God’s throne and role as judge, was claiming to be equal with God. If it was false, it was blasphemy. If it was true, they were condemning God.

And they all condemned him as deserving death. “All”: the verdict was unanimous, among those present. (Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, did not consent, Luke 23:51; perhaps he was absent.)

And some began to spit on him. Spitting in someone’s face was the ultimate insult (Numbers 12:14; Deuteronomy 25:9). Isaiah 50:6 had foretold it.

And to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, Prophesy! A cruel game: blindfold him, hit him, and demand that he say who struck him. Luke makes this explicit (Luke 22:64). The irony: at that very moment, his prophecy about Peter (v. 30) was being fulfilled in the courtyard below. He is a true prophet.

And the guards received him with blows. Slaps across the face, the treatment of a slave.

In a sentence. The high priest declared Jesus’ claim blasphemy, the council condemned him to death, and some spat on him, blindfolded and struck him, mocking him as a prophet.

For worship. The King of glory was spat on, struck and mocked, in silence, for you. Let it break your heart, and stir your worship.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, "You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus." But he denied it, saying, "I neither know nor understand what you mean." And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came. Seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said: you also were with the Nazarene, Jesus. But he denied it, saying: I neither know nor understand what you mean. He went out into the gateway, and the rooster crowed.

And as Peter was below in the courtyard. While Jesus was confessing his identity upstairs, Peter was denying his below.

One of the servant girls of the high priest. Not a soldier or a member of the council. A slave girl, the lowest person there, with no power over him at all. And Peter, who had drawn a sword against an armed crowd, collapsed before her.

She looked at him. Closely, in the firelight.

You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus. “The Nazarene”: from the small town of Nazareth, perhaps with contempt. “With”: being “with him” was the purpose for which Peter was chosen (3:14).

I neither know nor understand what you mean. A legal form of denial: “I don’t know what you’re talking about.” Evasive, rather than a flat denial of Jesus, but a denial.

And he went out into the gateway. Away from the light, toward the exit.

And the rooster crowed. Some manuscripts omit this, but it matches Jesus’ “twice” (v. 30) and the second crowing in v. 72. The first warning. Peter did not notice, or did not heed it.

In a sentence. When a servant girl recognised him as one of Jesus’ followers, Peter pretended not to know what she meant and moved away, and a rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. Denials of Christ usually begin with small evasions in front of unimportant people. Watch your first steps.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, "This man is one of them." But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, "Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders: this man is one of them. But again he denied it. After a little while the bystanders again said to Peter: certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.

And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders. She followed him to the gateway, and now told everyone.

This man is one of them. The circle of accusation widens.

But again he denied it. The tense means he kept on denying.

For you are a Galilean. Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent. Matthew says: your accent betrays you (Matthew 26:73). Jerusalemites mocked the Galilean accent, which dropped certain guttural sounds. Peter could not disguise where he came from. Every time he spoke to deny it, he confirmed it.

In a sentence. The servant girl told the bystanders that Peter was one of them, he denied it again, and the bystanders insisted, pointing to his Galilean accent.

On a Tuesday. You can’t hide where you come from. If you belong to Christ, let your speech betray you, in the best sense (Matthew 5:16).
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he broke down and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear: I do not know this man of whom you speak. Immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times. And he broke down and wept.

But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear. Not swearing in the sense of bad language, but taking an oath: “May God curse me if I am lying”, calling down God’s judgement on himself. Some think the Greek could mean he cursed Jesus (the verb has no object). Either way, the third denial is the worst: an oath before God that he did not know Jesus.

I do not know this man of whom you speak. “This man”: he will not even say his name. At that very moment, upstairs, “this man” was confessing that he is the Son of God.

And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. Exactly as Jesus had said. Luke records that at this moment the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61).

And Peter remembered. The word of Jesus came back to him.

And he broke down and wept. The Greek is unusual (epibalōn eklaien): perhaps “he thought about it and wept”, or “he threw himself down and wept”, or “he began to weep”. The tense means he wept and went on weeping. Bitter tears of repentance (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62).

Peter and Judas. Both failed Jesus terribly on the same night. Judas betrayed him and despaired, and died by his own hand (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied him and wept, and was restored (16:7; John 21:15–19). The difference was not in the size of the sin, but in what they did afterwards. Godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation; worldly grief produces death (2 Corinthians 7:10). Peter returned to the one he had denied.

Why record this? The early church did not hide the failure of its greatest leader. Mark, probably writing from Peter’s own preaching, records it in detail. Peter told this story against himself, again and again, as a testimony to the grace that restored him. No Christian is too great to fall, and no fallen Christian is beyond restoration.

In a sentence. Peter swore with a curse that he did not know Jesus; the rooster crowed a second time, and, remembering Jesus’ words, Peter broke down and wept.

On a Tuesday. If you have denied Christ, in word or deed, don’t despair like Judas. Weep like Peter, and come back. He is waiting for you in Galilee.

14.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane turns on it, and it is not the general dread of dying. Thousands of his own martyrs have gone to worse deaths singing; if the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have a Lord less composed than his servants.

The cup is a fixed Old Testament image and it means the wrath of God: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine... and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8); you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17); take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jer. 25:15). That is what stands in front of him in the dark, and it is why a man who slept through a hurricane is on the ground shaking. And he drank it — for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21) — which is precisely why there is nothing left in it for anyone who is in him.

And Gethsemane reverses Eden. In a garden a man was told the Father's will and said, in effect, "not your will but mine", and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended.

Abba (v. 36) is one of the Aramaic words Mark preserves, and the most significant: the ordinary family word a child used for his father at home. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. And it did not stay his — twice the New Testament says the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians (Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he handed over.

And I am (v. 62) is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of silencing demons and hushing healed men — and now, under oath, in chains, when it can only cost him his life, he answers plainly, in the words of the burning bush, and fuses Psalm 110:1 to Daniel 7:13. He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
14.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has opened his mouth, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure happens. No condition attached — not if you repent, not if you come back. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards, and the word he uses is a shepherd's word: I will go before you, out in front, the way a shepherd leads. And not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong — Galilee, where they were called off their boats.

Now: the angel at the empty tomb repeats it with one addition — go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). The one named in the failure is named in the restoration.

And the chapter ends with two men who betrayed him. Both of the twelve, both warned to their faces, both doing exactly what he said they would. One went out and hanged himself; one went out and wept.

The difference is not the size of the sin — denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. It is what each did with the wreckage. Remorse drove Judas away from Christ, to a rope. Grief drove Peter back.

So if you have failed him badly, notice where Peter was standing when it started: at a distance (v. 54), and then warming himself at the fire — near enough to keep his conscience quiet, far enough to keep his safety. Nobody stays there long. And notice that the man who told this story against himself, with the numbers in it, for the rest of his life, is the man whose memories became this Gospel.

15.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. <sup>2</sup>And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>3</sup>And the chief priests accused him of many things. <sup>4</sup>And Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.” <sup>5</sup>But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed. <sup>6</sup>Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. <sup>7</sup>And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. <sup>8</sup>And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. <sup>9</sup>And he answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?” <sup>10</sup>For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. <sup>11</sup>But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. <sup>12</sup>And Pilate again said to them, “Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” <sup>13</sup>And they cried out again, “Crucify him.” <sup>14</sup>And Pilate said to them, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him.” <sup>15</sup>So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. <sup>16</sup>And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. <sup>17</sup>And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. <sup>18</sup>And they began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>19</sup>And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. <sup>20</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. <sup>21</sup>And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. <sup>22</sup>And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). <sup>23</sup>And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. <sup>24</sup>And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. <sup>25</sup>And it was the third hour when they crucified him. <sup>26</sup>And the inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.” <sup>27</sup>And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>29</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, “Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, <sup>30</sup>save yourself, and come down from the cross!” <sup>31</sup>So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. <sup>32</sup>Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. <sup>33</sup>And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <sup>34</sup>And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>35</sup>And some of the bystanders hearing it said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” <sup>36</sup>And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” <sup>37</sup>And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. <sup>38</sup>And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. <sup>39</sup>And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>40</sup>There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. <sup>41</sup>When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. <sup>42</sup>And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, <sup>43</sup>Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>44</sup>Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. <sup>45</sup>And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph. <sup>46</sup>And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. <sup>47</sup>Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
15.overview:
Fifteen hours from the garden to the grave, and Mark tells it almost without adjectives.

At first light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular and hands him to Rome, because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry one out. Pilate asks one question, gets four words, and then nothing at all — and it astonishes him, because he has never seen a prisoner decline to save himself.

He knows the case is malicious; Mark says so plainly (v. 10). He tries the festival amnesty and the crowd, worked by the chief priests, asks for a murderer instead — a man called Barabbas, guilty of exactly the crime Jesus is falsely charged with. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning and, getting no answer, hands him over anyway, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Then a cohort of soldiers stages a coronation as a joke and gets every detail right; a pilgrim from Africa is pressed into carrying the beam and his sons end up in the church at Rome; and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words.

At noon the light goes out. At three he shouts the first line of Psalm 22 into the dark, and then shouts again and dies — and sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down, and a Roman officer who has watched him for six hours says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Before Pilate and the Mocking
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transfer (vv. 1–5). As soon as it is light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular, and hands him to Rome — because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry out an execution. Pilate asks one question and gets four words, and then nothing at all, and it astonishes him.

Barabbas (vv. 6–15). Pilate has read the situation correctly — he perceived that it was out of envy — and tries to release him through a festival custom. The chief priests work the crowd, and the crowd asks for a murderer. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning, what evil has he done?, gets no answer, and hands him over anyway.

The mockery (vv. 16–20). Then the whole battalion is called together for a game: a purple cloak, a crown twisted out of thorns, a reed, mock salutes and real spitting.

Every element of it is accurate. He is the King; he does receive homage; he will wear purple and a crown. A cohort of Roman soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got every detail right.
verseByVerse.theology:
Barabbas is the atonement acted out on a platform in Jerusalem.

Mark tells us exactly what he was: a rebel, in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection — guilty of precisely the crime Jesus is falsely charged with, and guilty in fact.

So two men stand before the crowd. One is guilty; the other is the Son of the Father and is innocent. The crowd is offered a choice, chooses the guilty man, and condemns the innocent one — and the innocent one dies in the guilty man's place, on the cross that had been prepared for him.

Nobody in Jerusalem understood what they were watching. But somewhere in that city, by nine o'clock that morning, there was a murderer walking around free, and the only reason he was free is that Jesus of Nazareth was on his cross.

That is the whole gospel, and it happened to one man literally before it happened to anybody else spiritually. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What evil has he done? (v. 14) — the right question, asked by the one man in Jerusalem with the authority to act on it, who then did the opposite.

Mark is careful to show that Pilate knew. He perceived that it was out of envy (v. 10). He tried the amnesty. He put the question twice. The Roman governor of Judea conducted a better assessment of the evidence than the Sanhedrin had, and reached the correct conclusion, and signed the order anyway.

Now: and the reason Mark gives is five words long — wishing to satisfy the crowd. Not conviction, not deception, not a legal error. He wanted the noise to stop, and his position was already precarious enough that a riot at Passover could have finished him.

That is the commonest failure of people in authority, and it has never needed a Roman governor to perform it. The doctrine not defended because of who would leave. The wrong not named because of whose son it was. The decision made by counting the room rather than weighing the case.

Pilate did not decide that Jesus was guilty. He decided that being right was more expensive than being popular — which is a different sin, and a far more available one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders, the scribes and the whole council. They bound Jesus, led him away and handed him over to Pilate. Pilate asked him: are you the King of the Jews? He answered him: you have said so.

And as soon as it was morning. Early, perhaps around 6 a.m. Roman officials began their working day at dawn. The night hearing (14:53–65) is now made formal by a morning session, perhaps to give the verdict legal standing, since trials at night were irregular.

Held a consultation. They agreed how to present the case to Pilate. Blasphemy would mean nothing to a Roman governor. So they turned it into a political charge: Jesus claims to be a king, a rival to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

And they bound Jesus. Like a criminal. Isaac was bound on the altar (Genesis 22:9); the true sacrifice is bound now.

And delivered him over to Pilate. “Delivered over” again (9:31; 10:33). Under Roman rule, the council could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31). Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect (governor) of Judea from AD 26 to 36. He normally lived at Caesarea on the coast, but came to Jerusalem at festivals with extra troops, to keep order. Ancient writers describe him as harsh, stubborn and contemptuous of the Jews; Luke mentions Galileans whose blood he mingled with their sacrifices (Luke 13:1). An inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.

Are you the King of the Jews? The political form of the charge. “King of the Jews” is a Gentile phrase; Jews said “King of Israel” (v. 32). The title runs through this chapter (vv. 2, 9, 12, 18, 26, 32). Rome tolerated no king without Caesar’s permission. Pilate’s “you” may be emphatic: you, a bound, beaten Galilean, a king?

You have said so. A guarded yes. The words are true, but not in the sense Pilate means. Jesus is a king, but his kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36–37). He is not the rebel Pilate fears.

In a sentence. At dawn the council bound Jesus and handed him over to Pilate, who asked if he was the King of the Jews, and Jesus answered, you have said so.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the King, though not the kind the world expects. Ask yourself in what sense he is your king.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chief priests accused him of many things. And Pilate again asked him, "Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you." But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests accused him of many things. Pilate again asked him: have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you. But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.

And the chief priests accused him of many things. Luke lists some: misleading the nation, forbidding tribute to Caesar, claiming to be Christ, a king (Luke 23:2). The second was a lie (12:17).

Have you no answer to make? Roman law gave the accused the right to defend himself; a man who did not was normally convicted.

But Jesus made no further answer. As before the high priest (14:61). Isaiah 53:7 again: he opened not his mouth. His silence is not weakness but dignity, and submission to the Father’s will. He would not defend himself against lies, or try to escape the death he came to die.

So that Pilate was amazed. Pilate had seen many prisoners plead, protest and bargain for their lives. Never one like this. Isaiah 52:15: so shall he sprinkle many nations. Kings shall shut their mouths because of him.

In a sentence. Faced with many accusations, Jesus gave no answer, and Pilate was astonished.

On a Tuesday. There are times when silence is the right answer to false accusation. Trust God to vindicate you (1 Peter 2:23).

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. And he answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?" For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the feast Pilate used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. Among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. The crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. He answered them: do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews? For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed him over.

Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner. A Passover amnesty. It is not mentioned outside the Gospels, but such amnesties were known elsewhere in the Roman world, and it fits a festival celebrating liberation from slavery.

Among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection. “The insurrection”: one of the many uprisings against Rome in those years, well known to Mark’s source. Barabbas was a revolutionary, perhaps a Zealot, who had killed someone in a riot. Exactly the kind of man Pilate should have feared, and exactly the kind of “king” the crowd wanted.

A man called Barabbas. An Aramaic name meaning “son of the father” (bar abba). Some manuscripts of Matthew give his first name as Jesus (Matthew 27:16–17): Jesus Barabbas. The crowd is offered a choice between two “sons of the father”: a murderer, and the true Son of the Father (14:36).

And the crowd came up. “Came up” to the governor’s residence. This crowd was perhaps not the same as the Galilean pilgrims who had welcomed Jesus; it may have come specifically to ask for the release, and perhaps for Barabbas.

Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews? Pilate thought he could free Jesus this way. The title is also contemptuous of the Jews: this is your king?

For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. Pilate saw through them. They were not loyal to Caesar; they were jealous of Jesus’ popularity and authority. Envy, one of the sins Jesus listed from the heart (7:22), sent him to the cross.

In a sentence. Pilate, knowing the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy, offered to release him under the Passover amnesty instead of Barabbas, a murderer and rebel.

On a Tuesday. Envy is a deadly sin. When you resent someone else’s gifts or success, remember what envy did to Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Barabbas means “son of the father.” The “insurrection” was one of many uprisings against Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. And Pilate again said to them, "Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?" And they cried out again, "Crucify him." And Pilate said to them, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Crucify him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas for them instead. Pilate again said to them: then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews? They cried out again: crucify him. Pilate said to them: why? What evil has he done? But they shouted all the more: crucify him.

But the chief priests stirred up the crowd. “Stirred up” (aneseisan): shook them up, incited them. The leaders manipulate the crowd.

What shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews? The question of every person who hears of Jesus: what will you do with him?

Crucify him. The crowd that shouted Hosanna (11:9), or a different one, now shouts for the most shameful death the Romans knew. Crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels and the worst criminals, and was meant to deter by its horror. Roman citizens could not be crucified. The Jewish law said a man hanged on a tree was cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). They wanted not only his death, but his disgrace.

Why? What evil has he done? The judge declares him innocent. Luke records that Pilate said three times that he found no guilt in him (Luke 23:4, 14, 22). The judge’s own words testify that Jesus died not for his own sins, but as the righteous for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18).

But they shouted all the more, Crucify him. No answer to “why?” Only louder shouting. The mob does not reason.

In a sentence. Stirred up by the chief priests, the crowd chose Barabbas and, when Pilate asked what evil Jesus had done, only shouted louder for his crucifixion.

On a Tuesday. What will you do with Jesus? Every person must answer, and there is no neutral answer.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released Barabbas for them, and having scourged Jesus, he handed him over to be crucified.

So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd. Pilate chose politics over justice. He knew Jesus was innocent, but a riot at Passover could cost him his position. John records the crowd’s threat: If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend (John 19:12). Matthew records that he washed his hands to declare himself innocent (Matthew 27:24). But a judge who condemns a man he knows is innocent is not innocent. The church has confessed for centuries that Jesus suffered under Pontius Pilate.

Released for them Barabbas. The guilty man goes free; the innocent man dies in his place. Barabbas is the first person in history who could say, literally: Jesus died instead of me. And every believer can say the same. This is substitution in a picture.

And having scourged Jesus. Roman scourging (flagellatio) was the normal preliminary to crucifixion. The prisoner was stripped, tied to a post, and beaten with a whip of several leather thongs weighted with pieces of bone or metal. It tore the flesh to the bone. Men sometimes died under it. Mark records it in a single word, without description. Isaiah 53:5: with his wounds we are healed.

He delivered him to be crucified. The final “handing over”. The Father gave the Son (Romans 8:32), Judas handed him to the priests, the priests to Pilate, and Pilate to the soldiers.

In a sentence. To satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas, had Jesus scourged, and handed him over to be crucified.

For worship. You are Barabbas. The guilty one went free because the innocent one took his place. Give thanks.
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor's headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. And they began to salute him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers led him away inside the palace, that is, the governor’s headquarters, and called together the whole battalion. They clothed him in a purple cloak, twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on him. They began to salute him: hail, King of the Jews! They struck his head with a reed, spat on him, and knelt down in homage to him. When they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.

Inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters). The praetorium, the governor’s residence in Jerusalem, either Herod’s palace on the west side of the city or the Antonia fortress next to the temple. Mark uses the Latin word for his Roman readers.

And they called together the whole battalion. A cohort (speira): in theory 600 men, though probably only those on hand. These were not Romans from Italy but auxiliaries, recruited from non-Jewish people in the region, who had no love for Jews.

And they clothed him in a purple cloak. Purple was the colour of royalty, made from an expensive dye. This was probably a faded red soldier’s cloak (Matthew 27:28 says scarlet), passed off as a king’s robe.

And twisting together a crown of thorns. A parody of the laurel wreath that the emperor wore, perhaps woven from the long thorns of a date palm, sticking out like the rays of a crown on coins. Thorns were the sign of the curse on the ground after Adam’s sin (Genesis 3:17–18). The King bears the curse on his head.

Hail, King of the Jews! A parody of the greeting to Caesar: Ave, Caesar! Hail, Caesar!

And they were striking his head with a reed. The reed was his mock sceptre (Matthew 27:29), then used to beat him, driving the thorns in.

And spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. Mock worship. The irony: every one of them will bow the knee to him one day, in truth (Philippians 2:10–11).

And they led him out to crucify him. Out of the city (Hebrews 13:12).

In a sentence. The soldiers dressed Jesus as a mock king in a purple cloak and a crown of thorns, saluted him, beat him and spat on him, before leading him out to be crucified.

For worship. They mocked him as king, and he is the King. Bow to him in truth where they bowed in mockery.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. Purple was the colour of royalty.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The road and the cross (vv. 21–27). A man on his way in from the country is pressed into carrying the beam, and Mark names his sons, probably because his readers knew them. At Golgotha he refuses the drugged wine, the soldiers gamble for his clothes, and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words: and they crucified him.

The mockery (vv. 29–32). Three groups take their turn — passers-by, the chief priests, and the two men dying beside him. The taunt is always the same, and it is the wilderness temptation for the third time: come down; save yourself.

The darkness (vv. 33–37). At noon the light goes out for three hours. And at three o'clock he cries out in Aramaic the opening line of Psalm 22, and Mark preserves the sound of it. Then a loud cry, and he is dead.

What the death did (vv. 38–41). Sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down. A Roman officer says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said. And the women who have been there all along are named.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cry of dereliction (v. 34) is the sentence a suffering reader stops at, and two errors must be kept off it.

The first would soften it — as though Jesus were merely reciting a comforting psalm and was not truly forsaken. He was. The abandonment was real; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer.

The second would break God in two — as though the Trinity were torn apart, the Father ceasing to love the Son, the Son ceasing to be God. That did not happen and could not. The Son remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment of the darkness; what he lost was not his Father's love or his own deity but the felt light of the Father's face, borne in our place.

Both are true at once: he entered a real forsakenness, and he entered it still holding on — for notice the word he uses. He does not cry God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God: twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark.

And that is the word for the believer who has prayed into silence. The blackest hour a soul can know — real God-forsakenness, the full weight of it — has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb. 13:5) is bought with this cry. If you must pray in the dark, pray as he did — my God — to the God you cannot feel, and know that he prayed it first, and prayed it there, so that you would never have to pray it alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, standing at the foot of the cross, jeering.

And they have stated the gospel with complete accuracy without meaning a word of it.

Every clause is true. He did save others — a leper, a paralytic, a legion, a dead girl, a boy with a spirit. And he could not save himself — not because the power was gone, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done.

Now: the mockers thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the mechanism. The one who saves others cannot save himself; that is not a failure of power but the shape of substitution, and it is why there is a gospel at all.

And notice the demand attached: come down now from the cross that we may see and believe (v. 32). They had the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand — show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes. Had he come down they would have seen a miracle and gone home unforgiven. He stayed up, and by three o'clock a Roman officer who had asked for no sign at all was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull).
verseByVerse.commentary:
