They compelled a passer-by, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull.

And they compelled a passerby. Roman soldiers had the right to force civilians to carry loads for them (Matthew 5:41 uses the same word). Normally the condemned man carried his own crossbeam (patibulum), weighing perhaps 75–100 pounds (35–45 kg), to the place of execution, where the upright post was already standing. Jesus, weakened by the scourging, could not.

Simon of Cyrene. Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in modern Libya, with a large Jewish community. Simon was probably a Jewish pilgrim, or had settled in Jerusalem. People from Cyrene were among those at Pentecost (Acts 2:10), and some of the first to preach to Gentiles (Acts 11:20).

Who was coming in from the country. Into the city, as Jesus was being led out.

The father of Alexander and Rufus. Only Mark has this. Why name his sons? Because Mark’s readers knew them. They were Christians. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Romans 16:13). If this is the same family, as is likely if Mark wrote for Rome, then Simon’s forced service to Jesus led to the faith of his whole family. He literally took up the cross and followed Jesus (8:34).

To carry his cross. Luke says he carried it behind Jesus (Luke 23:26), the picture of a disciple.

Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). Golgotha is Aramaic; “Calvary” comes from the Latin word for skull, calvaria. Perhaps a rocky hill shaped like a skull, or a place of execution. It was outside the city wall then, but near it, on a main road, so that passers-by could see (v. 29). The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, inside today’s Old City (but outside the wall of Jesus’ day), has a strong claim to be the site.

In a sentence. The soldiers forced Simon of Cyrene, whose sons became known Christians, to carry Jesus’ cross to Golgotha.

On a Tuesday. Simon was forced to carry the cross; you are invited. And God can use an unwanted interruption to change a whole family.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” Rufus may be the man Paul greets in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.

And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh. A drugged drink, to dull the pain. Jewish tradition records that the women of Jerusalem provided it as an act of mercy for the condemned, based on Proverbs 31:6: give strong drink to the one who is perishing.

But he did not take it. Jesus chose to face the cross with a clear mind, and to drink the full cup the Father had given him (14:36). He would not dull what he had come to bear. He had also said he would not drink wine again until the kingdom (14:25).

And they crucified him. Mark describes the most terrible death in the ancient world in three Greek words, with no detail. His first readers knew exactly what it meant. The victim was stripped, laid on the crossbeam, and nailed through the wrists and feet, or tied; then the beam was hoisted onto the upright post. He hung there, often for days, in agony, struggling to push himself up to breathe, until he died of exhaustion and suffocation. Cicero called it the cruellest and most disgusting penalty. The Gospels focus not on the physical suffering, but on its meaning.

And divided his garments among them, casting lots for them. The clothing of the executed belonged to the soldiers. A man’s clothes were among his few possessions: an outer cloak, an inner tunic, a belt, sandals, a head covering. They gambled for them, probably with dice. Psalm 22:18: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. The psalm of the righteous sufferer (Psalm 22) runs through this chapter. Jesus was crucified naked, the final shame. Adam and Eve were clothed by God after the first sin (Genesis 3:21); Christ was stripped to clothe us in his righteousness.

In a sentence. Jesus refused the drugged wine and was crucified, and the soldiers gambled for his clothes, as Psalm 22 foretold.

For worship. He was stripped naked so that you could be clothed in his righteousness (Isaiah 61:10). Worship him.
verseByVerse.note: Wine mixed with myrrh was a drugged drink to dull pain; Jesus refused it. The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And it was the third hour when they crucified him. And the inscription of the charge against him read, "The King of the Jews." And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the third hour when they crucified him. The inscription of the charge against him read: The King of the Jews. And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.

And it was the third hour when they crucified him. About 9 a.m. by Jewish reckoning, counting from sunrise. Mark marks the hours carefully: the third (v. 25), the sixth (v. 33), the ninth (v. 34). John says it was about the sixth hour when Pilate handed him over (John 19:14). Perhaps John used Roman reckoning, from midnight; or both are approximate, since people reckoned time in three-hour blocks.

The inscription of the charge against him. A placard (titulus) stating the crime was carried before the condemned man or hung around his neck, then fixed to the cross. John says it was written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek (John 19:20).

The King of the Jews. Meant as mockery and a warning: this is what happens to rebel kings. But it was the truth. Pilate proclaimed to the world, in three languages, who Jesus is. On the cross, he is enthroned as King, ruling by giving his life.

And with him they crucified two robbers. “Robbers” (lēstas), the same word Jesus used at his arrest (14:48), probably meaning rebels like Barabbas. Perhaps Barabbas’ companions.

One on his right and one on his left. James and John had asked for these places in his glory (10:37). Jesus told them they did not know what they were asking. This was his glory, and those were the places beside him.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add verse 28: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, He was numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, quoted in Luke 22:37). It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added from Luke. The ESV puts it in a footnote. It is true, though not original to Mark.

In a sentence. Jesus was crucified at about 9 a.m. under the charge “The King of the Jews”, between two rebels, in the places James and John had asked for.

For worship. The charge against him was the truth. He reigns from the cross. Worship the crucified King.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 28: “And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors.’”

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying: aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!

And those who passed by. Crucifixions took place by roads, for maximum publicity.

Derided him. The word is eblasphēmoun, literally “blasphemed him”. Jesus was condemned for blasphemy; now the real blasphemers are those who mock the Son of God.

Wagging their heads. A gesture of scorn. Psalm 22:7: All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads. Also Lamentations 2:15.

You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days. The false charge from the trial (14:58). The irony is total: at that very moment, the temple of his body was being destroyed, and in three days he would raise it.

Save yourself, and come down from the cross! The temptation of the wilderness, of Peter at Caesarea Philippi (8:32–33), and of Gethsemane, one last time: avoid the cross. He could have. Twelve legions of angels were at his command (Matthew 26:53). But if he saved himself, he could not save us.

In a sentence. Passers-by mocked Jesus with the false charge about the temple and taunted him to save himself and come down from the cross.

On a Tuesday. The world still says to Christians: save yourself. Jesus shows the other way: lose your life and save it (8:35).

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe." Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying: he saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, that we may see and believe. Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.

So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him. The religious leaders, at the foot of the cross, gloating. They speak to one another, not to him: he is beneath their address.

He saved others; he cannot save himself. The most profound irony in the Gospel. They mean it as a sneer. But it is the deepest truth of the cross. Precisely because he would save others, he could not save himself. He chose not to. Love bound him to the cross more firmly than nails. They admit, without meaning to, that he saved others.

Let the Christ, the King of Israel. The Jewish form of the title (compare v. 26). They mock his claim before the council (14:61–62).

Come down now from the cross that we may see and believe. Another demand for a sign (8:11–12). But they would not have believed (Luke 16:31). In three days he would do something greater than coming down from the cross: he would come up from the grave. And still they would not believe.

Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. Even the dying criminals joined in. Luke records that one of them later repented and was promised paradise (Luke 23:39–43). Mark, focusing on Jesus’ total abandonment, records only the reviling.

In a sentence. The religious leaders mocked Jesus, saying he saved others but could not save himself, and challenged him to come down so they might believe; even the criminals beside him reviled him.

For worship. He did not save himself, so that he could save you. That is the gospel in the mouth of his enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. At the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice: Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? which means, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

And when the sixth hour had come. Noon, the brightest time of day.

There was darkness over the whole land. Not an eclipse, which cannot happen at Passover, when the moon is full. A supernatural darkness, for three hours. In Scripture, darkness is a sign of God’s judgement. The ninth plague on Egypt was darkness (Exodus 10:21–23), just before the Passover. Amos prophesied: On that day, declares the Lord God, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight … I will make it like the mourning for an only son (Amos 8:9–10). The darkness shows that God’s judgement on sin is falling, and it falls on Jesus.

Until the ninth hour. About 3 p.m., the time of the evening sacrifice in the temple (Acts 3:1).

Jesus cried with a loud voice. Not the faint whisper of a dying man, but a cry.

Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani? Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, preserved by Mark as he preserved other words of Jesus (5:41; 7:34; 14:36). The only words of Jesus from the cross that Mark records. They are the first line of Psalm 22, which he quotes in his own tongue.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? The darkest words in Scripture. Jesus, who always called God “Father” (“Abba”, 14:36), now says “my God”. He is not doubting the Father or losing faith; he still says “my God”, twice. But he experiences what no one else ever has: being forsaken by God. Why? Because he was bearing our sin. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). He became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The holy God turns away from sin, and Jesus, bearing it, experienced the abandonment that sinners deserve. This is hell: separation from God. Jesus endured it, in the place of his people, so that they would never be forsaken. This is penal substitution at its heart.

Psalm 22. Quoting the first line of a psalm brought the whole psalm to mind. Psalm 22 moves from abandonment (vv. 1–21) through mockery (vv. 7–8), the dividing of garments (v. 18) and pierced hands and feet (v. 16), to victory and praise: all the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord (vv. 22–31). Its last words are: he has done it. Jesus’ cry is real dereliction; but it is also the cry of one who knows the end of the psalm.

What it does not mean. Not that the Trinity was broken, or that the Father stopped loving the Son. The Father was never more pleased with the Son than in this act of obedience (John 10:17; Ephesians 5:2). The Son, in his human nature, bore the Father’s wrath against sin and experienced the withdrawal of all sense of his favour. The mystery is beyond us. But the fact is clear: he was forsaken so that we would be accepted.

In a sentence. After three hours of supernatural darkness, Jesus cried out in the words of Psalm 22, asking why God had forsaken him, as he bore the judgement of God against sin.

For worship. Because he was forsaken, you never will be (Hebrews 13:5). Let this cry move you to grateful, wondering worship.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders hearing it said, "Behold, he is calling Elijah." And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the bystanders who heard it said: look, he is calling Elijah. Someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying: wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.

Behold, he is calling Elijah. “Eloi” sounds like “Elijah” (Eliyahu). They misheard, or deliberately misunderstood. Popular Jewish belief held that Elijah, who had not died, came to help the righteous in trouble. They mock even his dying cry.

The irony. Elijah had come, in John the Baptist, and they did to him whatever they pleased (9:13). He will not come now.

And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine. “Sour wine” (oxos): cheap, vinegary wine diluted with water, which soldiers and labourers drank. It may have been an act of kindness, to moisten his lips, or to prolong his life, and the mockery. Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. John records that Jesus said “I thirst” and received it (John 19:28–30).

Put it on a reed. To reach his mouth. Crosses were not necessarily very tall.

Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down. Mockery to the end.

In a sentence. Mishearing his cry, bystanders said Jesus was calling Elijah, and someone gave him sour wine, mocking to see whether Elijah would come.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was misunderstood and mocked even in his dying words. If you are misunderstood for your faith, he knows.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.

And Jesus uttered a loud cry. Crucified men usually died of exhaustion, drifting into unconsciousness, unable to speak. Jesus died with a loud cry, in strength. John records the word: It is finished (John 19:30), tetelestai, which was written on receipts: paid in full. Luke records: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (Luke 23:46), from Psalm 31:5. His death was not defeat, but completion. He gave up his life; it was not taken from him (John 10:18).

And breathed his last. Exepneusen: he breathed out. He died. A real death, of a real man. The Son of God died.

Six hours. From the third hour to the ninth. Crucified men often took days to die. Pilate was surprised he had died so soon (v. 44). He had suffered terribly before the cross, but his early death also shows that he laid down his life at the moment he chose, when the work was finished.

In a sentence. With a loud cry, Jesus died.

For worship. It is finished. Nothing is left to pay. Rest in his finished work.

verseByVerse.quote: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.

And the curtain of the temple. There were two curtains in the temple. The outer one hung at the entrance of the Holy Place. The inner one separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, the inner sanctuary that represented God’s throne room, where the ark of the covenant had stood. Only the high priest could pass through that curtain, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with the blood of sacrifice (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). It was a barrier that said: sinners cannot come into God’s presence. Most interpreters take this to be the inner curtain. According to Jewish tradition, it was enormous: 60 feet (18 m) high, and as thick as a man’s hand.

Was torn in two. The same word (eschisthē) Mark used when the heavens were torn open at Jesus’ baptism (1:10). At the beginning and the end of his ministry, God tears open a barrier.

From top to bottom. From top to bottom: torn by God, not by man. No human hand could reach the top of it.

Its meaning. Two things together. First, access: through the death of Jesus, the way into God’s presence is open to all who come through him. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). No more priests, no more sacrifices. The one sacrifice is complete. Second, judgement: the temple’s system is finished, as Jesus foretold (13:2). The fig tree has withered. God has left the building. The true temple is now Christ, and his people.

In a sentence. At the moment of Jesus’ death, God tore the temple curtain from top to bottom, opening the way into his presence and signalling the end of the old temple.

For worship. You can come into the presence of God today, not by your own merit or through a priest, but through the torn flesh of Jesus. Come boldly (Hebrews 4:16).
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said: truly this man was the Son of God!

And when the centurion. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers, the backbone of the Roman army. He was in charge of the execution. A Gentile, a pagan soldier, who had probably supervised many crucifixions.

Who stood facing him. He had watched everything, close up.

Saw that in this way he breathed his last. How Jesus died: the loud cry, the darkness, the manner of his death, his dignity, his words. Something in the way Jesus died convinced him.

Truly this man was the Son of God! The climax of Mark’s Gospel. The first line of the Gospel announced Jesus as the Son of God (1:1). God said it at the baptism (1:11) and the transfiguration (9:7). Demons said it (3:11; 5:7). But no human being has said it, until now. And the first person to say it is not a disciple, not a Jew, but a Gentile soldier, at the cross. The cross reveals who Jesus is. You cannot understand him as Son of God except as the crucified one.

What did he mean? Some translate “a son of God”, since a Roman might mean only a divine man, a hero. And “was” (past tense), as of a dead man. But in Mark’s story, his words carry their full weight. Whatever the centurion understood, Mark wants us to hear the full confession. And the emperor was called “son of god” (divi filius) on coins. A Roman soldier gives the title to a crucified Jew instead.

The secret revealed. All through Mark, Jesus silenced those who would announce him. Now, at the cross, the secret is out. He can be proclaimed as Son of God, because the cross shows what that means: not a conqueror, but one who gives his life as a ransom for many.

In a sentence. Seeing how Jesus died, the Roman centurion in charge of the execution confessed that he was truly the Son of God, the first human being in Mark to say it.

For worship. Stand where the centurion stood, look at the cross, and make his confession your own: truly this man is the Son of God.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were also women looking on from a distance, among them Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.

There were also women looking on from a distance. The men had fled; the women stayed. At a distance, perhaps because they were not allowed closer, or for safety. But they stayed. They are witnesses of his death (here), his burial (v. 47) and his resurrection (16:1–8). The Gospel’s chain of eyewitness rests on them.

Mary Magdalene. From Magdala, a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her (Luke 8:2). Not the sinful woman of Luke 7, as later tradition wrongly assumed. She was the first to see the risen Lord (16:9; John 20:11–18).

Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses. “The younger” (or “the less”) distinguishes this James from James son of Zebedee. Perhaps the wife of Clopas (John 19:25). Mark’s readers knew her sons.

And Salome. Probably the mother of James and John (Matthew 27:56 lists the mother of the sons of Zebedee here), who had asked for their seats at his right and left (Matthew 20:20–21). She saw who was on his right and left.

When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him. “Followed” and “ministered” (diēkonoun, served) are the two words of discipleship (1:18; 10:45). These women were true disciples. Luke says they supported Jesus and the Twelve out of their own means (Luke 8:3). In a culture where women were not normally disciples of a rabbi, Jesus welcomed them.

And there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. Many.

In a sentence. Women who had followed and served Jesus since Galilee, including Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome, watched his death from a distance when the men had fled.

On a Tuesday. Faithful service that no one notices is noticed by Christ, and he made these women the first witnesses of his resurrection. Thank God for the faithful women in your church.
verseByVerse.note: Salome may be the mother of James and John, named in Matthew as “the mother of the sons of Zebedee.”

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The request (vv. 42–43). Evening is coming and with it the Sabbath, and a body left on a cross overnight would defile the land under the Law. And a member of the very council that condemned him goes to the governor and asks for the corpse.

Mark says he took courage, and he needed it. Joseph of Arimathea is a man of standing who has kept his hopes to himself, and he chooses the moment when Jesus is a convicted criminal and every one of his friends has run — to go public.

The verification (vv. 44–45). Pilate is surprised that he is dead already and sends for the officer in charge to confirm it. So the death of Jesus of Nazareth is certified by a professional executioner and reported to a Roman governor before the body is released.

The tomb (vv. 46–47). A linen shroud, a grave cut in rock, a stone rolled across — and two women sitting where they can see, memorising the address.
verseByVerse.theology:
The burial is not a postscript. It is evidence, and Mark reports it like a man building a case.

Four facts are established in six verses, and every one of them closes off an objection that would be raised later.

He was really dead. Pilate was surprised, because crucifixion normally took two or three days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. A professional soldier who had stood facing him for six hours confirmed it to the governor before the body was signed over. Any theory that Jesus survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.

He was really buried, in a known place. Not a common grave, which is where crucified bodies usually went, but a rock-cut tomb belonging to a named man of the council — a man the authorities could have produced and questioned.

The tomb was sealed. A stone rolled across the entrance.

And the location was witnessed. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid — Mark's last sentence of the chapter, and it exists to say that the women who go to the tomb on Sunday morning went to the right one.

There is no room in this account for a mistaken address, a swoon, or a grave nobody could find.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council... took courage and went to Pilate.

John tells us he had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38), and Luke that he had not consented to the council's decision (Luke 23:51). So here is a man who had believed quietly for some time and had never said so.

And of all the moments to come out, he chooses this one.

Not the Sunday, when the tomb is empty and there is something to be glad about. Not the triumphal entry, when the crowds were shouting and it would have cost him nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a convicted blasphemer executed by Rome, when the movement is finished, when every one of the twelve has vanished — and he does it by walking into the governor's residence and asking, as a member of the Sanhedrin, for the body of the man his own colleagues had just killed.

Now: he had everything to lose and nothing to gain. There was no upside. Association with a crucified criminal ended a career in that city, and he must have known it.

Which is worth putting to any Christian who has been quiet for a long time and is waiting for an easier moment to speak. The easier moment does not come, and it is not supposed to. Joseph's courage arrived on the worst possible day, and it is why he is in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage, went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

And when evening had come. Late afternoon, before sunset. The Sabbath would begin at sunset, and no burial could be done on it.

Since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath. Friday. Mark explains for Gentile readers. The law said a body hanged on a tree must not remain overnight but must be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), even more so on a Sabbath. The Romans often left crucified bodies to rot, or threw them in common graves.

Joseph of Arimathea. Arimathea was a town in Judea, probably about 20 miles (30 km) north-west of Jerusalem. He appears in all four Gospels only here, at the burial. Matthew says he was rich (Matthew 27:57), a disciple of Jesus. John says secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38).

A respected member of the council. A member of the Sanhedrin that had just condemned Jesus. Luke tells us he had not agreed with their decision (Luke 23:50–51). Isaiah 53:9: they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death.

Who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God. Waiting for it, expecting it, a devout man of faith, like Simeon and Anna (Luke 2:25, 38).

Took courage and went to Pilate. “Took courage”: it was a dangerous request. To ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to identify yourself with him, before both Pilate and the council. The disciples had fled; Joseph came out of hiding. The cross made a secret disciple brave.

And asked for the body of Jesus. The bodies of the executed could be given to family or friends, at the governor’s discretion. Jesus’ family was not there to ask.

In a sentence. As the Sabbath approached, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member looking for God’s kingdom, courageously asked Pilate for Jesus’ body.

On a Tuesday. If you have been a secret disciple, let the cross make you brave. Come out and identify yourself with Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate was surprised to hear that he had already died. Summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. When he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.

Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. Crucified men often lingered for two or three days. Six hours was unusually short.

And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. Pilate checks with the officer in charge, a professional in killing who had watched it all.

And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead. Official confirmation. Jesus really died. This matters, because from early times some have claimed that he only fainted on the cross and revived in the cool of the tomb (the “swoon theory”). Mark gives the official Roman verification: the centurion confirmed it, Pilate accepted it. John adds that a soldier pierced his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). He was dead.

He granted the corpse to Joseph. “Corpse” (ptōma), a stark word: a dead body. The Son of God was a corpse. Perhaps Pilate, believing him innocent, was glad to grant it.

In a sentence. Surprised that Jesus was already dead, Pilate confirmed it with the centurion before giving the body to Joseph.

For worship. Jesus truly died. And so his resurrection is real resurrection, a real victory over real death, and the hope of all who die in him.
verseByVerse.note: Crucified men often lingered for days; a death within hours surprised Pilate.

parallels.desc: the soldiers find him already dead

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. He rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.

And Joseph bought a linen shroud. Fine linen, costly. Bought quickly, before the shops closed for the Sabbath.

And taking him down. John tells us that Nicodemus, another member of the council, helped, bringing about 75 pounds of spices (John 19:39). A rich man’s burial for a criminal.

Wrapped him in the linen shroud. In haste, because of the Sabbath. The women would come to complete the anointing after the Sabbath (16:1).

And laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. Wealthy families had tombs carved into the limestone hillsides around Jerusalem: a chamber, with ledges or niches for bodies. Matthew says it was Joseph’s own new tomb (Matthew 27:60); John, that no one had yet been laid in it, in a garden near the place of crucifixion (John 19:41–42). An unused tomb meant there could be no confusion about which body was there.

And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled down a groove in front of the entrance. Easy to roll in; very hard to roll out, uphill. Several men might be needed (16:3–4). Matthew adds that the authorities sealed it and set a guard (Matthew 27:62–66).

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid. Eyewitnesses again. They knew the right tomb. On Sunday morning they would not go to the wrong one. Mark carefully records witnesses of the death (v. 40), the burial (v. 47) and the empty tomb (16:1): the same women. The Apostles’ Creed preserves the sequence: crucified, dead and buried. Paul’s summary of the gospel: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

In a sentence. Joseph wrapped Jesus’ body in linen, laid it in a rock tomb, and rolled a stone across the entrance, while two of the women watched where he was laid.

For worship. Jesus lay in a tomb, so that the grave would hold no terror for those who belong to him. He has made the grave a bed of rest.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled into a groove.

15.theology:
The cry of dereliction (v. 34) has two errors to be kept off it. The first would soften it, as though he were merely reciting a psalm and not truly forsaken — he was; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer (2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13). The second would break God in two, as though the Trinity were torn and the Father ceased to love the Son — that did not happen and could not. He remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment; what he lost was the felt light of his Father's face, borne in our place.

And notice the word he uses. Not God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God — twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark, and it is the only place in the Gospels where he addresses the Father as anything but Father.

The curtain (v. 38) may be the most important sentence in the book. Sixty feet of woven fabric, a handbreadth thick, whose entire purpose for fifteen centuries was to say you cannot come in — torn at the instant he died, and torn from the top, which is beyond human reach. The way in was not forced from our side; it was opened from his. And it is the second thing in Mark torn from above: the heavens being torn open at the baptism (1:10), the same violent word, at the beginning and the end. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

And the burial is evidence, not postscript. Pilate was surprised he had died so soon — crucifixion normally took days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. The death was doubted by the governor, examined on his order, and certified by the officer who had stood facing him for six hours, before the body was released. Mark even switches words in v. 45 to ptōma, corpse. Any theory that he survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.
15.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, jeering at the foot of the cross, stating the gospel with complete accuracy and believing none of it.

Both halves are true. He did save others, and his enemies concede it at the moment they have nothing to gain by conceding anything. And he could not save himself — not for lack of power, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done. They thought they had found a contradiction; they had found the mechanism of the atonement.

Now: and the demand attached to it — come down now from the cross that we may see and believe — has the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand. Show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a miracle and gone home impressed and unforgiven. He stayed up; and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign whatever was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

And notice what converted that officer. Not a wonder — Mark is precise: he saw that in this way he breathed his last. He saw how he died. That is the answer to the question this Gospel keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. The crowds saw the healings and stayed baffled; the scribes heard the teaching and planned a murder; and at the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a pagan finally sees it — and he is the first human being in fifteen chapters to say the words Mark opened his book with (1:1).

16.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. <sup>2</sup>And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. <sup>3</sup>And they were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” <sup>4</sup>And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large. <sup>5</sup>And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed. <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. <sup>7</sup>But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” <sup>8</sup>And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. <sup>9</sup>Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. <sup>10</sup>She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. <sup>11</sup>But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. <sup>12</sup>After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. <sup>13</sup>And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. <sup>14</sup>Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen. <sup>15</sup>And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. <sup>16</sup>Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. <sup>17</sup>And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; <sup>18</sup>they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” <sup>19</sup>So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. <sup>20</sup>And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
16.overview:
Three women buy spices when the shops reopen on Saturday evening, and set out at first light to finish a burial. Not one of them expects a resurrection — he had told them three times and it had gone in nowhere. They are carrying ointment for a corpse, and the only thing on their minds is a stone they cannot move.

They arrive and find it moved, and a young man in white sitting inside, and the most important sentence in the book: He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. Not a symbol and not an experience — an event with an address, and an invitation to inspect the evidence.

Then a message with two extra words in it: tell his disciples and Peter. And they run away and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified — which is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop.

The twelve verses that follow are printed in brackets in the ESV and most modern Bibles, and the question they raise is answered here in full rather than buried in a footnote. They summarise appearances recorded elsewhere, give the commission, and end with the Lord Jesus taken up and seated at the right hand of God — exactly as he had told the high priest he would be, on the night they condemned him for saying it.

And the last sentence of Mark is the reversal of verse 8: the people who said nothing went out and preached everywhere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The errand (vv. 1–4). The Sabbath ends at sunset on Saturday, the shops open, and three women buy spices. They set out at first light on Sunday to finish a burial, and the only thing worrying them on the road is a practical problem they cannot solve: the stone. They arrive and find it solved.

The announcement (vv. 5–7). Inside the tomb a young man in white is sitting on the right, and what he says is the most important sentence in the book. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. And then a message with one name added to it that has comforted failing Christians for two thousand years.

The silence (v. 8). And they run, and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified.

That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop — mid-sentence, almost, on the word afraid. Which raises the question this chapter cannot avoid, and which is dealt with plainly below rather than left in a footnote.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible?

Open the ESV at this page and you will find, before verse 9, a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. That deserves a straight answer, because a reader who meets it for the first time can feel the ground move.

Here are the facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament we possess — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at verse 8. Eusebius and Jerome, writing in the fourth and fifth centuries, both say that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts have a different, shorter ending; a few have both. And the Greek of verses 9–20 does not read like Mark: it uses more than a dozen words found nowhere else in the book, and verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named in verse 1.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these twelve verses, and that they were added early — early enough to be widely known and read in churches by the second century.

And here is what that does not mean. It does not mean anything has been smuggled into your Bible. Every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere: the appearance to Mary Magdalene (John 20), the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission to all nations (Matt. 28), the ascension and session at God's right hand (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20). No doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here.

So take the reassurance the right way round. The reason you know about this is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of quietly tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one puts the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest of the text can be trusted.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: tell his disciples and Peter (v. 7).

Two extra words, and they are there because somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain he had forfeited his place.

Peter had denied him three times with oaths and a curse, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, and had gone out and wept. As far as he knew, he was finished — not merely ashamed, but out.

And the first message from the other side of the grave has his name in it, added on, as though the general term might not reach him. In effect: tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter.

Now: and notice that this is not new. Jesus had promised it before the failure happened: you will all fall away... but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats his promise, and adds the name.

So if you are a Christian who has failed badly enough to wonder whether there is a road back, the answer is in two words at the empty tomb. The road was mapped before you took the wrong turn, and when the message came, the one who had failed worst was named.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might go and anoint him. Very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.

When the Sabbath was past. The Sabbath ended at sunset on Saturday. Then the shops could open, and the women bought spices that evening.

Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. The same women who watched the crucifixion (15:40) and the burial (15:47). They are the link of eyewitnesses: they saw him die, saw where he was laid, and now go to the same tomb.

Bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. Fragrant oils to pour over the body, an act of love and honour, to offset the smell of decay. They had not been able to finish this on Friday. Notice: they came to anoint a dead body. They were not expecting a resurrection. Jesus had foretold it three times (8:31; 9:31; 10:34), but no one had grasped it. This is important evidence. The resurrection was not invented by people who expected it.

And very early on the first day of the week. Sunday. The day after the Sabbath. From this day on, Christians met on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), calling it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10), the day of resurrection and new creation. The Sabbath, the seventh day, commemorated God’s rest after the first creation; the Lord’s Day celebrates the beginning of the new creation in Christ’s resurrection.

When the sun had risen. Just after dawn. John says it was still dark when Mary set out (John 20:1); by the time they arrived, the sun was up.

In a sentence. After the Sabbath, three women who had watched Jesus’ death and burial brought spices to anoint his body, and went to the tomb early on Sunday morning.

For worship. Every Lord’s Day is a celebration of the resurrection. Gather with God’s people on the first day of the week as a joy and a privilege, not a burden.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were saying to one another: who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb? And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back. It was very large.

Who will roll away the stone for us? A practical problem, and a picture of every human impossibility. They had not thought it through: they set out to do what love required, without knowing how. The stone was too heavy for three women. And Matthew tells us it was sealed and guarded (Matthew 27:66).

And looking up. The tomb was perhaps up a slope, or they had been walking with their heads down in grief.

They saw that the stone had been rolled back. The passive voice: rolled back by God. Matthew says an angel rolled it away (Matthew 28:2). Not to let Jesus out (he would not need it), but to let the witnesses in.

It was very large. Mark adds this to show that it could not have been moved by accident, or by the women.

In a sentence. Wondering who would roll away the heavy stone for them, the women looked up and saw it had already been rolled back.

On a Tuesday. What stone are you worried about? Go forward in faithful love; God often removes the obstacle before you reach it.

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.

And entering the tomb. They went into the outer chamber of the rock tomb.

They saw a young man. An angel, in human form, as angels often appear in Scripture (Genesis 18:2; Daniel 9:21). Matthew says an angel (Matthew 28:2–5); Luke, two men in dazzling clothes (Luke 24:4). Mark’s “young man” may recall the young man who fled naked from Gethsemane (14:51–52): the frightened follower who lost his linen cloth gives way to a heavenly messenger in white.

Sitting on the right side. The side of favour and good news.

Dressed in a white robe. The colour of heaven and glory, like Jesus’ clothes on the mountain (9:3).

And they were alarmed. “Alarmed” (exethambēthēsan): utterly astonished, overwhelmed with awe. The same strong word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:33). The natural human response to a messenger from heaven.

In a sentence. Entering the tomb, the women were overwhelmed to see an angel in the form of a young man in white sitting on the right.

For worship. The resurrection is not ordinary news. Let it astonish you again.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.

Do not be alarmed. The first word of the resurrection message is comfort.

You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. The perfect participle (estaurōmenon) means “the one who has been crucified”, and remains the crucified one. The risen Lord is the same Jesus, from Nazareth, who was crucified. He is still the crucified one, now risen. His scars remain (John 20:27). The cross is not erased by the resurrection; it is vindicated.

He has risen. The heart of the gospel. Literally “he has been raised” (ēgerthē), a passive: God raised him (Acts 2:24; Romans 10:9). The resurrection is the Father’s verdict on the Son: the rejected stone has become the cornerstone (12:10). It proves that he is who he claimed to be (Romans 1:4), that his sacrifice for sin has been accepted (Romans 4:25), that death has been defeated (1 Corinthians 15:54–57), and that all who belong to him will be raised as he was (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

He is not here. The empty tomb. A bodily resurrection. Not merely that his spirit lived on, or that his disciples felt his presence, or that his message survived. His body was gone. Something had happened to it.

See the place where they laid him. An invitation to examine the evidence. The faith of the church does not rest on feelings but on facts, on a real tomb, really empty. John records that the grave clothes were still there, lying in place (John 20:5–7). The women knew it was the right tomb, because they had watched him laid in it (15:47).

Evidence for the resurrection. The empty tomb, which the authorities never disputed but explained by claiming the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11–15). The appearances to many witnesses, including over five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). The transformation of frightened, scattered disciples into bold witnesses ready to die. The conversion of sceptics like James and Paul. And the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday by Jewish believers. None of this is explained except by the resurrection.

In a sentence. The angel told the women not to be alarmed: Jesus the crucified one had been raised, was not there, and they could see the empty place where he had lain.

For worship. He is risen. Your sins are paid for, death is beaten, and he lives for ever. Worship the risen, crucified Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.

But go, tell his disciples. The women become the first messengers of the resurrection. In a culture where women’s testimony was not accepted in court, God chose women as the first witnesses. No one inventing the story would have done that. It is a mark of truth.

His disciples. Still his disciples, though they deserted him.

And Peter. Key words. Only Mark has them. Peter is named: the one who had denied him three times, with oaths and curses, who might have thought he was no longer a disciple. The message is: especially Peter. Jesus singles out the one who failed most. And Mark probably heard the story from Peter himself, who never forgot those two words. The risen Lord appeared to Peter personally (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5), and restored him publicly (John 21:15–19).

That he is going before you to Galilee. As he had promised on the night of his arrest (14:28). Like a shepherd going before his sheep. The scattered sheep will be gathered (14:27). Galilee, where it all began, where they were first called. They will begin again.

There you will see him, just as he told you. His word has proved true in everything: the colt (11:2–6), the room (14:13–16), the betrayal, Peter’s denial, his death, and now his resurrection. Every word he spoke can be trusted.

In a sentence. The angel sent the women to tell the disciples, and especially Peter, that the risen Jesus was going ahead of them to Galilee, where they would see him, as he had promised.

On a Tuesday. “And Peter.” Put your own name there, especially if you have failed him. The risen Lord is calling you back.
verseByVerse.note: Peter is named — the one who had denied him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.

And they went out and fled from the tomb. Not from unbelief, but from overwhelming awe.

For trembling and astonishment had seized them. “Trembling” (tromos) and “astonishment” (ekstasis, ecstasy, being beside oneself). The fitting response to a direct act of God. In Mark, fear and amazement are the constant reaction to Jesus’ divine power (4:41; 5:15, 33, 42; 9:6).

And they said nothing to anyone. At first, at least, on the way. Matthew and Luke tell us they went and told the disciples (Matthew 28:8; Luke 24:9). Their silence was temporary, a stunned silence, not disobedience.

For they were afraid. In Greek, the sentence ends with the small word gar, “for”: “they were afraid, for”. An extraordinarily abrupt ending.

Textual note: the ending of Mark. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament (Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century) end Mark’s Gospel here, at verse 8. Early church writers, Eusebius and Jerome, said that most of the Greek manuscripts they knew ended here. Other manuscripts have a short ending of a sentence or two; most later manuscripts have the longer ending (vv. 9–20), which differs from Mark’s style and vocabulary and appears to be a summary drawn from the other Gospels and Acts. The ESV prints verses 9–20 in brackets.

Where Christians differ: did Mark end here? Some think Mark meant to end at verse 8. Others think the original ending was lost, perhaps from the end of a scroll, or that Mark could not finish. Verdict: the evidence is strong that verses 9–20 were not written by Mark, but were added early, probably in the second century. Whether Mark meant to end at verse 8 is less certain. But if he did, it is a powerful ending. The resurrection has been announced; Jesus has been seen to be who he said; and the story leaves the reader with the question: what will you do? The women were silent for fear; will you be? Mark’s Gospel began with “the beginning of the gospel” (1:1). It ends where the church’s preaching begins.

In a sentence. Seized with trembling and astonishment, the women fled from the tomb and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid, which is where the earliest manuscripts end Mark’s Gospel.

On a Tuesday. The women were silent at first. You have heard the news: Christ is risen. Don’t be silent. Go and tell.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some of the earliest manuscripts end the Gospel here, and brackets verses 9–20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What this passage is. Before verse 9 your Bible prints a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. It is the most significant textual question in the New Testament, and it is dealt with fully at verses 9–11 rather than hidden in a note, because a reader who meets it for the first time deserves a straight answer.

What it contains. A summary of resurrection appearances — to Mary Magdalene, to two men walking into the country, and to the eleven at table — with the disciples disbelieving every one of them until Jesus stands in front of them and rebukes them for it.

Then the commission: go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Then a promise of accompanying signs, including the two sentences about serpents and poison that a handful of churches have built a lethal practice on.

And then the ending. He is taken up into heaven and sits down at the right hand of God — which is exactly what he told the high priest would happen, on the night they condemned him for saying it (14:62).

And the last verse of Mark is the disciples doing the one thing the women in verse 8 could not.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (v. 16) can sound, read at speed, as though baptism were half of what saves you. Read closely it says something more careful.

Believing and being baptized are named together in the first half because in the New Testament they belong together — nobody in Acts comes to faith and then quietly declines to be baptized; the washing is the ordinary, public, commanded seal of the faith professed.

But look at the second half, which is where the sentence settles the matter. The condemnation clause is not whoever is not baptized. It is whoever does not believe. Baptism drops out of it entirely.

That asymmetry is doing deliberate work. What saves is Christ, received by faith; baptism is the sign and seal of that faith, not the ground of it. Which is why a dying thief with no water within reach could be told, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43).

So take the verse whole and let it cut both ways: do not despise baptism, because your Lord commanded it and it is no empty ceremony — and do not lean your weight on it, because it was never the thing holding you up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them (v. 18).

On the strength of that sentence, a handful of churches — mostly in the Appalachian hills — have taken up handling rattlesnakes and drinking strychnine in their services to prove their faith. People have died doing it.

Now: two things must be said, and they are enough.

First, these are among the words whose place in Mark is most doubtful of all. To build a practice on a passage the earliest manuscripts do not contain is unwise twice over.

Second — and this holds even reading the verse at face value — it describes what may happen to Christ's servants, not what they are to seek out. When a viper fastened on Paul's hand on Malta and he shook it off unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), it was an accident of ministry he neither courted nor expected, not a stunt to test God.

Deliberately reaching for a snake or a poison cup to prove one believes is precisely what Satan urged in the wilderness — throw yourself down — and precisely what Jesus refused, with the words you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Luke 4:12).

Faith trusts God. It does not dare him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it.

About verses 9–20. These verses are not found in the earliest manuscripts, and were very probably not written by Mark (see the note on v. 8). They were added early, and have been read in the church for centuries, so they are included in our Bibles, in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels and in Acts. Where they agree with the rest of Scripture, they are true and useful. But no doctrine should rest on these verses alone.

He appeared first to Mary Magdalene. As John 20:11–18 records. The first person to see the risen Lord was a woman once possessed by seven demons (Luke 8:2). Grace chooses the unlikely.

As they mourned and wept. The disciples were grieving. They thought it was over.

They would not believe it. As Luke also records: these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them (Luke 24:11). The disciples were not gullible. They doubted. It took the risen Lord himself to convince them.

In a sentence. The risen Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene, but when she told the grieving disciples, they would not believe her.

On a Tuesday. If you struggle to believe, so did the first disciples. Bring your doubts to the risen Christ himself.
verseByVerse.note: These verses are not found in some of the earliest manuscripts; the ESV prints them in brackets. They largely summarise appearances recorded in the other Gospels.

parallels.desc: Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord
from whom seven demons had gone out

verseByVerse.quote: After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After these things he appeared in another form to two of them as they were walking into the country. They went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. Afterwards he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.

He appeared in another form to two of them. The two disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35), who did not recognise him at first. “In another form”: his risen body was the same, but changed, glorified (1 Corinthians 15:42–44), and he could be recognised only when he chose.

But they did not believe them. Luke’s account suggests that by the time they returned, the others had already heard that he had appeared to Simon (Luke 24:34). This summary emphasises the disciples’ slowness to believe.

Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves. The Twelve minus Judas (Luke 24:36–43; John 20:19–29).

And he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart. The same rebuke as in 8:17. Unbelief in the face of credible testimony is not a mere intellectual difficulty, but hardness of heart. And the risen Christ still rebukes it, lovingly.

In a sentence. Jesus appeared to two disciples on the road and then to the eleven, and rebuked them for refusing to believe those who had seen him risen.

On a Tuesday. The testimony of the eyewitnesses has come down to you in Scripture. Believe their word (John 20:29).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. Whoever believes and is baptised will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. The Great Commission, in the form found in Matthew 28:18–20, Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8. “The whole creation” means all people everywhere. The gospel that Jesus said must first be preached to all nations (13:10) is now the church’s task.

Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved. Faith and baptism belong together in the New Testament: those who believed were baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12; 16:31–33). Baptism is the public sign of faith and union with Christ.

But whoever does not believe will be condemned. Notice: it does not say “whoever is not baptised”. The decisive issue is faith. The thief on the cross was saved without baptism (Luke 23:43). Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9). Unbelief condemns (John 3:18, 36).

What it does not mean. Not that baptism itself saves, or that a believer who dies unbaptised is lost. Baptism is commanded, and a believer will want to be baptised in obedience. But it is the sign, not the cause, of salvation. And this verse, from the longer ending, is not a foundation for any doctrine of baptism on its own.

Where Christians differ: the order of believing and baptism. Paedobaptists baptise the children of believers before faith; credobaptists baptise on profession of faith. Verdict: this verse, like the New Testament pattern generally, places believing before baptism, which fits the credobaptist position, held charitably toward brothers who differ.

In a sentence. Jesus sent his disciples to proclaim the gospel to all people, promising salvation to those who believe and are baptised, and condemnation to those who do not believe.

On a Tuesday. The commission is yours too. Who in your world needs to hear the gospel?

verseByVerse.quote: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.

These signs. The signs listed are found in Acts: casting out demons (Acts 16:18), speaking in tongues (Acts 2:4; 10:46), surviving a snake bite (Paul on Malta, Acts 28:3–6), healing by laying on of hands (Acts 28:8). Drinking poison unharmed is not found in the New Testament, though a later legend told it of Barsabbas (Acts 1:23).

Will accompany those who believe. Signs confirmed the apostles’ message in the founding of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12).

What it does not mean. Not a command to handle snakes or drink poison to prove one’s faith, as some groups in the Appalachian mountains have done, with fatal results. That would be putting God to the test, which Jesus refused to do (Matthew 4:5–7). And these verses, not part of Mark’s original text, should not be made the basis of any practice.

Where Christians differ: do the signs continue? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians hold that the miraculous gifts, tongues and healing continue in the church today as normal. Cessationists hold that the sign gifts were given to confirm the apostles and their message while the New Testament was being written, and ceased with the apostolic age. Verdict: the cessationist position fits Scripture best. The signs authenticated the apostles as the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3–4). God still answers prayer, and still heals according to his will (James 5:14–15), but not through the apostolic sign gifts. This is held charitably toward brothers and sisters who differ.

In a sentence. These verses promise that signs, such as those recorded in Acts, would accompany the first believers, confirming their message.

On a Tuesday. The greatest sign of the gospel’s power is a changed life. Pray for the sick, trusting God’s will, and let your life show the power of the risen Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.

So then the Lord Jesus. The full title, “the Lord Jesus”, common in Acts.

Was taken up into heaven. The ascension, forty days after the resurrection (Luke 24:50–51; Acts 1:9–11). As Elijah was taken up (2 Kings 2:11).

And sat down at the right hand of God. Psalm 110:1, the verse Jesus quoted in the temple (12:36) and before the high priest (14:62). What he claimed at his trial has come true. He is enthroned, reigning, interceding for his people (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 1:3; 7:25), until all his enemies are under his feet.

And they went out and preached everywhere. The book of Acts in a sentence. The frightened, scattered disciples became bold preachers across the world.

While the Lord worked with them. The ascended Lord was not absent. He worked with them by his Spirit (Matthew 28:20; Acts 1:1, where Luke says his first book told what Jesus began to do and teach).

And confirmed the message by accompanying signs. As Hebrews 2:3–4 describes.

The end of Mark. Whether one reads to verse 8 or 20, Mark’s Gospel ends at a beginning. Jesus is risen and reigning, and the gospel goes out. The story of Jesus continues in the preaching of his church, and in every person who hears it and believes.

In a sentence. The Lord Jesus ascended and sat at God’s right hand, and the disciples preached everywhere while he worked with them and confirmed their message.

For worship. Jesus reigns at God’s right hand now. Go out today knowing that the Lord works with those who serve him.

16.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible? The facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament — Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at v. 8, as do the oldest Syriac, Armenian and Georgian versions. Eusebius and Jerome both report that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts carry a different, shorter ending; a few carry both. And the Greek does not read like Mark: more than a dozen words appear nowhere else in the book, and v. 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named twice.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these verses, though they were known and read by the middle of the second century.

And here is why that need not unsettle anybody. Nothing has been smuggled in: every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere — Mary Magdalene (John 20), the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission (Matt. 28; Acts 1), the ascension and session (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20; Heb. 1:3). No doctrine stands or falls here. And the reason you know about it at all is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them; this one prints the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest can be trusted. Nothing in the discussion touches vv. 1–8, which are in every manuscript there is.

Does Mark end at v. 8? The last word is gar — for — an extraordinarily abrupt way to end a book, rather like closing on because. Three explanations are offered and we do not know which is right: the last leaf of an early codex was lost; the author was interrupted (tradition places him in Rome under Nero); or he meant to stop there. The third has grown stronger the longer people look at it, because an ending at v. 8 leaves the resurrection announced and not described, the appearances promised and not narrated, and the story unfinished in the reader's hands. Mark called his book the beginning of the gospel (1:1) — and the women are sent to Galilee, where chapter 1 began.
16.examples:
Then: and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid (v. 8).

There is a superb irony in that sentence, and it is Mark's last word about human beings. All through this Gospel, people commanded to be silent could not keep quiet — the cleansed leper went out and began to talk freely about it so that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly (1:45); the Decapolis crowd was charged to tell no one, and the more he charged them, the more zealously they proclaimed it (7:36).

And here, where the women are commanded to speak, they say nothing at all.

Now: and the last verse of the chapter is the exact reversal — they went out and preached everywhere. The same frightened company. Something happened in between, and it was not a change of temperament.

These were not credulous people. They dismissed the women, dismissed the two from the road, and had to be confronted in person and rebuked to their faces for unbelief and hardness of heart (v. 14). Every account we have says the apostles were the hardest audience in the story, not the softest.

And he sent them anyway — a company of men who had run from a garden, denied him in a courtyard, spent the weekend weeping and refused three separate eyewitness reports. He did not wait for better material. There was none, and there never has been.
